- `run_status(run_dir: str) -> status.json content + last history line`. It also has `job` (section 24.1), `checkpoint` and `verdict` (section 24.2), and `time_left` with `time_left_note` (E1-P2, section 24.5).
  After a run that an input check refused in a folder with an earlier run, it also has `earlier_run`: the facts of that earlier run, which are then not at the top level (P9-18, section 24.1).
  `run_topopt` takes `resume`, `allow_changed_inputs` and `stop_rules` too (section 24.2), and `continue_from` and `more_iterations` (since P4b-5, section 24.3),
  and `fine_from`, `fine_pass`, `fine_voxel`, `fine_passes` and `fine_tol` (#318, section 24.6). `run_status` of the first folder of `fine_pass=true` has `fine_run`; `run_result` has `fine_pass` and, for a fine run, `fine_from`.
- `run_result(run_dir: str) -> metrics.json content + path of final.stl`. With machining stock (section 23) it also gives
  `nominal_stl` and `nominal_stl_rel`. With `regions.not_printed` (section 9.1) the content of `metrics.json` holds the key
  `part_only`, and the reply also gives `part_only_stl` (absolute path) and `part_only_stl_rel` (relative to the work folder) when
  `result/part_only.stl` exists. A run without the key has none of these.
  The reply also gives `report_md` (absolute path) and `report_md_rel` (relative to the work folder) of the part card `result/report.md` (since P9-7a,
  section 9.2). The call writes the card again first, with the facts the run folder has now (verify, buckling, renders), and does not touch the file when its
  bytes do not change. If the write fails, the reply has `report_md_note` (the error) and still names an older card when there is one. A run folder under `<code folder>/recordings/` (the shipped, committed recordings) gets no write: the reply
  has `report_md_note` that names `topopt report <run folder>` (for a copy that the user can write), and names a card that is already there. The rest of the code
  folder is not blocked: the runs of a user can live inside a clone. A run with no result has none of these keys.
  For a run that a request stopped it returns `{"done": false, "stopped": true, "run_dir", "run_dir_rel", "message", "levers"}` (no `result/` exists).
  The reply has the key `levers` (since P7 PR-3, section 41.10): the facts of the run folder that the engine flags, each with the keys, kinds and layers of the lever cards
  that name it (and the `when` text of a symptom that has one), cheapest layer first, and a line that points to the resource `topopt://levers` and to the template `topopt://levers/{query}`. A fact that the engine does not flag is not listed. A fault while the block
  is made gives `{"entries": [], "error": "..."}` in place of the block, and the rest of the reply is as before.
  The reply has the key `end_fact` (since #380) only when `metrics.verdict.state` is `iteration_limit`: one plain sentence of fact, `The run stopped at its pass limit
  (pass N of M). The objective had settled: yes|no|not known. Every constraint row is met: yes|no|not known.` (N is `final_iteration`, M is
  `iterations`, the two tests are `converged` and `feasible` of the verdict). It is the line `Result` of the part card (one writer: `result_sentence` of
  `topopt/part_card.py`), and it names no stop rule (the rules are off by default). It is a fact and not an order. A run in any other state (`converged`, `stopped_by_rule`,
  `stopped_by_request`, `unfinished`) and a run with no `verdict` have no such key, and their replies keep their bytes. The instructions of the server (limit: 2,048
  characters, `tests/test_plugin_manifest.py`) name the rule in a short form; the sentence is the place where the client reads it in full.
  `metrics.stress.cases.<case>.independent_check` and `summary` in the reply are read again from `verify/verify.json` at each call (F4-29, section 17: `stress_report.refresh_from_verify`; in memory, `result/metrics.json` is not changed).
  `metrics.print` has `partial` and `coverage` (TC-2, section 44), and `independent_check` has `verify_partial` and `verify_coverage` when the verify result is partial.
- A run that ended with no result (since P9-6, section 24.4): `run_status` has `log_tail`, `failure`, `options` and, for a stop by a signal
  or an unseen end with no message, `possible_causes` and `possible_causes_note` (and `dashboard_note`). `run_result` returns `{"done": false, "state", "run_dir",
  "run_dir_rel", "summary", "message", ...}` with the same keys, in place of `No result yet. Call run_status.`. A run that is at work,
  a done run, a run that a request stopped and a folder with no run keep their replies.
- `stop_run(run_dir: str | None) -> dict` (since P4b-4): ask a running run to stop at the end of its current pass. It returns at once. It sends
  no signal and waits for nothing. The reply and its states are in section 24.2, "Stop on request".
- `environment(yaml_path: str | None) -> dict` (added after version 1.5). The dict has `code_folder`:
  the folder with the `topopt` package and, in a checkout or a plugin, `examples/` and `tools/`. Facts about the
  machine and the solver backends. It starts no optimizer run (with `auto` on a GPU it runs the short self-test of gpu-mg in a child process, at most 60 s: seconds the first time on a device and driver, then the cached pass) and installs and builds nothing. Keys:
  `topopt_version`, `checkout` (below), `python` (`version`, `executable`, `implementation`), `platform` (`name`,
  `system`, `machine`, `release`, `apple_silicon`, `linux_x86_64`, `mac_python`, `hint`), `packages` (version or
  `null`), `tet` (the state of the optional tet mesher, section 14), `backends` (`cholesky`, `pardiso`, `amg`; each `available`, `note`, `resolved_by` =
  the values of `settings.solver` that end in this solver; `auto` counts with its CPU solver), `solver_setting` (for each value of
  `settings.solver`: `resolved` or `error`; for `auto` also `cpu_solver`, `fallback`, `why` and `choice`, below), `experimental_solvers`
  (an empty object since P9-4d: gpu-mg is a value of `settings.solver` and has its entry in `solver_setting`; the key stays for readers of
  the old data), `opencl` (the OpenCL facts of section 20), `auto_solver` (the solver that `auto` uses
  first: `gpu-mg` on a GPU that passes the self-test, else the CPU solver), `auto_choice` (the `SolverChoice` of `auto` as data:
  `solver`, `cpu_solver`, `fallback`, `device`, `case`, `self_test`, `reason`, `line`; section 20), `gpu_solver` (the facts about the GPU solver,
  section 20, "Environment"), `ram` (`total_bytes` and
  `available_bytes` for this process: the host value, or the cgroup limit if lower; also
  `host_total_bytes`, `host_available_bytes`, `cgroup_limit_bytes`; `null` if unknown. In a cgroup the room is the
  limit minus the working set, as cAdvisor and the kubelet count it (Docker subtracts the same value): `cgroup_used_bytes` = `cgroup_current_bytes`
  (memory.current, v1: memory.usage_in_bytes) minus the inactive file pages (`cgroup_inactive_file_bytes`; memory.stat
  `inactive_file`, v1: `total_inactive_file`), not below 0; also `cgroup_room_bytes`, `cgroup_source`, and `cgroup_facts`,
  a list of texts that says what is missing when memory.stat has no such line (the used memory is then the raw count)
  and when the inactive file pages are more than the raw count (the used memory is then 0). In a cgroup with a limit,
  `available_bytes` is the smaller of `host_available_bytes` and `cgroup_room_bytes`; `cgroup_room_bytes` is `null`
  without a limit or without a used value), `cores`
  (`logical`, `affinity`, `cgroup_cpu_limit`, `usable`), `threads` (`env`,
  `openblas_threads_in_run`: the same rule as `cap_blas_threads`, and the text of the variable if the
  user set it; `note`), `run_interpreter` (the Python of the runs, TOPOPT_PYTHON; the data is for it), `work_folder` and `server` (the MCP tool only; section 10.1), `preferences` (the MCP tool only; section 10.2),
  `other_servers` and `other_servers_note` (the MCP tool only; section 43.5),
  `problem`, `recommendations`, `note`, `ok`.
  `problem` is `null` without `yaml_path`. With it: `ok`, `name`, `free_dofs`, `iterations`,
  `solver`, `time_estimate_s` (total seconds for each backend; model values, CONTRACTS section 11),
  `time_estimate`, `memory_estimate`, `solver_setting_problem` (why `settings.solver` cannot run
  here, else `null`; the estimates are still given), `backend_warnings`, `recommendation`. On a
  wrong YAML: `{"ok": false, "error": ...}`.
  `recommendations` is a list of offers as data: `install_pypardiso` (same fields as the `check`
  recommendation) on Linux x86_64 without `pypardiso`, `build_accelerate_shim` (`command`
  quoted for a shell, `needs`, `reason`, `license_note`; no `speedup_factor`, the reason says that
  `auto` runs `amg`, slower by the factor of the time estimate above, an estimate) on Apple silicon without a
  library that loads,
  `install_pyamg` (`command` with `--python` and the pin). The two offers for gpu-mg of the time when it was opt-in are gone: the facts
  are in `gpu_solver` (section 20). The tool never installs or builds anything
  (on macOS it reads the free RAM with `vm_stat`). The agent runs the command after the user agrees.
  The same data is `topopt.environment.environment_data(yaml_path=None)`.
  `checkout` (since L1b; `topopt.doctor.checkout_facts()`, the function that `topopt doctor` also calls; read-only, it fetches
  nothing): `code_folder`, `kind` (`git checkout`, a source folder without git such as a plugin copy or a ZIP, or an installed
  package), `git` (a `.git` file or folder is there), `has_tools`, `has_pyproject`; for a git checkout `head` (short revision),
  `head_date`, `branch` (`null` when `detached` is true), `dirty` (tracked files changed), `changed_files`, `untracked_files`,
  `default_branch_ref` (what `origin/HEAD` points to, else `origin/main` or `origin/master`), `ahead` and `behind` (commits, against that
  ref AS OF THE LAST FETCH), `last_fetch_utc` and `last_fetch_age_s` (the newest time of the `FETCH_HEAD` files: the common one and the one of each
  linked worktree, because git writes `FETCH_HEAD` in the git folder of the worktree where `git fetch` ran, and the remote-tracking
  refs are shared; `null` when nothing was fetched since the clone), `fetch_command`, `update_command` (`git -C <folder> pull
  --ff-only` when HEAD is on the default branch, or on a branch that follows it and has no commit of its own; else it goes to the
  default branch, because `behind` counts against that branch: `git -C <folder> switch <default branch> && git -C <folder> pull
  --ff-only` on another branch or a detached HEAD, or `git -C <other worktree> pull --ff-only` when another worktree has the default
  branch checked out) and `notes` (text facts, for example that a
  folder has no git data and the clone command). The facts are `null` when git does not answer; the function never raises.
- `save_preferences(print=None, material=None, quality=None, outputs=None, filaments=None) -> dict` (since P9-7b, section 10.2; `filaments` since
  PM-2): keeps the print bed, the material, the quality, the outputs and the filaments of the user in `<work folder>/topopt-preferences.yaml`. It
  has no path argument.
- `find_printer(name) -> dict` (since PM-1, section 18.7): finds a printer by name in the shipped catalog and in the user printers of the work
  folder. It reads and changes nothing. `save_printer(profile) -> dict` (since PM-1): keeps a printer that the catalog does not have, with its sources, in
  `<work folder>/topopt-printers.yaml`. It has no path argument and strict arguments.
- `find_material(name) -> dict` (since PM-2, section 18.8): finds a filament by name in the shipped catalog and in the user filaments of the work
  folder. It reads and changes nothing. `save_material(profile) -> dict` (since PM-2): keeps a filament that the catalog does not have, with its
  sources, in `<work folder>/topopt-filaments.yaml`. It has no path argument and strict arguments. `printer_materials(printer=None) -> dict`
  (since PM-2): every current filament of the catalog and the user file grouped by its state on a printer (`ok`, `care`, `no`, `unknown`), with
  the reasons; the rows of an older sheet of a listed product are left out and counted in `note`. It reads and changes nothing.
- `find_features(stl_path) -> dict` (since I2, section 45): lists the cylindrical holes, the bosses and the flat faces of an STL file, in mm. It reads the file and writes
  nothing; no work folder is made. A wrong input gives `{"ok": false, "error": ...}`.
- **Title and hints (since P9-11).** Every tool has a `title` and the four hints of the MCP specification (`readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`,
  `idempotentHint`, `openWorldHint`). All four are set on every tool; none is left to the defaults of the specification (destructive and
  open-world). They live in one table, `TOOL_SURFACE` in `topopt_mcp/server.py`, and `_TopoptServer.tool` gives them to the SDK: an
  `@mcp.tool(...)` line does not pass them. A tool with no row stops the import, and `tests/test_mcp_tool_surface.py` fails for a row with no
  tool. The table is not copied here; the code is its one home. The sort is made from the code of the tool, not from its name, and the
  hint is for the whole tool, over all its arguments. When two values fit, the table has the safe one (not read-only, destructive).
  - read-only: the tool creates, changes and deletes no file, folder, process or lock. A cache or log file counts as a write.
  - destructive (only for a tool that is not read-only): the tool can delete or overwrite a file or folder that it did not create in the
    same call, or stop a process. An `overwrite` argument counts. A tool that only adds new files is not destructive.
    The lock file of a job that has ended holds no data: `verify_status` and `ratchet_status` remove such a lock, so they are not read-only,
    and they are not destructive. `environment` removes the registry entry of a server that has ended (P9-14), which holds no data either:
    the same holds. A tool that only writes again its own derived output (a file that topopt makes from the facts of the folder) is not
    read-only, and it is not destructive for that: `run_result` writes the part card `result/report.md` again (P9-7a); it is not
    destructive and it is idempotent.
  - idempotent: a second call with the same arguments has no more effect on the environment than the first.
  - open-world: the tool can reach the network or a system outside this machine. A local file or a local process does not count.
- **Strict argument names (since #174, step 4).** Every tool refuses an argument name that it does not have. The MCP SDK drops such a
  name, and a call that only looks right then does a wrong thing (a typo such as `stop_rule` for `stop_rules` gives a run with the stop rules of the YAML). `_TopoptServer`
  makes it the rule: `@mcp.tool()` is strict, and `strict_arguments=False` turns it off for one tool (no tool does today). The input schema
  of the tool has `additionalProperties: false`. `_TopoptServer.call_tool` answers an unknown name with the tool's own reply
  `{"ok": false, "error": "<tool> did nothing: it has no argument 'x'. The argument names are: a, b, c."}` before the tool runs, so no
  file, run folder or process is made. The refusal is the tool's own reply, so `isError` is false, as for every `"ok": false` reply of
  this server (the 3 save tools did the same before #174). Before #174, a misspelled REQUIRED name gave the validation error of the SDK,
  with `isError` true. "did nothing" is true for a read-only tool too. A tool with no parameter says "It takes no
  arguments." The reply carries the work folder note as every reply does. The server check reads the parameter names of the tool, never
  the schema keyword: a schema without `additionalProperties` refuses the same. Gemini CLI sends the same keyword in the schema of
  its own tool `write_todos` (public source, read 2026-10-28). A real call of a topopt tool from Gemini CLI is not checked yet.
  - **Client control keys.** The constant `CLIENT_CONTROL_KEYS` in `topopt_mcp/server.py` lists the argument keys that a client adds to
    the input schema of every MCP tool for its own use, so that the model can send them (today `wait_for_previous`: Gemini CLI; the
    key is in a call only when the model writes it). `call_tool` drops such a key first, before the name
    check and before the tool runs, and only when the tool has no parameter of that name; a tool parameter of the same name is kept and
    passed. The refusal does not list a control key as a valid name, and does not name it as unknown.
  - **Adding an entry.** Only for a client that is documented (public docs or public source) to add a key of its own to the input
    schema of every tool, or to the arguments of every call. The comment of the entry has the client, the file of its source, the version and the read date. A test covers the key
    (`tests/test_mcp_strict_arguments.py`). A key that only one model wrote by mistake is not an entry.

- **Reply key guides (since P9-11).** The resource template `topopt://replies/{tool}` (text/markdown, `topopt_mcp/replies.py`) gives the lines
  that explain the keys of the reply of `check_problem`, `build_regions`, `apply_marks`, `render_part`, `marks_to_hints`, `run_result` and `environment`. The text of each of
  these tools names its address, so that the tool text stays well under the 4,096 characters that the client keeps. A name with no guide gives
  a short text that names the tools that have one. The guide `run_topopt` (since #318) holds the detail of the fine pass (section 24.6): its
  arguments, the keys `fine`, `fine_run_dir` and `fine_run` and the other tools that show the fine pass, and (since #174) the keys
  `brief_stated` and `brief_facts`. The tool text of `run_topopt` names `fine_from` and `fine_pass` and the address. The address of a guide ends inside the first 2,048
  characters of the tool text (`test_the_address_of_each_reply_key_guide_ends_inside_the_first_2048_characters`).

### 10.1 The work folder (added with P9-1a; the words for each surface with P9-1b)

The work folder holds `runs/`, the lock files of the verify and ratchet jobs, and the start of every relative path in a tool call. One
rule decides which folder it is: `topopt/workfolder.py`, `resolve(env=None, cwd=None, home=None, check=True)`. `workspace()` of
`topopt_mcp/server.py` and `key_root()` of `topopt/runinfo.py` both call it, so they give the same folder. The module does not import
`mcp` (it imports `topopt.runjob` only to look for old runs). It reads the environment at each call and creates no folder: a tool that
writes makes the folder where it writes.

- **Order.** The env var `TOPOPT_WORKSPACE` if it can be used, else `TOPOPT_DEFAULT_WORKSPACE`, else the current folder of the process
  (the Claude Code plugin, the CLI and Cursor start the server in the folder to work in; this was the only rule before P9-1a).
  `source` says which: `TOPOPT_WORKSPACE`, `TOPOPT_DEFAULT_WORKSPACE` or `current folder`.
- **The text of a variable.** An empty text, a text of blanks, and a whole `${user_config.<key>}` mean "not set" (Claude Desktop gives
  the last one for an option that the user left empty). They have no note. Blanks are cut for these two tests only: any other value keeps
  its blanks (a folder name can end in a blank), and the texts show the value as it was given. Otherwise a leading `~` and the MCPB variables `${HOME}`,
  `${DOCUMENTS}` (`<home>/Documents`), `${DESKTOP}`, `${DOWNLOADS}`, `${/}` and `${pathSeparator}` are replaced, in exact case (`expanded`
  lists them). A `${` that is left, or a `~name` that no home folder replaces (no such user), means the value cannot be used: the next
  variable of the order is used, and `fix_needed` has a text with the value as it was given. If both values cannot be used, one text names
  both values, names the folder in use, and gives the fix once. A relative path (after the replacement) starts at the current folder of the
  process, as before, and `notes` says so; when `TOPOPT_DEFAULT_WORKSPACE` is set it adds that the current folder is the folder of the
  extension, that an update of the extension can remove it, and the full path from the home folder as the option. The current folder is read
  only when a rule needs it (no usable value, a relative path, the old-runs check). If it is gone, `fix_needed` says that the server has no
  work folder, and nothing raises. The home folder is `Path.home()` (a test gives a fake one).
- **Facts** (`WorkFolder.facts()`): `path`, `source`, `raw` (the text of `TOPOPT_WORKSPACE`, or null), `expanded` (list), `exists`,
  `writable` (an existing folder that the process can write in, or a missing one that it can make; the check writes nothing), `fix_needed`
  and `notes` (lists of texts), `old_runs` (null, or `{path, run_folders}` of the first place that holds runs, with `also`: a list of the same
  items when other places hold runs too). `writable` is a fact of the work folder itself: a work folder that the process cannot write, with a
  `runs/` that it can write, has `writable` false, no `fix_needed` and no refusal, and a note says that the lock files of `verify_run` and
  `ratchet_run` cannot be written there. On macOS, when the check gets `EPERM` for a folder in the home folder, the cause adds that System
  Settings > Privacy & Security > Files and Folders shows if Claude may use it.
- **Two levels of text.** `fix_needed`: the value could not be used and another folder was taken, or the folder cannot be created or
  written and `runs/` cannot either. Every dict reply of every tool has `work_folder_note` with these texts while they persist. `notes`: what the server did (it
  replaced a variable, it started a relative path at the current folder, it found runs in an old place, the folder is a scratch workspace of Claude Desktop). They are added to
  `work_folder_note` in the replies of `environment`, `list_runs` and `run_topopt` only. A text names the cause, the folder in use and the
  fix. When `TOPOPT_DEFAULT_WORKSPACE` is set the Desktop extension started the server, and the fix is: "Open Settings > Extensions >
  topopt, choose the Work folder with the folder button, then quit Claude completely (Cmd+Q on a Mac) and open it again. A new chat or a
  new Code tab session is not enough: it keeps the old server process." Else it is: "Start the client in the folder that you want to use as
  the work folder. Or set TOPOPT_WORKSPACE to a full path in the env of the topopt server in the settings of your client. Then restart the
  server." (P9-1b: the first text of P9-1a, "Set TOPOPT_WORKSPACE in the MCP server settings", was not true for the Claude Code plugin,
  which gives the server no env to edit and starts it in the folder where Claude Code runs.) One place adds the key: the subclass of `MCPServer` in `topopt_mcp/server.py` wraps each function that
  `@mcp.tool()` registers; the schema and the description of a tool stay as they were.
- **The words for each surface (P9-1b).** The server can tell two cases apart: the Desktop extension, and every other start. The sign is
  `TOPOPT_DEFAULT_WORKSPACE`: only `packaging/mcpb/manifest.json` (`mcp_config.env`) sets it. The plugin (`.claude-plugin/plugin.json`
  gives the server no env), the repo `.mcp.json` (`env` is empty), `.cursor/mcp.json` (`TOPOPT_WORKSPACE` only), `.codex/config.toml` and
  `scripts/topopt-env.sh` set no variable that names the client, so the server cannot tell the plugin from a checkout, Cursor, Codex CLI or
  Gemini CLI. They get one text that is true for all of them. `topopt/workfolder.py` has the words (`FIX_DESKTOP`, `FIX_OTHER`) and three
  functions: `is_desktop_extension(env=None)`, `fix_text(env=None)` (the text of the surface) and `change_text(env=None)` ("To change the work
  folder: " and the text). Every reply that offers a change of the work folder takes its words from them: the `fix_needed` texts, the
  scratch workspace note, the error of `run_topopt`, `record_brief` and `case_status` for a YAML that is not found ("YAML file not found:
  <path> (work folder: <folder>). Give an absolute path." and `change_text()`), the error of `run_topopt` for a run folder that cannot be
  made ("Cannot create the run folder <folder>: <cause>. Give out_dir a folder that you can write." and, only when that folder lies in the
  work folder, `change_text()`: for a folder outside it the caller chose the folder, and another work folder would not help), and the option of
  `record_brief` for a YAML in the code folder. "Give an absolute path" and "give `out_dir` a folder that you can write" work on every
  surface, so they stay. When the work folder has a `fix_needed` text, `work_folder_note` of the same reply holds the fix, so those two
  errors do not add `change_text()`. No tool description, no instruction text and no skill or role names `TOPOPT_WORKSPACE`; the
  description of `run_topopt` says that relative paths start at the work folder and that `environment` shows it. The README section "The
  work folder" has the steps for each surface.
- **The one refusal.** `run_topopt` (when the run folder lies in the work folder) and `build_regions` return `error` when the folder that
  they write cannot be created or written: for `run_topopt` the folder that holds the run folder (the log, the pid file and the run folder go
  there), for `build_regions` `runs/` (or its nearest existing parent). The work folder itself is not the test. The error holds the cause
  and the fix. No other case refuses.
- **A child process.** `run_topopt`, `verify_run`, `ratchet_run` and `export_step` start a child with the work folder as its current folder.
  Each makes the work folder just before the start (a new install has none yet). If that fails, the reply has the work folder text, not the
  raw error of the system. The `TOPOPT_PYTHON` probe of `environment` is a read: it starts in the work folder when that is there, else in
  its nearest existing parent, and makes nothing.
- **A child process: the module path.** Every Python child of the server (the five starts above, and the import probe of `TOPOPT_PYTHON`) gets
  `PYTHONSAFEPATH=1` in its environment (`_child_env`), so the work folder is not on its module path. A user file there (`timeit.py`, `json.py`,
  `random.py`) cannot take the place of a standard or dependency module. The Python processes that the child starts (the gmsh worker and probe)
  inherit the variable. `PYTHONPATH` still works. The launcher `scripts/topopt-env.sh` starts the server (`mcp`) and the command line
  (`topopt`) with `python -P -m`, for the same reason: the client starts the server in the project folder of the user. The `python` case of the
  launcher gives the arguments of the user, so it has no `-P`. Test: `tests/test_child_safe_path.py`.
- **Old runs.** For a raw value with `${` the server before P9-1a resolved the text against its current folder (for the Desktop
  extension: `<extension folder>/${DOCUMENTS}/topopt/runs/...`). When `TOPOPT_DEFAULT_WORKSPACE` is set, the server also looks at
  `<current folder>/${DOCUMENTS}/topopt`, the text of the first default, because a person who typed a folder later still has runs there.
  A place that exists, is not the folder in use and holds run folders or a non-empty `runs/` is reported once: `old_runs` has its path and
  the number of run folders (`also` has the other places), and a note for each place says that an update of the extension can remove it
  (this sentence is only in the Desktop case). The server moves and copies nothing.
- **Scratch workspace.** When the work folder lies inside a path that has the parts `.../Claude/scratch-workspaces/...`, `notes` says that
  the app removes this folder when the session ends and the runs in it are lost, and gives the options: a folder that the user keeps
  (the Desktop extension: choose it in the Work folder field; the other surfaces: open the session in a project folder), then
  `change_text()`. It is a fact from the path, an info note at the same level as a
  relative path, and no refusal. Source: Claude Desktop scratch workspace (observed 2026-10-23, Desktop 3.6556.2): a Code tab session that
  the user starts with no project folder runs in `/Users/<user>/Library/Application Support/Claude/scratch-workspaces/<id>/<id>/scratch-<date>-<hex>`,
  and the app says the folder "starts empty, belongs to this session only, and is removed once the session ends". With no
  `TOPOPT_WORKSPACE` (the Claude Code plugin route) the work folder is that current folder.
- **At start** the server writes one line to stderr: `python: <exe>; work folder: <path> (from <source>)`, then `; fix needed: <text>` and
  `; note: <text>` for each text. Claude Desktop keeps stderr in `mcp-server-*.log`.
- **`environment`** (the MCP tool, not `environment_data`) adds `work_folder` (the facts above) and `server` (`pid`, and `started_utc`:
  ISO 8601 with `Z`, the time the process imported the server module). A person can compare `started_utc` with the time of a change of
  the extension setting to see whether this is the old server process.
- A child process (`topopt run`, a verify or ratchet job) gets the same env vars. A relative `TOPOPT_WORKSPACE` starts at the current
  folder of the child, which is the work folder of the server; this was so before and is not changed here.

### 10.2 Preferences: the file, the tool and the rule (added with P9-7b)

The agent asked the same things in each session (the print bed, the printer, the material, the quality), or assumed them, so the print
facts of every run said "assumed". One file in the work folder keeps the answers of the user once. The code is `topopt/preferences.py`
(it does not import `mcp`). It is not a way to run with other values: a preference does not change a run by itself (the rule below).

- **The file.** `<work folder>/topopt-preferences.yaml`, visible, so a person can find it and edit it. `topopt_mcp/server.py` reads it at
  each call (no restart), through `workspace()` of section 10.1. `save_preferences` writes it with `runinfo.write_atomic`; it writes this one
  path and no other, and it makes the work folder if it is not there. Comments that a person adds are not kept when the tool writes the file. A save replaces the file: if the name is a symlink, the
  link is read through (the values are used), and a save replaces the link with a plain file and does not write the file that it pointed to.
- **Keys** (`format: 1`, the integer 1: `1.0`, `true` and the text `'1'` are another format; every section is optional):
  - `print`: `printer_model`, `printer_type`, `bed_mm`, `build_direction`, `self_supporting_angle_deg`. The names, values and checks of the `print` block of
    section 18 (`topopt.config.parse_print_block`). A print LIMIT key (`min_wall_mm`, `max_bodies`, ...) belongs to one part, so it is not a
    preference. `printer_model` is checked with the resolver of section 18.7 against the shipped catalog and the user printers of the folder
    of the file: the file keeps the id (also when the user gave an alias), and a text that is not one printer is a refusal that lists the
    candidates or the suggestions. A FILE with a `printer_model` that is not found now (for example a user printer that was removed, or an id
    that a later catalog renamed) is not a problem of the file: only that key is not used. `environment.preferences` has `values` (without
    that key) and `not_used` (the text of the refusal), the other print keys, the material, the quality and the outputs stay in use,
    `build_regions` says in a fact that the printer was not used, and the reply of `save_preferences` has `not_used` too. The INPUT of
    `save_preferences` with such a printer is still a refusal.
  - `material`: `E` (MPa), `nu`, `density` (g/cm3) with the checks of section 2 (`parse_material_block`), `filament` (since PM-2) and an optional
    free text `name` (for example `PETG`). The name is for the facts; it is not written into a problem YAML. `filament` is a filament of the
    catalog of section 18.8 (an id, or a name or an alias): it is checked with the resolver of that section against the shipped catalog and the
    user filaments of the folder of the file, and the file keeps the id. A text that is not one filament is a refusal that lists the
    candidates or the suggestions. A FILE with a `filament` that is not found now (a user filament that was removed, or an id that a later
    catalog renamed) is not a problem of the file: only that key is not used, like a `printer_model` that is not found (above).
    `environment.preferences` has `values` (without that key) and `not_used`, the other keys stay in use, and `build_regions` says in a fact
    that the filament was not used.
  - `filaments` (since PM-2): `available`, a list of the filaments that the user has (ids of the catalog or of the user filament file; names
    and aliases are turned into ids, a filament once, in the order given). A FILE with an id that is not found now (a user filament that was removed) loses only that id: it is named in `not_used`, and the other ids stay in the list. The agent shows `printer_materials` for them and does not ask for
    a filament again. It is a fact about the user: it fills no YAML and sets no number of a run.
  - `quality`: `voxel_size` in mm with the check of `settings.voxel_size` (`parse_voxel_size`). Nothing else.
  - `outputs`: a list of `renders` (`render_part`), `step` (`export_step`) and `verify` (`verify_run`). The final STL and the part card
    `result/report.md` are made in every run, so they are not choices. `[]` means none of the three. An unknown name in the INPUT of `save_preferences` is an
    error that lists the allowed names. An unknown name in the FILE (a name of a later format) does not make the file invalid: `environment`
    names it as `outputs.<name>` in `kept_not_used` and the server uses the known names. A save that does not give `outputs` leaves the
    list as it is, with that name; a save that gives `outputs` replaces the list.
  - A key that the code does not know (a key that a person added, or a key of a later format) is kept in the file as it is. `environment`
    names it in `kept_not_used`. It does not make the file invalid. An unknown key in the INPUT of `save_preferences` is a refusal that
    names the key and the allowed keys. An unknown argument NAME (a key at the top of the call, for example `preferences`, `printer` or
    `path`) is a refusal too: every tool does this (section 10, "Strict argument names"). `_TopoptServer.call_tool` answers
    `{"ok": false, "error": "save_preferences did nothing: it has no argument 'x'. The argument names are: ..."}` with the allowed names
    (`print, material, quality, outputs, filaments`) before the tool runs, so no file is made (the MCP SDK drops such a name, and a call
    that only looks empty would make the "keep the defaults" file).
- **Reading: the key `preferences` of `environment`.** `path`, `exists`, `values` (the sections, in the stored form: `bed_mm` is a list of
  two numbers, `printer_type` is lower case), `problems` (a list of texts, when the file is not valid: `values` is then absent and the server
  uses no value from the file), `kept_not_used` (only when there are such keys) and `note`. A file that a person broke (not YAML, not a
  mapping, a wrong value, `format` other than 1) is a fact in `problems`, never a crash. A file that the system does not let the server READ is
  a fact in `problems` too, but it is not called broken: the text says "cannot read the file" with the cause (on macOS, a blocked read names the
  Files and Folders setting, as the write does), the note blames the rights and not the content, and `save_preferences` does not write over it
  and does not advise to remove it. With no file the note says in one sentence that no
  preferences are saved and that `save_preferences` keeps the answers of the user for the next runs. The descriptions of `environment`,
  `build_regions` and `check_problem` do not name `preferences` or `preferences_facts` (other items add text there, and the limit is 4,096
  characters); the reply keys carry the text, and the description of `save_preferences` names them.
- **Writing: `save_preferences`.** A section that is not given stays as it is. A mapping section that is given is merged key by key: a given
  key replaces the key, a key with the value `null` is removed, and `{}` removes the section (a key that the code does not know stays). The
  list `outputs` replaces the list; `{}` removes it. Every given value is checked first with the rules above; one wrong value refuses the
  call, writes nothing, and names the key, the value and the rule. With no section at all the call makes a file with `format: 1` and no
  section when there is none (the user kept the defaults, and `exists` becomes true so nobody asks again). The call refuses (writes nothing):
  a work folder with a `fix_needed` text (the error is that text, section 10.1) or a folder that cannot be written; an existing file that
  is not valid YAML or not a mapping (the error names the file and the YAML error; the file of a person is not overwritten); a file with
  another `format`. A write that fails is a refusal with the cause (on macOS, a blocked write names the Files and Folders setting, as section 10.1 does). The reply: `ok`, `path`, `values` (the file now), `changed` (the sections), `created`, `kept_not_used`, `problems`
  (what is still wrong in the file) and `note`. When `problems` is not empty after the save, the note names the keys, says that the server
  uses no value from the file until they are fixed, and does not say that the values are live; `values` is then the valid part only. There is no CLI command: a CLI user edits the file.
- **The rule: a preference does not change a run by itself.** `run_topopt`, `check_problem`, `topopt run` and `topopt check` do not read
  the file to fill a YAML. The problem YAML is the full record of a run. For the same YAML, with and without a preferences file, the
  loaded problem, the run settings, `run.json` (but `started_at`), the reply of `run_topopt` and the result of `check_problem` are the same;
  the only difference is the key `preferences_facts` of `check_problem` (a guard test covers this). Two places use the file, and both
  say so in the reply:
  - `build_regions` (the MCP tool; the CLI wrapper does not read the file) fills only a block that the spec does not have at all: the
    `material`, the `print` block, or `settings.voxel_size` (absent or null; an empty `{}` block gives no value, so it counts as missing; the
    text `auto` is a value of the spec). The values go into the YAML. The `material` block of the file may hold a `filament`: it is written
    into the YAML as `material.filament`, and the fact says what the run takes from it (the numbers of `parse_filament_block`, and that a key
    of the file wins over the filament). A spec with a `material` block of its own, also with a `filament` only, gets nothing from the file.
    The reply has `preferences_facts`: one text for each block, with the file and the
    values. A block that the spec gives, also a part of one, is not changed and gets no value of the file: the material and the print
    values are requirements of the user for this request, and the spec always wins. A key that the file does not hold keeps the default of
    the problem YAML, and the fact says so. A file with a problem is not used, and one fact says so.
  - `check_problem` adds `preferences_facts` (one text) when the printer model, the printer type, the bed, another print value or the material of the YAML
    differ from the preferences (a printer model is compared by id: an alias in the YAML is the same printer; a YAML without a model and
    preferences with one is a difference; since PM-2 the filament is compared by id in the same way, and a number that the filament of the YAML
    gives is the number of the YAML for this compare), or when the YAML has no `print` block (so the print report assumes the bed) and the preferences have one.
    It is a fact: not a warning, not a stop. The YAML is not changed; the text offers to edit it. The key is absent when there is no
    difference, no file or a file with a problem. The voxel size and the outputs are not compared.
- **The user printer file is not a preference.** `<work folder>/topopt-printers.yaml` (section 18.7) is a second catalog, not an answer of the
  user: `print.printer_model` of a YAML is looked up in the shipped catalog and in that file, as `topopt run`, `topopt check` and `load_config` do.
  The YAML still names the model, and `run.json` keeps the full profile, so the rule above is not broken: the same YAML in a work folder with
  the same two files gives the same run. `save_printer` writes the file; nothing else does. One thing is different from a preference: when
  `save_printer` REPLACES an entry, a YAML that names its id gets the new values at its next check or run, and the YAML text is the same, so
  `yaml_sha256` of the checkpoint, the case record and the ratchet pins do not see it. The reply of `save_printer` says so (`note`), old
  runs keep their record, and `run.json` `print.profile_sha256` (section 18.7) tells whether two runs used the same printer facts.
- **The lever reference.** A preference is not a lever (it changes no run), so `save_preferences` has no card. It is listed with the tools that
  judge nothing (`READ_ONLY_TOOLS` in `topopt/levers_cards.py`, like `record_brief`), as section 41 asks for a tool that has no card.
- **The skills.** `start-here` (Step 1b) asks the user once, in one message, when `environment.preferences.exists` is false, then calls
  `save_preferences`; with a file it does not ask again. Since PM-1 it asks for the printer model only (section 18.7), not the bed and the
  printer type. `part-to-topopt` uses the preferences or lets `build_regions` do it, tells the user
  which values came from there, and offers the outputs that the file lists. Both are offers (tools inform, the agent decides).

## 11. Time model and the time budget

The time estimate of `topopt check`, `check_problem` and the part builder is a model, given as an estimate and not as a promise: a run can
take less or more time (the fixed part is `SETUP_S` 10 s and `POST_S` 15 s, and the loop is fitted to the table below).
The engine has no time budget of its own. The only budget is the one of the user, `settings.stop_rules.time_budget_s` (section 24.2).
When the YAML sets it and the estimate is above it, `topopt check` and the part builder print a warning with the voxel size where the
estimate is the budget (`cli.fit_voxel_size`, about). Without it there is no budget warning and the time estimate is a fact in plain words.
(Until P9-8 a fixed budget of 240 s on an M1 16 GB gave a warning for every user.)

The budget is also a stop rule (section 24.2), not a note. Every budget warning says what it does in this YAML, with one text
(`cli.budget_effect`, used by `topopt check`, MCP `check_problem` and the part builder, after the fact and before the offers):

- The stop rules are on (a `stop_rules` mapping turns them on; `enabled` is true in a mapping unless it says false): the run stops at the
  first pass that ends after the budget (rule `time_budget`), and the part is the design of that pass. The rule `converged` is on too.
  `topopt run --no-stop-rules` (MCP `run_topopt(stop_rules=false)`) turns the rules off for one run, and then all passes run.
- `enabled: false`: the budget is set but the rules are off, so the run does not stop at it. `--stop-rules` (MCP
  `run_topopt(stop_rules=true)`) turns the rules on for one run.

The clock of the rule is not the clock of the estimate. The rule reads the run time at the end of each pass (`RunWriter.elapsed()`): the
time since `topopt run` started, so it counts the loading, the setup and the passes, and the time before a resume. It does not count the
post step after the last pass. The estimate counts `SETUP_S`, the passes and `POST_S`. So a run whose estimate is a little above the budget can
still make all its passes, and the rule fires only at the end of a pass (a pass is not cut short).

Measured on the real hook (2026-10-08, Cholesky, quiet Mac; assemble + factor
+ 2 solves, steady state). Free dofs set the cost, not active voxels:

| voxel_size | active | free dofs | s/iteration | peak RSS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.0 | 65,930 | 193,839 | 4.74 | 3.2 GB |
| 1.1 | 50,455 | 147,945 | 2.51 | 2.3 GB |
| 1.2 | 37,505 | 109,548 | 1.30 | 1.7 GB |
| 1.25 | 33,188 | 96,924 | 1.04 | 1.4 GB |

The hook uses 1.2 mm: about 110 s of loop time.

## 12. Refine (added after version 1.5)

The refine step makes a page to mark the final part. See `topopt/refine/README.md`.

- `topopt refine <run_dir> [--yaml FILE]` writes `result/refine.html` and `result/stress.npz`.
  It exits 1 with one line if `result/final.stl` is missing or the YAML changed after the run, or if the YAML of the run is not
  at the path of `run.json` (section 5: a relative path starts at the run folder): the line gives the path that it tried and
  `--yaml`. `--yaml FILE` is the YAML at its new place (a moved run folder, a recording made on another machine).
  When the voxel grid of the YAML is not the grid of the run, it exits 1 with one line that shows the path once (resolved,
  absolute) and the grid of the run and of the YAML (shape, voxel size, origin, and the number of voxel labels that differ when
  the shapes are equal). With `--yaml` the line says that the given file does not fit the grid of the run; without it, that the YAML
  or the STL files changed after the run.
  If the YAML is read again, `refine` prints one `note: the YAML differs from run.json: ...` line for each difference on stderr
  (the lines of `topopt verify`; the path of `refine.html` stays the only line on stdout), and the page data (`META` in
  `refine.html`) has the key `yaml_vs_run` (`matches`, `differences`, `note`; no path). `topopt run` does not read the YAML again
  for this step, so its page has no such key. The material (`E`, `nu`) and `penal` are not compared (section 5).
- `topopt run` calls the same code after the status is `done` and after `metrics.json`.
  The run time does not change. A failure logs one `warning: refine failed: ...` line and the run still ends with exit code 0.
- With `--dashboard`, a successful refine also opens `<dashboard url>refine` in the browser.
- `result/stress.npz`: `centers` (n, 3) in the mm frame of `final.stl`, `rho`, `vm_case_<i>` (MPa), `vm_max`,
  `case_names`, `compliance_cases`, `E`, `nu`, `penal`, `h`. Only voxels with density 0.5 or more.
- Dashboard server: `GET /refine` returns `result/refine.html` (404 if missing).
  `GET /api/refine` returns `{"exists": true|false}`.

## 13. Constraints and the objective form (added with A1)

This section holds the A1 additions to sections 2, 5 and 9. The other sections stay as they are.
The Python API is in `topopt/formulation.py` (`Constraint`, `Objective`, `Formulation`,
`Response`, `DesignPoint`), `topopt/mma.py` (`Mma`, `MmaState`) and `topopt.optimize.minimize`.
`examples/custom_constraint.py` is a script
that adds a custom constraint.

A row that uses the displacements `U` (an adjoint solve, `DesignPoint.stiffness_derivative`) returns
`wrt="rho_stiff"` and reads `point.rho_stiff`. `stiffness_derivative` is the slope with respect to
`rho_stiff`: it equals `rho` in a default run, bit for bit, and it is the eroded density in robust mode
(section 22b). A row that uses only the density (a volume, a box mean) keeps `wrt="rho"` and reads
`point.rho`. A row with an explicit term in the density and an adjoint term (the stress row of PR #22) has
two slopes, to `rho` and to `rho_stiff`, and one `wrt` cannot give both. In robust mode its gradient is wrong
unless both terms use the same density (section 22b, "Objectives and rows").

### YAML keys

```yaml
load_cases:
  - name: pull_off
    compliance_limit: 5.0       # optional. float > 0, N*mm. The compliance c_i of this case stays at or below it.
                                # Write 0.005 or 5.0e-3. A text that float() reads ("5e-3", or a bare 5e-3 that
                                # YAML 1.1 loads as text) is read as that number. Only this key does that.
settings:
  case_combine: sum             # optional. sum (default) | max. How the load cases join in the objective.
  objective_scale: stage        # optional. stage (default) | first. When the objective scale is taken (below).
```

- `sum`: minimize `sum(w_i * c_i)`. This is the objective of every run before A1.
- `max`: minimize the worst case `max_i(w_i * c_i)`. The weight `w_i` scales the case before the max.
  MMA gets this as the bound form: one row `w_i * c_i / ref - z <= 0` for each case and the
  objective `z`. `ref` is the largest `w_i * c_i` at the first pass of the beta stage (at pass 0 only with `objective_scale: first`, below).
- A case with `compliance_limit` adds the row `c_i <= limit`. The volume row is always there.
  Rows of all kinds can be used together. The YAML key `limits` (section 31) adds displacement and alignment rows after
  these rows, and `settings.perimeter_max_mm2` (section 26.3) adds the perimeter row last.
- With `max` and one load case, the run uses the `sum` form (the problem is the same, and the
  `sum` form is the plain path). `run.json` then shows `objective_form: sum`.
- The loader checks the keys. Messages (one line, with the file name, as in section 2):
  `'load_cases[1].compliance_limit' must be > 0, got -2.0`,
  `'load_cases[1].compliance_limit' must be a number, got 'big'`,
  `'settings.case_combine' must be sum or max, got 'minmax'`. A key that is not listed is still an error.
- `topopt check --json` (and `run.json` `derived`) show `compliance_limit` for each load case
  (`null` if none) and `case_combine`. The part builder (`build_regions`) passes `case_combine`
  and `beta_schedule` from the spec `settings` to the YAML.

#### Prices of the rows (facts)

MMA treats every row as a soft constraint: a row that cannot be met is violated, and its price says
how hard MMA works against that. When rows cannot all be met, the row with the lower price gives way first.

- The volume row has price 1000 and the linear form. The volume is the budget.
- A compliance-limit row has price 100. MMA gets `ln(c_i / limit)` (form "log"); the report keeps
  the linear `g = c_i / limit - 1`. A limit that cannot be met at the given volume leaves the
  volume at its target and only the limit row is unmet. The value of that row is then the best
  compliance of the case that MMA reached at this volume. (Cantilever, 40 iterations, side limit at
  0.3 times the free result: volume 0.300, side row `g = +1.59`. With one price 1000 and a linear
  row it was volume 0.479, `g = +0.60`, and both rows unmet; with a limit of 1e-6 the volume
  went to 1.0.)
- A custom constraint (Python API) stays linear with price 1000 unless it sets `form` and `price`.
  The form "log" needs a value and a limit above 0.
- The bound form (`max`) needs objective terms above 0 (the bound variable z is at least 0). A
  term at or below 0 stops the run with a message. Its rows have price 1000.
- Two rows that are linear copies of each other make the dual system of MMA nearly singular
  (measured: condition number 1.6e14, against 6e7 for one row; the 40-iteration run differed by
  1.7e-7 in compliance). A YAML can make such a pair: two load cases with equal loads or exact opposite loads and the same
  compliance limit (see "Load cases that repeat another case" below, which gives a fact). No guard exists.
- A limit that the design cannot meet is not an error. The run ends, reports the violation
  (below), and the exit code stays 0.
- A force that sits on fixed nodes is lost (section 5, `lost_force`). A case compliance, and so its
  limit, uses the force that is left.
- The default (no key) gives the same run as before A1: same rows, same iteration count, same
  beta and move schedule.

#### The scale of the objective (`settings.objective_scale`, added with P3a)

MMA gets the objective divided by a scale (`MmaState.f0_ref`). So `f0 = objective / scale`. In the `max` form the rows are `term_i / scale - z`.
The scale is the value of the objective at one design: `abs(value)`, or 1.0 if that is 0.

- `stage` (default): the scale is taken at pass 0. It is taken again at the first pass of each beta stage, from the design of that pass.
  That pass is one where the beta is not the beta of the pass before. Between stage starts the scale does not change.
- `first`: the scale is taken at pass 0 only. It stays for the whole run. This is the behaviour before P3a.
- Why: a beta jump removes much of the projected volume. In tests with a phone stand at a low volume fraction the loss was 25 to 60 percent.
  The volume row is then below its limit and has no force. So only the objective moves the design.
  The scale of pass 0 is the objective of a near-void start. It is 2 to 3 orders above the objective of a design that has been optimized.
  So the scaled gradient is far below the absolute regularization `raa0` (1e-5) of MMA. The step is then very small.
  The volume came back at about 1 percent of the limit for each pass. Nine runs of about 200 000 active voxels or more ended with 0.55 to 0.88 of the allowed volume.
  A scale from the design of the stage start gives a gradient of the size that MMA expects.
- Measured on a small CPU copy of the stand (`tests/test_objective_scale.py`). It has 6307 active voxels, penal 6, Linux and PARDISO.
  After the last jump the volume is 0.73 of the limit with `first`. It needs 5 passes to reach 0.95.
  With `stage` the volume is 0.94 at the jump, and it is above 0.95 one pass later.
- The MMA state is not reset. The asymptotes, `xold1`, `xold2` and the move limit stay. Only the scale changes.
- After a stage start the projected volume can be above its limit for a few passes. Measured: g up to +0.022 on the CPU stand.
  On the full-size stand g is up to +0.043, with four passes above 0.005 in the stage that starts at pass 30.
  This is normal MMA behaviour: MMA does not keep each step feasible. The volume row is active again at the next pass, and the volume comes back.
  `first` does it too, but less (g +0.0074 on the full-size stand). The verdict tests the last pass only.
- A run with one beta stage is the same run in both modes. That is a schedule with one entry, or a run that ends before the second breakpoint.
- Resume: the pass number and the beta schedule alone decide (`optimize.objective_scale_resets`).
  A run can resume from the checkpoint of the pass before a stage start, or of the stage start itself. It then has the same scale as a run that was not stopped.
  The checkpoint holds the scale in force after the pass (`mma.f0_ref`).
- Old checkpoints: the effective settings (section 24.2) leave the key out at its default `stage`. This is the rule of `gpu_tol` and `gpu_backward_error` (section 20).
  So a checkpoint of a build from before P3a resumes with no override. The `meta_json` of a checkpoint of this build has `objective_scale` with the value of the run.
  A resume of a checkpoint with no such key writes one `resume:` fact. The fact says that the first part kept the scale of pass 0, and that the run goes on with `stage`.
  It says that `settings.objective_scale: first` keeps the old behaviour. A checkpoint of a finished run gets no such fact, because no pass is left.
- `first` stays in the effective settings. So a change from `first`, or to it, is a change of the inputs. It needs `--allow-changed-inputs`.
  The refusal names two ways out. The first is `settings.objective_scale: first` in the YAML: it keeps the rule of the checkpoint (a key that is not set means `stage`).
  The second is `stage` with the override. The scale of the checkpoint then stays until the next beta stage start, and each stage takes its own after that.
  A checkpoint of a build from before P3a, resumed with `first`, is refused for the new key. With the override the run goes on as the old build did.
- The log and the tests read the physical value of the objective, not the scaled one. This holds for `obj=` in the log line.
  It holds for `objective.value` and `compliance` in the history. It holds for the `objective_change` test of the verdict and of the stop rule `converged` (section 24.2).
  So they do not step at a stage start because of the scale.
  The objective does change at a beta jump, because the design is projected anew. The stop rule needs `window + 1` passes in a row at one beta, so it never compares across the jump.
- Nothing else reads the scale. The rows have their own scales: the stress row takes its KS scale `c` at each stage start by itself. Step acceptance and the verdict do not read it.
- `minimize(..., objective_scale=...)` takes the same two values and overrides the setting. `build_regions` passes the key from the spec `settings`.
- The loader refuses another value: `'settings.objective_scale' must be stage or first, got 'every'`.

#### Facts at the end of a beta stage and of the run (`stage_end`, added with P3a)

`run()` makes the facts below at the last pass of each beta stage. That pass is one where the beta of the next pass is not the beta of this pass.
It makes them also at the last pass of the run, and at the pass where a stop rule ended the run. A run with one beta stage has them at the last pass only.
The facts come from the design of that pass (`topopt/stage_facts.py`). They read the density and the snapshot bytes: no solve.
Not one of them is a test, a limit or a warning rule. The verdict tests (section 24.2) do not read them.

- `volume` (only a run with a row named `volume`): how much of the allowed volume the design uses.
  The allowed volume is the `limit` of the row, a mean density of the design voxels. `projected` is the mean density of the projected design (the value of the row).
  `thresholded` is the share of the design voxels with a density of 0.5 or more (the print threshold, the snapshot byte 128 or more).
  `used_projected` and `used_thresholded` are each of them divided by `limit`.
  The sentence is `volume: 0.47 of the allowed volume used (projected design), 0.40 (thresholded part at 0.5)`.
  The volume row is a ceiling, and the verdict counts a row under its limit as met. So this is the one place that says how much of the volume the run used.
  There is no threshold: the tool does not say that a number is too low. A mass objective with no volume row has no `volume` fact; it has the `material` fact below.
- `material` (F1-3a; only a run with `settings.objective: mass` and no row named `volume`): the material that the run uses. `volume_mm3` is the volume of the thresholded part
  (the design voxels with a snapshot byte of 128 or more, plus the fixed and load voxels) as a voxel count times h^3, the rule of `threshold_stability` at 0.5. `mass_g` is that volume times
  `material.density` (g/cm3), and `density_g_cm3` is the density. It is not the mass of the finished mesh (`metrics.mass_final_g`). The sentence is
  `material: the thresholded part (density 0.5) has 7724 mm3 and 9.58 g (material density 1.24 g/cm3)`. A mass run with the volume fallback (no other row, so the ceiling at
  `settings.volume_fraction` is a row named `volume`) has the `volume` fact and no `material` fact.
- `grey` (F1-3a; only a run with `settings.objective: mass`, and only when the grayness of the pass is above `settings.stop_rules.grayness_max`, the default 0.1): the design is grey, so the
  thresholded part depends on the cut. The keys: `grayness` (`mean(4 rho (1 - rho))`, the number of the verdict "Tests:" sentence), `grayness_max`, `levels` (the `levels` of `threshold_stability`,
  section 5: `level`, `volume_mm3` and `bodies` at the cuts 0.4, 0.5 and 0.6) and `volume_spread` (the volume at 0.4 minus the volume at 0.6, divided by the volume at 0.5; null when the part is void
  at 0.5). A fault of the cut check gives `grayness`, `grayness_max` and `error`. The cost is three labelings of the grid (no solve). No new number: the limit and the three cuts exist already.
  The sentence is `grey design: grayness 0.739 is above grayness_max 0.1 at beta 2, so the thresholded part depends on the cut. Its volume is 9270 mm3 at the cut 0.4, 7993 mm3 at 0.5 and 6846 mm3 at 0.6,
  a spread of 0.30 of the volume at 0.5. Its body count is 1 at 0.4, 1 at 0.5 and 1 at 0.6`. At the last pass of the run, and in the verdict, it ends with `. The mesh step keeps only the bodies that touch a
  frozen region (a fixed, load or solid region): the body count of final.stl comes after the post step (metrics.grey_design.final_stl_bodies)`. The run log line of the last pass adds one sentence of options (more passes with
  a beta schedule that reaches a higher beta, or the compliance objective with a volume fraction or a target mass). A design that is grey is a fact, not an error: the numbers say how far the part
  depends on the cut, and the agent decides.
- `load_path` (every run): the rule of `stress_report.load_path_facts` (section 17). It is one face-connected labeling (6-connected `scipy.ndimage.label`) of the thresholded design.
  The thresholded design has the design voxels with density 0.5 or more, and all fixed and load voxels.
  A load region is joined when one body holds a voxel of the region and a voxel of a support. A support is a fixed region, a spring region or a joint region (`springs.support_mask`).
  The keys: `regions` is `{name: joined}` for each load region, and `not_joined` has the names of the regions that are not joined.
  The other keys are `bodies` and `bodies_with_a_support`. A failed check gives `{"error": text}`. The check never raises.
  The sentence names the regions that are not joined, and the beta of the stage. For example:
  `load path: load region 'tip' is not joined to a fixed, spring or joint region in the thresholded design (density 0.5) at beta 2. A low beta gives a grey design: the thresholded part is then not the final part`.
  A grey design is expected at a low beta. So the fact is about the thresholded part of that pass, not about the final part.
  At the last pass the beta is the last beta of the schedule. The check uses the snapshot of the pass. It does not read `final.stl` (the report of section 17 does).
  Cost: one labeling of the full grid takes 5 to 10 ms on the phone stand at 0.7 mm. That grid has 325 000 voxels, and 143 000 of them are design voxels.
  It takes about 40 ms on 2.5 million voxels. Measured on Linux, one thread.

Where they are:

- `history.jsonl`: the record of that pass has the key `stage_end`.
  Its value is `{"beta", "next_beta" (null at the last pass), "volume": {...} (only with a volume row), "load_path": {...}, "material": {...} (F1-3a: a mass run with no volume row), "grey": {...} (F1-3a: a mass run, when the grayness is above `grayness_max`)}`. No other record has it. `minimize()` does not make it, because it has no run folder, log or verdict.
- `run.log`: after the line of that pass, one line for each fact.
  The lines look like `fact: end of the beta 1 stage, pass 29: volume: ...` and `fact: last pass 80: load path: ...`. The order is volume, material, grey design, load path.
  The post step of a grey mass run adds one line `fact: grey design: the thresholded part has 13 bodies at the cut 0.5 (15 at 0.4, 8 at 0.6), and final.stl has 1 body. ...` (`metrics.grey_design.text`, section 5).
- `verdict.json` key `facts` (and `metrics.verdict.facts`, so `run_status` and `run_result`): `{"iteration", "beta", "next_beta", "volume", "load_path"}` of the last pass, and `material` and `grey` where the run has them (F1-3a).
  It is null for a run that did not finish, and for a history with no `stage_end`.
  The text of the verdict ends with ` Facts: <the volume sentence>; <the material sentence>; <the grey design sentence>; <the load path sentence>.`
  The volume sentence is in the text of every run with a volume row. The material sentence is in the text of a mass run with no volume row (F1-3a). The grey design sentence is in the text
  of a mass run whose last pass is grey (F1-3a). The load path sentence is in the text only when a load region is not joined, or the check failed.
  The state of the verdict, `converged` and `feasible` do not read these facts. The body count of `final.stl` is not in the verdict: `verdict.json` is written before the post step
  (`metrics.grey_design`, section 5). A history of a run from before F1-3a has no `material` and no `grey`: its verdict text is as it was.
  A history of a run from before P3a has no `stage_end`. Its verdict has `facts: null` and no `Facts:` sentence.
- Resume: the decision (the pass number and the schedule) is the same as in a run that was not stopped. The numbers (the design) are the same too.
  The records that were written keep their `stage_end`.

#### Load cases that repeat another case (facts, added with F4-5)

The model is linear. A load case whose loads are the exact opposite of the loads of another case gives the displacements `-u`, and a
case with equal loads gives `u`. `loads.repeated_load_cases(config)` finds these cases. Two cases match when they have the same
entries of `forces` and `pressures`, in any order (the entries are compared as a multiset: the load region, `force`, `moment` and `at` of
each entry, and the region and value of each pressure), and each force, moment and pressure is equal (relation `"equal"`) or equal with
the other sign (`"opposite"`). A remote force keeps its point `at` in both cases. The test is exact float equality: there is no
tolerance and no new number. Two entries on one region against one entry with their sum, or an extra entry with a zero force, give no
match. A **group** is the first case and every later case that matches it, so three cases with one load make one group of three. A case
with an all-zero load matches both signs and is called `"equal"`. Cases that are proportional with another factor are not matched:
a float test would need a tolerance (0.3 and 3 * 0.1 are not equal), and the effect would be different (the weight `wA + k^2 * wB`, the
limits scaled by `k^2`).

These rows give the same value and the same gradient for every case of a group: the compliance, the relaxed von Mises stress
(`ks_stress.py`), the springs and joints (they are part of `K`), and the displacement and alignment rows with the sense `abs`. These rows
follow the sign, so they give another value for an opposite case: the buckling row (`buckling.min_factor`, one row for each case), the
buckling check after the run (`buckling.check`), and a displacement limit with the sense `max` or `min` that lists a case of each kind
(the kind of the first case, and the opposite kind; a missing `cases` key lists every case). A limit with the sense `max` or `min` that lists one
kind only gives the other kind nothing: it is no sign row, and the text names it among the `limits` rows that list a case (below). The
reactions of springs, joints and clamps have the other sign in an opposite case (they are a report, not a row).

The group is a fact with options, not a refusal and not a cap. The run goes on. The text (`loads.repeated_load_lines`, one `fact:` line for
each group) says why the cases repeat, what differs, the effect of the case settings, the cost, and the options:

- The weights: in the `sum` objective the group acts like one case with the weight of all the weights added. In the `max` objective the
  largest weight counts. With the mass objective the weights do not count.
- The limits: a `compliance_limit` or a stress limit of any case holds for all the cases of the group (they have the same compliance and the
  same stress), so the lowest one counts. Two equal compliance limits give two rows that are copies of each other (see "Prices of the rows").
  A weight or a limit in the text is its shortest exact text (`repr` of the float), so a value that you copy equals the YAML value.
- The cost: each case after the first adds one load column to the forward solve of every pass, and one adjoint solve for each stress,
  displacement, alignment or buckling row that it has. With the buckling row, each case also does one eigen solve in every pass.
- The options do not choose a case by its order: keep one of the cases and remove the others, and give the kept case the added weight and
  the lowest limits; or, if a row above follows the sign, keep all the cases. The text names the `limits` rows that list a case of the group in a
  `cases` list that is shorter than the list of all cases (the loader stops on a `cases` list that names a removed case), and, if one of them has
  the sense `max` or `min`, says to swap `max` and `min` for a kept case that has the opposite load. A `limits` row that lists all the cases of
  the YAML is not found: the loader fills a missing key with every case, so the two look the same.

One function, `repeated_load_lines`, writes the text for all of these places:

- `optimize.problem_facts(config)` appends the lines. `topopt check` prints them, `topopt check --json` has them in `facts`, and
  `run.log` has them at the start of the run, before the first pass.
- `cli.check_data` (so `topopt check --json`, the MCP tool `check_problem` and `build_regions` `check`) has the key `repeated_load_cases`: a list with one
  dict for each group (`[]` if none), JSON-safe: `cases` (the first is the first case of the group), `relations` (one for each later case: its
  relation to the first), `weights`, `compliance_limits`, `stress_limits_mpa` (one value for each case, `null` if none), `objective` (`"sum"`,
  `"max"` or `"mass"`), `objective_weight` (the weight of the group as one case; `null` for `"mass"`), `remote_force` (a case has a force with
  `at`), `buckling_row` (the YAML has `buckling.min_factor`), `sign_rows` (texts; only if a case is an opposite) and `limit_rows` (one dict
  `{name, kind ("displacement" or "alignment"), sense ("abs", "max", "min" or `null`), cases}` for each `limits` row that lists a case of the
  group). The same lines are in `warnings`. `topopt check` (the text) prints each line once, from `problem_facts`.
- The part builder (`regions_builder.check_yaml`) prints the lines with its other facts.

#### Load cases that apply no load (a fact and a refusal, added with U21; the reduced load vector and the compliance of 0.0, F4-37)

A load case **applies no load** when every component of every `force` and every `moment` of its `forces` is exactly `0.0`, and no entry of
`pressures` has a value other than `0.0`. The test is `LoadCase.applies_load` (false for such a case). It has no tolerance and no new number: any other value counts as a load for this test, `1e-300` too. A value that small can still give a compliance that is 0.0 or subnormal (an underflow), and a force can land on fixed nodes only or cancel on the nodes: see "A load that does no work for another reason" below.
`weight` is the share of the case in the objective (a number above 0) and is no load; the engine has no body force. The sum of the nodal forces
(`derived.load_cases[].total_magnitude_n`) is no test: it is `0.0` for a pure moment, which is a load, and two equal and opposite forces on two
regions (a squeeze) are a load with a force sum of 0. Neither gets a word.

What follows was measured on the hook (4 passes, CPU): the compliance of such a case is 0 for every design, so the case adds nothing to the objective
(its weight counts for nothing), and its stress limit is met by any design. A case next to a normal case gives the same pass-0 compliance as the normal case
alone. With no load at all, the objective scale is 1 (`abs(value) or 1.0` in `Formulation.respond`), no number is NaN or inf, and under the compliance objective
the run minimizes a constant: only the volume row moves the density, and the thresholded part is the fixed regions. Four rows cannot work with such a case: a
`compliance_limit` on it (the log form needs a value above 0), `settings.case_combine: max` with the compliance objective (the max form needs terms above 0),
the buckling row `buckling.min_factor` and the buckling check `buckling.check` (the eigen solve has no start vector). Each of the first three stopped the run at
pass 0 with an internal error (exit 2) (the buckling row before pass 0). The buckling check ended with an error record and no factor for any case (exit 0).

- **The fact.** `loads.no_load_lines(config, reach=None)` gives one `fact:` line for all the cases that apply no load. It names the cases, says that each adds nothing to the
  objective (compliance 0 and stress 0 for every design), that the weight counts for nothing (compliance objective with `case_combine: sum`), that a stress limit
  and a displacement or alignment limit that lists these cases only are met by any design, the cost (one load column in the solve of every pass, and one adjoint
  solve for each stress, displacement or alignment row that the case has), and the options: give the case a force, a moment or a pressure, or remove the case (with
  the `limits` rows that list it in a `cases` list). With the mass objective and no load at all, the line also says that the part has nothing to carry and the
  objective gives the lightest design that the rows allow. `ok` stays true. The same text is in `topopt check` and `check --json` (`facts`), in `run.log` before the first
  pass, in the `warnings` of `cli.check_data` (so the MCP tool `check_problem`) and in the part builder (`regions_builder.check_yaml`). `derived.load_cases[]` has the
  key `applies_load` (boolean) for each case, in `check_problem` and in `run.json`; no key is renamed. F4-37 adds the keys `load_reaches_free_dofs` and `load_reach` (see below).
- **The refusal.** `loads.no_load_refusal(config, reach=None, runtime=())` gives the text of a loader error (`UserError`, one line, with `(file: ...)`) where the cases that apply no load are next to
  a row that cannot work with them: (1) no case applies a load and `settings.objective` is `compliance` (the objective is 0 for every design, so nothing in the
  YAML shapes the part); (2) a case with no load has a `compliance_limit`; (3) `settings.objective` is `compliance` with `case_combine: max`; (4) `buckling.min_factor` or
  `buckling.check` is set. The text names the cases, gives each reason and the options: give the case (each case) a force, a moment or a pressure; remove the case (the cases); and the option of
  each reason (remove the `compliance_limit`, use `case_combine: sum`, remove the buckling key). When no case applies a load, "remove the case" is not offered (`load_cases` would be
  empty, and the loader stops on that), and under the compliance objective only "give a force, a moment or a pressure" is offered, because no other option gives a run that depends on a load.
  The sentence "A `limits` row that lists a case you remove must name another case in `cases`" follows the option "remove the case", and only a YAML with `limits` gets it. `topopt check`, `topopt run` and `check_problem` stop with it before any mesh (`check_problem` returns `ok: false` and the text in
  `error`); `run_topopt` starts the process, which stops with exit 1 and the text in its log, and the reply has the text in `derived_error`; the part builder prints it as an `ERROR:` line. Every other YAML with a case that applies no load gets the fact only, among them the mass objective with no load at all (with or
  without a `stress_limit`: the run goes on and gives the lightest design), and a case with a `stress_limit` next to a normal case.
- **Levers.** The card `load_cases[].forces[].force` has the symptom "the load case does nothing, zero force" with the facts `check_problem.derived.load_cases[].applies_load`
  and `run.derived.load_cases[].applies_load`; the second is a run flag (41.10). F4-37 adds `load_reaches_free_dofs` in the same two places (the `when` text names both causes) and a second run flag; the second flag is the entry and `applies_load` joins it, so a YAML zero case is one entry (a run.json without `load_reaches_free_dofs` keeps the `applies_load` entry).
- **The reports.** A case with no load has `stiffness_cases[].N_per_mm` null with a `reason` ("the case applies no load: every force is 0, so its compliance is 0 and |F|^2 / c is not
  defined"); F4-37 gives the same null to a case whose load reaches no free dof (`load_reaches_free_dofs` false in the `derived` of `run.json`), with the reason "the load of the case reaches no free dof
  (load_reaches_free_dofs is false), so its compliance is 0 and |F|^2 / c is not defined" (a `run.json` without the key gives no reason). With a stress limit, such a case has `physical.peak_MPa` 0.0 in the stress section of `metrics.json` and no ratio of the limit to the grey peak in its `summary`. Before U21 that
  ratio divided by 0.0, and the stress section of every case of the run became an error record. `topopt verify` prints "n/a" for the change of the p99.9 and for the stiffness of such a
  case in the line of a load band (`verify.json` has `null`); before U21 the summary stopped with exit 2 (`TypeError`) after `verify.json` was written. With `--levels`, the `levels` block has
  `null` for each relative change of such a case (the coarser value is 0), and the summary prints "n/a"; before, `levels_block` stopped with exit 2
  (`ZeroDivisionError`; found during the U21 fix round).
- **The solver gpu-mg.** It skips a zero column. `GpuSolver.solve` (`gpu_mg/model.py`) solves only the live columns of the block of load cases and repeats a live column in a short block;
  `solve_refined` (`gpu_mg/engine.py`, case C) gives a column with a zero residual a copy of a live column. So the PCG stop test (`residual < rtol^2 * |b|^2`, which a zero column would
  never meet) does not see it. Measured on the pocl CPU device (cantilever, 3 passes, case B and case C): a case with no load next to a normal case gives the same inner iteration counts
  as the normal case alone, and the pass-0 compliance is the same. The cost sentence of the fact stays true: the block holds one column for the case.
- **The resume of an old run.** A YAML with a case with no load and `buckling.check` ran before U21 (exit 0, with an error record and no factor for any case). The loader refuses it now,
  so every reader of that YAML stops with the refusal: `topopt run --resume` and `topopt verify --yaml` (measured, exit 1). Option: write a new YAML without `buckling.check` (or with a
  force in the case, or without the case) and run `topopt run <new yaml> --out <run folder> --resume --allow-changed-inputs` (measured: exit 0; the resume names the changed key).
- **A load that does no work for another reason (F4-37).** The test above reads the YAML numbers. Other reasons get the same answer: the same rows refuse, the same
  `fact:` line for every other YAML, the same options. Each test is exact; there is no tolerance and no new number, apart from the one use of `np.finfo(float).tiny` in (2).
  (1) **The load vector on the free dofs.** `loads.reaches_free_dofs` is false for a case whose load vector is exactly `0.0` on every free dof (`not np.any(f[free])`; per dof: a roller
  loses a force along its axis only). `problem.build_problem` tests it, so one place serves `topopt check`, `check_problem`,
  `topopt run` (the refusal comes before pass 0: exit 1, `status.json` says `error`, the job record `failed`), `--resume`, `--continue-from` and the part builder. The words say why, and
