  `loads.reach_kinds` chooses them from the vectors that the test already has (no tolerance): `nodal_zero` is `not np.any(f)`: "the nodal forces of the case add up to 0.0 at every node (opposite
  forces on the same nodes cancel, or a force is so small that its nodal share is 0.0 in double precision)", and the options are to put opposite forces on different load regions or to give the
  case a larger force (no word about fixed regions, no "100 percent": no force lands on a fixed dof). `fixed` is `np.any(f)` with `not np.any(f[free])`: "every force of the case lands on fixed dofs, so the
  solver drops all of it and no free dof gets a load; the `lost_force` fact says 100 percent", and the first option is to move the load region off the fixed regions (for a case with a moment the fact is
  `lost_moment_percent`). `fixed_net` is the same, but the `lost_force` fact of the case does not say 100 percent: a squeeze on fixed nodes (two opposite forces) has a net force of 0, so the fact says 0 percent,
  and the words say "the forces cancel in the net sum that the `lost_force` fact measures, so that fact does not say 100 percent" (same first option). The test for `fixed` reads what the fact prints (`100.0`), so
  a round-off of its sum cannot change it. Where the YAML has no such row, the case gets the `fact:` line (and a normal run). A YAML zero case is not reported twice: the loader answers for it, and a
  message that names both kinds gives each case its own words. `derived.load_cases[]` has `load_reaches_free_dofs` (boolean; `null` where there is no grid; `false` also for a case with a YAML
  zero) and `load_reach` (`free`, `nodal_zero`, `fixed` or `fixed_net`; `null` where there is no grid; a YAML zero case is `nodal_zero`) in `check_problem` and in `run.json`; `topopt check` reads `load_reach` for
  its facts. A case that loses only a part of its force keeps the `lost_force` fact and warning, gets no refusal and no fact (the key is `true`): the
  rule is "no free dof gets any load", never a share.
  (2) **A compliance that is 0.0 or subnormal at run time.** A force of `[0, 0, 1e-300]` reaches a free dof, but `c = f.u` underflows to `0.0`, and a force of `1e-160` N gives `2.57e-322`, a subnormal value: it is below
  `np.finfo(float).tiny` (`2.2e-308`, the smallest normal double: the IEEE 754 bound of a subnormal value, not a tuned number). A subnormal compliance has lost its precision: the log form divides the slope by it
  (`formulation.py`, `d / r.value`) and the eigen solve of the buckling row breaks on it (ARPACK error -9). `optimize.run` asks `loads.zero_compliance_refusal` at every pass, before the rows are evaluated, for each case that has a
  load by (1) and a compliance with `abs(c) < np.finfo(float).tiny`; it gives the refusal of the rule above, with the words "the compliance of the case is 0.0 or subnormal in double precision, so its load does no measurable
  work on the part" and the first option "give the case a larger force, moment or pressure". The run stops at the first pass where that holds, with exit 1 (`UserError`): at pass 0 in most measured cases, but a force of `1e-153` N has a
  normal compliance at pass 0 (`2.4e-308`) and a subnormal one at pass 2, when the design has become stiffer. `status.json` says `error` with the text, the job record `failed` with exit code 1, and `run_status` shows both. A case
  with such a compliance and no row that needs a load runs as before (no fact, no refusal). A force whose compliance is a normal double runs as before (`1e-150` N to `3e-153` N in the scan below).
  Measured, one scan for each row (cantilever of the tests, voxel 2 mm, 3 passes, CPU, one thread; the force `[0, 0, x]` N of the case `tiny` next to a normal case; exit code before the F4-37 review fix (`cb65ea0`), then after).
  Scan 1: `compliance_limit` on `tiny`, 26 forces from `1e-150` to `1e-162` N: before, 0 down to `9e-161` N, then **2** ("MMA got a value or gradient that is not finite") for `8e-161` (pass 2), `5e-161` and `3e-161` N (pass 0), and 1 below;
  after, 0 down to `3e-153` N, 1 for every force from `1e-153` N down (`1e-153` N at pass 2, the others at pass 0). Scan 2: the buckling row, the same 26 forces: before, 0 down to `2e-160` N, then **2** ("ARPACK error -9") for `1e-160`, `9e-161`, `8e-161`
  (pass 1), `5e-161` and `3e-161` N (pass 0), and 1 below; after, the same cells as scan 1. Scan 3: `case_combine: max` and the buckling check, 8 forces each (`1e-150`, `1e-154`, `1e-155`, `1e-158`, `1e-160`, `8e-161`, `3e-161`, `1e-161` N):
  before, 0 down to `8e-161` N and 1 below (`3e-161` N at pass 2); after, 0 for `1e-150` N and 1 for the others (at pass 0). **No cell gives exit 2 after the fix**, so the two old windows (the log form from `3e-161` to `8e-161` N, found by the
  review, and the buckling row at `1e-160` N and `9e-161` N) are closed by the one rule, and no catch of `ArpackError` is needed. The forces from `1e-153` N to `9e-161` N ran before with a subnormal compliance at some pass and a met row; they are refused now.
  At the start of F4-37 (cantilever, 4 passes; exit code before F4-37, then after): (a) force `1e-300`: `compliance_limit` 2 (`the log form needs a value above 0, got 0.0`), `case_combine: max` 2
  (`the 'max' form needs terms above 0`), `buckling.min_factor` 2 (`ARPACK error -9: Starting vector is zero`), `buckling.check` 0 (an error record with `cases` empty), no case with a load under
  the compliance objective 0 (a part that does not depend on a load), no such row 0; after: 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0. (b) all force on fixed nodes: the same exit codes before (2, 2, 2, 0, 0, 0 with the
  same texts); after: `topopt check` and `topopt run` give 1 for the first five, and 0 (the fact, a normal run) for no such row and for the mass objective with a `stress_limit`.
  The part builder prints the refusal as an `ERROR:` line. A run folder of a YAML with a lost case and `buckling.check` (before F4-37 it ended with exit 0 and an error record) is refused by every
  reader that builds the problem: `topopt run --resume` and `topopt buckling <run folder>` (measured: exit 1); the option is the one of "The resume of an old run" above.
  A refusal of `build_problem` for a fresh `topopt run` leaves an earlier run in the same folder as it is, as every other check of the input does (F4-43: the checks come before `out.clean()` when the folder holds an earlier run, section 24.1;
  before F4-43 the refusal came after `out.clean()` and removed the earlier run); the U21 refusal of the loader comes first and leaves the folder as it is. `--resume` and `--continue-from` build the problem before they touch the folder and leave it as it is. The reply of the MCP tool `run_topopt` has no
  `derived_error` for the reasons of this item: it reads the YAML without a grid (`derived_numbers(cfg)`), so `load_reaches_free_dofs` and `load_reach` are `null` in its `derived`, the process starts and stops with exit 1, and `run_status` has the
  state `error` and the text (the loader's refusal of U21 reaches the reply as `derived_error`). `history.jsonl` of `examples/hook/hook_short.yaml` (one thread, pardiso) is equal before and after (time keys apart), and so is
  `result/final.stl`; `tests/data/root_guard_history_f367b2d.json` holds the history of one small case that `f367b2d` (before F4-37) wrote, and a test compares this code with it.


#### A run that ends before the last beta stage (fact before the run, added with P7-4, F4-18)

`settings.beta_schedule` gives the pass at which each beta stage starts. The run makes the passes 0 to `settings.iterations`; a stop rule can only
end it earlier. The verdict test `last_beta_stage` (section 24.2) is met when the last pass is at or after the start of the last stage. A run with
`iterations` below that start cannot meet it: the design never sees the last beta, and it can stay grey (measured below). This happens when `iterations`
is lowered and the schedule stays as it was (the default schedule `[[0, 1], [30, 2], [50, 4], [65, 8]]` fits 80 passes). Before P7-4 only the verdict at
the end of the run said so.

`verdict.beta_stage_fact(iterations, schedule)` gives one `fact:` line before the run, or `[]`. The fact is due when `iterations` is below the start of
the last stage. At `iterations` equal to the start pass the verdict says "reached", so there is no fact. Both use one function,
`verdict.reaches_last_beta_stage(last_pass, schedule)`. A schedule with one stage never gets the fact. The line gives, in this order (about 1100
characters for the hook on 20 passes, so that the options come before the price):

- the fact: the pass count, the schedule, the pass and beta where the last stage starts, the pass and beta where the run ends and the pass where
  that stage starts, and that the verdict will say that the schedule has not reached its last stage;
- the options, as `options:`. First: `settings.iterations` at the start pass or more. At the start pass the last pass is the first pass at the last
  beta: it measures and does not change the design, and each pass above it is one change of the design at the last beta. Second: the schedule scaled to
  the passes, as YAML (`beta_schedule: [[0, 1], [8, 2], ...]`) that you can paste, with the factor and the span;
- the price that was measured on the hook example (`examples/hook/hook_short.yaml`, 2 mm voxels, one part, one run each, origin/main 4f6d39d): the
  stiffness of `hang` / `pull_off` against the 40-pass run with its own schedule (grayness 0.025). 20 passes with the schedule as it was (ends at beta 2):
  x0.791 / x0.834, grayness 0.142 (run IT20 of the P7 series E1). 20 passes with the schedule that the line offers for the hook,
  `[[0, 1], [8, 2], [12, 4], [16, 8]]`: x0.989 / x0.970, grayness 0.026 (run IT20o, made for P7-4).
  40 passes with the default schedule (ends at beta 2): x0.801 / x0.869, grayness 0.138 (run BSc of E1). These are facts about one part, not limits.
  The grayness was measured for runs that end at beta 2; the line says "can stay grey".

`verdict.scaled_beta_schedule(iterations, schedule)` makes the second option from the schedule of the user (the default schedule when the key is
absent): each start pass is multiplied by `iterations / span` and rounded half up to a whole pass; the betas stay. The span is the last start plus the length of
the stage before it, so the last stage is as long as that stage (the default schedule gives 65 + 15 = 80 passes, the length that it fits; the schedule of
`hook_short.yaml` gives 34 + 8 = 42, and it was written for 40). The line gives the span. **The last start is rounded down**, not half up: `last * iterations / span` is below
`iterations`, so the last start is at most `iterations - 1` and the design changes at least once at the last beta (a half-up rounding could put the last start on the
last pass, which only measures; the default schedule on 40 passes gives 32 and not 33). An earlier start is held at the last start, and stages that fall on one
pass become one stage: the later one stays, and the line says so, and names the beta that the run then starts at when the stage on pass 0 is replaced. A beta is
printed so that YAML reads the same number (`8`, `2.5`, `1.0e-05`). The result starts at pass 0, its starts increase (the loader takes it), and its last start is
at most `iterations - 1`: the verdict test is met. No other number enters, and nothing is refused. With `iterations` 1 the offer is the last beta from pass 0.

Where it shows (one function, two call sites, as for F4-5):

- `optimize.problem_facts(config)` appends the line. `topopt check` prints it, `topopt check --json` has it in `facts`, and `run.log` has it at the
  start of the run, before pass 0. A run that is resumed prints it again at the start of the resumed part, with the `settings.iterations` and the
  schedule of that part.
- `cli.check_data` (so `topopt check --json`, the MCP tool `check_problem` and `build_regions` `check`) has the same line in `warnings`. `topopt check` (the text) prints it once, from `problem_facts`.
- A continuation (`--continue-from`, section 24.3, and the resume of one) has K + `more_iterations` passes, and `settings.iterations` of the YAML is not used. `optimize.run` gives `resume.continued_from` (the `continued_from` record of run.json) to `problem_facts(config, continued_from)` and so to `beta_stage_fact(iterations, schedule, continued_from)`, and the line in `run.log` reads: `fact: the pass count of this run is 25 (20 + 5 more_iterations); settings.iterations of the YAML is not used. ...`. Its first option is `more_iterations {last - K} or more` (the same clause: pass {last} only measures), its second is a new run, not a continuation, with the schedule scaled to its passes (`topopt check` of the YAML with that settings.iterations gives the list: a changed `beta_schedule` is a changed input of a continuation, so the line has no YAML list). The numbers and the price are the same. Without the record (`topopt check`, `check_problem`, a run that is not a continuation) the text does not change.

Resume (not changed by P7-4): `settings.iterations` and `settings.beta_schedule` are inputs that decide the numbers (`checkpoint.diff_inputs`). A resume
of a run that did not finish with another value needs `--allow-changed-inputs`; a resume of a finished run with another `settings.iterations` is refused
(`checkpoint.plan_resume`). With the override the resumed part uses the new values from its first pass.

### Run folder (additive; a reader ignores keys it does not know)

`run.json`: `"objective"` (`weighted_compliance` or `worst_case_compliance`), `"objective_form"`
(`sum` or `max`), `"constraints"`: `[{"name": "volume", "limit": 0.25}, {"name": "compliance:pull_off", "limit": 5.0}]`.

`history.jsonl`, every line, two new keys:

```json
{"objective": {"name": "weighted_compliance", "form": "sum", "value": 1.23e2},
 "constraints": [{"name": "volume", "value": 0.2503, "limit": 0.25, "g": 0.0012, "violation": 0.0012},
                 {"name": "compliance:pull_off", "value": 4.1, "limit": 5.0, "g": -0.18, "violation": 0.0}]}
```

- `objective.value`: the physical value (the largest `w_i * c_i` for `max`). `compliance` keeps
  its meaning: the weighted sum.
- `constraints[].value`: the physical value (volume fraction, compliance in N*mm). `g` =
  `(value - limit) / scale` (scale = `limit` for the built-in rows). The row is met when `g <= 0`.
  `violation` = `max(g, 0)`. Order: volume first, then the cases in YAML order.
- The values of pass `it` belong to the design of snapshot `it` (the last pass only measures).
- `run.log`: at the end, one line for each constraint with the linear `g` above 0.005:
  `constraint not met: compliance:pull_off  value 6.2  limit 5  (+24.00% of the limit)`.
  When every unmet row is a compliance limit (so the volume row is met), one more line gives the
  cause and the options: `the other rows are met, so this limit does not fit at this volume;
  options: raise settings.volume_fraction, relax the limit, or use the mass objective (A2)`.
  This text is for the compliance objective. Under the mass objective (A2) the line is `the other rows are met, and this limit is not met at the end of the run; options: relax the limit`
  (there is no volume budget in a mass run), and with a perimeter row (section 26.3) it names that row as a possible cause.
  It is a fact. The exit code stays 0 and the post-process runs.
- `result/metrics.json`: `"constraints"` is the list of the last history line (`null` for a run
  from before A1).

## 14. Tet mesher (optional, added after version 1.6)

Package `topopt/tet/`. It is for scripts and for later steps (stress check, buckling). It has no CLI flag,
MCP tool or YAML key. User text: `docs/reference/print-step-tet.md`, section "Tet mesher". The state of the extra is also in the
`tet` field of the `environment` tool (`topopt/environment.py`).

**Rules.**

- gmsh is GPL-2.0-or-later. It is only in the extra `tet` of `pyproject.toml`
  (`gmsh==4.15.2`, marker: macOS, and Linux x86_64). It is never a main dependency, never in `requirements.lock`,
  and never vendored. The core does not import it.
- `import topopt`, `topopt.cli`, `topopt_mcp.server` and `topopt.tet` do not put `gmsh` into `sys.modules`
  (`tests/test_tet.py`). gmsh is imported in `topopt/tet/gmsh_probe.py` (`import_gmsh`) and inside the functions of
  `topopt/tet/mesher.py`, after the probe says `ok`.
- `mesh_stl` runs gmsh in a child Python by default (`isolate=True`, `topopt/tet/worker.py`): the calling process never
  loads libgmsh, and a crash of gmsh (a SIGSEGV in the Netgen optimizer was seen on the hook at 0.6 to 0.75 mm) kills only the child.
  The child gets the prepared surface and the settings as an .npz file and writes nodes and tets as an .npz file. The mesh is the same
  as in-process (same hash). Cost: about 0.1 s for the first probe and about 0.1 s for each attempt.
- The child starts with the soft limit RLIMIT_CORE at 0 (the hard limit does not change). `limit_core_dumps` in
  `topopt/tet/worker.py` sets it first in `main`, before gmsh is imported, on macOS and on Linux. On Linux it also calls
  `prctl(PR_SET_DUMPABLE, 0)` through ctypes, so the kernel starts no core-dump helper for the child (a `core_pattern` that
  pipes to systemd-coredump gets the soft limit as `%c` and stores no core when it is 0). A crashed child leaves no core file.
  If a call fails, the failure goes into the return value and the meshing runs. The parent process keeps its limits, and
  `isolate=False` does not use the worker. To get a core file of the child for a debug session, set `TOPOPT_TET_KEEP_CORE=1`
  in the environment of the parent and run `ulimit -c unlimited` in its shell: the child then keeps the limits and the flag of
  the parent (the flag 0 also stops a debugger without CAP_SYS_PTRACE from attaching to the child, and the variable allows it).
  `python -m topopt.tet.worker --limits` prints one JSON line with the core limits (`core_soft`, `core_hard`; -1 is
  unlimited), the dumpable flag and the result of each step, and does not mesh.
- gmsh is started with `readConfigFiles=False` (a `~/.gmshrc` cannot change a mesh) and `interruptible=False`
  (the interrupt handler works in the main thread only). In-process (`isolate=False`), one mesh at a time per process: `GMSH_LOCK` serializes
  the calls, because the state of gmsh and the capture of stdout are global to the process.
- Tests that call gmsh use the marker `needs_gmsh` (`tests/helpers.py`). It runs the probe in a child Python
  (`probe_subprocess`). They never use `pytest.importorskip("gmsh")` (it raises `OSError` when a system library is missing).

**Probe.** `topopt.tet.probe() -> TetProbe(state, version, detail, fix)`. It never raises. `state` is:

| state | meaning |
|---|---|
| `ok` | `import gmsh` works and the package finds libgmsh. `version` is the gmsh version string. |
| `missing` | gmsh is not installed. On a platform that the extra does not cover (for example Linux arm64), `detail` says so and `fix` lists other options (conda-forge gmsh, which is another OCC build so its meshes differ; a source build). |
| `load_failed` | gmsh is installed but does not load (`OSError`, another error, or libgmsh not found). On Linux `detail` lists ALL missing libraries (from `ldd`) and `fix` has the Debian package names; on Linux x86_64 it also gives the GUI-free (nox) build as an alternative. On macOS `fix` says to run `otool -L` (the arm64 wheel needs macOS 12 or newer). |

`TetProbe.line()` gives one line. `probe_subprocess()` gives the same result from a child Python.
`require_gmsh()` returns the module or raises `TetUnavailable`.

**API.** `mesh_stl(path, size=None, threads=1, optimize="Netgen", eps_factor=0.1, max_attempts=10, size_field=None, min_edge_mm=0.05, isolate=True, fallback_optimize=("Gmsh+Netgen", "Gmsh"), log=None) -> TetMesh`.

- Input: a closed, oriented, manifold STL in mm. Output: `TetMesh(nodes (n, 3) float64, tets (m, 4) int64, facts dict)`.
  Every tet has a positive signed volume (a tet of zero volume is a failed attempt, F4-27). `TetMesh.save(path)` writes an `.npz` file (suffix added; `nodes` float64, `tets` int64,
  `facts` as JSON text). `TetMesh.load(path)` reads it.
- `size` is the target edge length (mm). Default: 2.5 times the mean edge of the STL. For a `final.stl` of the `blur` method that is about
  1.15 to 1.25 voxels (the STL edges are about half a voxel). For the `sdf` method the mean edge is larger (section 19, "Snap to the region faces"):
  hook 1.94 mm (1.6 voxels), ladle 4.28 mm (1.3 voxels), bracket of `examples/interfaces` 2.16 mm (2.2 voxels) at `c080f62`. The pipeline rule is h <= d_min / 3 (d_min: thinnest member).
- `size_field(P) -> sizes` (optional) sets a local edge length of the surface. It is combined with the retry patches by `np.minimum`.
- `min_edge_mm` is an absolute limit (not scaled with `size`).
- `optimize` is None, `"Netgen"` (default), `"Relocate3D"`, `"Gmsh"` (the default optimizer of gmsh during meshing) or steps joined by `+`.
  If the child dies on a signal, each setting of `fallback_optimize` is tried on the same surface, in order.
- `threads` default is 1. At 1 thread two runs on one machine with one gmsh build give the same mesh
  (equal `facts["sha256"]`). At more threads they can differ (measured on large meshes). There is no cap.
- `facts` keys: `tets`, `nodes`, `quality_min`, `quality_mean`, `quality_p01`, `below_0p1`, `below_0p05`,
  `volume_fraction_below_0p05` (mean-ratio quality, 1 is a regular tet; 0.05 is the cut of the P2 report),
  `volume_mm3`, `volume_stl_mm3`, `volume_ratio` (tets over the prepared surface; 1 within 1e-12; the acceptance limit is 1e-3),
  `volume_ratio_stl` (tets over the input STL), `deviation_from_input_mm` (`mean_mm`, `p99_mm`, `max_mm`, `samples`),
  `stl_sha256`, `inverted_fixed`, `threads`, `repeatable_expected` (True at 1 thread; a prediction), `sha256`, `size`, `size_given`,
  `size_field_given`, `algorithm`, `attempts`, `failed_attempts` (a list: `attempt`, `kind` (`crossing`, `zero_volume`
  or `other`; F4-27), `points`, `error`), `optimize`, `optimize_used`, `crashes` (list of `attempt`,
  `signal`, `returncode`, `size`, `optimize`, `algorithms`, `threads`), `isolated`, `gmsh_version`, `seconds`, `seconds_surface`,
  `seconds_gmsh`, `seconds_isolation`, `surface_faces`, `surface_weld_retry` (only when the weld retry below ran: the step
  of `PreparedSurface.steps` that has `step: weld_short_edges`), and `surface_clean_retry` (only when the clean retry below ran: the
  step that has `step: clean_short_edges`), and `surface_shell_retry` (only when the shell retry below ran).
- Errors (all subclasses of `UserError`, one line of text): `TetUnavailable` (the text has the probe state and the fix),
  `SurfaceRejected` (the STL is not a closed manifold; its subclass `PreparedSurfaceRejected` is a refusal of the prepared surface, which depends on the mesh size), `MeshingFailed` (gmsh failed on all attempts), `MeshingCrashed`
  (a `MeshingFailed`: the child died on a signal with every optimize setting; `crashes` lists them, the text has the options), and `UserError` for a bad
  argument or a file that is not an STL.
- Weld retry (added with C3c). `prepare_surface` refuses a prepared surface that has an edge under `min_edge_mm`
  (`MIN_EDGE_REJECT_MM`, 0.05 mm). An edge collapse cannot remove every such edge: marching cubes on a flat face that lies on the
  node lattice (the output of `apply_marks`, CONTRACTS 29.1) makes clusters of two to five vertices 1e-5 to 3e-5 mm apart, and a
  hair-thin tube among them fails the link condition of the collapse. After that one refusal, and only after it, `prepare_surface`
  welds the INPUT surface (`weld_short_edges`) and prepares the welded surface again. The weld acts on every edge of the input that is
  under `min_edge_mm`, not only on the edges that the collapse could not remove: the vertices that such edges join (a chain of
  any length) become one vertex at their mean, a face with two equal vertices goes, and so does a face that occurs twice on the same
  three vertices; this repeats while an edge is under the limit. The weld has the radius `min_edge_mm`: no new number. It is refused, and
  the first refusal stays, when:
  - a vertex of the input that is welded ends more than `min_edge_mm` from where it was (a welded vertex whose faces all go counts at
    the place where its group was welded). The radius bounds the move of the vertices that are welded. It is not a bound on the change
    of the surface: a vertex that is on no short edge is a group of one and does not move, also when all its faces go. The weld then
    removes it, as the apex of a spike whose base edges are under the limit, and the surface changes there by the height of the spike
    (measured: 0.178 mm on the plain-boolean `bowl_smooth` of `tests/test_apply_marks_seam.py` at 1.2 mm, where the largest move
    was 0.042 mm). The facts give the volume change and the vertices dropped. A fine ring of a through-hole of
    0.6 mm radius is a chain of short edges, and its weld moves the ring by 0.3 mm and fills the hole: it is refused. The same holds for
    a pin of 0.6 mm (0.3 mm), a 3 mm through-hole (1.5 mm) and a dome of 1 mm radius (1.11 mm);
  - the welded surface is not a closed manifold (the text names the place of the first open edge, non-manifold edge or pinch vertex);
  - the number of bodies changes, the welded surface has more fold edges than the input, or its volume is not positive (the clean retry
    below calls the weld with `check_folds=False`: it judges the fold edges itself, after the fold repair).
  The weld does not refuse a change of topology. A hair handle that goes is a change of the genus of its body, and that is the purpose
  of the weld (the candidates c001 and c002 of 29.3 limit 5 go from genus 2 to genus 0). Only a feature that is smaller than the radius
  can go this way: a hole is filled only when its ring is within 0.05 mm of its centre.
  Measured on the posts case of 29.3 limit 5 (16 candidates): the 4 candidates that the retry rescues move at most 0.0335, 0.0376,
  0.0349 and 0.0427 mm. The largest, 0.0427 mm at the shift (0.11, 0.17, 0.23) mark 1, is 85 % of the radius (a margin of 0.0073 mm).
  The weld of the candidate with the largest move (0.0475 mm, the shift (0.07, 0, 0.11) mark 2) is refused for its pinch vertex. Another
  part can meet the bound; the refusal then has the first text and the move.
  If the weld is not refused, the usual steps run on the welded surface and the weld is the first entry of `steps`: `step`, `limit_mm`,
  `passes`, `short_edges_in_input`, `edges_welded`, `vertices_before`, `vertices_after`, `vertices_merged` (input vertices that joined
  another vertex), `vertices_dropped` (input vertices with no face left), `faces_before`, `faces_after`, `bodies_before`, `bodies_after`,
  `max_vertex_move_mm`, `euler_before`, `euler_after`, `genus_before`, `genus_after` (the last four are lists with one value for each
  body of the input, in the same order), `volume_before_mm3`, `volume_after_mm3`, `volume_change_mm3` and `refused_first`.
  `mesh_stl` copies it into `facts["surface_weld_retry"]` and `topopt verify` into `verify.json` `mesh.surface_weld_retry`, prints one
  line that starts with `surface:` in its summary (the facts above in short), and the ratchet row has the same line in `facts.notes`
  (a note: no rule reads it). An input that passes at the first try never reaches the retry: its prepared surface, its facts and the
  verify text are the same as before (no `surface_weld_retry` key, no `surface:` line). If the weld cannot give a surface to prepare,
  the clean retry below runs. If that cannot help either, `SurfaceRejected` keeps the first refusal and adds the reason of the weld:
  "<first refusal>; the weld retry was tried and did not help: <reason>" (and the reason of the clean retry, see below).
  The volume change of the weld is a fact in the step (about 0.003 mm3 of 1180 on the posts case), and there is no volume or thickness
  limit for it. Known limit: when two sheets of the part touch each other at a hair cluster, the weld
  leaves a pinch vertex or a non-manifold edge and the refusal stays. The cause is in `apply_marks` (29.3 limit 6). On the 16
  candidates of the posts case at eight positions of the whole case, 2 stay refused for this reason and 14 are prepared (4 of them only
  through the retry; 6 were refused before). The clean retry below was not measured on the 2 that stay refused.
- Clean retry (F1-5). The weld of the input does not help when the preparation itself makes the short edges. The collapse of
  `prepare_surface` removes the edges under `min_edge_mm` first. The steps after it (the flips, the tangential smoothing, the fold
  repair) move vertices and can make new edges under the limit. Measured on a public part: a block with a bore (`interfaces.apply_step`)
  and a keep-out STL with a socket of 256 segments and a radius 1e-5 mm over the bore; the bore has 92 segments; `size` 1.0 mm. The
  booleans leave 436 edges under 0.05 mm (4 under 3e-5 mm, 8 from 1e-4 to 1e-3 mm, 424 from 1e-3 to 5e-2 mm): the two polygons of one wall
  cross each other every few hundredths of a millimetre. The collapse leaves 1 edge. The smoothing makes 22 (the shortest is 0.0227 mm).
  The weld of the input then joins hundreds of vertices in chains, and it is refused ("the welded surface has more fold edges (2) than
  the input (0)"). So the cause is the smoothing, and the weld of the input cannot help.
  After the weld retry is refused, and only after it, `prepare_surface` cleans the surface that the first try refused
  (`clean_short_edges`). It does not prepare again from the start. (1) The first phase of `collapse_decimate` runs again (the link
  condition and the normal check; a vertex moves onto its neighbour, so there is no new position). Its sliver phase can turn a face over,
  and that makes fold edges. When the collapsed surface has more fold edges than the refused surface and the input have (the lower
  number), the fold repair of the first try (`repair_folds`, see "Fold repair" below) runs on it (F4-27; before, the retry was refused at
  this point). (2) The edges that stay are welded with the weld of `weld_short_edges` and its rules: the radius `min_edge_mm` for the
  vertices that are welded, a closed manifold, the same number of bodies, a positive volume. The weld has no fold rule here
  (`check_folds=False`). When the welded surface has more fold edges than the surface before the weld, the fold repair runs on it
  (F4-27). One more rule: no face that stays may turn over. Its normal must not have a negative dot product with its normal before
  the weld (a sign test). The test runs on the result, after the fold repair. A face that the repair removes is not in the result, so
  it is not tested. The reason names the stage that turned the face: "the weld of them turns N faces over", or "the fold repair after
  the weld turns N faces over" (the first one is the weld, the second is a collapse of the repair; a face counts for the weld when the
  weld already turned it). A turned face is not always a sliver of no area. For f7c at 0.977 mm, attempt 2, the repair turned a face
  of 0.011 mm2 with the cosine -0.91 between its normals: one vertex moved 0.19 mm. The weld moves a vertex by 0.05 mm at most.
  The weld of the refused surface has few edges to join, so it makes no long chain. On the part above the collapse
  removes all 22 edges. On other parts of the same kind 1 to 12 edges stay, and the largest move of the weld was 0.025 mm. The limit is
  `min_edge_mm` and the fold rule is the one of the first try: there is no new number. The result must be a closed manifold with no more
  fold edges than the refused surface and the input have (the lower number), and with no edge under the limit. Else the refusal stays,
  and its reason gives the fold edges that the collapse or the weld made and the fold edges that the repair leaves ("the collapsed
  surface has more fold edges (3) than the refused surface has (0), and the fold repair leaves 3"), or the edge that the repair left
  under the limit.
  The radius bounds the move of the vertices that are welded. A vertex whose faces all go (the apex of a spike whose base edges are
  under the limit) is removed, and its distance to the cleaned surface is not bounded by the radius. The step gives the change as facts
  (below). Measured on the plain-boolean `bowl_smooth` of `tests/test_apply_marks_seam.py` at 1.2 mm: the weld moved a vertex by
  0.0419 mm, and the surface changed by 0.178 mm (two spike apexes were removed).
  The step is the last entry of `steps`: `step` (`clean_short_edges`), `limit_mm`, `short_edges_before`, `short_edges_after_collapse`,
  `collapse_rounds`, `edges_welded`, `passes`, `vertices_merged`, `vertices_dropped`, `max_vertex_move_mm` (the weld of the edges that
  stay; 0 when none stayed), `vertices_before`, `vertices_after`, `faces_before`, `faces_after`, `volume_before_mm3`, `volume_after_mm3`,
  `volume_change_mm3`, `fold_repairs` (F4-27; a list, empty when no repair ran: for each repair `stage` (`collapse` or `weld`),
  `fold_edges_made` (the fold edges of the surface before the repair, whoever made them), `fold_edges_left`, `vertices_removed` and
  `faces_turned` (the faces that stay and that the repair turned over; a fact, and a rule only in the stage `weld`, see above)),
  `removed_vertices` (the vertices of the refused surface that have no vertex of the cleaned surface at the same
  place: collapsed, welded or dropped), `removed_vertex_distance_max_mm` (the largest distance from one of them to the cleaned surface;
  exact, all of them, no sample), `deviation_from_refused_mm` (`samples`, `mean_mm`, `p99_mm`, `max_mm`: the distance from a sample of at most
  8,000 vertices of the refused surface to the cleaned one), `refused_first` and `weld_refused`. `mesh_stl` copies it into
  `facts["surface_clean_retry"]`.
  `topopt verify` puts it in `verify.json` `mesh.surface_clean_retry` and prints one line that starts with `surface:` in its summary
  (the edges cleaned, collapsed and welded, the faces and the vertices removed, the fold edges that the fold repair removed and the
  faces that it turned over, the largest distance of a removed vertex, the volume change; the weld part is left out when no edge was
  welded, the fold part when no repair ran). The
  ratchet row has the same line in `facts.notes` (a note: no rule reads it). An input that passes at the first try, or by the weld
  retry, never reaches the clean retry: its prepared surface, its facts and its verify text are the same as before. If the clean retry
  cannot help, `SurfaceRejected` keeps the first refusal and the reason of the weld, and adds the reason of the clean retry: "<first
  refusal>; the weld retry was tried and did not help: <reason>; the clean retry of the prepared surface did not help: <reason>".
  Known limit: a hair-thin tube among the edges that stay (the link condition fails, and the weld joins
  two sheets or changes the number of bodies) is still refused, as before. The `final.stl` of an `sdf` run of `examples/hook/hook.yaml`,
  meshed at 3.0 mm, which the weld retry left refused ("an edge of 0.0399 mm"), is prepared by the clean retry: it collapses that one
  edge (volume change -0.0031 mm3 of 19985, largest distance to the refused surface 0.0048 mm).
  A cleaned surface can still fail in gmsh. The plain-boolean `bowl_smooth` does at 1.2 mm: its surface has a near-fold (two faces
  with the cosine -0.9944 between their normals) that the fold rule (cosine under -0.999) and the search for crossings (faces that share
  a vertex are not tested) do not see; the refused surface of the first try has it too. The error of `mesh_stl` then names the retry
  and the first refusal (see the crossing retry below).
- Fold repair (F4-27). A fold edge is an edge of two faces whose normals are opposite (cosine under -0.999). The first try of
  `prepare_surface` runs `repair_folds` after its collapse. The clean retry above runs it after its own collapse and after its weld.
  `repair_folds` collapses edges of the fold faces and the edges around them. It keeps a collapse only when the surface stays a closed
  oriented manifold and the number of fold edges goes down. A collapse moves a vertex, so it can turn a face over. Neither the repair
  nor the first try tests this. In the clean retry only the stage `weld` refuses a turned face (see above). The count is the fact
  `faces_turned` of each repair. Measured: the repair after the collapse of the clean retry turns 3 faces of the f6a surface of
  attempt 1 (cosines -0.17, -0.15 and -1.00), and f6a meshes. So a refusal for these faces would refuse f6a.
  Since F4-27 the repair judges one collapse on the faces around the two vertices (`_collapse_is_good_local`). The test has three
  parts: no directed edge twice, the reverse of each directed edge at the vertices of the star, and no bow-tie vertex there. The fold
  edges must be fewer in the patch. Before, the judge took the whole surface (`_collapse_is_good_global`: a closed-manifold test and a
  count of the fold edges, about 60 ms for 28,000 faces). A surface that is not a closed oriented manifold at the start still gets
  the judge of the whole surface. There is no new number.
  The two judges give the same answer. The implementer compared them on 10,238 candidates (stage surfaces of f7c, f0_root, f6a and a
  sphere, 3,313 accepted), and the repaired surface of f6a is equal. The review compared them on 56,273 candidates: no difference.
  Measured on one Linux x86_64 host (revision `f86ac04` against this change; `prepare_surface` of the f6a `final.stl`, 0.973 mm): the
  first try has 315 fold edges, needs 143 fixes and leaves 3 fold edges. It took 959 s with the whole-surface judge and 96 s with the
  local judge. That time, and not gmsh, was the "hang" of `topopt verify` on f6a (1154 s before the refusal). The cost grew with the
  fold pairs that cannot be fixed: they are tried again before each new fix.
- Phone stands of the F-series (F4-27; one host; revision `f86ac04` against this change; `topopt verify --no-buckling --no-sensitivity
  --solver pardiso`, CPU). The `final.stl` of the `sdf` mesher has about 5 % of its edges under 0.05 mm (f7c 19,681 of 387,900 edges;
  f0_root 18,480; f6a 19,346). 98 % of them are within 0.02 mm of an exact face of a `fixed`, `load` or `keep_out` region (f7c: 81 % at
  the `load` slab). This is the seam where the smooth surface (2 to 20 um off the face) meets the exact union or cut. The first try
  removes most of these edges. The few that stay (12 for f7c) sit on the region faces, where the surface has sheets some um apart.
  Result: f6a (0.973 mm) is meshed and checked (exit 0, 310 s, 50,803 tets, 290,892 dofs; before: exit 2 after 1154 s). The clean retry
  cleaned 25 edges (19 collapsed, 6 welded). The fold repair removed 9 fold edges. The volume change is -0.0023 mm3 of 8508.9. The
  largest distance of a removed vertex is 0.0049 mm.
  f7c (0.977 mm) and f0_root (0.927 mm) are still refused (exit 2, 2 to 3 minutes). Before this change the preparation of attempt 1 was
  refused. Now attempt 1 gives a surface, and gmsh stops on it: the surface crosses itself at 11 places (f7c) and at 33 places
  (f0_root), at the seam. The preparation of attempt 2 (refined around the crossings) is then refused by the clean retry. For f7c the
  fold repair after the weld turns a face over (see above). For f0_root the weld makes a non-manifold edge at a corner of the seam. The
  error says so (see the crossing retry). The cause of the refusals is the seam that `smooth_sdf.make_mesh_sdf` writes: sheets 1 to
  20 um apart, micro-steps, fold edges and self-crossings in the float32 STL. A change there is not part of F4-27. F4-27b makes it: the
  writer moves the vertices that lie just outside a region face into the region before the exact boolean (section 19, "Snap to the region
  faces"; the numbers there are of public parts).
- Crossing retry (P4, F2-6). gmsh stops on a surface where an edge goes through a face ("PLC Error: A segment and a facet
  intersect"). It names ONE place for each call.
  After a failure that is not a crash, `mesh_stl` finds all such places of the prepared surface at once.
  The finder is `find_crossings` in `topopt/tet/intersect.py`. It finds pairs of faces that share no vertex and where an edge of one
  goes through the other. A touch is not a crossing. It does not find folds, or faces that overlap in one plane.
  It needs about 10 s for 600,000 faces. The next attempt refines around every place, not only the one that gmsh named.
  The retries end at once, with a `MeshingFailed` that has the places, in two cases.
  - (1) The STL itself crosses itself near a place. The preparation keeps the shape of the STL, so no retry helps.
    The text says to repair the STL, or to try another mesh size.
  - (2) An attempt does not have fewer crossings than the best earlier attempt that had any.
    Also, all its crossings are within the mesh size of a place that an earlier attempt refined.
    The same number at other places is a crossing that the refinement moved, so the retries go on (P4 review, L2).
    The text gives the counts of all attempts. It says that the STL itself does or does not cross itself. It gives the places.
    It says to try a mesh size nearer to the mean edge of the STL, because the surface preparation then collapses fewer edges.
    It names the options (`topopt verify --mesh-size`, MCP `mesh_size_mm`).
  The error of the attempt limit (`gmsh failed on every surface attempt (N)`) gives the crossings found in each attempt.
  - (3) The prepared surface of an attempt is equal to the prepared surface of the attempt before (the same `V` and `F`). The
    refinement around the places did not change the surface, so the next attempt would repeat this one. The stop has the reason
    `no_progress` and the fact `same_surface_as_attempt`. The surface may have no crossing that the search finds: gmsh can fail on a
    defect that the search does not test (faces that share a vertex), as on a near-fold. The text then says so and gives the places that
    gmsh named. No number is used (F1-5 review, MJ1: the plain-boolean `bowl_smooth` at 1.2 mm made 10 attempts, and the surfaces of
    the attempts 2 to 10 were equal, 14.7 s; now it stops at attempt 3, 5.1 s, on the Linux host of the review).
  When the prepared surface of the failed attempt came from the weld retry or the clean retry (section 14), every `MeshingFailed` of
  `mesh_stl` has one more sentence: "The surface that gmsh got is the prepared surface that was refused (<first refusal>), with its N
  edges under 0.05 mm cleaned (clean retry)", or the same for the input surface that was welded (weld retry). `crossings["surface_retry"]`
  has the step. `topopt verify` and `errors.verify` of the ratchet row keep the sentence, because they keep the text.
  A tet of no volume, or that the stress check cannot use, is a failed attempt too (F4-27). gmsh can give such a tet: the determinant of
  its 3 x 3 matrix of edge vectors or of its 4 x 4 matrix `[1 x y z]` is exactly 0, as for four nodes in one plane. The 4 x 4 matrix is
  the one that `verify.p2.tet_geometry` inverts, and `numpy.linalg.inv` raises "Singular matrix" for the same tets. The two matrices
  are not the same test in floating point: of 20,000 random tets in a tilted plane, `inv` refuses 5,230. The 3 x 3
  determinant is exactly 0 for 74 of them (it misses 5,156), and it is exactly 0 for 37 more tets that `inv` inverts (review MN1). A tet is listed when one of the two is exactly 0. With the
  4 x 4 matrix alone, f6a at 0.973 mm (`Gmsh+Netgen`, as `topopt verify` uses) lost one of its three listed tets at attempt 2, the
  refinement of the next attempts changed, and the part was refused at attempt 4. `mesh_stl` finds these
  tets. It fails the attempt with "gmsh made N tet(s) of zero volume, the first at (x, y, z) mm". The next attempt refines at the
  centres of these tets. The centres are places to refine and not crossings of the STL, so they do not stop the retries as a crossing of
  the input. f6a at 0.973 mm: attempt 2 gives one such tet at (71.99, 14.994, 0.269), and attempt 3 meshes (50,803 tets). The tet comes
  from a face of exactly zero area in the prepared surface (three vertices on one line of the plane y = 15 at z = 0.1244 to 0.1253). A
  check for such a face before gmsh would name the cause. It is not done here.
  When the surface preparation of attempt 2 or later is refused (`SurfaceRejected`), the text starts with what happened before: "gmsh
  failed on the prepared surface of attempt K (it crosses itself at N place(s)), and the surface preparation for attempt K+1 (local
  refinement at M point(s)) was refused: <the refusal>". After a tet of zero volume it starts "gmsh made N tet(s) of zero volume on the
  prepared surface of attempt K". The exception has the `crossings` facts of the attempts before, so `topopt verify` names the regions
  near the crossings. A refusal in attempt 1 is not changed. The log line of an attempt with such a tet is the error text, not
  "intersection point(s) reported".
  The old behaviour was `max_attempts` attempts, each with the full surface preparation. `max_attempts` is unchanged.
  Measured on the case-2 `final.stl` (576,000 faces, 4.5 mm): one attempt took 2.7 minutes on the user's machine.
  It took 3.8 to 4.4 minutes here. 10 attempts took 27 minutes, and the text named one point.
  The STL has no crossing. The prepared surface has 11 crossings.
  A collapse of the decimation puts a large triangle through a small one at an angle of 11 to 27 degrees.
  The second attempt has 1 and the third has 1. The retries now stop after 12 minutes.
  The search is a help. If it cannot run (for example `MemoryError`), the retry refines at the place that gmsh named, as before.
  The attempt has the count `null`. The log, the error text and `search_failed` (`attempt`, `surface`, `error`) have a note.
  The grid cell is `max(3 x median edge, (box volume / faces) ** (1/3))`.
  So the grid has about as many cells as the surface has faces, also in a large box around small faces.
  The crossings do not depend on the cell size.
  `MeshingFailed.crossings` has `prepared` (`count`, `points`, `attempts`: the count of each attempt), `input` (`count`, `points`),
  `stopped` (`input_crosses_itself` or `no_progress`), `same_surface_as_attempt` (with `no_progress`, when the surface of the attempt
  before was equal), `surface_retry` (the step of the weld retry or the clean retry that made the surface, when one did) and `search_failed`.
  `topopt verify` adds to its error the two YAML regions that are nearest to each of the first ten places.
  It uses the places of the STL if the stop is `input_crosses_itself`, else the places of the prepared surface.
  It gives the distance to the region surface, or "inside", so the reader sees which bodies meet there.
  That text is a fact to help and never an error.
- Shell retry (F4-45). gmsh gets the prepared surface as one volume. A surface with more than one closed shell (a set of faces that
  share vertices) can fail in two ways. HXT stops on a second shell ("duplicate volume"), and the Delaunay algorithm (algorithm 1)
  meshes the solid of the outer shell only. The check of `VOLUME_TOLERANCE` then compares the tets with the volume of the surface,
  which is the sum of the signed volumes of the shells. For a shell that lies in the material of another shell (a nested shell, normals
  out) that sum counts the material twice, so the mesh is refused by the volume of the nested shell. Measured: `result/nominal.stl` of
  a bracket run (mass objective, voxel 0.7 mm) has a sheet of 14.74 mm3 (1.82e-3 of the STL volume, 0.2 mm thick on average, 0.5 mm from
  any face of the main shell) inside the material of the main shell. The prepared surface at 0.973 mm has 12.54 mm3 in the sheet, the
  tet volume of algorithm 1 is the volume of the main shell to 1e-15, and the refusal was -1.56e-03 (the sheet over the prepared volume).
  After every algorithm failed, and only when gmsh named no crossing (`MeshingFailed.points` is empty), `mesh_surface` calls
  `shell_relations`: for each shell it takes the winding number of all the other shells at one vertex of the shell, rounded to the
  nearest whole number (no limit). Normals out and 0: `outer`. Normals out and 1 or more: `nested`. Normals in and 1: `cavity`. Any
  other value: `other` (shells that cross each other; gmsh names such crossings, so the shells are not looked at). If there are
  nested shells, `mesh_surface` leaves them out (they add no boundary to the solid under the rule that a point is inside when the
  winding number is not 0) and runs the same algorithms with the same check on the rest. A surface that one try meshes is never
  changed: its mesh, its hash and its facts are the same as before (the retry runs only after the failure). `mesh_stl` copies the
  facts into `facts["surface_shell_retry"]`: `step` (`drop_nested_shells`), `shells_in_surface`, `volume_before_mm3` and
  `volume_after_mm3` (the volume of the prepared surface), `left_out` (a list: `shell`, `volume_mm3`, `faces_count`, `bbox_min_mm`,
  `bbox_max_mm`) and `whole_surface_errors` (the text of each failed algorithm on the whole surface). `volume_ratio_stl` is then the
  volume of the mesh over the STL volume, and the STL volume counts the nested shell twice. A nested shell that was meant as a thin
  void in the part is not a void in this mesh; the verify line says so.
  When the retry cannot help, the error of `mesh_stl` names the shells: "the surface has N closed shells (volumes ... mm3): shell k
  (V mm3, x .. to .., y .. to .., z .. to .. mm) lies in the material of another shell ... / is a cavity (an enclosed void) ...
  Options: ...". A cavity is not meshed: gmsh fills the void of the one volume it gets (a cube of 1000 mm3 with a cavity of 64 mm3 gets a
  mesh of 1000 mm3, +6.8e-02 over the surface), so a cavity always ends here, and the text gives the option to fill the void in
  the STL. Two bodies that are apart (`outer` and `outer`) are meshed by algorithm 1 as before; HXT stops on them. Known limit (no
  change in F4-45): a nested shell whose volume is under `VOLUME_TOLERANCE` of the volume passes the check on algorithm 1, so the
  retry does not run. HXT is not used, and the mesh is the solid of the outer shell with the faces of the nested shell inside it. The
  `final.stl` of a hook run (`hook_R_v12`, voxel 1.2 mm) has such a shell (1.21 mm3 of 26,373): HXT stops, algorithm 1 gives
  `volume_ratio` -7.8e-06 at 2.0 mm, and the mesh has no `surface_shell_retry` fact.
- Origin: ported from `pipeline/lib/p2_surface.py` (`prepare_surface`) and `pipeline/lib/p2_mesh.py` of an earlier pipeline of the same author (d43bcf3).
  The vtk method of `prepare_surface` is not ported.

## 15. Render (added with V1)

`topopt/render.py` draws STL meshes as PNG images, so an agent or a person can look at a part.
It uses numpy, numba, trimesh, manifold3d (for `section`) and Pillow. It needs no display, no
OpenGL and no VTK. The CLI and the tool check the input with `topopt/render_input.py` (standard library only)
before they import `topopt.render`, so a wrong input gives one line at once and `import topopt.cli` stays light.
It is an orthographic z-buffer with flat shading and crease and silhouette lines.

- Library: `render(sources, *, roles=None, views=None, section=None, size=None, out_dir=None, regions=None, max_triangles=None, loads=None) -> dict`.
  `sources` is a run folder, or a problem YAML (below), or an STL path, or a list of STL paths. A list item can be `(path, role)`.
  A wrong input raises `UserError`.
- CLI: `topopt render <stl...|run_dir|problem.yaml> [--role ROLE[,ROLE...] ...] [--views LIST] [--section SECTION] [--size WxH] [--out DIR] [--regions ghost|solid|off] [--max-triangles N] [--loads|--no-loads]`.
  It prints the facts as JSON and exits 0. A wrong input prints `error: ...` and exits 1.
  `--role` is given once for all files or once for each file. It takes a comma list (`--role design,fixed,load`) or repeated flags
  (`--role design --role fixed`), and the two forms can be mixed. A role item of the library and of the MCP tool can be a comma list too.
- MCP tool: `render_part(run_dir=None, stl_paths=None, roles=None, views=None, section=None, size=None, out_dir=None, regions=None, max_triangles=None, inline=True, yaml_path=None, loads=None)`.
  The answer is one text content (the facts as compact JSON) and, with `inline` true, one image content (`image/png`, the montage).
  A wrong input gives the text `{"ok": false, "error": ...}` only. With neither `run_dir` nor `stl_paths`, the last run is used
  (`no run yet: give run_dir or stl_paths` if there is none). Relative paths start at the work folder.

**Input.** A run folder renders `result/final.stl` as role `part`, and the region STLs that `run.json` names
in `regions` (`design`, `fixed`, `keep_out`, `load`). A region file is `<folder of the YAML of the run> / name` (the YAML is `run.json` `yaml_path`; a relative path starts at the run folder).
A missing region file is a fact (`missing_files`), not a stop. A run folder without `result/final.stl` is an error.
For a list of STLs the role is `part` unless given.

**A problem YAML** (`topopt render problem.yaml`, `render_part(yaml_path=...)`; any `.yaml` or `.yml` path alone). It draws the problem
before a run, so that a wrong cut is visible: the region STLs of the YAML (`design`, `fixed`, `keep_out`, `load`; a `solid` region has the role
`load`), and the interface shapes of section 23. A union shape (a `boss`, the ring of a `tube`, an `stl` union) has the role `interface`
and is drawn solid, green (50,160,90). A cut shape (a `bore`, the hole of a `tube`, a `face`, an `stl` cut) has the role `cut` and is
drawn as a strong ghost, red (235,70,110). A `face` is its cut zone, clipped to the grid box (the bounds of the regions and the union shapes), so a
plane that goes through a sleeve is visible. With `radius_mm` the zone is the disc. The shapes are those of the labels
(`interfaces.add_meshes`, `interfaces.cut_meshes`; `interfaces.render_shapes` clips them). The roles `design` and `keep-out` are light
ghosts, `fixed` and `load` are solid. No role can be given for a YAML (`--role` with a YAML is an error), and `regions` has no effect (a note says so).
The facts have `input.kind` `yaml` and `input.yaml`; each mesh has a `file` such as `interface <name>` and `path` null for a shape; the stem of the
PNG files is the YAML name; `<out>` is `renders` beside the YAML. The YAML is loaded like `topopt check` loads it (a bad YAML is an error); no voxelization and no solve run.

**Force arrows** (a problem YAML only; P9-16). Before a run, a wrong sign or axis in a force vector is the most common load error, so the
render of a problem YAML draws the forces. The rule is the one of the dashboard (`addLoadArrows` in `topopt/dashboard/js/app.js`), so the picture
before the run and the picture during the run agree:

- One arrow for each force entry of each load case that has a force (`force` is not the zero vector). The arrow points along the force.
  Its tip is at the point where the force acts: `at` for a remote force, else the volume centroid of the STL of the load region (the center of the
  bounding box when the mesh is not a closed solid, and a note says so). The run takes the mean of the load voxels, so the point can differ by about
  one voxel, and by more when the region sticks out of the grid. The tail is `length_mm` before the tip.
- The length is `ARROW_LENGTH_SHARE` (0.18) of the diagonal of the bounding box of all drawn meshes, and it is the same for every arrow. It does **not**
  show the size of the force: a note says so when the sizes differ, and `size_n` gives the size. The shape is a shaft and a cone head with the
  dashboard proportions (shaft radius 0.045 of the length, head length 0.32 of the length, head base radius 3 times the shaft radius, 16 sides). The
  numbers are drawing constants in `topopt/render.py` (`ARROW_*`), not limits. Arrows are drawn last, over everything (no hidden-surface test, as in the dashboard), in
  every view, with the line grey of the solid meshes at their edge. They count in the fit of the view, so an arrow that sticks out of the part stays in the tile.
- One color for each load case, in the order of the load cases (`CASE_COLORS`, five colors that repeat after the fifth; a note says so): violet 120,0,200,
  gold 176,150,0, teal 0,140,150, plum 120,0,80, dark green 0,100,40. None of them is a color of the table below (each is 60 or more away in RGB). The color
  follows the case number, so a case with no arrow does not move the colors of the next cases. The legend of the montage has one line
  `force: <case name>` (style `arrow`) for each case that has an arrow, and the second header line says `force arrows N`.
- A moment (`moment`), a pressure (`pressures`) and a case with no force have no arrow. The facts say so (`not_drawn`, and a note for a case with no arrow
  at all). The moment of a force with a moment is not drawn (`moment_drawn` false).
- `loads=false` (CLI `--no-loads`) draws no arrow: the render is the same, byte for byte, as a render of a YAML with no arrow to draw, and `load_arrows` is
  `{"drawn": false, "note": ...}`. `loads=true` is the default. For an STL or a run folder `loads` has no effect (a note says so) and `load_arrows` is null.
  A value that is not a boolean is a `UserError`.
- Facts, `load_arrows`: `drawn`, `arrow_count`, `length_mm`, `length_rule`, `tip_rule`, and `cases`: for each load case in YAML order, `case` (the name),
  `color` (hex; null when the case has no arrow), `arrows` and `not_drawn`. An arrow has `region`, `kind` (`force`, `remote_force`, `force_moment` or `remote_force_moment`, as
  in `run.json`), `force_n` (the vector, N), `size_n`, `point_mm` (where the force acts), `point_source` (`at`, `region centroid` or `region bbox center`),
  `arrow_tail_mm`, `arrow_tip_mm` (the tip is `point_mm`), `color` and, with a moment, `moment_nmm` and `moment_drawn`. An entry of `not_drawn` has `region`, `kind` (`moment` or
  `pressure`), `moment_nmm` or `value_mpa`, and `reason`. These are the numbers that the agent reads out when it asks the user to confirm the directions.
- A section does not move the arrows: they are drawn at the true points, also when the section removes the region.

**Roles, colors and how they are drawn** (RGB; shading changes the brightness of solid meshes):

| Role | Color | With a part (`regions=ghost`, default) | Without a part (`regions=solid`, default) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `part` | grey-blue 154,167,180 | solid | solid |
| `design` | light blue 120,165,235 | light ghost | light ghost if other meshes are drawn, else solid |
| `keep-out` | brown 150,100,40 | light ghost | solid |
| `fixed` | dark blue 40,90,200 | strong ghost | solid |
| `load` | red 214,39,40 | strong ghost | solid |
| `interface` (YAML only) | green 50,160,90 | | solid |
| `cut` (YAML only) | red 235,70,110 | | strong ghost |
| back face | magenta 217,26,191 | any solid mesh: a flipped or open surface | |
| cut face | orange 232,140,60 | flat, full color, with `section`; roles `part` and a solid `design` | |

A light ghost is a tint (alpha 0.14) and thin lines. A strong ghost is a tint (alpha 0.35) and lines in the role color.
No ghost hides the part. `regions=solid` draws fixed, load and keep-out solid (the design space stays a ghost when other meshes
are drawn, so it never hides them). `regions=off` draws the part only. The cut faces of regions keep their role color.
Regions are drawn a little behind the part where faces touch, so the part wins. The legend swatch of a role shows
how it is drawn: a pale fill with an outline for a ghost (`legend` in the facts has the style), the full color for a solid.

**Views.** `iso` (1,-1,0.8), `front` (0,-1,0), `back`, `right` (1,0,0), `left`, `top` (0,0,1), `bottom`.
Default: `iso, front, right, top`. `NAME:dx,dy,dz` is a direction from the part to the camera (z up);
the name has letters, digits, `_` and `-` only (it is part of the file name). A list of views is split at `;` when the
text has a `;`. Else it is split at `,`, and a `NAME:dx,dy,dz` view keeps its two next numbers. So `fl:-0.5,-1,0.25` is one view and
`iso,fl:-0.5,-1,0.25,top` is three. Before, a custom view needed a `;` in the list (P4, F4-10). An item of the list that the MCP
tool gets is read the same way. Z is up.

**Section.** `x=30` or `x>=30` keeps the side x >= 30. `x<=30` (or `x<30`) keeps x <= 30. The axis is x, y or z; the value
is a finite number in mm. Each mesh is cut with manifold3d. A mesh that has no material on the kept side is not drawn
(`meshes[].drawn` is `removed`, `section.kept_triangles` is 0). An inside-out mesh (negative volume) is flipped for the cut,
and `section.note` says so. A mesh that is not a valid closed solid is not cut: the facts say so (`section.applied` false,
`notes`), the part is drawn whole, and for a region the triangles whose center is on the removed side are dropped.
The render still completes.

With a section and no `views`, the views are: `cut` (straight at the cut face from the removed side), `iso-cut` (the iso
direction with the cut axis turned to the removed side) and two side views of the kept part (x: front, top; y: right, top;
z: front, right). The names `cut` and `iso-cut` can be given in `views`. `cut_face_visible_px` (in `views[]` and in
`section`) counts the visible cut-face pixels. If a section is made and the total is 0, `notes` names a `cut:dx,dy,dz` view to add.

**Scale.** All tiles of a montage have one scale. A scale bar (a round length, 1, 2 or 5 times a power of 10 mm, near one
fifth of the tile width) is in each tile. `scale` has `px_per_mm` and `bar_mm`.

**Files.** `<out>/<stem>_<view>.png` for each view and `<out>/<stem>_montage.png`. `stem` is the file name of the
first mesh without extension (`final` for a run folder). A section adds `_section-<axis><value>` (and `-below` for a
`<=` section) after the stem. `<out>` is `<run>/renders`, or `renders` beside the first STL; `out_dir` or `--out` overrides it.
A render overwrites PNGs with the same names. It stops with an error rather than overwrite an input file, and with a
`UserError` (not a traceback) when it cannot make or write the folder. The same inputs give the same PNG bytes
(on one machine and one Pillow version).

**Montage.** Tiles in 2 columns, a header (file name, bbox in mm, triangle count, watertight; a second line with the
roles, missing files, the number of force arrows and the section with the number of views that show the cut), the view name in each tile, a legend.
The text is 18 px. One tile is 640x480 by default. The tile size is reduced until the long edge of the montage is 1568 px or less.

**Fonts.** `load_font(size)` tries the file in env var `TOPOPT_FONT`, then `FONT_CHAIN` (macOS Helvetica and Arial,
DejaVu and Liberation on Linux), then `ImageFont.load_default(size=N)` (Pillow bundles a font). It never raises.
The facts name the font that was used (`font`: a path, or `pillow-default`). The look of the text differs between fonts.

**Facts** (all keys): `ok`, `input` (`kind` run, stl or yaml, `run_dir`, and `yaml` for a YAML), `out_dir`, `montage` and each of `views`
(`path`, `width`, `height`, `bytes`; a view also has `name`, `direction`, `back_face_share`, `cut_face_visible_px`), `section`
(`axis`, `value`, `keeps`, `applied`, `cut_face_visible_px`, `views_with_cut`, or null), `meshes` (each: `file`, `path`,
`role`, `drawn` solid, ghost, off or removed, `bbox_mm` min, max, size of the mesh as loaded, `triangles`, `watertight`,
`winding_consistent`, `volume_mm3` and `inside_out` (only for a watertight mesh with a consistent winding, else null),
`section`), `load_arrows` (a problem YAML: the force arrows above; else null), `back_face_share` (back-face pixels of solid meshes over all their visible pixels, all views),
`missing_files` (`role`, `file`, `path`), `notes`, `regions`, `colors`, `ghost_style`, `legend`, `scale`, `tile_size`,
`triangles_drawn`, `memory_estimate_mb`, `font`, `elapsed_s` (not part of the repeatable result).
The MCP tool adds `inline`, `out_dir_rel` and `montage_rel` (relative to the work folder when inside it, like the `*_rel`
keys of the other tools).

**Size.** `memory_estimate_mb` is a rough model: 450 MB plus 450 MB per million triangles drawn (measured: 477 MB for the
85,610-triangle hook, about 1.0 GB for 1.4 million triangles; a section adds about 15 %). `max_triangles` stops the render with a
`UserError` when the meshes have more triangles. The default is no limit.

**Time.** The hook `final.stl` (85,610 triangles) with 4 views takes 2 to 4 s. The first call with an empty
numba cache adds under 1 s to compile the rasterizer. The cache goes next to the package. If that folder cannot be
written, numba falls back to a user cache folder (`~/.cache/numba` on Linux, measured; macOS not measured), and the
cache is reused on the next start. The env var `NUMBA_CACHE_DIR` sets the folder.

## 16. Verify (added with B2)

Package `topopt/verify/`. It checks the final STL of a finished run with quadratic tets (P2), independent of the voxel
model: another mesh and another element. It does not depend on the linear solver: the factor can be the one of the optimizer. User text: `docs/reference/verify.md`, section "Verify the result".

**Rules.**

- The extra `verify` of `pyproject.toml` holds gmsh (`gmsh==4.15.2`, same marker as `tet`; GPL-2.0-or-later), `scikit-fem==12.0.2`
  (BSD-3-Clause) and `cholespy==2.2.0` (GPL-2.0-or-later in effect: the wheel bundles CHOLMOD Supernodal, SuiteSparse 5.4.0; the
  code of cholespy itself is BSD-3-Clause; the same rule as gmsh). They are never main dependencies, never in
  `requirements.lock`, never vendored.
- `import topopt`, `topopt.cli`, `topopt_mcp.server` and all `topopt.verify` modules import none of them (`tests/test_verify_run.py`).
  scikit-fem is imported inside `P2Model` and `quadrature`; cholespy inside `CholespyFactor`; gmsh only through `topopt.tet`.
- The P2 model is a port of `pipeline/lib/p2_core.py` (d43bcf3). `tests/fixtures/verify_golden.npz.b64` (base64 text of an .npz) (made by `tools/make_verify_golden.py`)
  holds results of the pipeline code: K, stress at quadrature points, stress at vertices, `weighted_percentile` and von Mises
  are bit-identical (also with small assembly chunks). K also equals the scikit-fem assembly, and the traction equals the scikit-fem
  `FacetBasis` load, on a jittered mesh.
- A message that names an option names the one of the reader: `--max-gb` in the command, `max_gb` in the MCP tool (`topopt/verify/names.py`).
  The MCP server sets the style for its calls and for its child (env var `TOPOPT_VERIFY_STYLE=mcp`).

**CLI.** `topopt verify <run_dir> [--mesh-size MM] [--levels MM,MM,...] [--region-band-mm MM] [--allowable-mpa X] [--percentile P]
[--solver NAME] [--max-gb X] [--force] [--estimate-only] [--yaml FILE] [--near-mm MM] [--no-sensitivity] [--buckling | --no-buckling]
[--bore-checks | --no-bore-checks] [--part-only] [--gate]`.

- `run_dir` needs `run.json` and `result/final.stl`. If `result/nominal.stl` exists (a run with machining stock, section 23), `verify` meshes it, because it is the part in service; else it meshes `final.stl`. `run.verified_file` of `verify.json` names the file (`final_stl` and `final_stl_sha256` are those of that file), and the text result has a `mesh file:` line when it is not `final.stl`. The problem YAML is the `yaml_path` of `run.json` (a relative path starts at the run folder). `--yaml` gives another file (a run folder
  that was moved, or a recording made on another machine). The YAML is compared with `run.json` (case names, weights, forces, region
  files): a difference is a fact (`yaml_vs_run`, and a `note:` line), not an error.
- `--mesh-size`: one size in mm. Default: the size of the tet mesher (2.5 times the mean STL edge: about 1.3 to 2.2 voxels for an `sdf` STL, see section 19; `verify` prints it). `--levels`: several
  sizes (not with `--mesh-size`). The finest is the reference level.
- `--region-band-mm`: default 0.5 times the voxel size of the run.
- `--allowable-mpa`, `--percentile` (default 99.9): your limit. No default limit. Without `--allowable-mpa`, the result has the key
  `no_allowable`, which names the resource `topopt://materials/reference` (section 25.7). With `--gate` and no `--allowable-mpa`, the result has no `no_allowable`: the gate has its own limits (below).
- `--gate` (added with K1-B): the opt-in hard gate. See "The gate" below. Without it, `verify.json` and the exit codes are as before.
- `--solver`: `auto` (default), `cholesky`, `pardiso`, `cholespy` or `superlu`. `amg` is refused: it is an iterative method, so its error
  depends on its tolerance, and every direct factor gives the same refined solution. AMG is listed as a later low-memory option (not built).
- `--max-gb`, `--force`: see the memory model. `--estimate-only`: print the estimates and stop, nothing is meshed.
- `--near-mm` (default 2): the distance from a fixed or load region for `near_regions`. `--no-sensitivity`: no load-band sensitivity.
- `--buckling`, `--no-buckling` (added with B3): the linear buckling check of the tet model (section 33, "In `topopt verify`"). Without a flag, the YAML
  block `buckling` of the run decides (`buckling.check`, default false). `buckling.modes` and `buckling.max_seconds` are its settings. The flag overrides
  the YAML for this call. The estimate lines and `buckling_check` of the result say which one switched it on. The A5 rows (section 31) need no flag: they run when
  the YAML of the run has `limits.displacement` or `limits.alignment` rows.
- `--bore-checks`, `--no-bore-checks` (added with B4): the bore checks of the block `bore_checks` of the YAML (section 40). Without a flag, the block decides (on when it is there). `--bore-checks` needs the block
  (else an error that names the YAML); `--no-bore-checks` turns the block off for this call. The estimate lines and `bore_checks` of the result say which one switched them on.
- `--part-only` (added with P4b-3): mesh `result/part_only.stl` (section 9.1) instead of `nominal.stl` or `final.stl`. The default does not change.
  `run.verified_file` is `part_only.stl`, and `run.final_stl`, `run.final_stl_sha256`, `mesh.stl_sha256` and `stl` are those of that file. If the file
  is not in the folder (a run without `regions.not_printed`, a cut that failed, a file that is gone), the command stops with exit code 1 and a text that
  gives the fact (from the block `part_only` of `run.json`) and the options. A run that has the file, verified without the option, gets one `note:` line that names `--part-only` and the file that verify meshes ("Verify meshes final.stl"; with `--estimate-only`, which meshes nothing: "Verify would mesh final.stl")
  (the MCP reply has it in `notes`). The line is not in `verify.json`, so that file is the same as before this option, except for the time fields.
  With machining stock (a `nominal.stl`), `part_only.stl` is cut from `final.stl` and keeps the stock (section 9.1): the report says so as a fact in
  `part_only.notes` and makes no second cut. The removed bodies are the ones of `regions.not_printed` in the YAML that verify reads. A difference from the list that the run cut out
  (`run.json`, `part_only.removed`) is a fact in `part_only.yaml_vs_run`, not an error. See "Region rule with `--part-only`".
- The mesh optimizer is `Gmsh+Netgen` (`DEFAULT_OPTIMIZE`).
- The command prints the estimates (memory and time) to stderr, and the summary to stdout. When the surface
  preparation welded the input (section 14, weld retry) or cleaned the refused surface (section 14, clean retry), the summary has one
  more line that starts with `surface:`. It has one such line too when the mesh was made without a shell that lies in the material of
  another shell (section 14, shell retry; `mesh.surface_shell_retry` in `verify.json`): the line names the shell (volume, faces, box),
  says that gmsh failed on the whole surface and why, and gives the volume of the surface before and after. A cavity or a shell that gmsh
  cannot take stops `topopt verify` with exit code 2 and the text of section 14 (the shells, the cause and the options).
- A real run removes the files of an earlier run from `verify/` first (see Files).
- The result depends on the `final.stl`, so on the mesh method of the run (`settings.mesh_method`, `blur` or `sdf`, section 19; `run.json` has the key `mesh_method` and `metrics.json` has `mesh.method`;
  a run made before section 19 has neither key and was made with `blur`). `blur` makes thin members (2 to 3 voxels) thinner than the voxel design. On the hook, the lowest buckling load factor of the tet model is 0.61 to 0.63
  of the voxel one on the `blur` STL of the recorded run and 0.71 to 0.79 on the `sdf` STL of the same design, and the tip displacement of a row differs by tens of percent (sections 31 and 33). Compare runs of the same method.

**Exit codes.** 0: it ran. 1: bad input or usage (also an argparse usage error of this command, and `--part-only` on a run without `result/part_only.stl`), a part that the tet model cannot solve
(`UnsolvableMesh`, a `UserError`: a body with no fixed node, a load region that no body touches, a singular matrix; see "Bodies and a singular matrix"),
and a linear solver that cannot run (`SolverUnavailable`, a `UserError`: no factor can run here, or the one that `--solver` names cannot; the text
holds the note of every factor and the options). 2: it could not run
(`VerifyError`: `VerifyUnavailable` for a missing gmsh or scikit-fem, `MemoryRefused`, `EmptyRegion`, and a SuperLU factor that ran out of memory; the errors
of `topopt.tet` are wrapped in it; the text has the install step or the options). A meshing failure reads "meshing the final STL at <size> mm failed: <reason>". When
the reason can change with the mesh size (`PreparedSurfaceRejected`: the prepared surface is refused; `MeshingFailed`: gmsh failed), the text adds the next step that fits the call: for a call with one size (or the default) set `--mesh-size`
(`mesh_size_mm` in the MCP tool) to a value other than the one that failed; for a call with levels change that size in `--levels` (`levels_mm`),
because the two options cannot be given together. `topopt verify` does not retry. A missing gmsh and a
refusal of the input STL itself (`SurfaceRejected` that is not a `PreparedSurfaceRejected`) have no size hint. 3: `--allowable-mpa` is given and a case is above it at the percentile (by volume, reference level). The peak is information only. 3 also when `--gate` is given and the gate fails (a check is not met, or a check that the gate asked for could not run). The meaning of 3 is "a limit failed".

**The gate (added with K1-B; `topopt/verify/gate.py`).** `topopt verify --gate` (MCP `verify_run(gate=true)`) gives a pass or a fail for
the stress, the buckling factor and the A5 rows, from limits that the YAML already has. There is no new YAML key. The switch is opt-in: without it the result has no `gate` key and the exit codes are as before
(the rule "no `met`, no new exit code" of the buckling and alignment checks holds for a run without `--gate`).

- *Limits.* Stress: for each load case, `load_cases[].stress_limit_mpa` (section 17: `stress_limit`, or `allowable_mpa / safety_factor`) against the stress by volume at `--percentile` (default 99.9), at the reference level;
  `--allowable-mpa` replaces the limit of every case (the old `limit` block stays and its exit code 3 stays). Buckling: the lowest tet load factor of each case (`load_factors[0]` of the case in the key `buckling`, section 33: the measured value, also when the rigid-body rule of section 33 ran) is at least `buckling.min_factor`;
  the gate turns the check on when the YAML has `min_factor` (the same check as `--buckling`; `--no-buckling` with it is a `UserError`). Displacement and alignment: the `tet_value` of each row of the key `motion` (section 31)
  is at most the limit of its row. The test is strict: a value on the limit passes, a value past it fails, there is no tolerance.
- *A limit that the call replaces* (D-2). When `--allowable-mpa` replaces a limit that the YAML gives, the record of the case keeps `replaced_limit`, `replaced_source` (for example `load_cases[hang].stress_limit`) and `loosened` (true when the new limit is above the replaced one;
  false when it is equal or below). The line `gate: stress ...` and the plain text of the case say it. This is a fact and not a refusal: a larger value loosens a requirement of the YAML, and that needs the consent of the user (section 41.2); a smaller one tightens it.
  A case whose YAML has no limit has no such keys. A `--percentile` other than 99.9 gives the stress record `replaced_percentile` (99.9) and `percentile_loosened` (true for a lower percentile, which cannot give a higher value). The text of `source` follows the style of the caller (the rule of `topopt/verify/names.py`):
  `--allowable-mpa (all cases)` for the command and `allowable_mpa (all cases)` for the MCP tool (D-7).
- *The limits are for the voxel model; the gate compares tet values* (the voxel-to-tet gap). The limits in the YAML are the limits of the optimizer, which solves the voxel model. The gate reads the same numbers as limits of the tet value, and the two models differ by a measured amount. Measured on the hook (one part, one host, not re-run for this text):
  the p99.9 stress of `pull_off` was 2.45 to 2.67 times the limit (0.5 MPa) in six runs while the relaxed row of the optimizer said met (card `load_cases[].stress_limit`); the lowest buckling factor of the tet model was 0.61 to 0.63 of the voxel factor on the `blur` STL and 0.71 to 0.79 on the `sdf` STL (section 33);
  and the tet value of a displacement row was 1.23 times (`sdf` STL) and 1.63 times (`blur` STL) the voxel value, which was at its limit (section 31). So a design that met its limits on the voxel model can fail the gate. The gate changes no limit and the YAML has no key for a tet-specific limit in this version.
- *Not gated.* A check with no limit is listed in `not_gated` (`check`, `case`, `reason`) and does not fail the gate: a case with no stress limit (and no `--allowable-mpa`), no `buckling.min_factor`, no `limits.displacement` or
  `limits.alignment` rows, a case that applies no load (for buckling), and a case of status `no_positive_factor` (a pure tension state: the buckling check ran and found nothing that can buckle; the reason is "no compression in this load case, nothing can buckle"; it is neither a failure nor a pass; D-1).
  A gate that gates no check at all is refused before the run (`UserError`, exit code 1, with the options). Only a check that can run counts: a `buckling.min_factor` with no load case that applies a load does not (D-5). If every check turns out to be `not_gated` only after the solve
  (every case of the buckling check has no compression), `passed` is false, `failed` is empty and the key has a `reason` that says so.
- *A check that could not run* When the gate asked for a check and the record is `skipped` or `error` (for example the buckling check above the memory limit, or rows that cannot work), or the row, the case or the value is missing or not a finite number,
  the check has `met: null` and a `reason`. It fails the gate.
