  and the levers of the run (`run_result` `levers`, `topopt levers --run`). A case whose `independent_check` differs from the file gets the new `independent_check` and the `summary` made again.
  It compares the forces and the material of the YAML with `run.json`; if they differ it says so as a fact (`input_changed`) and gives
  no physical numbers for that case. A `run.json` from before A2 R1 has no E and nu: the check then compares the density only, and `input_check.not_compared` says so.
  The check reads `verify.json` whatever file `topopt verify` meshed, and records that file as `verified_file` (`run.verified_file` of `verify.json`: `final.stl`, `nominal.stl` or
  `part_only.stl`; null when there is no value, or the file has no such key). The `note` names it. After `topopt verify --part-only` (section 16) the P2 value is the one of `part_only.stl`,
  a part without the removed bodies and with their boundary conditions at the contact faces, while the voxel value is the one of the whole problem. The note says so:
  `p2_over_voxel` then compares two different models (added with P4b-3).

## 18. Print report (added with V2)

The print report gives plain numbers about printing: overhang area, plate contact, a support-volume estimate,
bed fit and a thinnest-member estimate. It reads the final mesh. It does not change the optimizer, the
snapshots or the mesh. All values are facts or estimates: nothing in it stops a run.
Code: `topopt/print_report.py` (numpy and trimesh; the ray queries use the pinned `rtree`; no VTK). The ray queries run in
passes of at most 2,000 rays and 2 million (ray, triangle) pairs (`RAY_CHUNK`, `PAIR_BUDGET` in `print_report.py`; a lone ray with more pairs
runs alone). The memory of a pass grows with its pairs, not with its rays: the hook mesh needs 160 MB, a mesh of 1.4 million triangles
1.0 GB, and a disk whose caps are triangle fans (200,000 triangles, long slivers with big boxes) 1.0 GB and 43 s.

**YAML: the optional `print` block** (a top-level key, after `assumptions`). Unknown keys inside it are an error,
as at the top level. A YAML with no `print` block, or a block with some keys, uses the defaults below.
The report labels each default as "assumed" (`settings.assumed` in the report).

```yaml
print:
  build_direction: [0, 0, 1]      # vector of 3 numbers (any length, not zero) or an axis name: +x -x +y -y +z -z (x = +x). Up, away from the plate. Default [0, 0, 1].
  bed_mm: 220                     # mm. One number (square bed) or [x, y]. Default 220 (220 x 220).
  printer_type: fdm               # fdm | sla | lpbf | sls (any case). Default fdm.
  printer_model: bambu-lab-p1s    # optional: a printer of the catalog or of the user file (section 18.7). Fills bed_mm and printer_type when the block does not give them.
  self_supporting_angle_deg: 45   # optional, 0 to 90. The angle from the plate; wins over the printer-type default.
```

- `build_direction` is normalized. The plate is the plane through the lowest vertex along it.
- The self-supporting angle is measured from the plate (0 = flat, 90 = vertical). A face with an angle below it needs
  support. Default by printer type (the same number for each type today; a different value in the YAML wins):

  | `printer_type` | Default angle | Support | Source |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `fdm` | 45 | yes | Stratasys: "The general rule for the minimum self-supporting angle is around 45 degrees from horizontal" (https://www.cati.com/?p=122249). Also `printability.py:22` and `orientation_study.py:18` of the earlier pipeline of the same author. The real limit depends on layer height, material and cooling. |
  | `sla` | 45 | yes | Wikipedia, DFM analysis for stereolithography: "Generally, beyond a certain angle (usually around 45 degrees), the surface doesn't require support". Isolated islands also need support. |
  | `lpbf` | 45 | yes | The rule of thumb in LPBF papers, for example Materials 2023, 16(3), 1039 (DOI 10.3390/ma16031039; found as a search snippet, the page was not fetched: HTTP 403). The earlier pipeline of the same author uses 45 degrees for its metal part. New machine parameters allow lower angles. |
  | `sls` | 45 (reference only) | no | Wikipedia, Selective laser sintering: the part "is surrounded by unsintered powder at all times". The report says "no support needed" and still gives the overhang area at this reference angle. |

- `topopt/config.py`: `load_config` returns `Config.print_settings` (a frozen `PrintSettings`; `given` names the keys
  that the YAML had). `PRINTER_TYPES` holds the table above.
- `run.json` has the key `print` (`build_direction`, `bed_mm`, `printer_type`, `self_supporting_angle_deg` or null, `given`; with a `printer_model`
  also `printer_model`, `catalog_version`, `profile` and `derived`: section 18.7).
  `post.finish` reads it. A run folder without it (an old recording) uses the defaults, all assumed.
- The part spec of the `part-to-topopt` skill can carry a `print` block. `regions_builder.write_outputs` copies it to the
  problem YAML as it is, and `load_config` checks it.

**Rules (all on the triangle mesh of `result/final.stl`; `n` is the outward face normal, `b` the unit build direction):**

- Overhang: a face is an overhang if `n.b < -cos(angle)`. The test is strict `<`: a face at exactly the angle is not an overhang
  (a flat underside with the angle 0 is not an overhang). A face within about 1e-15 of the limit can fall on either side (floating point):
  a cube turned 45 degrees about y has two such faces, and their count depends on the position of the cube. Plate-contact faces are not counted. This is `Study.metrics`
  (`orientation_study.py:64-90`).
- Plate contact: faces with `n.b < -0.99` whose centre is less than 0.3 mm above the lowest point along `b`. The pipeline
  tests this inside the overhang set; here it does not depend on the angle (the same result for any angle of 8.1 degrees or more).
- Support volume (mm3) is the "gap" measure of `printability.py:46-61`: each overhang face casts one ray from 0.05 mm below its
  centre along `-b`. The gap is the distance from the face centre to the first hit on the part, or the height above the plate if
  nothing is hit. Volume = sum of (gap x |n.b| x face area). For more than 30,000 overhang faces, a random sample of 30,000
  (seed 0) is scaled to the full overhang area. It is a solid-column upper bound: real supports use less material.
  The pipeline's other measure (height above the lowest point, in cm3) counts the part under an overhang as support and is not ported.
  The unused arcsin `angle_from_plate` of `printability.py:32` is not ported.
- Bed fit: the part extents in the build frame are two in-plane extents and the height (`extents_mm`). For an axis direction the in-plane
  axes are the other two world axes in the order x, y, z (the sign of `v` makes the frame right-handed, `u x v = b`). For another
  direction `u` is perpendicular to `b` and to the world axis least aligned with `b`, and `v = b x u`. The footprint is the part projected
  on the plate. The footprint is turned about `b` from 0 to 89 degrees in 1-degree steps (the convex hull of the footprint is turned, as
  `footprint()` in `orientation_study.py:26-40`). At each turn the margin is the smaller of the two spare lengths, bed side minus footprint
  side, the two sides sorted against the two bed sides (so a turn of 90 degrees counts as 0). For a part in the middle of the bed the
  gap to each edge is half of the spare length. `bed_turn_deg` is the turn with the largest margin (of equal margins, within 1e-6 mm,
  the smallest turn). If the part fits as it is (turn 0 has a margin that is not negative), a turn is reported only if it gains at least
  `BED_TURN_MIN_GAIN_MM` = 10 mm of margin over turn 0; otherwise `bed_turn_deg` is 0 and the footprint and the margin are those of turn 0.
  If turn 0 does not fit, `bed_turn_deg` is the turn with the largest margin. `bed_footprint_mm` is the footprint at the reported turn and
  `bed_margin_mm` that margin, in mm. `bed_fit` is true if the margin is not negative. If no turn fits, `bed_fit` is false and
  `bed_margin_mm` is negative: the footprint is that many mm longer than the bed at the best turn (`bed_turn_deg` and `bed_footprint_mm`
  are those of the best turn). The height is not limited, unless the run has a printer profile with a build height (section 18.7).
- Thinnest member: the pipeline ray-thickness method (`thick.py`), with trimesh instead of VTK. 60,000 surface points (by area,
  seed 1; the number that `printability.py` gives to `ray_thickness`, whose own default is 30,000). At each point a chord goes along the negative face normal to the first wall (hits closer than 0.03 mm are the surface itself;
  no wall within 12 mm gives 12 mm). The thinnest-member number is the 1st percentile of the chords, in mm. It is an estimate. It means: 1 percent of the sampled
  surface area has a thinner chord. A thin feature on less than about 1 percent of the area does not move it (a 1.0 mm rib on 0.5 percent of
  the area reads 12 mm), so read `area_below_mm2` too. `min_mm` is the shortest chord of the sample and includes noise from sharp edges
  (0.07 to 0.5 mm on the hook for different seeds). A value equal to `max_chord_mm` (12) means 12 mm or more.
- Area below a thickness: `area_below_mm2` maps the thresholds "0.8", "1.2" and "2.0" (mm) to the surface area (mm2) whose chord is
  thinner. It is the share of the sampled chords below the threshold times the total area; `area_below_pct` gives the share in percent.
  The sampling error of a share f is about sqrt(f (1 - f) / samples): 0.04 percentage points of the area at f = 1 percent with 60,000 samples
  (4 percent of that value).
  The pipeline blends vertex normals; this port uses the face normal because the blend gives wrong chords near sharp edges (plan, measurements).

**`metrics.json`: the new key `print`** (added after the 13 existing keys; they do not change). Fields:

- `ok` (true). If the report fails, `print` is `{"ok": false, "error": "<text>"}` and the run goes on.
- `partial` and `coverage` (TC-2, section 44), right after `ok`: which of the five sub-checks `bed_fit`, `overhang`, `plate_contact`, `support_volume` and `thinnest_member` ran, failed or were not run.
  A report that failed as a whole has them too: `partial` true and one failed check, `print_report`.
- `settings`: `build_direction`, `build_direction_label`, `bed_mm` [x, y], `printer_type`, `self_supporting_angle_deg` (the angle
  used), `angle_source` (`yaml` or the default of the printer type), `assumed` (the keys of `build_direction`, `bed_mm`,
  `printer_type` that the YAML did not give and that no printer profile filled) and `assumed_note` (when `assumed` is not empty). With a
  `printer_model` there are more keys (section 18.7).
- `support_needed` (false for `sls`), `support_note` (for `sls`: "no support needed ..."), `warning` (an inside-out mesh was flipped), `total_area_mm2`.
- `configured`: the entry of the configured direction. `options`: six entries, in the order +x, -x, +y, -y, +z, -z. An entry has
  `label`, `direction`, `extents_mm` (in-plane u, in-plane v, height), `height_mm`, `bed_fit` (true or false), `bed_turn_deg`,
  `bed_footprint_mm`, `bed_margin_mm` (see the bed-fit rule above),
  `overhang_area_mm2`, `overhang_fraction` (of the total area), `plate_contact_area_mm2`, `support_volume_mm3` (null if no
  support is needed) and `support_rays`.
- `thinnest_member`: `thinnest_member_mm`, `percentile` (1.0), `min_mm`, `samples`, `percentiles_mm` (`p0.1`, `p1`, `p5`, `p50`),
  `area_below_mm2`, `area_below_pct`, `seed`, `max_chord_mm`, `method`, `estimate` (true). If the estimate stops with an error, the block keeps these keys (the numbers are null, `samples` is 0)
  and has `error` (TC-2): the other numbers of the report stay.
- `definitions` (a short text for each number) and `elapsed_s` (the time of the report; it is part of `run_time_s`).
- The MCP tool `run_result` returns the key with the rest of `metrics.json`.

**Before the run:** `topopt check` prints two lines (`print settings:` and `print bed fit:`). `check_data` and `check --json`
(and the MCP tool `check_problem`) have the key `print`: `bed_mm`, `assumed`, `printer_type`, `box_extents_mm`, `configured` and
`options` (each `label`, `direction`, `extents_mm`, `bed_fit`, `bed_turn_deg`, `bed_footprint_mm`, `bed_margin_mm`) and a `note`. The box is the box around the design, fixed and load
voxels. The part lies inside it, so a fit is certain and a misfit can go away when the optimizer removes material. It is a fact, not a refusal.

**`tools/check_part.py`** reads `print.bed_mm` and `print.build_direction` when the YAML has them (`--bed` wins over the YAML). With
no `print` key its output does not change (a test compares it byte for byte with the output of `7555b19`; the line keeps the old strict
"<" rule with the two smallest extents). With `print` keys the bed line uses the rule of the report (at most, "<="); with a build direction
it uses the extents in the build frame and the turn about the build axis, and says "fits turned N degrees (margin M mm)" when N is above 0
and "does not fit at any turn (best: N degrees, X mm over)" when no turn fits (`topopt check` says the same). A wrong
`print` block gives one `error:` line and exit 1 before any check, as `tools/print_section.py` does.

**Not in V2:** a `min_member_mm` key, a voxel-size check against it, a filter change and a pass/fail gate (these are in A3 and E1).

### 18.7 Printer profiles: the catalog, the lookup, the key and the user file (added with PM-1)

The user names the printer. The tool finds the model and fills the print parameters itself. The facts about a printer come from a catalog
that ships with topopt, and from a file of the user for a printer that the catalog does not have. Code: `topopt/printers.py` (it does not
import `mcp`; it imports `topopt.config` only inside a check, because `config` imports it). Tests: `tests/test_printers.py`.

**The catalog.** `topopt/data/printers.yaml` is package data (`pyproject.toml`: `data/*.yaml`; the Desktop bundle holds the whole
`topopt/` tree). The keys: `format: 1` (the integer 1), `catalog_version` (text, the date of the last edit), `vendors` (a vendor name
mapped to its words) and `models` (a list). A model has every field of the list below. A fact that no maker page states, or that two
maker pages state differently, is `null`, and the `note` of the row names the field and says why. Nothing is guessed: a null is
"unknown". `chamber_max_c` and `nozzle_options_mm` may be null without a note (no chamber heater stated; no sizes stated).

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id`, `vendor`, `model`, `aliases` | The id is a lower-case slug (the value of `print.printer_model`). The name is "`vendor` `model`". `aliases` are other exact names. |
| `printer_type` | `fdm`, `sla`, `lpbf` or `sls` (the values of `print.printer_type`). |
| `bed_mm` | `[x, y]` in mm. |
| `build_height_mm` | The build height in mm. |
| `nozzle_mm`, `nozzle_options_mm` | The stock nozzle and the sizes that the maker sells. |
| `max_nozzle_c`, `max_bed_c` | The highest temperatures that the maker states. |
| `enclosure`, `chamber_max_c` | `open`, `enclosed` or `heated`. `chamber_max_c` is a number exactly when the enclosure is `heated` (the maker states a chamber heater). |
| `stock_nozzle_material`, `extruder` | `brass`, `stainless`, `hardened_steel` or `tungsten_carbide`; `direct` or `bowden`. |
| `source_url`, `opened`, `tag` | The maker page (http or https), the date it was opened (`YYYY-MM-DD`) and `maker doc` or `third party`. |
| `field_sources`, `note` | Optional: a field mapped to its own page, and a text. |

- Catalog 2026-10-24 has 15 printers (Bambu Lab, Prusa, Creality, Elegoo, Voron). The values and pages are from the research file
  `A-printers.md`. A file with a fault raises `CatalogError` with the place of the fault; it is a defect of the package.
- **Licence.** The file is our own list of facts, written by hand from maker pages, and it is MIT like the rest of topopt. It holds no
  data of a slicer profile set (OrcaSlicer, Bambu Studio, PrusaSlicer and SuperSlicer profiles are AGPL-3.0; Cura profiles are
  LGPL-3.0). A printer name names a product.

**The lookup.** `printers.resolve(text, catalog=None)` returns a `Resolution` with `status` `match`, `ambiguous` or `none`.

- The text is cut in lower-case words (letters and digits; `+` reads as the word `plus`; accents are dropped). The words `my`, `the`,
  `printer`, `3d` and the shop words `combo`, `bundle`, `ams`, `cfs` and `kit` are dropped (so `P1S Combo` is the P1S, and a user entry
  `P1S Combo` of the vendor Bambu Lab is refused: it is a name of the shipped printer, and the refusal names it). The vendor phrases (the vendor name and its words, the longest first) are taken out and kept as a hard
  filter: a text that names a vendor looks only at the printers of that vendor. A word is cut where letters meet digits, so `p1s`,
  `p1 s` and `P1-S` are one name. The names of a printer are indexed without the words of ITS OWN vendor only (a shipped printer with
  the shipped table), so the `vendors` of the user file change no shipped name. If the text is not a `match` with the vendor words taken
  out, it is read again for each printer with only the words of that printer's own vendor taken out; an exact name from that is a
  `match`. So a vendor named `Plus` or `Carbon` does not hide `MINI+` or the alias `K1 Carbon`.
- An exact id (case ignored) is a `match` by `id`. Else the text is compared with the model name and the aliases of the printers that pass
  the vendor filter: one printer is a `match` by `name` or `alias`; the exact name of printers of two vendors is `ambiguous`.
- Else the printers with a name that has the text as a part are the `candidates` of an `ambiguous` answer. The text is a part of a name when its
  words, in this order, are the start of a run of the words of that name (`x1` is a part of `X1 Carbon`; the last word may stop inside the
  word: `p` is a part of `P1S`). The order matters and a run does not start inside a word, so `p1p`, `s1`, `1s` and `carbon x1` are no
  part of `P1S` or of `X1 Carbon`. A text that is only a vendor word gives all printers of the vendor. One candidate is also `ambiguous`: a
  part of a name is not an exact name, so the caller asks the user. The reply says it in `matched_by`: `partial` (a part of a name),
  `name` (the exact name of printers of more than one vendor) or `vendor` (only a vendor word). `differs` names the facts (`bed_mm`, `build_height_mm`, `nozzle_mm`, `max_nozzle_c`, `max_bed_c`, `enclosure`, `chamber_max_c`,
  `stock_nozzle_material`, `extruder`) on which the candidates differ.
- Else the answer is `none`. `suggestions` are the printers whose compact names have a difflib `SequenceMatcher` ratio of at least
  `SUGGEST_CUTOFF` (0.6) to the text, at most `SUGGEST_MAX` (5), the best first. They are module constants, not YAML keys. A suggestion is never taken by itself. An empty text is `none`.
- `Resolution.to_dict()` is the reply of `find_printer`. It has the same keys for the three statuses: `ok`, `status`, `query`,
  `catalog_version`, `matched_by` (`id`, `name`, `alias` for a match; `partial`, `name`, `vendor` for `ambiguous`; null for `none`), `origin`, `profile`, `derives`, `candidates`, `differs`, `suggestions`,
  `vendors`, `user_file` and `note`. `derives` is `{sets, missing}`: what `print.printer_model: <id>` sets in a run, and what the profile
  cannot give (`print.bed_mm`, the build height).

**The key `print.printer_model`.** A text: an id, or a name or an alias that is one printer. `PRINT_KEYS` holds it; the lever card is
`print.printer_model` (section 41).

- With a printer, `bed_mm` and `printer_type` come from the profile when the YAML does not give them. A key that the YAML gives wins. A
  profile whose `bed_mm` is null gives no bed (the default and the label `assumed` apply).
- The source label of a value from the profile is `profile:<id>`, not `assumed`. `PrintSettings.given` stays the keys of the YAML (it holds
  `printer_model`). `PrintSettings.derived` holds the keys that the profile filled (`bed_mm`, `printer_type`; `PRINT_DERIVABLE_KEYS`).
  `PrintSettings.profile` holds the `PrinterProfile`; `printer_model` and `build_height_mm` are properties; `key_source(key)` gives
  `profile:<id>` for a key in `derived`. `assumed` in the report and in `check` does not list a derived key.
- A text that is not one printer is a `UserError` of one line: the key, the text, the candidates or the suggestions, and the ways on
  (`Use an id from the catalog, or remove printer_model and give bed_mm and printer_type`, and the way to add a printer to the user file).
  A value that is not text is an error too. The error names the user printer file and its problems when it has any.
- `run.json`, key `print`: a run with a printer also has `printer_model` (the id), `catalog_version` (text, or null for a user printer
  whose file has no version), `profile` (the facts, below), `profile_sha256` and `derived` (a list). A run without a printer has none of the
  five keys, so the file is the one of V2. `profile_sha256` is the sha256 of the name and the capability facts of the profile
  (`FACT_FIELDS`) as JSON with sorted keys and no blanks; the sources, dates, note and origin are not in it, so two runs with the same
  digest used the same printer facts. The profile facts are `name`, `vendor`, `model`, `origin`, every fact field, `source_url`, `opened`,
  `tag`, and `source`, `field_sources` and `note` when the printer has them. The reader (`PrintSettings.from_dict`) takes the profile from this
  record and does not read a catalog: the record is the truth for that run, also when the catalog or the user file changed later. A bad
  value reads as "not stated"; a missing record reads as no profile.

**The build height.** A profile with a `build_height_mm` adds a height test to the bed fit (`print_report.bed_fit_turn(points, b, bed_mm,
build_height_mm=None)`). The part height is the third extent in the build frame (a turn about the build axis does not change it). The
entry gets `height_fit` (true if the height is not above the build height) and `height_margin_mm` (build height minus part height, in mm),
and `bed_fit` is false when the part is too tall. Without a profile, or with a null build height, the keys are absent and the height is
not limited; the output is as before, byte for byte where a test pins it.

- The report: `metrics.json` `print.settings` gets `printer_model`, `printer_name`, `catalog_version`, `printer_origin`, `profile_from`
  (`catalog 2026-10-24` or `user printer file`), `build_height_mm` and `derived` (a key mapped to `profile:<id>`). `definitions` gets
  `height_fit`. Without a printer the section has none of these.
- `topopt check` and `check_problem` (`print`): the same settings keys. The line is `print settings: bed 256 x 256 mm, build direction +z,
  printer: Bambu Lab P1S (profile bambu-lab-p1s, catalog 2026-10-24), type fdm (from the profile: bed_mm, printer_type)`. The fit line
  says `fits the bed but is X mm too tall for the build height`, or `..., and is X mm too tall for the build height`.
- `topopt printcheck` and `print_check` (section 32): the `bed_fit` check value has `height_fit` and `height_margin_mm`; the limit gets
  `build_height_mm` and `build_height_source` (`profile:<id>`); the reason names both heights; the text report has a `printer:` line. The
  `source` of `bed_mm` and `printer_type` in `settings` is `profile:<id>` when the profile filled them. In a run folder the printcheck takes
  the profile from `run.json`; for a YAML it resolves `printer_model` again. If `run.json` and a YAML name two printers, the YAML printer
  is the profile of the report, and a key that the `run.json` printer filled keeps the label of that printer (`profile:<its id>`).

**The user printer file.** `<work folder>/topopt-printers.yaml` has printers that the catalog does not have.

- **Where.** The work folder is the one of `topopt.workfolder.resolve(check=False).path` (section 10.1: `TOPOPT_WORKSPACE`, else
  `TOPOPT_DEFAULT_WORKSPACE`, else the current directory). The MCP server (`workspace()`), `load_config` and so `topopt run`,
  `topopt check` and `topopt printcheck` all call it. The CLI has no option for the folder, so it reads the file of the current directory
  when no variable is set. The server starts its runs with the work folder as the current directory and with `TOPOPT_WORKSPACE` set to that
  folder as a full path (also for a verify or ratchet job, `topopt step` and the environment probe), so a run finds the same file also when
  the setting of the server is a relative path.
- **The schema** is the one of the catalog (`format: 1`), with these differences. The file needs no `catalog_version` and no `vendors`
  (both are optional; a vendor of the file that is not in the table becomes a vendor with its own name as its word; a vendor name or word
  that the table has maps to the table's vendor, for example `bambu` to `Bambu Lab`). A printer needs `id`, `vendor`, `model`,
  `printer_type`, `bed_mm` and a source: `source_url` (the maker page that the agent found) or `source: user` (the user said the values).
  The other fields are optional; a field that is not given is `null`, which means unknown. A null needs no note. `opened` is optional
  (an unquoted date is read as text). `tag` is optional (`maker doc`, `third party` or `user`; the default is `user` for a printer with
  `source: user` and no page). `field_sources` maps a fact field to a page address or to the word `user`. `chamber_max_c` needs the
  enclosure `heated`; a `heated` printer may leave the chamber temperature null.
- **Merge.** `printers.catalog_for(folder)` returns the shipped printers first, then the printers of the file, as one `Catalog`
  (`resolve` takes it as its second argument; `printers.work_catalog()` uses the work folder). Every profile has `origin`: `catalog` or
  `user`. The file is read at each call (no cache), so a change is live at once.
- **No shadowing.** A printer of the file with the id of a shipped printer is not used: the problem names the shipped printer and offers
  another id (`<id>-user`). A printer whose name or alias is already a name of another printer of its vendor is not used either. Two
  entries with one id: the first is used.
- **A fault is a fact.** `Catalog.user_file` (`path`, `exists`, `entries`, `problems`) holds what is wrong. A fault of the whole file (not
  valid YAML, not a mapping, another `format`, an unknown top key, a wrong `vendors` or `models`, or a clash of the names when the
  vendors and the printers are indexed together) leaves the file unused. A fault of one
  entry leaves that entry out and the others in. Nothing is raised; the shipped catalog works as without the file. `find_printer` shows
  `user_file`, and the refusal of `load_config` names the problems.
- **Writing.** `printers.save_user_printer(folder, profile)` (the MCP tool `save_printer`) checks the printer as the loader does, merges
  by id (it replaces a user printer with the same id; the other entries, bad ones too, and the top keys stay as they are), and writes the
  file with `runinfo.write_atomic` (a temporary file in the same folder, then a rename). The entry has every fact field, null when
  unknown. It refuses, and writes nothing, for: a profile that is not a mapping; a file that cannot be read or is not valid YAML, has
  another `format` or a `models` that is not a list (the file is not changed); a fault of the entry; a shipped id; a name that another
  printer of the vendor has. The reply is `{ok, path, profile, created, replaced, note}` (+ `problems` of the rest of the file), or
  `{ok: false, error}`. `note` names the fields that are null.

**Tools.** `find_printer(name)` (read-only; `ok`, the keys of `Resolution.to_dict()` above) and `save_printer(profile)` (strict arguments, as every tool: an unknown
argument name is a refusal that does nothing (section 10, "Strict argument names"); it needs a work folder that the server can write). Both are in `READ_ONLY_TOOLS` (section 41): a printer entry changes no run until a YAML names it.
Each description is under 2,048 characters. The mock `evals/mocks/topopt/_tools.json` lists them.

**Preferences and skills.** `print.printer_model` is a preference (section 10.2). `start-here` (Step 1b, "The printer model") asks the user
only for the printer name, calls `find_printer`, shows the derived values and saves the id. On `ambiguous` it offers the candidates. On
`none` the agent looks up the maker page, shows the values with their sources to the user, and calls `save_printer` after the user agrees;
a value it cannot find stays null, and the agent asks the user for it. Then it saves `printer_model`. `part-to-topopt` says the same
(its section "The printer"). Both are offers: tools inform, the agent decides.

### 18.8 Filament profiles: the catalog, the lookup, the key, the compatibility check and the user file (added with PM-2)

The user names the filament. The tool finds the product and fills the material numbers itself. The facts about a filament come from a
catalog that ships with topopt, and from a file of the user for a filament that the catalog does not have. This is the same plan as for
the printers (section 18.7), and the two share the code of the name lookup. Code: `topopt/materials_catalog.py` (the catalog, the lookup
and the user file), `topopt/catalogs.py` (the name index and the lookup that `topopt/printers.py` uses too), `topopt/compat.py` (the
compatibility check of a printer and a filament; it imports nothing but `dataclasses`). None of them imports `mcp`;
`materials_catalog` imports `topopt.config` only inside a check, because `config` imports it. Tests: `tests/test_materials_catalog.py`,
`tests/test_compat.py`, `tests/test_filament_key.py`, `tests/test_filament_preferences.py`, `tests/test_material_tools.py`.

**The catalog.** `topopt/data/materials.yaml` is package data (`pyproject.toml`: `data/*.yaml`; the Desktop bundle holds the whole
`topopt/` tree). The keys: `format: 1` (the integer 1), `catalog_version` (text, the date of the last edit), `makers` (a maker name mapped
to its words) and `materials` (a list). One row is one product and one sheet version: a product with two sheet versions has two rows.
Every row has every field of the list below. A fact that no source states, that two sources state differently, or that a sheet gives in
a way that does not fit the field is `null`, and the `note` of the row names the field and says why. Nothing is guessed: a null is
"unknown". Eight fields are plain nulls that need no note: `nu`, `chamber_c_min`, `hardened_nozzle`, `drying`, `direct_drive`,
`conditioned`, `bending_modulus_xy_mpa` and `bending_modulus_z_mpa`.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id`, `maker`, `product`, `family`, `aliases`, `sheet_version` | The id is a lower-case slug (the value of `material.filament`). The name is "`maker` `product`". `family` is a label (`PLA`, `PETG-CF`, `PA6-CF`, ...). `aliases` are other exact names. `sheet_version` is the version that the sheet prints (`none stated` if it prints none). |
| `E_xy_mpa`, `E_z_mpa` | The tensile modulus in MPa. XY: the load runs in the layer plane. Z: the load runs across the layers. A sheet bar that loads the layer plane is not a Z value. |
| `bending_modulus_xy_mpa`, `bending_modulus_z_mpa` | The bending (flexural) modulus of printed bars in MPa, with the same XY and Z meaning. A shipped row has it only when its sheet gives no tensile modulus and gives a bending modulus of printed bars; it is `null` in every other row. A run takes E from it when the row has no tensile modulus. |
| `strength_xy_mpa`, `strength_z_mpa`, `strength_kind` | The tensile strength of printed bars in MPa, and what the sheet calls it: `yield`, `peak` or `not stated`. |
| `elongation_xy_pct`, `density_g_cm3`, `hdt_18_c`, `hdt_045_c` | Elongation of the XY bar, density, and the heat deflection temperatures at 1.8 MPa and 0.45 MPa. |
| `density_range_g_cm3` | Optional: `[min, max]` in g/cm3 of a sheet that gives a range and no single density (then `density_g_cm3` is `null`, and the note says so). A run takes the middle of the range, and the reason says "the middle of the sheet range a-b". A user entry may have it. It is not a fact field, but the digest of the facts holds it (a run reads it). |
| `conditioned` | The wet values of a polyamide: `condition`, `strength_xy_mpa`, `strength_z_mpa`, `E_xy_mpa`, `E_z_mpa`. |
| `nu` | Poisson's ratio. No data sheet gives it, so it is `null` in every row. |
| `nozzle_c`, `bed_c` | `[min, max]` in C for a 0.4 mm nozzle (a sheet value "x +/- y" is stored as `[x - y, x + y]`). |
| `enclosure`, `chamber_c_min` | What the maker says about an enclosed printer: `"no"` (write it with quotes: an unquoted `no` is a YAML 1.1 false, and the loader reads it as `"no"`), `recommended` or `required`; and the lowest chamber temperature that the maker names as a need (entered for a filament that needs an enclosure; a chamber that a sheet lists only among its print conditions, for a filament with no enclosure need, is not entered). |
| `hardened_nozzle`, `drying`, `direct_drive`, `abrasive`, `soft` | `true` when the maker asks for a hardened nozzle, `false` when it says it is not needed; the drying setting as text; `true` when the maker recommends a direct drive extruder; `true` for a product with fibre; `true` for a rubber-like filament (TPU). |
| `source_url`, `opened`, `tag` | The page (http or https), the date it was opened (`YYYY-MM-DD`) and `maker TDS`, `maker page` or `third party`. |
| `field_sources`, `note` | Optional: a fact field (or `enclosed_note`) mapped to its own page, and a text. |
| `enclosed_note` | Optional text: what the sheet or the product page of this one product says about printing in an enclosed printer, in its words (for example to leave the door open). On an `enclosed` or `heated` printer the `enclosure` check is `care` with this text. Only a page of the product itself counts: a general guide of a maker, for a whole family or with a condition that the check cannot know, does not. A user entry may have it. It is not a fact field, but the digest of the facts holds it (the check reads it). |
| `superseded_by` | Optional, shipped rows only: the id of the row of a NEWER sheet of the same product. The row is an older sheet. The id must be a row of the catalog that is not itself superseded (no chain, not the row itself). A user entry may not have it. It is not a fact: the digest of the facts does not hold it. |

- Catalog 2026-10-25 has 69 filaments of six makers (Polymaker, Bambu Lab, Prusament, Elegoo, AzureFilm, eSun) in 25 families. The values
  and pages are from the research files `B-materials.md` and `reference.md` (and the saved copies of the same sheets). A file with a
  fault raises `CatalogError` with the place of the fault; it is a defect of the package.
- **Licence.** The file is our own list of facts, written by hand from maker data sheets, and it is MIT like the rest of topopt. It holds
  no data of a slicer profile set (OrcaSlicer, Bambu Studio, PrusaSlicer and SuperSlicer profiles are AGPL-3.0; Cura profiles are LGPL-3.0).
  It has no price anywhere. A filament name names a product. Every sheet says that its numbers are not for design: they describe printed
  test bars of one maker and one set of print settings, not the part of the user.

**The lookup.** `materials_catalog.resolve(text, catalog=None)` returns a `Resolution` with `status` `match`, `ambiguous` or `none`. The
words of the text are cut, and the maker words are taken out as a hard filter, by `topopt.catalogs` with the rules of section 18.7 (case,
punctuation, accents, the word `my` and the shop words do not matter; a word is cut where letters meet digits; the order of the words
matters, and a run does not start inside a word).

- An exact id (case ignored) is a `match` by `id`. Else the text is compared with the product name and the aliases of the filaments that
  pass the maker filter: one filament is a `match` by `name` or `alias`; the exact name of filaments of two makers is `ambiguous`.
- A text that is only the name of a material family (`PLA`, `PETG-CF`), with no maker word, and that fits two filaments or more, is
  `ambiguous` with `matched_by: family`: a family is not a product, so every filament of it is a candidate.
- A row with `superseded_by` is an older sheet. An exact id selects it (`match`; the `note` says that a newer sheet exists), and so does the
  exact name or alias of the old sheet (`PLA Basic 2.0`). A list of candidates (family, maker or partial name) leaves out an older row whose
  newer row is in the list, and the `note` names the rows left out, so the current row of a product is the one that is offered.
- Else the filaments with a name that has the text as a part are the `candidates` of an `ambiguous` answer (`matched_by` `partial`,
  `name` or `vendor`; a text with only a maker word gives all filaments of the maker). One candidate is also `ambiguous`: a part of a
  name is not an exact name, so the caller asks the user. `differs` names the facts (`E_xy_mpa`, `E_z_mpa`, `strength_xy_mpa`,
  `strength_z_mpa`, `density_g_cm3`, `enclosure`, `hardened_nozzle`) on which the candidates differ.
- Else the answer is `none`. `suggestions` are the filaments whose compact names have a difflib ratio of at least
  `printers.SUGGEST_CUTOFF` (0.6) to the text, at most `printers.SUGGEST_MAX` (5), the best first; the two numbers are the ones of the
  printer catalog and no new number. A suggestion is never taken by itself. The `note` says how to go on: look up the data sheet of the
  maker, show the user the values with the address of the sheet, and call `save_material` after the user agrees. An empty text is `none`.
- `Resolution.to_dict()` is the reply of `find_material`, with the same keys for the three statuses: `ok`, `status`, `query`,
  `catalog_version`, `matched_by`, `origin`, `profile`, `derives`, `candidates`, `differs`, `suggestions`, `makers`, `user_file` and
  `note`. `derives` is `{sets, assumed, missing}`: what `material.filament: <id>` sets in a run (`material.E`, `material.density`),
  what stays at the default (`material.nu`), and what the profile cannot give.

**The key `material.filament`.** A text: an id, or a name or an alias that is one filament. `MATERIAL_OPTIONAL` holds it; the lever card is
`material.filament` (section 41; kind `requirement`, confidence `code`).

- With a filament, `material.E` and `material.density` come from the profile when the YAML does not give them. A key that the YAML gives
  wins. `E` is the LOWER of `E_xy_mpa` and `E_z_mpa` (a part loaded across the layers is the weaker case, and the engine has one isotropic
  modulus); with one of the two only, that one is taken, and the reason says which. A profile with no tensile modulus takes the same
  rule from `bending_modulus_xy_mpa` and `bending_modulus_z_mpa`; the label stays `filament:<id>` and the reason says
  "the bending modulus of the sheet; the sheet gives no tensile modulus" (and which value). `nu` is the profile value when the profile has one;
  the catalog has none, so it is the default 0.35 of the `material` block, labelled `assumed` with the reason "no data sheet gives it".
  A number that the profile does not have is labelled `assumed`. A density is the one of the sheet; a sheet that gives a range gives the middle of it (source `filament:<id>`, reason "the middle of the sheet range a-b"). Only a sheet with neither has a null density, and then it is the MEDIAN density of the shipped rows of the same
  `family` (read without case) that state one (the filament itself, the user rows and the rows of an older sheet are left out); the reason says "the median of N <family> rows of the
  catalog (<ids>)". With no such row it stays at the default 1.24 of the block, with the reason "the catalog has no density for this
  filament; the default of the problem file". `find_material` shows the value in `derives.assumed` and in `note`.
- The source label of a number is `yaml` (the YAML gave the key), `filament:<id>` (the profile gave it) or `assumed` (the default of the
  block, or the median density of the family of the filament). `Config.filament` is a `FilamentUse` (`profile`, and `keys`: one `(key, value, source, reason)` for each of `E`, `nu`, `density`);
  it is `None` without the key. `Config.material` stays a `Material` with the three numbers: the engine reads no other field.
- A filament with no tensile modulus and no bending modulus is an error when the YAML gives no `E`: a default modulus would change the result
  by a wrong factor.
  The error names the filament, the note of the profile and the ways on.
- A text that is not one filament is a `UserError` (`FilamentNotFound`) of one line: the key, the text, the candidates or the
  suggestions, and the ways on (`Use an id from the catalog, or remove material.filament and give E and density in the material block`,
  and the way to add a filament to the user file). A value that is not text is an error too. The error names the user filament file and
  its problems when it has any.
- `run.json`, key `filament` (at the top level; a run without the key `material.filament` has no such key, so the file is the one of
  before PM-2): `id`, `name`, `origin`, `catalog_version` (or null), `facts` (the profile: `name`, `maker`, `product`, `family`,
  `sheet_version`, `origin`, every fact field, `source_url`, `opened`, `tag`, and `source`, `field_sources` and `note` when the profile
  has them), `profile_sha256` and `material` (for each of `E`, `nu`, `density`: `value`, `source` and `reason` when there is one).
  `profile_sha256` is the sha256 of the name and the fact fields (`FACT_FIELDS`) as JSON with sorted keys and no blanks; the sources,
  dates, note and origin are not in it, so two runs with the same digest used the same filament facts. `FilamentUse.from_dict` takes the
  profile from this record and does not read a catalog: the record is the truth for that run, also when the catalog or the user file
  changed later. A bad value reads as "not stated". `run.json` has no `material` key (the three numbers are part of `problem_key`, which hashes `Config.material`, so a run with other numbers has another key); the key `filament` is the only record of where they came from.
- `topopt check` and `check_problem`: with a filament the result has the key `material` (`filament`, `name`, `origin`, `profile_from`,
  `catalog_version`, `sheet_version`, `tag`, `source_url`, `profile_sha256`, `material` with the source of each number, `printer` and
  `compat`, and `superseded_by` when the filament is an older sheet: the id of the newer row). The text has two lines. The first is `material: <name> (filament <id>, catalog <version>, sheet <v>): E 2080.9 MPa
  (filament:<id>, the lower of the XY and Z modulus), nu 0.35 (assumed, no data sheet gives it), density 1.04 g/cm3 (filament:<id>, the
  density of the sheet)`. The second is `material fit: <state>: <filament> on <printer>`, with one line for each check that is not `ok`;
  without a printer profile (`print.printer_model`) it says that no fit was checked. A filament that is an older sheet adds the line
  `material sheet: a newer sheet of this filament exists: <id>; the spool may be of either`; the YAML works as written. Without a filament the key and the lines are absent
  and the output is as before. They are facts: no run is refused because of them.

**The compatibility check.** `topopt.compat.check(printer, filament)` takes a `PrinterProfile` and a `FilamentProfile` and returns a
`Compat` (`state`, `printer`, `filament`, `reasons`, `drying`). It reads nothing else: no file, no catalog, no clock. Each check compares
two values that a source states, and the reason names both values and the source of each. There is no threshold of our own: a margin, a
factor or a "close enough" would be a new number. A value that a catalog does not state gives `unknown`, never a guess.

| Check | Rule |
|---|---|
| `printer_type` | A filament is for an `fdm` printer; another type is `no`. |
| `nozzle_temperature`, `bed_temperature` | The printer maximum against the filament range `[min, max]`: a maximum below the minimum is `no`; between the two is `care` (only the lower part of the range); at or above the maximum is `ok`. A missing value on either side is `unknown`. |
| `enclosure` | An `enclosed` or `heated` printer meets any enclosure need: `ok`, also when the sheet states nothing; but a filament with an `enclosed_note` is `care` there, with the text of the sheet. On an `open` printer: `required` is `no`, `recommended` is `care`, `"no"` is `ok`, and a sheet that states nothing is `unknown`. A printer that does not state its enclosure is `unknown` unless the sheet says `"no"`. |
| `chamber` | Only when the sheet names `chamber_c_min`. A `heated` printer whose maximum is at least the value is `ok`, below it is `no`; a printer without a chamber heater is `care`; a missing value is `unknown`. |
| `nozzle_wear` | A filament that asks for a hardened nozzle (or has fibre, with no word of the sheet about the nozzle) against the stock nozzle: a hardened steel or tungsten carbide nozzle is `ok`, any other is `care`, none stated is `unknown`. A filament that says nothing about the nozzle and does not say whether it is abrasive has `unknown`; one that needs no hardened nozzle has no line. |
| `extruder` | A soft filament, or a filament with `direct_drive: true` (the maker recommends a direct drive extruder), is `care` on a bowden extruder and `ok` on a direct one; no extruder type stated is `unknown`. |
| `material_model` | A soft (rubber-like) filament, `soft: true`, is `care` on every printer: a linear model does not fit this material. |
| `moisture` | A filament with `conditioned` values is `care` on every printer, and the reason gives the dry and the wet values. |

The state of the answer is the worst state of its checks: `no`, then `unknown`, then `care`, then `ok`. `no` means that a stated need is
above a stated limit of the printer as it ships; the user may have changed the printer. The check never stops a run. `drying` is the
drying setting of the maker as text; it is information and never changes the state. A test pins that `compat.py` imports nothing but
`__future__` and `dataclasses`.

**The user filament file.** `<work folder>/topopt-filaments.yaml` has filaments that the catalog does not have. It follows the rules of
the user printer file (section 18.7), with these points.

- **Where.** The work folder is the one of `topopt.workfolder.resolve(check=False).path` (section 10.1), the same as for the printers.
- **The schema** is the one of the catalog (`format: 1`), with these differences. The file needs no `catalog_version` and no `makers`
  (both are optional; a maker of the file that is not in the table becomes a maker with its own name as its word). A filament needs `id`,
  `maker`, `product`, `family` and a source: `source_url` (the data sheet that the agent found) or `source: user` (the user said the
  values). The other fields are optional; a field that is not given is `null`, which means unknown. A null needs no note. `opened` is
  optional. `tag` is optional (`maker TDS`, `maker page`, `third party` or `user`; the default is `user` for an entry with
  `source: user` and no page). `field_sources` maps a fact field to a page address or to the word `user`.
- **Merge.** `materials_catalog.catalog_for(folder)` returns the shipped filaments first, then the filaments of the file, as one `Catalog`
  (`resolve` takes it as its second argument; `materials_catalog.work_catalog()` uses the work folder). Every profile has `origin`:
  `catalog` or `user`. The file is read at each call (no cache), so a change is live at once.
- **No shadowing.** A filament of the file with the id of a shipped filament is not used: the problem names the shipped filament and
  offers another id (`<id>-user`). A filament whose name or alias is already a name of another filament of its maker is not used either.
  Two entries with one id: the first is used.
- **A fault is a fact.** `Catalog.user_file` (`path`, `exists`, `entries`, `problems`) holds what is wrong. A fault of the whole file leaves the
  file unused. A fault of one entry leaves that entry out and the others in. Nothing is raised; the shipped catalog works as without
  the file. `find_material` shows `user_file`, and the refusal of `load_config` names the problems.
- **Writing.** `materials_catalog.save_user_filament(folder, profile)` (the MCP tool `save_material`) checks the entry as the loader does,
  merges by id (it replaces a user filament with the same id; the other entries and the top keys stay as they are), and writes the file
  with `runinfo.write_atomic`. It refuses, and writes nothing, for: a profile that is not a mapping; a file that cannot be read or is not
  valid YAML (the file is not changed); a fault of the entry; a shipped id; a name that another filament of the maker has. The reply is
  `{ok, path, profile, created, replaced, note}` (+ `problems` of the rest of the file), or `{ok: false, error}`. `note` names the fields
  that are null, says when the filament has no tensile modulus, and says when a replaced entry changes what a YAML that names its id
  gets at its next check or run (the YAML text is the same, so `yaml_sha256` of the checkpoint, the case record and the ratchet pins do
  not see it; old runs keep their record, and `profile_sha256` tells whether two runs used the same facts).

**Tools.** `find_material(name)` (read-only; the keys of `Resolution.to_dict()` above), `save_material(profile)` (strict arguments, as every tool: an
unknown argument name is a refusal that does nothing (section 10, "Strict argument names"); it needs a work folder that the server can write) and `printer_materials(printer=None)` (read-only). All three are in `READ_ONLY_TOOLS`
(section 41): a filament entry changes no run until a YAML names it. Each description is under 4,096 characters. The mock
`evals/mocks/topopt/_tools.json` lists them. `printer_materials` takes a printer as `find_printer` does (a name or an id; without it, the
`print.printer_model` of the preferences) and returns `ok`, `printer` (`id`, `name`, `origin`, `from`, `named_by`), `catalog_version`,
`counts`, `groups`, `available`, `user_file` and `note`. `groups` has the keys `ok`, `care`, `no` and `unknown`; each holds a list of
`{id, name, family, origin, available, source, reasons}` for every current filament of the catalog and the user file in that state (a row with
`superseded_by` is not listed; `note` says how many are left out and names them), and `reasons`
lists the checks that are not `ok` with both values (the printer source is in `printer.from`, and the filament source in `source`, so the
long list names each only once). `available` lists the filaments of `filaments.available` of the preferences with their state (an id of the list that is not
found now is left out of the list by the read of the file and named in `not_used`, and the other ids stay; an older sheet has its state and a note with the id of the newer sheet; a direct call of `materials_catalog.printer_fit` with an unknown id gives state null and a note). A printer that is not one printer of the catalog is `{ok: false, status, candidates,
suggestions, error}`.

**Preferences and skills.** `material.filament` and `filaments.available` are preferences (section 10.2). `start-here` (Step 1b, "The
filaments") asks the user for the filament names, calls `find_material`, shows the derived values and `printer_materials` for the printer,
and saves the id with `save_preferences`. On `ambiguous` it offers the candidates. On `none` the agent looks up the data sheet of the
maker, shows the values with their sources to the user, and calls `save_material` after the user agrees; a value it cannot find stays
null, and the agent asks the user for it. `part-to-topopt` says the same (its section "The filament"). Both are offers: tools inform, the
agent decides. A state of `printer_materials` is a fact for the user to weigh, not a stop.

## 19. SDF mesh step (added with C1)

The mesh step of `topopt.post.finish` makes the final mesh from the last density snapshot. It has two methods.

- `blur`: the method of section 9 (Gaussian blur of the density, one global iso level, Taubin, exact keep-out cut).
- `sdf` (default): volume-preserving smoothing of a signed distance field (SDF). Code: `topopt/smooth_sdf.py`. The only other
  change in `topopt/post.py` is the choice of the method (`mesh_step`) and the `mesh` record.

**Choice of the method.** YAML key `settings.mesh_method` (`sdf` or `blur`, default `sdf`). CLI flag
`topopt run --mesh-method sdf|blur` (it wins over the YAML key). `run.json` has the key `mesh_method` (added in section 19). A run
folder without `mesh_method` gets `sdf`. The envelope fill (below, F4-55) has its own key, `settings.envelope_fill`: a run folder from before F4-55 has no
`envelope_fill` in `run.json` and gets `off`, so a post step on it (a resume of a finished run, `post.finish`) makes the mesh it made before F4-55. With `blur`, `result/final.stl`, `preview.bin` and the old keys of `metrics.json` are
bit-equal to the output of the code before section 19 (the key `mesh` is new). The optimizer files do not change: with
`OMP_NUM_THREADS`, `MKL_NUM_THREADS`, `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS` and `NUMBA_NUM_THREADS` at 1, the labels, the snapshots and the
compliance are bit-equal to the code before section 19, in both modes. With more threads, the compliance differs by about
1e-12 (relative) from run to run (also the code before section 19 against itself); the uint8 snapshots stay equal.

**Region files.** `run.json` has `region_files` (paths of the region STL files: relative to the YAML folder, or absolute if they are
outside it; the keys are `design`, `fixed`, `keep_out`, `solid` and `load`). The post step looks at the stored path, then at the YAML folder plus the file name. A file that is not there gives a
warning and the voxel labels give the shape of that group.

**Method `sdf`.** The lengths are in voxel sizes `h`; `up` is 2 (the fine pitch is `h/2`, `post.UPSAMPLE`).

1. The density is made finer (trilinear) and cut at 0.5. This is the sharp field. Solid islands that do not touch a frozen region
   (fixed or load) are removed.
2. Frozen regions (fixed and load) keep their exact shape. If the STL files of all fixed and load regions exist, the field uses
   them (within 3 fine voxels of the surface the distance to the nearest of dense samples of the surface, ray-cast sign; this is not
   the exact distance to the triangles: it is never smaller than that distance, and it is larger in 99 % of the voxels of the band on the
   hook, the ladle and the bracket, by 3 % of a fine voxel on average and by up to 0.7 of a fine voxel in the worst voxel; measured at
   `c080f62`, one Linux x86_64 host); else it uses the voxel labels. Keep-out regions
   work the same way. A keep-out region wins where it overlaps a frozen region (as in the labels of section 3).
   `metrics.json` says which source was used (`mesh.sources`). A missing STL gives a warning.
3. The sharp field becomes an SDF (negative inside, half a voxel from the voxel centres). It is smoothed with the low-pass
   `2G - G^2` (G is a Gaussian of sigma `1.0 h`; the pipeline uses 0.9 mm on a 0.5 mm voxel).
   The second-order shrink of a plain Gaussian cancels in this form.
   A local level shift `c(x)` then keeps the solid volume in a moving Gaussian window (sigma 1.67 sigma) equal to the volume of the
   sharp field. 13 levels from -0.67 sigma to +0.67 sigma are tried. The test of a level counts the frozen solid as solid and the
   keep-out solid as empty, so these regions do not disturb the shift. With the limit of the field to the envelope (below, "Limit of the
   field to the envelope"), it counts only the solid inside the envelope.
   (Source: `smooth_vp` of the s9 print pass of the pipeline. The ratios of the pipeline are kept; the lengths scale with `h`.)
   Members of 2 voxels or more stay at sigma 1.0 h. At sigma 1.5 h a 2-voxel member
   that joins a frozen region can break near the joint.
4. Blend: the field is `max(min(F, U), E, -C)`, with F the smooth field, U the frozen SDF, E the SDF of the envelope (only with the
   limit of the field) and C the keep-out SDF. The frozen solid blends into the smooth part because it was part of the field when it was smoothed.
5. Marching cubes at level 0. Taubin smoothing (10 passes, lambda 0.5, mu -0.53, uniform Laplacian). Vertices on a frozen or
   keep-out surface, or on the envelope with the limit of the field (closer than 0.35 fine voxels), stay. A body that does not touch a frozen region (the test is `U` under
   0.35 fine voxels at a vertex) is removed, in every source case. The step logs one warning with the count and the volume.
   A void (a closed shell that turns inward: its signed volume is negative) is not a body: it stays with the body around it, and
   step 6 decides on it. A void inside a removed body goes with that body, and the removed volume is the material of the body.
6. Exact shapes: with STL files, the mesh is united with each fixed and load STL and the keep-out STLs are subtracted
   (manifold3d, float32 input, as `subtract_keep_out` does). The frozen shape is then exact, and the keep-out cut is exact.
   Just before the booleans, with the limit of the field, the vertices that lie inside a plane that the design space shares with a region by
   less than the band are moved onto it (below, "Limit of the field to the envelope"); then the vertices near a region face are moved into the
   region (below, "Snap to the region faces"), and the
   mesh is cut at a plane that the design space shares with a region and that it stands past over a face of that region (below, "Cut at the shared planes"),
   and then cut to the envelope (below, "Cut to the envelope").
   After the booleans, each closed shell that holds empty space (a void: the faces turn outward from the material, so the signed volume of
   the shell is negative) is dropped before the mesh is oriented (`smooth_sdf._drop_voids`). The snap can close the narrow rim of a thin slit
   between a region face and the design, and the exact union then seals the rest of the slit as a void. Without this step, the orientation
   in step 8 turns the void the other way out, and the file holds a thin second body with outward normals inside the material. The volume of a
   filled void is material: the calibration (step 7) sees it. The fact is `mesh.voids_filled`; the step logs one warning when it fills a void.
   A void that encloses a closed cavity of the sharp field stays: a component of the empty fine voxels that does not reach the border
   of the grid (`smooth_sdf.closed_cavities`; a keep-out region that the solid encloses is one too), tested at its voxel farthest from the solid.
   The design has a cavity there, and the volume target (the sharp volume) does not hold it, so the mesh keeps it as a cavity: its volume is
   not material, in the mesh and in the target. The orientation (`_orient`, also in the interface step and `part_only`) keeps the faces of a
   closed shell with a negative volume inside a shell with a positive volume turned inward. The fact is `mesh.voids_kept`; the step logs one
   warning, and `print_check` reports the cavity (`closed_voids`). Before 0.5.1 the wall of such a void was removed as a body that does not
   touch a frozen region (step 5): the void was filled and its volume left the target, so the calibration flipped between about +30 % and
   -25 % as the shift opened and closed the skin over the void. With the fill (`settings.envelope_fill`), the shift of the fill thins the wall
   of a cavity from both of its faces, as any member (`mesh.envelope_fill.note`).
7. Volume: a global level shift is found by up to `calibrate_steps` rounds after the first build (3 by default; up to `calibrate_steps_fill`, 8, with the envelope fill or after a miss, see below; 3 secant steps and one full build each; a round can stop early, see `calibration[].stopped`), so that the volume of the final
   mesh meets the volume of the sharp field minus the volume of the removed bodies. The loop ends when the error is below 5e-4. A run without
   the fill that still misses by `SdfParams.extra_rounds_from` (1e-3, the bar of #348) or more after `calibrate_steps` rounds gets more
   rounds, up to `SdfParams.calibrate_steps_fill` (8), until the error is below 5e-4, and from then on moves the target by the miss divided
   by the measured slope of the final volume to the target, as a fill run does (below). So a run that misses by less than 0.1 % after the 3
   rounds keeps its bytes (#348: the cut to the envelope takes about half of each level change, and the bar of the envelope cut tests missed
   by 1.15 % after 3 rounds; it now meets the target in 6 builds, -0.03 %). Each extra round is one more build of the mesh, up to 5 more in a
   pass. An extra round that misses more than the best round from the third on ends the loop, and the best round is kept (its `calibration`
   entry gets `next_round_error`, the later rounds are not listed; the snap fact is measured at its level): the volume can jump with the
   level, for example when a slit closes and its void is filled, and then the rounds circle round the target. So within one pass the result
   is never worse than the round of the plain limit. The dry pass before a pass with cuts stops its extra rounds at the first round with a
   cut: the pass with the cuts starts again. `volume_error_pct` is the error to the sharp
   field. It is the residual of this calibration: a global shift can pay for a loss in one member with material in another. So
   `mesh.local_loss` gives the volume of the sharp field that lies more than 1.5 fine voxels outside the mesh (a shift cannot hide
   it). The sharp field of `sdf` has the exact STL regions, the sharp field of `blur` has the voxel labels (up to half a voxel more
   at each frozen face), so the two volumes are not the same number.
8. The file is made clean for float32. The mesh is made float32, `Manifold.simplify(1e-5 mm)` merges the near-coincident
   vertices that a float32 rounding would pinch (an exact union leaves them at seams), then the mesh is made float32 again.
   The STL is loaded again from the bytes that were written. `mesh.watertight` and the top-level `watertight` come from that
   reloaded file (watertight, consistent winding, positive volume). If it is not a closed manifold, the step logs one warning
   with the bodies, open edges, non-manifold edges and zero-area faces, and `watertight` is `false`. (For `blur`, the top-level
   `watertight` is still the old in-memory value, so that the old keys stay bit-equal.)

**Snap to the region faces (inside step 6; F4-27b).** The smooth surface does not lie on the exact faces of the regions (the field of step 2 is
not the exact distance, and the smooth surface runs into a face at a small angle). The exact union or cut of two surfaces that are almost
coplanar then leaves a strip of micro-steps and slivers along the seam (edges down to 5e-7 mm on the test part below), and on some parts fold edges and
self-crossings. The surface preparation of `topopt verify` removes most of these edges, and gmsh can still stop at the seam. The snap (`smooth_sdf.snap_into_regions`) moves each
vertex of the smooth mesh that lies OUTSIDE a region and within the band `pin_tol` x fine voxel (0.35 fine voxels, the band that pins vertices in
step 5) of the exact surface of the union of the fixed and load STL files, or of the union of the keep-out STL files (the nearer one wins),
to the point one band deep INSIDE the region: the closest point on that surface plus one band along the line from the vertex through that
point. "Outside" is a point-in-solid test of the whole region (`trimesh.proximity.signed_distance`): the side of the closest face where the closest
point lies in that face, and a ray test against the whole solid where it lies on an edge or at a corner, so a reflex edge (the tip of a notch
narrower than 90 degrees) does not move the vertices that lie inside the solid. The exact boolean then removes the sheet that lay off the face.
A vertex on the face (within 1e-8 mm of it, the merge tolerance of trimesh), a vertex inside a region and a vertex farther than the band do not move.
A vertex whose target point is not inside the region does not move either (a region thinner than one band); `snap.target_outside` counts them.
Where a region is thinner than two bands, the vertices from its two sides can cross each other inside it before the union (not guarded).
A move that would turn a face over (the normal of the face after the move has a dot product of 0 or less with its normal before) is halved,
for the vertices of the faces that turn, until no face turns over. The band, the depth and the rule have no setting and no number of their own.
The snap runs after Taubin and after the removal of the
bodies that touch no frozen region, and before the booleans, so the volume calibration of step 7 builds the mesh with the move: the global level
shift pays back the material that the move takes at the faces. A group of regions without STL files (labels) has no exact boolean and is not
snapped. The interface shapes of section 23 are not snapped: `interfaces.apply_step` makes their booleans after this step. If the exact step
fails, the smooth mesh is used as it was, not moved. If the snap itself fails, or the exact surfaces of the regions cannot be made, the
mesh is not moved and the exact step runs. `mesh.snap` has the facts (table below).

Measured at `c080f62` against `de085e1` (the same code without the snap), one Linux x86_64 host, manifold3d 3.5.4, on public parts (the hook
the recorded hook run (of an older build, `recordings/hook_*`; a clone may not hold it), the bracket of `examples/interfaces/bracket.yaml` at 1.0 mm, the ladle of `examples/ladle/ladle.yaml` at 3.25 mm;
`finish` on a copy of the run folder):

| part | edges under 0.05 mm | vertices moved | fold edges, crossings | volume of `final.stl` | new vertices to the old surface: mean, largest | old vertices to the new surface: mean, largest | final level shift (calibration) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| hook | 355 of 93,381 (0.38 %) -> 96 of 89,733 (0.11 %) | 3,083 of 46,114 (largest move 0.42 mm, band 0.21 mm) | 0, 0 -> 0, 0 | 20,322.7 -> 20,322.2 mm3 | 0.009, 0.33 mm | 0.005, 0.21 mm | -0.1051 -> -0.1035 mm |
| bracket | 204 of 30,927 (0.66 %) -> 169 of 29,652 (0.57 %) | 337 of 15,824 (0.35 mm, band 0.175 mm) | 0, 0 -> 0, 0 | 5,398.2 -> 5,398.3 mm3 | 0.006, 0.19 mm | 0.004, 0.15 mm | 0 -> 0.0024 mm |
| ladle | 1,623 of 102,039 (1.59 %) -> 185 of 57,273 (0.32 %) | 4,571 of 24,072 (1.14 mm, band 0.57 mm) | 0, 0 -> 0, 0 | 190,972.4 -> 190,977.0 mm3 | 0.035, 0.89 mm | 0.022, 0.64 mm | 0.0299 -> 0.0446 mm |

The edges that stay lie on the region faces (the retriangulation of the exact face along the union line) and are 0.01 to 0.05 mm long. The
distances are one-sided distances between the two STL files (vertices to surface). The vertices with the largest distance lie on a region
face, where the smooth surface meets the face at a small angle; probably the contact line then moves by about the band divided by the tangent of that
angle (an explanation, not a measurement; the 300 largest on the hook and the bracket all lie on a face; on the ladle most do, and the largest, 0.89 mm, is a vertex 12 mm from any region, not explained). The regions stay exact (`mesh.checks`: `uncovered_mm3` at most 2e-4 mm3, keep-out
`intersect_mm3` at most 1.3e-6 mm3 on these parts). The mean edge of the STL grows, so the default tet size of `topopt verify` grows (hook
1.75 -> 1.94 mm, ladle 3.36 -> 4.28 mm; the bracket, which `verify` meshes as `nominal.stl`, 1.61 -> 1.59 mm). At the same mesh size (the old
default) the stiffness of the verify runs changes by +0.7 % and +0.9 % (hook, two load cases), +2.9 % (bracket) and +0.05 % to +0.4 % (ladle, three
load cases), and no run is refused in either version. This is the difference of two tet meshes of two surfaces that differ by hundredths of a millimetre;
it is not a claim about the part. On a small test part (14 x 6 x 11.4 mm, `tests/test_tet_clean_retry.py`, shelf tilted by 8 degrees) the edges under
1e-3 mm go from 94 to 0 and the edges under 0.05 mm from 733 to 109.

**Cut at the shared planes (inside step 6; F4-50).** The smooth surface can go past the exact face of a frozen region, and the exact union with the
region does not take that material away. Three effects add up. The frozen voxels are a staircase: the exact face lies anywhere in the last voxel
that the field holds, up to half a fine voxel in front of the voxel boundary. The low-pass moves the zero level by a little more (on a plate that
is thin against the sigma, about 0.2 mm at a fine voxel of 1.25 mm). The level shift of the calibration adds its own. The snap takes only the
vertices within the band (0.35 fine voxels) into the region. What is farther out stays as a thin raised patch on the region face (footbridge
at volume fraction 0.15: a solid deck that is flush with the side planes of the design space, patches up to 0.56 mm high).
The step `smooth_sdf.shared_planes` finds the planes that a face of the design space shares with a face of a fixed, load or solid region: a face of
the design space lies in the plane, the whole design space is on its inner side (so also a non-convex design space has only its bounding planes), and a
face of a region lies in the plane with the same outward normal (all 3 vertices of the triangle on it). "On the plane" is the rounding of the
float32 STL files (`2 sqrt(3)` steps of `np.spacing` at the largest coordinate; 0 for round numbers); it is not a setting. Two faces that
differ by more are not one plane: a tilted pair from two CAD exports can be missed, and the cut then does nothing, as before. The planes
need the STL of the design space (`run.json` `region_files.design`) and the STL files of all fixed and load regions; else there are none
(`plane_clip.note` says why). For each plane it also gives the boxes of the region faces in it: one box (in the plane, `x . u` and `x . w`) for each
connected piece of coplanar region faces.
`smooth_sdf.clip_to_planes` runs in every build, after the snap and before the exact union. A vertex is a reason to cut a plane when it is
farther out than that rounding, lies over a face of a region (its place in the plane is in a box, grown by the band of the snap, `plane_clip.margin_mm`)
and is not in a region (a frozen region may go past a plane in another part of its shape, and the union puts it back). Then the whole mesh is cut
at the plane (manifold3d `trim_by_plane`, so the result is a closed body): the side face of the part is flat at the plane, also away from the
region face. A plane that the mesh goes past only away from the faces of the regions is not cut. There the mesh is past the design space by itself
(for example, a coarse voxel reaches past the design STL), not past the face of a region. `plane_clip.left` lists such planes, so that the agent
sees them. A mesh with no reason to cut is not touched (the same arrays).
A plane that a united interface shape of section 23 goes past (a boss or a tube that leaves the design space through that face) is not cut:
the shape is part of the field, the smooth surface joins it, and the cut would take away the join. `plane_clip.skipped_for_interfaces` counts
these planes. The interface shapes of section 23 are not cut: `interfaces.apply_step` unites them after this step. The union puts the exact region
back, also where it goes past the plane. If the cut fails, the mesh is not cut and `plane_clip.error` has the reason.
The volume calibration (step 7) builds the mesh with the cut: the global level shift pays back the material that the cut takes. Without the
limit of the field to the envelope (below), it first runs without the cut, in a dry run that only looks for the planes to cut. When the last
round of that pass has a part past a plane over a region face, the calibration runs again from its start with the cut (`plane_clip.passes` is 2).
Without such a part it runs once (`passes` 1), and the file has the same bytes as before F4-50. With the limit, the calibration runs once, with
the cuts from its first round, and the field stands past no plane (below, "Limit of the field to the envelope"). The reason: the cut of an early round would move the level shift of the later rounds, also when the
last round has nothing to cut. A round that cuts has the key `plane_clip_removed_mm3` in its `calibration` entry (the key is absent when the
round did not cut). `plane_clip` itself is the record of the last round, the one that gives the file.

**Cut to the envelope (inside step 6; F4-51).** The envelope is the room that the user gave: the design space, the fixed, load and solid regions, and the
union pieces of the interfaces of section 23 (a boss, the wall of a tube, an STL union) at their as-printed size (`interfaces.Context.union_meshes`,
with the stock). A part that sits next to other parts (a wall, a shelf, a housing) can collide with a result that goes past it, so the result of the
`sdf` method stays inside it by default. There is no key for this. Keep-out regions and the cut pieces of the interfaces (bores, the hole of a tube,
faces) are not in the envelope: they take material away, they do not give room. The smooth surface goes past the design space for the same reasons as
in "Cut at the shared planes", and on every kind of face: the voxel layer at the face, the low-pass and the level shifts. On 28 finished runs (after the cut at
the shared planes), 25 had a vertex more than 0.1 mm past the envelope. The largest excess of those runs was 0.04 to 0.71 of the voxel size (0.4 to 0.7 for
most), and 3.65 mm at most (voxel 6.5 mm).
`smooth_sdf.make_envelope` makes the envelope once (the union of the files, manifold3d) with the distance field of its surface. `smooth_sdf.cut_to_envelope`
runs in every build, after the cut at the shared planes and before the exact union with the regions. A vertex is past when it is outside the envelope by more
than the rounding of the float32 files (`_plane_tol` of all the files; the same rule as the planes, no setting). A mesh with no vertex past is not touched
(the same arrays). Otherwise the whole mesh is intersected with the envelope (manifold3d), so the cut face lies on the faces of the envelope. The region
STL files are united after it as before, so the regions stay exact, and the interface step (`interfaces.apply_step`) unites and cuts the exact interface
shapes after this step, for `final.stl` and for `nominal.stl` from the same mesh. The mesh is cut to the envelope with the as-printed pieces for both files:
`nominal.stl` is the same mesh with the nominal union pieces, which are not larger, so it lies inside the envelope too.
The envelope is made only when the design space has an STL file that is a closed mesh and the fixed, load and solid regions have STL files. Without them the
mesh is not cut and `reason` says why (a design file that is not there, or not closed, logs one warning). If the cut fails, the mesh is not cut and `error`
has the reason. Both cuts can act on one mesh: the cut at the planes goes first (it cuts the whole plane when a part is past it over a region face), and the
fact of the envelope counts what is past after it.
The volume calibration (step 7) builds the mesh with both cuts: the level shift pays back what they take, so the mass target holds and the members get a little
thicker. With the limit of the field (below) the calibration runs once, with the cuts from its first round (`passes` 1). Without it, the calibration first runs without any cut (a dry run that counts the vertices past a plane over a region face, and past the envelope). When the last
round of that pass has such a vertex, the calibration runs again from its start with the cuts (`envelope_cut.passes` and `plane_clip.passes` are 2). Without
one it runs once (`passes` 1) and the file has the same bytes as before F4-51, apart from a run that misses by 0.1 % or more after 3 rounds (step 7, #348). A round that cuts has the key `envelope_cut_removed_mm3` in its `calibration` entry.
After the cut, the exact union, the removal of the bodies that touch no frozen region, `_drop_voids` and the float32 clean-up of step 8 give one closed body for each
part of the design (the shell count of the file: `stl_roundtrip.bodies`, with the vertices merged).
The fact `mesh.envelope_cut` (table below) names, for each face of the design space, the vertices past, the largest excess before the cut and the volume that
the cut took. A vertex goes to the face of the design space with the closest point to it. A face is a plane facet (a connected group of two or more coplanar
triangles of the design STL; `kind` `plane`, with `normal` and `offset_mm`) or the `curved` part (all other triangles). The volume of each piece that the cut
takes is split between the faces by the vertices of the piece, so a piece at an edge counts for both faces and the parts add up to `volume_removed_mm3`.

**Limit of the field to the envelope (inside steps 3 to 5; #319).** Most of the material past the envelope comes from the optimized field itself: a design
voxel whose centre is inside the design space reaches up to half a voxel past the face. On 7 runs of the series (the post step on copies, the stages of the
kept build), this voxel layer gave 39 to 92 % of the largest excess. The low-pass added 0.03 to 0.54 mm, the global level shift up to 0.36 mm and Taubin at
most 0.07 mm, and the snap only took material away. The cut alone took that material after marching cubes, and the global level shift paid it back in a
second calibration pass, as a thicker part everywhere. So the `sdf` step limits the field to the envelope before marching cubes, by default
(`SdfParams.envelope_limit`; no YAML key):
- `smooth_sdf.envelope_sdf` gives the SDF E of the envelope on the fine grid: the sign of the ray-cast mask of `stl_sdf`, the exact distance to the
  triangles of the envelope (`_triangle_distance`) on the voxels within 2 fine voxels (2 layers of the 26 neighbours) of the voxels next to its
  surface, and the clip value of `stl_sdf` farther away. That holds every voxel closer than 2 fine voxels to a face that the mask resolves. The distance of `stl_sdf` goes to random surface samples and is too large by up to 0.7 of a fine voxel, so a limit made with
  it lay up to 0.4 of a fine voxel past the face. E needs no distance transform of the whole grid: it takes the distances in slabs of 16 grid planes.
  Measured on a generated lattice of 14 million fine voxels: E alone peaks at 18 bytes per fine voxel, and the grid stage of the step (before marching
  cubes) at 64 bytes per fine voxel (main: 57 to 59). A grid point on the face counts as just outside (1e-3 fine voxel): marching cubes on a value at
  the level makes faces of no area and a flat body that no boolean takes.
- Step 3: the local window of `c(x)` counts only the solid inside the envelope. So the volume that the limit takes goes back near the face where it was
  taken, to the member that lost it, not to the whole part.
- Step 4: the blend takes the maximum with E, so the surface does not go past a face of the envelope.
- Step 5: the vertices on the envelope (closer than 0.35 fine voxels) stay in Taubin.
