- Step 6: a vertex that lies inside a shared plane (a plane of the design space that a region face lies in too, see "Cut at the shared planes")
  by less than the band of the snap moves onto the plane (`smooth_sdf.flush_to_planes`), where its foot lies on the envelope and the vertex is not
  in a frozen region; a move that would turn a face over is halved, as in the snap. A vertex in a region stays: the union keeps the region there,
  and a member pulled back onto the plane out of a region left a loose body that touched the region face only in the plane. With the limit nothing stands past such a plane, so the cut at the planes, which made the side of
  the part flush with the plane before, does nothing. A surface that ends a hair inside the plane then met the region face in that plane with a
  strip narrower than a tenth of a millimetre after the exact union: on b2_bridge of the series 0.04 mm wide, and the surface preparation of
  `topopt verify` folded it at every mesh size from 4.75 to 5.25 mm. The fact is `envelope_cut.flush`.
- Step 7: the calibration runs once, with the cuts from its first round (`passes` 1). The cut to the envelope stays as the safety net: marching cubes
  cuts a concave edge of the envelope with a chamfer, so a few vertices can still lie past it there, and the cut takes them.
Without an envelope (above, `reason`), with `SdfParams.envelope_limit` off, or when `envelope_sdf` fails (one warning), the field is not limited, the
calibration runs as before the limit (the dry pass, then the pass with the cuts), and `envelope_cut.field_limit_note` says why. Such a run keeps its bytes.
The time of `envelope_sdf` is `envelope_cut.t_s.field_limit`; it runs before the mesh step, so `t_s.mesh_step` does not hold it. Measured on 28
finished runs (the post step on copies, against main with the cut alone, `d68bdc5`): `passes` is 1 in all 28 (main: 2 in 27). `vertices_beyond` is 0
in 9 runs and 3 to 59 in the others (main: 23 to 7340, 0 only in b1_bridge), the largest excess 0.60 mm (main: 3.65 mm), and the cut takes 0 to 418
mm3 (main: up to 19299 mm3). With main and this step run one after the other on each run, all of `make_mesh_sdf` takes 0.46 to 1.52 times the time
of main (median 0.78), `envelope_sdf` 0.2 to 3.9 s of it, and the peak memory of the post step is 0.78 to 1.02 times that of main. On the 9 runs
with nothing left past, the step takes 0.64 to 2.30 times the time before F4-51 (`0330dfa`, median 0.93): with the limit, the second round of the
calibration overshoots (on 7 of the 9 runs the volume of the build moves 2.1 to 6.4 times as far as its target, 2.1 to 2.5 on 5 of them; on
hook_CS it moves the other way), so some runs take 3 or 4 builds where they took 1 before.
The mass changes by -0.04 to +0.29 % (the largest: 0.02 g on the 6.9 g bracket_R_v14). In `topopt verify` (61 load cases, the tet mesh size of the
base of #300) the median change against main is -0.39 % (-3.99 to +1.91 %), and 9 cases are more than 2 % less stiff than the uncut result
(with the cut alone: 6). The 4 cases of phone_stand_CS and ladle_CS that the cut alone made 3.2
to 5.4 % less stiff than the uncut result are 2.2 to 3.9 % less stiff now, and stiffer than with the cut at 0.94, 1.00 and 1.06 times the mesh
size. bracket_R_v14 pull_down (+7.5 %; +4.0 to +7.6 % at the three sizes) and hook_R_v17 pull_off (+5.0 %) keep their price: the optimizer counts
the voxel layer past the face (up to half a voxel) as material, and no step after it can add that back inside the design space. shelf_bracket_R is
0.8 to 1.9 % less stiff than with the cut at the three sizes, and -0.5 to +1.1 % against the uncut result. Every run with an envelope gets new
bytes, also b1_bridge, which had nothing past after the snap: before the snap it had 9973 vertices up to 0.39 mm past.

**Envelope fill (before step 3; F4-55).** A face of the design space that is slanted to the grid axes (for example 2 to 4 degrees) gives a staircase in the density
field: the voxel layer at the face is full at some places and empty at others. The low-pass keeps the steps, and the cut to the envelope makes only the top of each
step flat, so the face shows panels, a step every few millimetres. A finer grid makes the steps denser. The key `settings.envelope_fill` switches the step: `off` (default: the step does not run; the file has the bytes it had before F4-55), `auto` (the step runs, but skips itself when the growth is a large share of the mass, see the cap below)
or `on` (the step runs also above the cap). `auto` or `on` make sense for a part with slanted faces whose look counts more than a few percent of stiffness (see the cost below). `topopt run --envelope-fill auto|on|off` wins over the key.
YAML 1.1 reads an unquoted `on` and `off` as booleans: the loader takes `true` as `on` and `false` as `off`. Any other value is an error of the loader that names the three values.
`run.json` has the key `envelope_fill` with the value.
When the envelope is known (the same conditions as the cut to the envelope: a closed design space STL and STL files for the fixed, load and solid regions), the sharp
field grows to the design space surface after the islands are removed and before the volume target is taken (`smooth_sdf.grow_to_surface`):
1. `d` is the signed distance of the design space surface on the fine grid (negative inside).
2. A candidate is a fine voxel that is not in the field and not in a keep-out region, with `-surface_depth * h < d < surface_overshoot * pitch`
   (`SdfParams.surface_depth` 1.0 coarse voxel, `SdfParams.surface_overshoot` 1.0 fine voxel; no YAML key).
3. For a candidate, `n` is the outward unit gradient of `d` (central differences). The candidate is grown when the field holds the nearest fine voxel of
   `v - k * n` for some `k` from 1 to `K = floor((surface_depth * h + surface_overshoot * pitch) / pitch)`. A candidate with a zero gradient is not grown.
   So the valleys under the steps are filled, and nothing grows sideways into a window where a gap meets the design space surface.
4. A group of grown voxels that does not join the field is dropped (it would be a loose body).
The growth has a cap: with `auto`, when the volume that it would add inside the design space (`grown_inside_mm3`) is above `SdfParams.fill_max_share` (0.05, 5 %; no YAML number) of the
volume target, the step skips itself, logs one warning and `reason` names the share and the cap. With `on` the step runs above the cap, logs one warning, and the fact has `cap_overridden` true. The field, the calibration rounds and the file are then the
ones of a run with the switch off. The reason: the mass-neutral calibration pays for the growth by thinning the members, and on a coarse, sparse part (measured:
the 2 mm cantilever of the optimizer tests, 36 % of the target) the thin members break away as loose bodies. On the measured parts the share was 0.98 % (bracket), 1.65 % (test bar), 2.05 % (drone arm), 2.29 % (ladle), 3.5 % (test part with slanted faces), 8.9 % (the short hook run) and 35.7 % (the 2 mm cantilever).
The overshoot voxels lie past the surface: the cut to the envelope takes them away and makes the face flat. The volume target stays the sharp volume
BEFORE the growth, so the mass target of the user does not change: the level shift of the calibration pays for the grown material. When the step ran, the
calibration takes up to `SdfParams.calibrate_steps_fill` (8) rounds instead of `calibrate_steps` (3); the loop still ends when the error is below 5e-4, so
a part that needs 3 rounds takes 3. With the fill the target of a round is moved by the miss divided by the measured slope of the final volume to the target
(the slope of the last two rounds, kept between `SdfParams.fill_slope_min` 0.2 and `fill_slope_max` 1.5; the first update uses the slope 1). Reason: the face lies on the envelope,
so about half of each level change is cut away, and the linear update (slope 1, used by every other run in its first `calibrate_steps` rounds) halves the miss in each round. Measured: the test bar 4 builds against 9
(last error -0.013 % against -0.062 %), the test part with slanted faces 5 against 9, the drone arm 5 against 9. When the step did not run, nothing changes: the mesh has the bytes it had before F4-55 (a run with the switch off, a run
without an envelope, or `blur`), apart from a run that misses by 0.1 % or more after 3 rounds (step 7, #348).
The step costs post-step time: the distance field of the design space, the growth, and more calibration builds (the dry first pass and the pass with the cuts both run). Measured side by side
on the same host (post-step time, with the fill against without it): the drone arm 334 s against 191 s (host load 9.9 at the start and 62 at the end), `examples/hook/hook.yaml` at 1.2 mm
93 s against 65 s (load 62 to 82). The slope update of the calibration keeps the builds at 4 to 5 for each pass. Cost near the cap: on `examples/interfaces/bracket.yaml` at 1.5 mm (12 passes) the fill adds 4.46 % of the target, just under the cap, and the mass-neutral calibration then moves the level by -0.157 mm,
so every member is that much thinner. Stiffness at the same mass: the grown skin carries little load, and the members pay for it. Measured with `verify` on one run of
`examples/ladle/ladle.yaml` (fill against `off`): at the example settings (3.25 mm, 80 passes, share 2.29 %) the stiffness of the three load cases falls by 1.7 to 3.6 %;
at 6.5 mm and 30 passes (share 3.51 %) it falls by 7 to 21 %, and the stress by volume rises by 28 to 42 %. The 5 % cap bounds the risk of loose bodies, not this cost. Thin walls: the area of the surface over a
wall thinner than 1.2 mm can change a little; read the print check on the result. The step does not change the joins with the frozen regions.
The fact `mesh.envelope_fill` (table below) records the step. A resume of a finished run reads the key again (the post step reads it). In the checkpoint
(`checkpoint.effective_settings`) the key is left out when it is `off`, so a run at the default has the hash it had before; `auto` and `on` are normal changes, like
`settings.mesh_method`.

**Guard.** The fine grid has about `8 x` the voxels of the coarse grid. The estimated peak memory of the step (`grid.est_peak_gib`) is
`smooth_sdf.BYTES_PER_VOXEL` = 70 bytes for each fine voxel plus `smooth_sdf.BYTES_PER_TRIANGLE` = 1,450 bytes for each estimated triangle
of the mesh (`grid.est_triangles`, #429). The triangle count is estimated before the fine grid is made: 2 x `up`^2 triangles for each face
between a solid (rho > 0.5) and a void coarse voxel, the outside counted as void (`surface_triangles`). The mesh has 1.08 to 1.09 times this
count on a generated lattice of thin straight members, 0.44 to 0.47 times on the hook, 0.44 to 0.90 times on 28 finished runs, and fewer on
a part with large flat faces. Measured as the rise of the step above its start (with the queries of #429): the grid stage takes 64 to 72 bytes
per fine voxel; the mesh stage grows with the mesh. On the lattice at 6.2 and 14 million fine voxels (2.0 and 5.0 million triangles) the
peak is 2,947 and 6,973 MiB: above 70 bytes per voxel that is 1,410 and 1,392 bytes per estimated triangle (1,302 and 1,273 per triangle
of the mesh), and the estimate gives 3,019 and 7,222 MiB. The hook refined to 9.6 and 22 million fine voxels takes 106 and 95 bytes per
voxel (975 and 1,999 MiB, the higher of two runs), and the estimate gives 133 and 119. Below about a million fine voxels other parts of the step set much of its
rise (0.05 to 0.54 GB on the 28 runs): there the estimate is 0.18 to 1.24 times the rise (125 bytes per voxel, the estimate before #429, gave
0.09 to 0.71). The estimate is a fact: the guard counts only the voxels. If the fine grid
has more than 30,000,000 voxels (env `TOPOPT_SDF_MAX_VOXELS` sets another limit; a value
that is not a number gives a warning and the default), the step does not run `sdf`. It logs one `warning:` with the voxel count,
the estimated peak memory, the limit and the options (a larger `voxel_size`, `mesh_method: blur`, the env var), and it uses `blur`
for this run. The guard runs before the fine grid is made. `mesh.method` is `blur`, `mesh.requested` is `sdf`, `mesh.fallback`
has the numbers. The same fallback happens on any other error of the `sdf` path that is not a resource error: one warning, `blur`,
`mesh.fallback` is `{"error": "<type>: <text>"}`. The run does not stop. A resource error does not go to `blur` ("Resource errors" below): after a failed thread start the
native libraries crashed the process on the `blur` path (measured on a test part under a 3.0 to 3.5 GiB address-space cap: 8 of 8 runs; `blur` alone and the step without `blur` ended cleanly).

**Resource errors** (#437, `topopt/resource_errors.py`). A fallback inside the `sdf` step is for a geometry problem (a mesh that is not closed, a boolean that fails).
A memory error or a failed thread start is not one: the same input gives the normal part when the resource is there. So after one, the mesh step stops and takes no fallback: not the
step's own fallback (the smooth mesh is not left unmoved, the cut is not left out, the field is not left unlimited), and not `blur`. A resource error is a `MemoryError`,
an `OSError` with `errno` ENOMEM or EAGAIN, an error of any type with the text of a failed thread start or allocation (for example the `RTreeError` of rtree: `std::bad_alloc`; "can't start new thread",
"bad_alloc", "Resource temporarily unavailable", "Cannot allocate memory", and "failed to map segment from shared object": the loader could not map a native library, for example
`libllvmlite` of numba under an address-space cap, #449), or an error with such a cause in its `__cause__` / `__context__` chain.
Each handler of the mesh step calls `reraise_if_resource(exc, step)` first; it raises `MeshResourceError` (a `RuntimeError`) with the step and the
original error (an error from an inner step keeps its own step). The steps outside the SDF path have names too: "the set-up of the interface shapes", "the blur mesh method",
"the exact interface step" and, for the SDF path outside its inner steps, "the SDF mesh step". The post step then fails, with one outcome:
- The message: "the mesh step ran out of a resource in <step> (<Type: text>). No part was written, because a fallback here would give a different part.
  Options: run one heavy job at a time, or give the run more memory; or use a coarser voxel size in a new run." The post step adds the route that repeats only the post step:
  "`topopt run <yaml> --out <run folder> --resume` ... It removes result/ first." A resume of a finished run runs no pass. The resume compares the settings of the checkpoint
  with the YAML, and the run options `--mesh-method`, `--envelope-fill` and `--solver` are in those settings. So the command gets each of them that the checkpoint holds and the YAML does not
  (for example `--mesh-method blur`), and then says that `run_topopt` has no argument for them; the text "(MCP: run_topopt with resume=true)" is there only when the command needs none.
  If the checkpoint or the YAML cannot be read, the text asks for the options of the first run. Options that the resume does not compare (`--buckling`, `--stop-rules`) are not in the command.
- `status.json` is `error` (step `postprocess`). Its `message` starts with "post-process failed: " when `post.finish` is called alone; under `topopt run` the CLI writes the status again and the
  message starts with "internal error: " (the same text after it). `final.stl`, `metrics.json` and `preview.bin` of this pass are not written. `topopt run` ends with exit code 2.
- An older `result/` of the same folder is not deleted by the failing step. `topopt run --resume` removes it before the post step, so after a failed resume no older result is left.
  `run_status` shows `state: error` (and, when the job ended as failed, `failure`); `run_result` then returns `done: false` and "The run failed: internal error: ..." (the message of the status). A call of `post.finish` alone
  on a folder whose job record is `done` and that holds an older result leaves them: `run_status` shows `error`, and `run_result` returns the older result as `done: true`.
A geometry error keeps its fallback and its fact as before. `SdfGridTooLarge` (the planned size check) keeps its path.

The steps after `final.stl` is written (#447, #449): the part-only cut (`result/part_only.stl`, section 9.1) and the stress report (the stress block of `metrics.json`,
its grey design and its thresholded estimate) give a file or a block that the run promises. Their handlers call `reraise_if_resource(exc, step, missing=...)` first; a resource
error there raises `PostResourceError` (also a `RuntimeError`), and the post step fails as above, with one difference in the message:
"the post step ran out of a resource in <step> (<Type: text>). result/final.stl is written, but <missing> is not, so the run stops here and does not end without it. Options: ..."
and the route. `<missing>` is `result/part_only.stl` or "the stress block of result/metrics.json". The steps are "the part-only cut", "the stress report" and "the thresholded
stress estimate of the stress report"; a `MeshResourceError` of a mesh helper that the cut calls (the float32 clean-up) becomes a `PostResourceError` whose step names both
("the float32 clean-up (simplify), in the part-only cut"). `final.stl` and `preview.bin` of this pass are written; `metrics.json` is not, and an older `part_only.stl` is
deleted. `stress_report.update_metrics` raises the same error and does not change `metrics.json`. Any other error of these steps keeps its record (`part_only.error`,
`stress.error`, `physical_thresholded.error` of a stress case) and the run ends as before. The checks, the verdict, the load path facts and the print check do not change a written file and keep their own handling.

**Fallbacks of the mesh step** (#445). An error that is not a resource error, in a step of `build` (the move onto the shared planes, the snap, the cut at the planes,
the cut to the envelope, the exact booleans, the float32 clean-up, the volume with the interface shapes, the build without the move), keeps the fallback of that step: the part
is written, and the mesh stays as it was before the step (the volume with the interface shapes: the calibration uses the mesh volume; the build without the move:
`snap.volume_change_mm3` is missing). The step does not fail for it, because a part from a fallback is not known to be unusable, and a failure would turn runs that end
with a part into failed runs. But the fallback is never silent. The mesh is built once in each round of the volume calibration, and `mesh.snap`, `mesh.plane_clip`,
`mesh.envelope_cut` and `mesh.exact` hold only the kept round: a fallback in an earlier round is not in them, and it moves the level of the later rounds. So each fallback of each round has:
- an entry in `mesh.fallbacks` (below);
- one warning line of the Python logger `topopt.smooth_sdf` (stderr of the process): "mesh fallback in round <k> of pass <n>, step <step>: <Type>: <text>; <what the mesh keeps>"
  (the build without the move: "in the build without the move").
The part card has a line "Mesh fallback: ..." in the section "Other checks that ran", `run.log` has its text after "warning: " (`topopt run` writes it after the post step),
and `run_result` has the key `mesh_fallbacks` (the same lines). These lines group the list: the same step with the same error in several rounds of a pass is one line that
names the rounds ("rounds 0, 1, 2 of pass 1 (2 is the kept round)"). Each line ends with an option: check the part with `topopt verify` (MCP: `verify_run`), or report the error
in an issue. The three are absent when the list is empty. The per-round keys stay as they were.
The fallbacks of the set-up before the first round (the envelope, the fill, the limit of the field to the envelope, the planes, the surfaces of the regions) are not in the list:
`envelope_cut.reason`, `envelope_fill.reason`, `envelope_cut.field_limit_note`, `plane_clip.note` and `snap.error` have them, and they do not depend on the round.

**`mesh` key of `metrics.json`** (both methods; keys that only `sdf` has are marked):

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `method`, `requested` | the method that ran, the method that was asked for |
| `params` | the numbers used (`sdf`: sigma, window, levels, Taubin, simplify tolerance, `up`, ...; `blur`: upsample, blur sigma, Taubin passes) |
| `volume_thresholded_mm3` | volume of the sharp field of the method (before smoothing), after island removal |
| `volume_smoothed_mm3` (`sdf`) | volume of the smooth mesh before the exact shapes |
| `volume_final_mm3`, `volume_error_pct` | volume of `final.stl`, and its error to the sharp field (a calibration residual for `sdf`, see 7) |
| `watertight` | the STL as loaded again is a closed manifold (see 8) |
| `sources`, `exact` (`sdf`) | `frozen` and `keep_out` are `stl`, `labels` or `none`; whether the exact union and cut ran. `exact` also has `error` (the exact booleans failed: the smooth mesh is kept), `cleanup_error` (the float32 clean-up failed: the mesh is as it was) and `interface_volume_error` (the volume with the interface shapes was not measured), each only when it happened |
| `snap` (`sdf`) | the facts of the move of the vertices to the region faces (above): `moved` (vertices that moved), `in_band` (vertices within the band of a region surface, inside or outside), `of` (vertices of the smooth mesh), `target_outside` (vertices outside a region and in its band whose target one band deep is not inside it; they did not move), `largest_move_mm`, `turned_faces` (faces that turned over in a trial of the move, each counted once) and `halving_rounds`, `band_mm`, `depth_mm` (equal to the band), and `volume_change_mm3` (the volume of the mesh minus the volume of the same marching-cubes mesh built without the move, at the last level shift; both volumes are the ones that the calibration uses, so with interface shapes (section 23) the volume with those shapes, which is not the volume of `final.stl`; the calibration has already paid it back; it costs one more build, present when a vertex moved). When that number is missing, `volume_change_error` has the reason: the extra build raised (`<type>: <text>`), or its exact boolean step failed. `{"error": "<reason>"}` when the mesh was not moved (the reason has the exception type). `null` when no region uses an STL file |
| `fallbacks` (`sdf`) | the list of the fallbacks that `build` took in any round of the calibration, in the order that they happened (`[]` when none; a run folder from before #445 does not have the key). Each entry: `pass` (1, or 2 for the second pass that starts with the cut), `round` (the index of the round in the calibration of that pass, from 0; `null` for the build without the move; `calibration` holds the rounds of the last pass up to the kept round, so an entry of pass 1 when pass 2 ran, or of a round after the kept round (#348), has no row there), `build` (`calibration`, or `without_move` for the extra build of `snap.volume_change_mm3`), `step` (`flush`, `snap`, `plane_clip`, `envelope_cut`, `exact`, `cleanup`, `interface_volume`, `snap_volume_change`), `error_type`, `error` (the text) and `kept` (true when the entry is from the kept round: the round of the last row of `calibration`, in the last pass) |
| `calibration` (`sdf`) | the rounds: level shift, volumes, target, error. A round that cuts has `plane_clip_removed_mm3` and `envelope_cut_removed_mm3` (the volume of the cuts of that round). A round that ended the calibration early has `stopped`, a text with the fact: the mesh volume does not follow the level shift (for example, the frozen and cut shapes hold the whole surface), or the marching-cubes volume target of the round is not above 0. That internal target is not `target_mm3`: the round moves it to pay for the residual of the round before. The mesh of that round is kept, and its residual is in `error`. A round with `next_round_error` is the kept round of a run that took extra rounds (section 19, step 7, #348): the round after it missed by that error, more than this round, so the loop ended there and that round is not listed. A `target_mm3` of 0 or less (the removed bodies hold the whole sharp volume) stops the `sdf` step with an error; the run then uses `blur` (see `fallback`) |
| `local_loss` (`sdf`) | `deep_lost_mm3`, `parts`, `largest_mm3`, `sharp_mm3`: sharp-field voxels more than 1.5 fine voxels outside the mesh (a lower bound: the mesh is sampled at 2 points per voxel) |
| `checks` (`sdf`) | with STL files: `fixed` has one entry per region with the key `fixed:<file name>` or `load:<region name>`: `uncovered_mm3` (volume of the region that the mesh does not hold), `max_outside_mm` (how far the missing part reaches from the mesh surface), `region_mm3`; `keep_out` has one entry per keep-out file with `intersect_mm3` (volume of the mesh inside it). Without STL files: `labels` has `fixed_missing_mm3` and `keep_out_inside_mm3` against the label voxel boxes (8 samples per fine voxel) |
| `stl_roundtrip` | facts of the written STL, as loaded again: `ok`, `watertight`, `winding_consistent`, `bodies`, `open_edges`, `nonmanifold_edges`, `zero_area_faces`, `volume_mm3`, `triangles`. A file with more than one body also has `body_volumes_mm3` (the signed volume of each body, the largest first; a body that turns inward has a negative volume) |
| `islands_removed`, `extra_bodies_removed`, `extra_bodies_volume_mm3` (`sdf`) | solid islands removed before the smoothing, and bodies removed after it (count and volume) |
| `plane_clip` (`sdf`) | the facts of the cut at the planes that the design space shares with a fixed, load or solid region (above), for the last build: `planes` (the shared planes found), `margin_mm` (the band of the snap: how far from the edge of a region face a vertex still counts as over the face), `vertices_beyond` (vertices farther out than a plane that was cut, not in a region, counted for each plane), `largest_excess_mm`, `volume_removed_mm3`, `clipped` (one entry for each plane that was cut: `normal`, `offset_mm`, `vertices`, `over_face` (the vertices over a region face: the reason to cut), `largest_excess_mm`), `left` (one entry for each plane that the mesh goes past only away from the region faces, so it was not cut: `normal`, `offset_mm`, `vertices`, `largest_excess_mm`), `passes` (1, or 2 when the calibration ran again with the cut) and `skipped_for_interfaces` (shared planes that an interface shape goes past: not cut). `planes` counts the shared planes that were found; `planes` 0 and the other numbers 0 when there is none. `note` (no design space STL, or the planes were not made) and `error` (the cut failed) appear only when they apply. A run folder from before F4-50 does not have the key |
| `envelope_cut` (`sdf`) | the facts of the cut to the envelope (above), for the last build, after the cut at the planes: `cut` (true when the mesh was cut), `vertices_beyond` (vertices outside the envelope by more than `tol_mm`), `largest_excess_mm` (the distance of the farthest vertex outside the envelope, before the cut), `volume_removed_mm3`, `volume_removed_pct` (`volume_removed_mm3` in percent of the mesh volume before the cut), `tol_mm` (the rounding of the STL files), `faces` (one entry for each face of the design space with a vertex past, the largest excess first: `kind` `plane` with `normal` and `offset_mm`, or `curved`; `vertices`, `largest_excess_mm`, `volume_removed_mm3`; the sums over the faces are the totals), `regions` (STL files of the fixed, load and solid regions in the envelope) and `interface_pieces` (union pieces of the interfaces, as printed), `passes` (1, or 2 when the calibration ran again with the cuts; 1 with the limit of the field), `field_limit` (true when the field was limited to the envelope, see "Limit of the field to the envelope"), `field_limit_note` (when it was not: the envelope is not known, `SdfParams.envelope_limit` is off, or the error of `envelope_sdf`), `flush` (with the limit and a shared plane: the move onto the shared planes, see "Limit of the field to the envelope": `vertices`, `largest_move_mm`, `turned_faces`, `halving_rounds`, `band_mm`; `error` when the move failed and the mesh was not moved), `t_s` (the time cost of the cuts, in seconds: `mesh_step`, the whole mesh step with both passes, `cut_pass`, the second pass, 0 with one pass, and `field_limit`, the time of the SDF of the envelope for the limit, which runs before the mesh step and is not in `mesh_step`; like the other `t_s` keys it differs from run to run). `reason` appears when the mesh was not cut: no vertex past, the first pass of the calibration, or why there is no envelope (no design space STL, an STL that is not a closed mesh, regions without STL files). `error` appears when the cut failed. A run folder from before F4-51 does not have the key, and one from before #319 has no `field_limit`, `field_limit_note` or `t_s.field_limit` |
| `envelope_fill` (`sdf`) | the fact of the envelope fill (above): `ran` (true when the field grew), `target_mm3` (the volume target, the sharp volume before the growth), and when the growth was measured `grown_inside_mm3` (the grown voxels inside the design space) and `grown_share_pct` (that volume in percent of `target_mm3`; also when the step skipped itself); `note` (when the step ran: the cost, "the fill moves material from the members to the skin of the design space: at the same mass the stiffness can drop, more on a coarse grid", with the option `settings.envelope_fill: off`; the post step logs the same text in one warning line with the share; a run where the step did not run has neither); `cap_overridden` (true when `on` ran the step above the cap); when it ran `candidates`, `grown`, `loose_dropped` (voxel counts) and `grown_overshoot_mm3` (the grown voxels past its surface; the cut to the envelope takes them). `reason` appears when it did not run: the switch is `off`, the share is above the cap with `auto` (above), or why there is no envelope (as in `envelope_cut.reason`); an error of the step is in `reason` too, and the field is then not grown. A run folder from before F4-55 does not have the key |
| `voids_kept` (`sdf`) | `count` and `volume_mm3` of the closed voids of the design that the last build kept as cavities (step 6); `0` and `0.0` when there is none. A run folder from before 0.5.1 does not have the key |
| `voids_filled` (`sdf`) | `count` and `volume_mm3` of the closed voids that the last build filled (step 6); `0` and `0.0` when there is none. A run folder from before F4-49 does not have the key |
| `grid` (`sdf`) | voxel count, estimated triangle count (`est_triangles`; a run folder from before #429 does not have the key), estimated peak memory (`est_peak_gib`, see "Guard"), limit (`options` only if the step cannot run) |
| `fallback` | `null`, the facts of the guard, or `{"error": ...}` (see above) |
| `keep_out_error` (`blur`) | only if the exact keep-out cut failed with a geometry error and the mesh was kept without the cut: `<Type>: <text>`; `keep_out_cut` is then false |
| `t_s` | seconds for the parts of the step |

`tools/check_final_stl.py <run_dir>` reads `result/final.stl` from disk and measures the same checks (exit code 1 if the mesh
is not one watertight body, or a region has a missing volume or a reach over its tolerance; the two numbers are reported
separately).
A design that does not connect all frozen regions gives more than one body. This is a fact in `stl_roundtrip.bodies`, not an error.
The mass changes by a few percent against `blur`, with either sign, because the regions now have their STL shape (hook -4.9 % at 1.2 mm voxels
and -8.8 % at 2 mm voxels, ladle +2.1 %; the size depends on the voxel size). The default tet size of `topopt verify` on the hook goes from 1.50 mm (`blur`) to 1.75 mm (`sdf`, `default_size` of the final mesh, at `de085e1`) and to 1.94 mm
(`sdf` with the snap, `c080f62`): the mesh has fewer, longer edges.

## 20. gpu-mg: GPU multigrid solver (added with G1d; the main solver on a GPU since P9-4d)

`gpu-mg` solves the linear system with a matrix-free geometric multigrid PCG on an OpenCL device. It is the main solver on a machine with a
usable GPU, and the CPU solvers (`cholesky`, `pardiso`, `amg`) are the fallback: `settings.solver: auto` runs `gpu-mg` on a GPU that passes
a short self-test, and goes on with the CPU solver of the platform when `gpu-mg` fails during the run ("Selection" and "Fallback during a run" below).
It was verified on a CPU OpenCL device (pocl), and on 2026-10-21 on one real GPU (below).
The code is `topopt/gpu_mg/`.

**Measured on a real GPU (one machine).** A MacBook Air M4 (16 GB, macOS 15.3, Python 3.12.15 arm64; Apple M4 GPU,
OpenCL 1.2, no 64-bit float, so case `C`), `main` at `cd349f9`. These are the figures of ONE machine. Another Mac or another GPU can
differ, and `topopt gpu-check` measures the machine it runs on.

- Parity (`tools/gpu_mg_parity.py --cases C`, 7,260 free dofs): the largest relative difference of the displacements 2.90e-11 and
  of the compliance 2.71e-11, against SuperLU and against Cholesky (limit 1e-6); PASS.
- The four gpu test files with `TOPOPT_TEST_REAL_GPU=1`: 98 passed, 10 skipped in 27.1 s. The 10 skips are the case B
  parametrizations (case B needs 64-bit floats).
- `tools/bench_gpu_mg.py` on the hook, 20 iterations, `max_active_voxels` 400000. Median seconds per optimizer iteration, default
  solver (Accelerate Cholesky) against gpu-mg; the relative difference of the final compliance is 1e-10 or smaller in each row:

| voxel mm | free dofs | default s/iter | gpu-mg s/iter | speed-up (median iteration) | default peak RSS | gpu-mg peak RSS | compliance rel. diff |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.2 | 115,836 | 0.765 | 0.287 | 2.67x | 1,895.6 MB | 655.8 MB | 9.61e-11 |
| 1.0 | 205,485 | 2.235 | 0.439 | 5.09x | 3,165.5 MB | 958.4 MB | 6.77e-11 |
| 0.8 | 386,142 | 9.241 | 0.658 | 14.04x | 6,428.4 MB | 1,523.9 MB | 1.20e-11 |
| 0.6 | 905,010 | not run: the memory estimate of the default solver (22.5 GiB) is above the RAM (16 GiB) | 1.919 | - | - | 2,415.5 MB | - |

  A full run of 80 iterations at 1.0 mm: default 218.62 s and 3,168 MB, gpu-mg 43.23 s and 987 MB (5.06x for the whole run);
  the final compliance 1.3466026943973426 against 1.346602694408493 (relative difference 8.28e-12). The 0.6 mm default run was
  skipped by `tools/bench_gpu_mg.py` (`--run-default fits`), not by `topopt run`, which only warns when the memory estimate is above the RAM.

**Selection.**

- YAML: `settings.solver: gpu-mg`. CLI: `topopt run <yaml> --out <dir> --solver gpu-mg` and
  `topopt check <yaml> --solver gpu-mg` replace `settings.solver` for that command. The flag takes
  `auto`, `cholesky`, `pardiso`, `amg` or `gpu-mg`.
- `solver_choice.SOLVER_SETTINGS` holds `gpu-mg` (since P9-4d). `solver_choice.EXPERIMENTAL_SOLVERS` is empty; the name stays for the key
  `experimental_solvers` of `environment`.
- `resolve_solver("auto")` is the CPU rule of section 4 and never gives `gpu-mg`. What a RUN uses first is `solver_choice.run_solver(setting, config)`,
  a `SolverChoice` (`setting`, `solver`, `cpu`, `fallback`, `device`, `case`, `self_test`, `reason`; `as_dict()` has `cpu_solver` for `cpu`, and `line`).
  An explicit value gives what `resolve_solver` gives. `auto` gives `gpu-mg` when ALL of these hold, else the CPU rule with `reason` as a fact:
  1. the YAML has no row that `gpu-mg` cannot run (today the buckling row `buckling.min_factor`, which needs a direct factor of the matrix);
  2. pyopencl loads, and the device that `settings.gpu_device` takes is a GPU (`gpu_mg.device.counts_as_gpu`: the kind is `GPU`; a CPU device such as
     pocl and an accelerator do not count, because the speed of `gpu-mg` is measured on GPUs) with the features of the engine, and
     `settings.gpu_case` fits it (`auto` takes case B on a device with 64-bit float, else C);
  3. the self-test passes (`gpu_mg.device.self_test`; a pass is cached, see "The child process and the cache of the self-test" below): one `gpu-mg` solve of a small in-memory cantilever
     (3,888 free dofs, 2 load cases) at the gpu tolerance `device.SELFTEST_TOL` (1e-8) against a SuperLU solve on the host. It passes when the largest relative
     difference of the displacements is at most `device.SELFTEST_MAX_DIFF` (1e-6). It never raises: a device error is a result with `passed` false and
     the text in `error`; the seconds of the test (with the kernel build) are in `seconds`.
  The child process and the cache of the self-test (#353). In `topopt run` and `topopt check` with `settings.solver: auto`, and in the MCP server (`check_problem`,
  `environment`), the parent process makes no OpenCL driver call and does not import pyopencl for the pick of `auto` and for the OpenCL facts of `check` and
  `environment`. One child process (`python -P -m topopt.gpu_mg.probe --device D --case C`, module `topopt/gpu_mg/probe.py`) lists the devices, makes the pick
  (`device.auto_gpu`), runs the self-test and prints one JSON answer: the last line of its stdout that starts with `TOPOPT-PROBE ` and parses as a complete answer (driver text on
  stdout and a later broken line do not break it). The parent uses that answer whatever the exit code of the child; a code that is not 0 is the fact `child_exit_code` in the answer and in its `facts` (so `check` and `environment` show it).
  When no line parses, the reason says "no answer that can be read" with the exit code. The keys are `facts` (the dict of `device.facts`), `device` and `case` (the pick, else null), `reason`, `self_test` and `timed_out`.
  The parent keeps the answer for the process, one child for each `gpu_device`, `gpu_case` and pick (`probe.probe`; `device.forget_devices` drops it).
  The limit is the constant `probe.PROBE_TIMEOUT_S` = 60 s (a constant, about 6 times the first self-test on an Intel Arc GPU, 9.8 s;
  not a settings field). At the limit the child is killed and the parent does not wait for it (a daemon thread reaps it). Then `auto` takes the CPU rule with the
  reason that names the limit, says that the child process was stopped, and gives the two ways out: an explicit `settings.solver`, or `TOPOPT_AUTO_GPU=0`
  (no wait: with this variable the parent starts no child for the pick and none for the OpenCL facts of `check`, `check_problem` and `environment`; the facts
  then have the pyopencl version from the package record, no device list, and `problem` = "not asked: TOPOPT_AUTO_GPU=0 is set in the environment"; an explicit
  `settings.solver: gpu-mg` is not changed). The child gets the folder that holds the parent's `topopt` package first on `PYTHONPATH`, so it imports the
  same topopt as the parent; when that folder is a site-packages folder of the running Python, nothing is added. After a timeout the OpenCL facts have `problem` = "the OpenCL device list did not finish in 60 s, and the
  child process was stopped". Without pyopencl (`importlib.util.find_spec`, no import) no child starts: the pick reason and the facts are "pyopencl is not usable here (missing: ...)".
  The timeout reason and the facts `problem` add that a new process asks again and that the MCP server asks again after a restart (the answer stays for the process).
  `environment` takes the `gpu-mg` entry of `solver_setting` from these facts (a device list exists, else the `problem` text), so it and
  `topopt doctor` ask no OpenCL driver in the parent. With `TOPOPT_AUTO_GPU=0` the entry has no `resolved`, and its `error` says that gpu-mg is not checked
  here (the device list was not asked) and that an explicit `settings.solver: gpu-mg` still asks the OpenCL drivers when the run starts; it does not say
  that gpu-mg cannot run. `check --solver auto` over a YAML with `solver: gpu-mg` uses the child (the effective setting counts).
  A child with no answer gives the CPU rule and the facts with the reason (exit code, last line of stderr).
  Not in the child: an explicit `settings.solver: gpu-mg` (the user asked for the GPU: `resolve_solver("gpu-mg")`, `gpu_mg.device.select`, `facts` for
  its `check` and the time model), the gpu-mg solve of a run after `auto` picked gpu-mg, and `topopt gpu-check`.
  The cache is the file `gpu-selftest.json` in `gpu_mg.check.state_dir()` (the folder of `gpu-constants.json`; `TOPOPT_STATE_DIR` moves it). It is written
  with the pattern of `save_calibration` (temporary file, `os.replace`, no lock). The file is `{"schema": 1, "passes": [{"key": {...}, "result": {...}}]}`.
  The key has `platform`, `device`, `device_version`, `driver` (`DeviceInfo.driver`, the `driver_version` of the device), `case`, `tol`
  (`SELFTEST_TOL`), `max_diff` (`SELFTEST_MAX_DIFF`), `topopt` (`topopt.__version__`) and `code` (the sha256 of the bytes of every `*.py` file of
  `topopt/gpu_mg/`, sorted by name: a change of the gpu-mg code tests again); a record is used only when every field is equal. Only a pass is
  written: a failure, an error or a timeout is not, so the next process tests again. A file that cannot be read or written, or has another schema, is no error:
  the self-test runs, and `cache_note` of the result says why the cache was not used. The self-test dict has `cached` (true for a record of the file),
  `tested_at` (the UTC time of the pass) and `cache_note`. The `solver choice:` line says "cached result of <UTC time>" in place of the seconds for a cached pass.
  The environment variable `TOPOPT_AUTO_GPU=0` is the first check, before pyopencl loads (`gpu_mg.device.auto_gpu`): `auto` then takes the CPU rule, with the
  reason `TOPOPT_AUTO_GPU=0 is set in the environment`, also in a subprocess. Any other value, or no value, gives the rule above. An explicit `settings.solver: gpu-mg`
  is not changed by it. The test session sets it to `0` (`tests/conftest.py`), unless `TOPOPT_TEST_REAL_GPU` is `1`; a value that the user set stays.
  `settings.gpu_device: auto` takes the first GPU; when the machine has no GPU it takes the best other device, and `auto` then does not use it. A user who
  wants `gpu-mg` on a CPU device or an accelerator sets `settings.solver: gpu-mg`. The pick, with its device, case, self-test numbers or reason, is the line
  `solver choice:  auto -> ...` of `topopt check`, the line `solver: auto -> ...` of `run.log` and `auto_choice` of `environment`.
- `resolve_solver("gpu-mg")` returns `"gpu-mg"` if pyopencl loads and one OpenCL device exists. Otherwise it raises
  `UserError` (section 4 rule: exit code 1, one line). It does not look at `gpu_device` or `gpu_case`: the check of the
  device and the case of the problem is in `cli.backend_problem(setting, backends, settings)` (called by `run` and
  `check`) and in `gpu_mg.device.select`. The OpenCL drivers are asked once for each process; for `auto` and for the OpenCL facts of `check` and `environment`, a child process asks them (see above).
- `run.json` field `solver` is `"gpu-mg"` when `gpu-mg` ran the run to its end. With `settings.solver` set to a CPU solver, the run is bit-equal to a run
  without this section (the hook at one thread: compliance 1.3891411615538347, every snapshot, `final.stl`). The same holds for `auto` on a machine where
  `auto` picks the CPU rule (no GPU, a CPU device only, a failed self-test, a buckling row): it runs the same code and the same solver as before P9-4d.

**Fallback during a run (P9-4d; `topopt/solver_fallback.py`).** Only a run with `settings.solver: auto` that `run_solver` sent to `gpu-mg` can fall back.
An explicit `settings.solver: gpu-mg` never falls back: it stops with the error, as before. `gpu_mg.device.GpuFailure` is a `UserError` with a `kind`:
`device_error` (an OpenCL error in an upload or a solve), `device_memory` (an OpenCL error that says the device is out of memory),
`not_accepted` (a solve reached neither the residual target nor the backward-error rule: `model.SolveFailure`) and `setup` (the engine cannot be made
on this device: the hierarchy, the largest buffer, the local memory of the joint kernel, the build of the program). A host `MemoryError`, an input error,
a request to stop (exit code 5), Ctrl+C and an internal error are not a `GpuFailure` and go up as before.

1. On a `GpuFailure` the device buffers are released and the run is not stopped yet. The memory estimate of the CPU solver (the number of `topopt check`,
   `cli.estimate_memory_bytes`) is compared with the RAM (`cli.physical_ram_bytes`). If it is above the RAM, the run stops with a `UserError` that names the
   estimate of the CPU solver, the estimate of `gpu-mg`, the RAM and the options (resume with `settings.solver: amg` and `--allow-changed-inputs`, a larger
   `settings.voxel_size`, a machine with more RAM). The checkpoint stays.
2. Else the run goes on with the CPU solver of the platform rule (`SolverChoice.fallback`) from the last checkpoint of the same run folder
   (`checkpoint.plan_resume` and `apply_plan`, as `--resume` does; this is not a swap inside the loop). A failure in the setup or in pass 0, before a
   checkpoint, starts again at pass 0. A continuation (`--continue-from`) with no checkpoint of its own yet goes on with its own plan.
   `history.jsonl`, the snapshots and `gpu_mg.jsonl` keep the passes of the GPU part; the pass that failed wrote no history line. The passes before the
   switch are those of a pure `gpu-mg` run.
3. The record. `run.json`: `solver` (the solver of the last part), `solver_setting` (`settings.solver`) and `solver_parts`, a list with one entry for each
   part, newest last: `{"solver", "device", "first_pass", "last_pass", "end"}`. `device` is the OpenCL device name for `gpu-mg`, else `null`. `first_pass` is
   `null` for a part that stopped in its setup. `last_pass` is the last pass that the part saved in a checkpoint. `end` is `null` for a part that ran to the
   end, else `{"kind", "text", "at_utc"}` (the `GpuFailure` kind, its text of at most 600 characters, the UTC time). The same `solver_parts` is in each checkpoint
   (`meta`). `run.log` gets one line `solver: gpu-mg stopped <where> (<kind>: <text>); the run goes on with <cpu> <from the checkpoint of pass N | from pass 0>`.
   `verdict.json` gets one note in `notes` that names each part, the passes it ran and the kind of the failure; a run with one part gets none.
   A resume and a continuation go on in the last part when the solver and the device are the same (the parts of a continuation start as the parts of the
   parent checkpoint), so a continuation with the same solver equals the run of full length, `run.json` included (section 24). Another solver or device, or a
   last part that ended with a failure, starts a new part. A resume of a finished run (no pass is left) starts no part: `solver` stays the solver of the last
   part that ran a pass. A fine pass (section 24.6) goes through the same runner: a failure at pass 0 starts again at pass 0 with a new start design (the parent
   is read again; the log lines of the start design appear once for each start), and a failure at a later pass restarts from the checkpoint of the fine pass,
   which holds the design and the `fine_from` record. The plan of a fine pass compares the inputs with the solver that `auto` picks, not with the CPU rule.
4. A resume (`--resume`) or a continuation with `settings.solver: auto` on both sides: another solver than the one of the checkpoint (after a fallback,
   or a GPU that is gone) is a NOTE with a fact, not a change that needs `--allow-changed-inputs` (`checkpoint.diff_inputs`, `plan_resume`, `plan_continue`).
   An explicit change of `settings.solver` stays a change.
5. The one-off stress solve of the post step (`refine/stress.compute_stress`) uses the solver that the run ended on when that is a CPU solver. Else `auto`
   follows the rule of a run (a GPU that passes the self-test, with the CPU rule as its fallback on a `GpuFailure`). An explicit setting has no fallback.

**Forced-failure check (for a real GPU).** To see the switch on a real GPU, give the YAML a tolerance that no device reaches: `examples/hook/hook_gpu_fallback.yaml`
is the short hook with `settings.gpu_tol: 1.0e-30` and `settings.gpu_backward_error: 1.0e-30` (the config accepts both; a 64-bit residual cannot go below about
1e-16, and the backward error of a solve at the rounding floor is about 4e-17). The rule of the backward error is on: with 0 it is off, and then the residual of the PCG
recurrence decides in case B, which can go far below the true residual, so a tolerance of 1e-30 is reached. The first solve is not accepted in case B and in case C,
`gpu-mg` stops with a `not_accepted` failure, and the run goes on with the CPU solver from pass 0 (the failure is in the first solve). The run ends with the
exit code 0 and `solver_parts` of two parts. On a machine where `auto` does not pick `gpu-mg`, nothing is forced. The text of the failure in the record is cut
at its last full sentence inside 600 characters.
**Device, precision case, stop test and iteration cap.** Five optional YAML keys under `settings`; they are used by `gpu-mg` only (the loader checks them for any solver).

| Key | Values | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gpu_device` | `auto`, a number, or a part of a name | `auto` | The number is the index in the list that `topopt check` prints. A name part matches the platform and device name (case does not matter). `auto` takes the first GPU, else the first accelerator, else the first CPU device. |
| `gpu_case` | `auto`, `B`, `C` | `auto` | The precision case (below). `auto` gives `B` if the device reports 64-bit float support, else `C`. |
| `gpu_tol` (G2) | a number, 0 < value < 1 | `1e-6` | The relative residual `\|r\| / \|f\|` that each solve of the optimizer loop reaches (the main, trial and adjoint solves). The one-off solve of the stress step of the post run (`solve_design`) keeps `GpuParams.tol`, 1e-8. |
| `gpu_backward_error` (G2) | a number, 0 <= value < 1e-6 | `1e-15` | A solve is also accepted when its normwise backward error is at most this number (**the stop test**, below). `0` turns the rule off, with its early stop and its check of the first pass: with `gpu_tol: 1e-8` too, the solver then behaves as at d19c7fb. It applies to the loop and to the stress step. |
| `gpu_max_iter` (P2b) | an integer, 1 or more | `1000` | The number of PCG iterations of the FIRST pass of a solve: the 64-bit outer PCG of case `B` (**the iteration caps**, below). It applies to the loop and to the stress step. Case `C` has no first pass, so the key does not apply to it. There is no upper bound. |

A value outside the range is a `UserError` from the loader (`'settings.gpu_tol' must be > 0` ...; `'settings.gpu_max_iter' must be an integer of 1 or more (the number of PCG iterations of the first pass of a gpu-mg solve; a pass of 0 iterations solves nothing), got 0`: a float, a string and a bool are errors too). YAML 1.1 reads `1e-6` as text: the loader accepts it as a number for the two tolerances. The three keys are in the effective settings of a checkpoint only when they differ from the default, so a checkpoint of d19c7fb (or of G2, for `gpu_max_iter`) still resumes (`settings.objective_scale` follows the same rule, section 13); a changed value is a changed input. Because that hides a change of a default, the `meta_json` of a checkpoint of a gpu-mg run has `gpu_mg` (`tol`, `backward_error`: the numbers of the loop; `max_iter`: the cap of the first pass, since P2b), and a resume with the solver `gpu-mg` writes one `resume:` line when they are not the numbers of this run: for a checkpoint from before G2 (no `gpu_mg`: the first part ran at the fixed target 1e-8 and without the backward-error rule) and for a checkpoint with other numbers (a default changed). A change that the YAML shows is a change of the inputs already (the override): a checkpoint with `gpu_mg` gets no second line for it. A checkpoint from before G2 gets both lines (the change line, which says `<not set>`, and the fact), because only the fact says how the first part ran. The cap has its own line, `resume: the first part of the run capped the first PCG pass of a gpu-mg solve at N iterations; this part runs at settings.gpu_max_iter M ...`: for a checkpoint of G2 (a `gpu_mg` record without `max_iter`: the cap was 300 then) and for a record with another cap (a default changed). The cap changes the path of a solve, not its target, so it is a fact and not a refusal. A change of `settings.gpu_max_iter` in the YAML of a run that you resume is a changed input, as for `gpu_tol` and `gpu_backward_error`: `topopt run --resume` stops until you give `--allow-changed-inputs` (MCP: `allow_changed_inputs=true`). The text of a failed solve offers a larger `settings.gpu_max_iter`, so a resume after that edit needs the flag.

- Case `C`: the V-cycle and the PCG run in 32-bit on the device. The CPU computes the residual in 64-bit and
  corrects (iterative refinement, at most 12 steps, inner tolerance 1e-2). It needs **no** 64-bit float on the device.
  The OpenCL C source of case C holds no 64-bit type and no extension pragma (a test checks this; it holds also for the deflation kernels of section 20).
- Case `B`: the V-cycle runs in 32-bit and the outer PCG in 64-bit, on the device. It needs 64-bit float support.
  A forced `B` on a device without it is a `UserError`.
- The program is built with `-cl-std=CL1.2` (Apple OpenCL is 1.2). The source uses no work-group function of
  OpenCL 2.0. The work-group sizes come from the device limit and the work-group query of each built kernel (a power
  of two, at most 128 for node kernels and 256 for vector kernels).
- Case `B` restarts: the 64-bit PCG has `settings.gpu_max_iter` iterations (default 1000) in its first pass. If it does not
  reach the tolerance, case `B` goes on in the refinement loop of case `C` (true residual in 64-bit on the CPU, inner tolerance
  1e-2, at most 12 steps of 300 iterations), from the result of the first pass. A solve that converges in the first pass is
  not changed (with the rule of the stop test on, it gets the check below).

**The iteration caps (P2b).** Two numbers cap the PCG iterations, and they are not the same number.

| Cap | Where | Value |
|---|---|---|
| First pass | case `B`: the one call of the 64-bit outer PCG at the start of a solve (`GpuParams.max_iter_first`) | `settings.gpu_max_iter`, default 1000 |
| Restart step | case `B`: each step of the refinement loop after the first pass. Case `C`: each refinement step (it has no first pass) (`GpuParams.max_iter`) | 300, a recorded default |

  Why two: the outer PCG of case `B` is in FP64, and a check of the true residual follows its first pass. So a large first pass loses no accuracy.
  A restart step is a cold PCG on the residual equation. When a solve needs more than about two caps of 300, the restart steps hit the cap again and make little progress.
  Measured on pocl (the cantilever at 0.5 mm, 52,920 free dofs, `gpu_tol` 1e-6, filtered random blobs, E 1 or 1e-6): the first pass with the cap 2000 needed 748 iterations.
  The cap 300 needed 1,200 (300 and three steps of 300).
  Measured in test runs on one Intel Arc iGPU (case B): there are 58 run folders, and 54 runs when a copy counts once. In 9 of the 54 runs,
  146 solve blocks hit the cap 300. A restart step hit its own cap again in 25 of 282 steps, all of them in one run.
  The mean PCG iterations of a block over the passes 0 to 2 were 205 to 328 for a start design with a stiffness contrast of about 1e4.5 to 1e5.5 against solid.
  The 1.35M-dof run needed 575 PCG iterations for each solve, on average, in the first pass and the restart steps together.
  The figures come from a check of the cap on real data.
  A cap of 100 failed on every hard design of the pocl experiment. A larger cap costs the iterations of a solve that would have converged late:
  at 1.35M dofs, 700 more iterations before the first true-residual check take about 14 s.

  The last restart step (P2b). A step with the inner tolerance 1e-2 divides the true residual by about 100. So a step that starts at less than 50 times the target
  (`gpu_tol`) overshoots. On the 1.35M-dof run it ended 9 to 32 times below the target.
  The loop (`engine.solve_refined`, called by the model with `last_step_margin=engine.LAST_STEP_MARGIN`) solves such a step to `max(1e-2, 0.5 * gpu_tol / rel)`.
  Here `rel` is the largest relative residual of the columns that no test accepts yet at the start of the step. The step ends near half the target.
  A step that starts at 50 times the target or more is not changed. No step is stricter than 1e-2.
  The 0.5 is a constant of the solver (`engine.LAST_STEP_MARGIN`), not a setting. It is a safety factor between the recurrence residual of the inner PCG and the true
  residual. It changes only the path of the last step, never its target: `gpu_tol` and the backward-error rule still decide acceptance on the true residual in FP64.
  A caller that gives no margin (`last_step_margin=None`, the default) gets the loop of d19c7fb.

**The stop test (G2).** The FP64 residual `|f - K u|` of any solver has a floor of about `eps * || |K| |u| ||`. On a design with a
near-void region around stiff strips (a soft start: start density = volume fraction, `penal` 5 or more) the floor is above 1e-8:
PARDISO gives 3.3e-8 and 4.0e-8 on two start designs of the phone-stand test, with a backward error of 7e-17. So a target of 1e-8
cannot be met by any FP64 solve there, and a run that tests only the residual stops at iteration 0. The rule:

- The solve is accepted when `rel = |r| / |f| < gpu_tol`, or (with `gpu_backward_error` > 0) when `eta = |r| / (|| |K| |u| || + |f|)` is at
  most `gpu_backward_error` (Rigal and Gaches). It is tested for each column of the block of load cases; all columns must pass.
  `|K| |u|` is the host matvec `apply_fine_abs` of `gpu_mg/hierarchy.py`: the sum of the absolute element matrices `E |ke|` applied to `|u|`
  (an upper bound of the entrywise `|K||u|`: `eta` is smaller than the entrywise value, by 1.25 on the d3b design and 1.25 to 1.28 on small test grids, never larger).
  No matrix is built. `eta` is computed only when some column has `rel >= gpu_tol`. The default limit 1e-15 is about 25 times the `eta` of the floor of a part without joints (3.5e-17 to 4.4e-17 on
  the d3b start and on 12 hook designs; a first pass that the device accepts on its recurrence has 9.3e-17 to 2e-16) and 2 to 6 times below the `eta` of a step before the floor
  (1.9e-15 to 5.8e-15 on the same designs).
- Where: the restart loop (`engine.solve_refined`: case C always, case B after a first pass that did not converge), and the first pass of case B.
  The first pass stops on the recurrence residual of the device, which can be about 10 times below the true residual (E2 of the research:
  6.9e-9 against 1.1e-7). With the rule on, `engine.check_solution` computes the true residual after every first pass that stopped on the
  recurrence (one host matvec for each column, and the absolute one when `eta` is needed; `check_s` in the record), and sends the solve to the restart loop
  when `rel >= gpu_tol` and `eta > gpu_backward_error`. Cost, measured on the hook at 1.0 mm (`check_s` against `solve_s`): pocl CPU device 0.46 % of the median solve
  (16.5 ms of 3.63 s). Intel Arc iGPU, case B, 30 passes, 31 solves of 28 to 60 PCG iterations, `gpu_tol` 1e-6: 7.6 ms of 0.29 s, 2.6 % median, 2.3 % smallest,
  5.3 % largest. The d3b soft start on the Arc (256 to 300 iterations): 2.6 % to 3.8 %. The host check does not get faster with the device, so the share is larger on a faster GPU.
- The restart loop stops early when the largest `rel` of the columns that no test accepts yet fell by less than 10 % over two steps and `eta` is above the limit
  (`stagnated`). A column that the backward error accepts (it sits at its floor and stays flat) does not count. This is an internal stop condition of the loop, not a
  setting. A loop that falls by 5 % per step from 1.5 times the target also stops, although it would reach the target in 8 steps: real restart steps fall by 10 to 100
  times until the floor. With the rule off the loop runs all its steps.
- `eta` at the limit does not mean a small `rel`: `rel` can be `gpu_backward_error * (|| |K||u| || + |f|) / |f|`. On the d3b start the ratio `(|| |K||u| || + |f|) / |f|` is 5.8e8:
  `rel` 3.3e-6 at `eta` 5.8e-15 on pocl, 3.0e-6 at 5.2e-15 on the Arc GPU. So the limit 1e-14 would accept a relative residual up to 5.8e-6 (above the default
  `gpu_tol` 1e-6), and the default 1e-15 accepts up to 5.8e-7. A solve at the floor has `eta` of 3.5e-17 to 4.4e-17 on the designs without joints measured so far. With joints the check has a noise of its own: see the next point.
- **The host check on a part that joints hold (F1-7).** The check computes `Kb u - C D^-1 C^T u` (`Border.add_to`). In a rigid motion of such a part the two terms are each far larger
  than the load (`|Kb u| / |b|` is 5e6 to 3e8 on the two-joint part) and they cancel, so the rounding of the sum `C^T u` over all bonded dofs shows in the residual. Up to d43f580 that sum was a BLAS
  product, which adds the bonded dofs one after the other. Since F1-7 it is the pairwise sum of numpy (`border.ct_dot`; numpy code, so the same on macOS and Linux; no long double). The device
  operator is not changed (case C has the same host check, and its 32-bit device operator keeps the rounding of section 38). Measured, linux-x86_64, numpy 2.5.3 with the OpenBLAS of the wheel, one host:
  - A cube of 8 to 32 voxels held by a joint (the beam 1e9 times softer than the block), a rigid motion of the body, against an exact reference (`fractions`): the noise of the host joint term is
    5.6, 19.7, 30.5 and 47.9 unit roundoffs of `|Kb u|` with the BLAS sum at 1,158, 4,614, 10,374 and 18,438 bonded dofs, and 1.6 to 1.8 with the pairwise sum (the rounding of `Kb u` alone is 1.1).
    A cube of 40 voxels with a soft axial beam (`tests/test_gpu_mg_border.py`, pocl): the true residual of the check 3.4e-6 on d43f580 (accepted by the backward error, `eta` 6.9e-16, above the target 1e-6) and 3.6e-7 now (accepted by `tol`).
  - The two-joint part (a part with 2 tube joints and no fixed region; 600,771 free dofs, 130k bonded dofs, 2 joints, 7 load cases; the answer of pardiso, checked by the host operator, two runs of each revision): the noise of the check over `|b|` was
    7e-9 to 3.6e-7 with the BLAS sum (LC5_side 9.5e-8 and 3.6e-7) and 1e-9 to 6e-8 with the pairwise sum (LC5_side 4.8e-8 and 6.0e-8). The `eta` of the noise alone (one run of each revision) was 3.6e-16 to 9.4e-16 and is now 4.4e-17 to 6.0e-17.
    What is left is the rounding of `Kb u` (3.3e-8 over `|b|` for LC5_side) and of the last product. The analysis of F1-7 measured 1.1e-6 for LC5_side in one run on the build of the stopped Arc run (the noise of the BLAS sum is the same for one answer on one host; it changes with the answer and with the BLAS thread count).
  - On the Intel Arc (one host, the two-joint part, one pass, case B): d43f580 stopped in the third block (LC5_side, FA_horiz) in 3 of 3 runs with the same numbers (first pass 84 PCG
    iterations, true residual 1.40e-6, restart steps 1.11e-6 and 1.31e-6, `eta` 1.28e-15, stagnated); with the pairwise sum the same block was accepted by `tol` at 4.97e-7 after the same 84 PCG
    iterations (1 run). So the device answer was right, and the stop was the noise of the check.
  - Since F1-7 the noise of the check shows in `rel` and not in `eta`: the denominator of `eta` holds `|Kb||u|` and `|C||D^-1||C^T||u|`, which are at least the size of the two terms that cancel,
    so a check noise of about 1.6 unit roundoffs of `|Kb u|` gives `eta` of about 1.6 unit roundoffs (1.8e-16) or less, for any amount of cancellation (cube, exact reference: 6.3e-16 and
    9.7e-16 with the BLAS sum, 5.2e-17 and 4.5e-17 now). The answer of pardiso for the two-joint part has `eta` of 6e-16 to 3.8e-15 (its own error, not the check).
  - Cost: `add_to` takes 0.6 to 1 ms more at the size of the two-joint part (6.7 to 7.7 ms for 130k bonded dofs and 12 border dofs, synthetic), and the host keeps one more copy of `C` (12.5 MB at that size).
    `add_to` runs 12 times on each level for each design (the power iteration of `setup_host`) and once for each column in each check and restart step: about 10 to 20 ms more for each design.
  - The rule is unchanged. The noise of the check is about 1.6 unit roundoffs of `|Kb u| / |b|` in `rel` (5e-8 on the two-joint part, where `|Kb u| / |b|` is 3.2e8). A part with about 17 times more
    cancellation (`|Kb u| / |b|` about 5.6e9) has a check noise near `rel` 1e-6; the backward-error rule then accepts the solve (`eta` about 1e-16, measured on a cube), and a run with
    `gpu_backward_error: 0` stops there. Removing the cancellation itself (not a better sum) is the work of P2d.
- Limit of the rule: it assumes a bounded solution. `eta` divides by `|| |K||u| ||`, so a solve with a large null-space part in `u` can have a small `eta` (a free rigid
  mode: the review of G2 measured `eta` 2.6e-15 at `rel` 0.18 for the inverse of `K + 1e-14 I`). `topopt run` stops a floating piece before the solve
  (`connectivity.floating_error`), and `E_MIN` keeps K regular, so a run does not meet this case.
- The one-off stress solve (`solve_design`, target 1e-8, rule on) is accepted by the backward error without a fact in `run.log` or `gpu_mg.jsonl`: it has no run
  writer, and the stress step has no log of its own (an option: return the record entry from `solve_design` to `compute_stress`; a change of the stress step). Its backward error
  is at most the limit, 1e-15, about 25 times the `eta` of the floor.

**What it does.** `GpuModel` (a subclass of `optimize.Model`, made by `optimize.make_model`) does not build `Assembler`
and does not call `LinearSolver`. `stiffness(rho)` returns the stiffness factor of each element (a vector) and
`solve(Ee)` makes the multigrid numbers on the CPU (numba, FP64), uploads them and solves. `m.solver` is a `GpuSolver`
with `solve(B, warm=True)` and `free()`. It solves with the operator of the last `Model.solve`, so
`DesignPoint.solve_adjoint` (and the stress rows of A2 that use it) work. There is no warm start. A load case with a
zero force is not solved. `numba` uses `NUMBA_NUM_THREADS`; the package sets no cap of its own.

**Stress step and refine page.** `refine.stress.compute_stress` (the stress step of the post run, used by the refine
page) takes the displacements from `gpu_mg.model.solve_design` when `settings.solver` is `gpu-mg`: one design, the same
solver, no global matrix and no factor. So the refine page and the physical stress numbers in `metrics.json` (A2) are
made with `gpu-mg`. `optimize.make_solver("gpu-mg", ...)` still raises a `UserError` for a caller that needs a matrix and a
factor.

**Springs and joints (P2b).** `gpu-mg` takes a YAML with springs (section 35) and with joints (section 38), alone or together, with a `fixed` region or without
(a part held by joints only). It takes a per-axis support (a `fixed` entry with `axes`) too, since P2c (the paragraph "Per-axis supports (P2c)" below). No support type is
refused any more: the texts `cli.GPU_MG_AXES`, `springs.GPU_MG_REFUSAL` and `springs.GPU_MG_JOINT_REFUSAL`, and `springs.gpu_mg_problem` that chose between them, are gone.

- The system. The solve is `A u = f` with `A = K + Kb - C D^-1 C^T`. `K` is the element stiffness (applied on the grid, as without these terms). `Kb` is
  the sparse matrix of the springs and of the bonds of the joints (it does not depend on the density). For `m` joints, `C` (3 dofs of a bonded node by
  `6 m` border dofs) and `D` (`6 m` by `6 m`, block diagonal: the bond and the beam of each joint) are the coupling and the self term of the rigid
  bodies. `A` is the grid block of the bordered matrix `[[K + Kb, C], [C^T, D]]` that pardiso, cholesky and amg factor, so `u` is the
  displacement of those solvers. A run with springs only has no border (`6 m = 0`).
- Every level. `Kb_l = P^T Kb_{l-1} P` and `C_l = P^T C_{l-1}` (Galerkin products of the trilinear transfer `P`, with the Dirichlet mask of the coarse
  level; made once on the host by `gpu_mg/border.py`, with the tables of `gpu_mg/transfer.py`). The terms are in the operator of each level, in the 3 x 3
  diagonal blocks of the smoother, in the dense inverse of the coarsest level, in the FP64 residual (`HostMG.apply_fine`) and in the absolute operator
  of the backward-error rule (`HostMG.apply_fine_abs`: `|Kb| |x| + |C| |D^-1| |C^T| |x|`). `K_l` stays rediscretized. The research of P2 measured that the
  terms in the coarsest matrix only are worse than none, and that a rigid motion of a bonded body cancels in `Kb x - C D^-1 C^T x` on a level only when
  the level has the Galerkin product, because the transfer keeps linear fields. A Schur complement or a Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury update of the
  coarse matrix is not used: the research found that it does not work.
- The device. Two small kernels run over the bonded nodes of a level: `bord_t_*` (`t = C^T x`, one work-group for each border dof) and `bord_w_*` (the
  3 x 3 blocks of `Kb x`, minus `C D^-1 t`); the operator kernels of the level add the result. A problem with no springs and no joints builds the
  program without the `BORDER` macro: the same kernels and launches as before P2b. Case C and case B use the same kernels (the outer operator of case B,
  level 0, has its own variants).
- After the solve. The border part of the answer, `q = -D^-1 C^T u`, is made on the host by `JointSet.border_terms` inside `reaction_facts`, so the
  reactions, the bond forces and `joint_wrenches` need only the displacement `u`. `GpuModel.kb` is the border of the solver, so the loop and
  `robust.finish_run` write the reactions as for the other solvers.
- Case C and the joint term (a fact, with measured cases; no rule). In a rigid motion of a bonded body, `Kb u` and `C D^-1 C^T u` are two terms of the size
  of the bond stiffness, and their difference is of the size of the beam. Case C computes the difference in 32-bit float, which rounds at 6e-8 of a term
  of the size of the bond stiffness, so it can lose the soft part of a joint. The solver has no threshold on the ratio of the beam to the bond. The ratio
  is the smallest generalized eigenvalue of (beam stiffness `B`, bond stiffness `D_bond`) over the joints: `GpuSolver.facts()["border"]["beam_over_bond_min"]`,
  in the `run.log` line below, in the text of a failed solve, and in a `topopt check` warning (`settings.solver: gpu-mg` with joints; the warning is a fact and
  does not predict a stop). The check of an accepted result is in 64-bit on the CPU, so a stop gives no wrong answer. A stop is the usual error (below): its
  cause is a value that is not finite, stagnation, or the target not reached, and its text has the ratio, the 32-bit fact, and the options (another solver,
  `settings.gpu_case B` on a device with 64-bit float, a stiffer beam: a larger section or a shorter beam).
  Measured on pocl in case C without the deflation (before P2d; next bullet), `gpu_tol` 1e-6 (the P2b review):
  a cube of 8 voxels on a side that only a joint holds (no fixed region), 4 load cases, only the beam E changed. Solved at 1.09e-5, 3.27e-6, 1.09e-6 and 3.27e-7
  (error of `u` at most 1.3e-6, true residual below 1e-6, 2 to 6 refinement steps). Stopped at 1.09e-7 (stagnation with the backward-error rule on; target not reached
  with the rule off), at 3.3e-8 to 1.1e-9 (not finite), and at 3.3e-10 and 1.1e-10 (not finite or stagnation, depending on the load case). The hook example with a fixed
  region and a joint on the tip (beam d 2 mm, L about 20 mm, E 3500) has the ratio 9.8e-9, and case C solved it in 6 steps (compliance 0.00724039 and 4.25502822; pardiso
  0.00724039 and 4.25502842); the beams d 4 mm (1.6e-7) and d 5 mm (3.8e-7) solved too. So the ratio decides the result only for a part that joints alone hold, where the
  limit lies between 1.1e-7 and 3.3e-7 on pocl; with a fixed region a beam far below 6e-8 solved. These are measurements of one device type, not a bound. Case B applies the
  outer operator in 64-bit: it solved the ratios down to 5.8e-11 in the tests (below).
- Deflation of the rigid modes and of the bonded patches in the inner PCG of case C with joints (P2d and P2d-D3h; `gpu_mg/deflation.py`, kernels `defl_dot`,
  `defl_coef`, `defl_apply`, `GpuMG.precondition`). It is a method setting, not a setting of the YAML: it has no switch, and its one number is the module constant
  `deflation.EXTENSION_TOL` (below). Every case C solve of a part with joints (a border with `k` > 0) removes from the inner PCG the rigid modes of each body and 6 harmonic
  columns for each bonded patch, and solves them in 64-bit on the host. Case B, and case C with no joints, have the program text, the launches and the buffers of
  before P2d (a test checks this). The cause is in the bullet above: in a rigid motion the operator is a difference of two large terms, and 32-bit float loses it.
  The rigid modes alone (P2d) solved the model cases below and did not solve the two-joint part (two tube joints on a part that no `fixed` region holds): the 32-bit error of the joint
  term is mostly a net force and a net moment on each bonded patch, and the part answers it in the soft motions where a sleeve moves against the rest, which no rigid
  mode of the whole body covers (research P2d-2).
  * `Z`, the rigid columns (P2d). 6 modes for each body (3 translations and 3 rotations about the centroid of the body, scaled by its radius of gyration). A body is a connected
    component of the active elements of level 0 (an element joins its 8 nodes). A mode is zero on every Dirichlet dof (for each dof, not for each node). The modes of a body are made
    orthonormal with a QR in 64-bit; a mode that the Dirichlet dofs make dependent is dropped by the numerical rank (a body with all dofs fixed has none). There is no
    cap on the number of bodies. The rigid columns depend on the topology only, so they are made once for a run.
  * `Z`, the harmonic columns (P2d-D3h). A bonded patch is the set of level-0 nodes that carry the coupling `C` of one joint (the bonded faces of its region): one patch for each
    joint. For each patch, 6 columns: its rigid motions (3 translations, 3 rotations about its centroid; cut at the Dirichlet dofs and reduced by the same numerical rank as the
    modes of a body) extended elastically into the part. The extension of a motion `u_s` of the patch is the field of minimum element energy `u^T K u`: the other patches and all
    Dirichlet dofs at zero, and no joint term, that is `K_ff x = -K_fs u_s` (`HostMG.apply_elements` is the operator, `K` only, with no support term). A column is zero on every other patch, except at a node that two patches share, and on every
    Dirichlet dof. Two joint regions that touch share nodes. `Deflation` writes the motion of each patch on all its nodes, so at a shared node the columns of both patches are not zero:
    each holds the motion of its own patch there (the two motions differ), and the node is no unknown of the extension. A patch with no free node (every bonded dof of its joint is Dirichlet, so the `C` block of that
    joint is cut) has no column; the facts list 0 columns for it (`columns_per_patch`). There is no cap on the number of patches or columns. The columns depend on the design (the density), so they are made again for every design (below).
  * The extension (P2d-D3h). For each design, after the numbers are on the device and before the first solve, `Deflation.extend` solves `K_ff x = -K_fs u_s` for all harmonic columns with a flexible PCG
    (Polak-Ribiere) in 64-bit on the host. The preconditioner is the V-cycle of the device (`GpuMG.precondition`: it runs the V-cycle for a block of `nr` residuals, in 32-bit, and reads
    the result back), so one iteration costs one V-cycle launch sequence and one product with `K` on the host for each block. The Krylov loop, the products with `K` and the residuals are 64-bit on the host; only the preconditioner is 32-bit. The columns go in blocks of `nr` (the load-case blocks of the engine).
    A block runs in chunks of at most `GpuParams.max_iter` iterations, with a restart between the chunks (the residual is made again from `x`), as the refinement loop does. A
    column is accepted at a relative residual `|K_ff x + K_fs u_s| / |K_fs u_s|` of `deflation.EXTENSION_TOL`, default 1e-4: this is the one new number of the method, one module constant used
    in one place; it is a method value and stays a module constant, not a setting. A block also stops when the largest residual of its columns that are not done fell by less than `engine.STAGNATION_FALL` (10 percent) over two chunks (the rule of
    the refinement loop), or when a direction has `p^T K p` not positive (a breakdown); the facts say why.
    There is no hard bound on the iterations of a block, and this contract adds no cap (no habitual cap while no run comes near the worst case; the `run.log` line of each extension gives its iterations and seconds). The worst case, as a fact: a residual that falls by exactly 10 percent over each two chunks
    passes the stagnation rule, and goes from 1 to 1e-4 in `ln(1e-4) / ln(0.9)` = 87 pairs of chunks, about 175 chunks, that is 52,500 iterations of one block (chunks of 300). At the measured 78.6 ms for an iteration (pocl, 4
    threads, 1.0 mm, the two-joint part: 2,385 iterations in 187.4 s, one run) this is about 69 minutes for one block, and the extension has one block for each `nr` columns (6 blocks for the 12 columns of that two-joint part). No run
    showed a fall that slow: every block of the two-joint part runs stopped by the tolerance, after 263 to 574 iterations for a block at 1.0 mm on pocl (one run) and 306 to 506 on the Arc (one run). A column above the tolerance is still a valid column of `Z` (any `Z` is right; only the
    speed changes): it is a fact in the record and in `run.log`, and the solve goes on. The start of the extension is the extension of the previous design (a warm start; the first design starts at zero). A
    value that is not finite in the V-cycle or in the residual is a `DeflationError`: that design runs without the deflation and the next design makes the extension again from zero.
  * `Z` of a design. `set_design` makes `Z` from the rigid columns, then an orthonormal basis of the harmonic columns made orthogonal to them (twice-projected Gram-Schmidt, then a QR and a
    numerical-rank rule; a harmonic column that the rigid columns and the others make dependent is dropped). The raw harmonic columns of all patches of a body that no Dirichlet dof holds add up to the rigid modes of that
    body (the extensions of the same rigid motion add up to that motion), so `E` of the raw columns is nearly singular; the orthonormal basis keeps `E` a compression of `A`, and its condition number is not above that of `A`
    on the span. The program of the device has `DK` = rigid + harmonic columns (a compile-time number); `k` <= `DK` of them are in use in a design, and the other rows of `Z`, `AZ` and `E^-1` are zero, so a
    dropped column costs nothing and breaks nothing. For each design: `AZ = A Z` (one `HostMG.apply_fine` for each column, with the joint terms) and `E = Z^T A Z`, with its Cholesky factor and `E^-1`. `Z` is
    copied to the device again for every design (when there are harmonic columns), with `AZ` and `E^-1`; a part with no bonded patch that can move copies `Z` once and has no extension.
