  written at once after the job lock (section 24.2, "Stop on request", reads it). A refusal gives the error status, the line `topopt run: <name>` in `run.log`,
  and the text of the error with no sentence about an earlier run.
- `--resume` does not call `clean()`. A continuation (`--continue-from`) calls it on NEW: when NEW holds an earlier run, its checks come before that call too.
- **The window (F4-47).** A check inside `optimize.run` needs the model or the first pass, so it stays after the call of `clean()`: the build of the model (the
  device of gpu-mg), the refusal of a case with a zero compliance at pass 0 (F4-37), and a failure of the factorization at the first solve. An error that
  nobody foresaw can come there too, also in the status line `starting` and in the first lines of `run.log` (an `OSError`, Ctrl+C). So `clean()` does not delete an earlier run. If the folder holds one (`old_run_files` is not empty), `clean()` moves
  every name of `RUN_FILES` (also `status.json` and `run.log`) and of `RUN_DIRS` that is in the folder into the hidden folder `.earlier-run/` of the run folder.
  It uses `rename` inside the folder: no copy and no new disk space. A `.tmp` file of a killed run is deleted. The window goes from that call to the first
  saved pass: `Checkpointer.save` calls `RunWriter.first_pass_saved()` after it wrote the first checkpoint, and that call deletes `.earlier-run/`. From then on the
  earlier run is gone, as it was before F4-47. A stop at a later pass (a compliance that is subnormal at pass 3, a request to stop, Ctrl+C) leaves the new run
  and its checkpoint. A folder with no earlier run never has `.earlier-run/`. `--resume` makes no hidden folder (it does not call `clean()`).
  - After a refusal, an error or Ctrl+C in the window, the run moves the earlier files back (`RunWriter.restore_earlier`). First it deletes the files that
    the run wrote at the names of `RUN_FILES` and `RUN_DIRS`. The folder then holds the same as after a refusal before the delete (the list above): the
    files of the earlier run with the same bytes (`run.log` has no line added), `status.json` with state `error`, iteration 0, the step where the run stopped
    (`setup`, or a step of pass 0, for example `solve`), the text of the error and the sentence `cli.EARLIER_RUN_KEPT`, and the job record. There is no
    `.earlier-run/`. The error text and the exit codes are the ones of a run in a folder with no earlier run (1, 2, 130), with the one sentence added. If the move
    back fails (an `OSError`), the status text says so, names `.earlier-run/` and `.earlier-run.moving/`, and has no sentence `EARLIER_RUN_KEPT`: the earlier files
    are still in these folders, and the next run moves them back.
  - After a kill in the window (SIGKILL, a power loss) the folder holds `.earlier-run/` with the earlier run, and at the normal names the files that the
    killed run wrote. Every state of a move is one `rename` of the folder: `.earlier-run.moving/` while the files move in or out, `.earlier-run/` when
    all earlier files are in it. A kill at any point of a move leaves a folder that the next run can read. The readers read the normal names, so they see the
    killed run and not the earlier run (`run_status`, `run_result`, the dashboard, `topopt verify` read `status.json`, `result/` and the other names of the
    folder; `list_runs`, `run_history` and `topopt dashboard` do not look into a folder whose name starts with a dot, and they do not look inside a run folder).
    `topopt cleanup` (section 29.3) reads `result/final.stl` by name and writes into `--out`, so it does not use the hidden folder. A run folder is a folder
    that holds `status.json` or `run.json`; the hidden folder lies inside one.
  - The next `topopt run` in the folder (fresh, `--resume` or `--continue-from`) calls `snapshot.recover_earlier_run` first, under the job lock, before it reads
    anything else in the folder. Three states can be there. (a) `.earlier-run.moving/`: a kill stopped a move; no file of a new run is in the folder; every entry
    goes back. (b) `.earlier-run/` and no `checkpoint.npz` or `checkpoint.prev.npz` in the folder: the run never saved a pass; the files that it wrote are deleted
    and the earlier run goes back. (c) `.earlier-run/` and a checkpoint in the folder: the run saved its first pass and the kill came before the delete; the earlier run
    is given up already, and the folder is deleted. After (a) or (b) the folder is as it was before the killed run, `status.json` of the earlier run included, and
    the run goes on as normal. A fresh run moves the earlier run aside again (or an input check refuses it, and the earlier run stays). `--resume` resumes the
    earlier run from its checkpoint, because the killed run saved no pass and has nothing to resume (the read-only plan of `cmd_run` is skipped while the folder
    holds a state of recovery; the plan runs under the lock, after the move back, with the pass count of the checkpoint of the earlier run). After (c) `--resume`
    continues the new run. One sentence says what the run did: a `warning:` line in `run.log` (the log of the new run, or the end of the log of the earlier run for
    `--resume`), or, if an input check refuses the run, the text "Before this run, a run stopped before it saved its first pass (...) and left the earlier run of
    this folder in .earlier-run/. The earlier run is back in place, and the files of the stopped run are deleted." after `EARLIER_RUN_KEPT`.
  - The job lock is as before (the lock, then everything above). A second `topopt run` in the folder stops at the lock and moves nothing.

**After a refused run, the reply says which facts are of the earlier run (P9-18).** The folder of a refused run holds the pass count, the verdict and the
checkpoint of the earlier run, and `status.json` and the job record of the refused job. `run_status` (and `run_result`, which reads it) must not give the
first as the result of the second. The case is found from what the folder holds, with no change of `cli.py` or `snapshot.py` (`server._refused_over_earlier_run`):
- `status.json` is `error`, pass 0, step `setup`, and its text ends with `cli.EARLIER_RUN_KEPT`. No other job writes that sentence: a failed resume that
  stops in its setup also has pass 0 and step `setup`, but no sentence;
- the job record is not `running`, and it did not begin before `status.json` was written (`started_at` has whole seconds, so the comparison allows one
  second: that is its resolution, not a setting): a later job, for example a resume that failed before it wrote a status, makes the status an old one;
- `snapshot.old_run_files` is not empty: the folder holds an earlier run now.

Then the reply of `run_status` is changed in these places. A folder that is not this case (no earlier run, a resume or a continuation that failed, a run that
failed at a later pass, a running job) gets the reply of before, key for key (`tests/test_refused_run_reply.py` compares it with the reply of the same code with
the detection forced off):
- `earlier_run`, the first key after `state`: `note` (whose facts these are), `summary` (one line: `pass 3 of 3, volume 29.5%, verdict iteration_limit,
  checkpoint at pass 3 of 3 (complete)`), and the facts `last_history`, `verdict`, `checkpoint` (with `yaml_path`) and `history_facts`, the same objects that
  the reply had at the top level before;
- `last_history`, `verdict` and `checkpoint` are `null` and `history_facts` is `[]` at the top level, as for any job that wrote no data;
- `summary`: `(iteration 0, 00:00)` (no pass count of `run.json`, no volume), then `job: ...`, then one clause `earlier run in this folder (this job did not
  change it; see `earlier_run`): <earlier_run.summary>`. The text of the verdict is not in the summary. A checkpoint of the earlier run that is not
  complete gets the clause `checkpoint at pass N of M: run_topopt with resume=true continues the earlier run`;
- `failure.run_data`: `setup only: no pass is done (the passes in the folder, up to pass 3, are of an earlier run: see earlier_run)`;
- `dashboard_note`: `topopt dashboard <run folder>` shows the passes of the earlier run in the folder (up to pass N);
- `options[0]` is the resume option, and it names the earlier run: `run_topopt with resume=true (yaml_path: earlier_run.checkpoint.yaml_path, out_dir:
  run_dir) continues the earlier run (not the refused job) from its checkpoint at pass N of M`, or `runs the post step of the earlier run (not the refused job)
  only: the checkpoint of the earlier run at pass N is complete`. The YAML must be the one of the earlier run: a resume with a changed YAML is refused and
  lists the changes (section 24.2);
- `log_tail` and the memory estimate do not read `run.log`: the refused job writes no line to it, so it is the log of the earlier run, also when its time is
  not older than the job.

`run_result` returns the same `earlier_run`, `summary`, `options`, `failure` and `dashboard_note` (`done: false`, `message: The run failed: <text with the
sentence>`, `checkpoint: null`); `earlier_run` is its third key, after `done` and `state`. No tool text changed: the key explains itself in `earlier_run.note`.

**After a refused run, the rows of the list tools say which keys are of the earlier run (P9-19).** A row of `list_runs` and of `run_history` (and a side
of `compare_runs`) reads `run.json`, `result/` and `history.jsonl`, which are the earlier run's, and `status.json`, which is the refused job's. It gave
the iteration count, the final mesh, the YAML, the settings and the metrics of the earlier run next to `state: error`. The rule that finds the case is
the one of P9-18. It lives in `topopt/earlier_run.py` (`refused_over_earlier_run`), because `topopt/feedback.py` does not import the server;
`server._refused_over_earlier_run` calls it. For a folder where it is true the row changes in these places. Any other folder gets the row of before, key
for key (`tests/test_refused_run_rows.py` compares it with the row of the same code with the rule forced off, and holds the keys of a plain row, recorded
from the start commit):
- `earlier_run`, after `state`, in the shape of the key of `run_status` (section 24.1, P9-18): `note` (the input check refused the job; the folder holds an
  earlier run that the job did not change; which keys are in the block; which keys stay with the refused job) and the keys that moved. Every fact stays
  in the row, in the block. `list_runs` moves `iterations`, `problem` and `final_stl_rel`; `run_history` moves the keys of section 21.1;
- the moved keys are `null` at the top of the row, as for a job that wrote no data. That includes `yaml_path`, `yaml_exists` and `yaml_newer_than_run`:
  the YAML of the refused job is not a field of the folder (the text of the error often names it, in `message`);
- `compare_runs`: see section 21.2 (the rows of its table form carry the same mark). `run_facts` and the other functions of `feedback.py` that give facts of a folder do not change;
- a fault in the rule gives the row of before, not a lost row. No tool text changed: the key explains itself in `earlier_run.note`. The dashboard has no
  list of runs: it serves one run folder (`dashboard_server`), and its pages are not part of this change.

**Facts for the data loop (DL1a).** `job.json` holds the facts of the machine and of the process, so that a later analysis of run time and
memory can tell a slow run on a busy host from a slow run on a quiet host. Code: `topopt/hostinfo.py` (the helpers; the standard library at
import time), `runjob.RunJob.start` and `finish`. A fact that cannot be read is `null`, and a sentence in `host.notes` says why (the helpers
never raise, and a fact never stops a job). Cost, measured on Linux x86_64 (22 threads, a busy host, load 23 to 33): about 6 to 16 ms
warm for the `host` block when the code is loaded (a median of 7 to 10 ms), and about 80 ms for the first call in a new process (it imports `cli` and
`environment`). In `topopt run` the first call costs about 12 ms, because those modules are loaded already. The end of the job costs 0.05 ms, the reset
0.01 ms. The largest part of the warm time is the package versions (`importlib.metadata`, 2 to 3 ms); the git commit is a file read (0.2 ms); the
process list is 0.7 ms. The cost on a Mac is not measured: there `sysctl`, `ps`, `pmset` and `vm_stat` are commands, each with the 5 s timeout, so a Mac
where all four hang waits at most 20 s (the guard is not held then).
The facts of the host are read BEFORE the job guard (`job.guard`) is taken, because a start fact can wait for a command (macOS: `sysctl`, `ps`,
`pmset`, `vm_stat`, each with the 5 s timeout) and a second start of the folder waits on the guard. A refused start (`JobHeld`) writes nothing and
resets nothing; its facts were read for nothing (about 7 ms). The read of the peak and its reset stay inside the guard, after the lock check.
The rule for the reply of `run_status` and `job_facts` (key `job`): the facts of the END of the job stay in it, all 11 keys (`peak_rss_reset`,
`cpu_time_s`, `cpu_time_children_s`, `ctx_switches_voluntary`, `ctx_switches_involuntary`, `load_avg_end`, `procs_running_end`, `setup_s`,
`loop_s`, `post_s`, `peak_rss_loop_bytes`; about 290 bytes), because they are short and say what the run cost. The block `host` is NOT in it
(about 640 bytes of facts for an analysis, not for a person or an agent): read `job.json` for it. A record from before DL1a has none of these
keys: a reader treats every key as optional.

The block `host` is written at the start (the keys are always there):

| Key | Type | Source (Linux / macOS) | `null` when |
|---|---|---|---|
| `started_by` | `"pytest"`, `"mcp"` or `"cli"` | env `PYTEST_CURRENT_TEST` set: `pytest`; else env `TOPOPT_STARTED_BY=mcp`: `mcp`; else `cli`. The MCP server sets `TOPOPT_STARTED_BY=mcp` once, at its start (`topopt_mcp.server.main`, `os.environ.setdefault`): the `topopt run` and the ratchet process that it starts inherit it, and so does `ratchet_approve`, which runs its job in the server process. Same on both systems. | never |
| `threads` | object: `OMP_NUM_THREADS`, `MKL_NUM_THREADS`, `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS`, `NUMBA_NUM_THREADS`, `GOTO_NUM_THREADS` (`cap_blas_threads` reads it) and `VECLIB_MAXIMUM_THREADS` (Apple Accelerate), each text or `null` | the environment of the process. `topopt.cli.main` sets `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS` to min(4, usable cores) itself on Linux (`cli.cap_blas_threads`) before numpy loads, if none of `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS`, `GOTO_NUM_THREADS` and `OMP_NUM_THREADS` is set; then that value is the OpenBLAS count of the run (when the user sets `OMP_NUM_THREADS`, `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS` stays `null` and OpenBLAS follows `OMP_NUM_THREADS`). The code has no other thread count: MKL (PARDISO), numba and OpenMP use their variable or all usable cores. On a Mac `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS` is usually `null` (no cap there), and `VECLIB_MAXIMUM_THREADS` is the variable that can be set. | a variable is not set (the library then uses its default) |
| `cpu_count` | int | `os.cpu_count()` | the call fails, or it gives `None` (a note in both cases) |
| `cpu_usable` | int | `cli.usable_cores()`: the CPU affinity, lowered by the CPU limit of a container | the call fails |
| `cpu_model` | text | Linux: first `model name` line of `/proc/cpuinfo`. macOS: `sysctl -n machdep.cpu.brand_string` | the source fails (a Linux kernel with no `model name` line, as some ARM kernels, gives `null` and a note) |
| `ram_total_bytes`, `ram_available_bytes` | int | `environment._ram()` (the function of the tool `environment`): the host value, or the limit of the container if it is lower | the system does not tell (a note for each one that is `null`) |
| `load_avg` | list of 3 numbers | `os.getloadavg()` (1, 5, 15 minutes), 2 decimals | the call fails |
| `procs_running` | int | Linux: `procs_running` line of `/proc/stat` (it counts the reader, so it is at least 1). macOS: no source | macOS (one note at the start of the job says so; the end adds none); a failed read |
| `other_jobs` | object `{count, by_kind, processes}` | the live topopt processes of the machine, without their command lines. Linux: `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`. macOS: `ps -axo pid=,command=`. `by_kind` has `run`, `verify`, `mcp_server` and `other` (a count for each, 0 for none); `processes` is a list of `{pid, kind}`; `count` is the sum. The process itself is not counted. A parent that is a topopt process (the MCP server of this run) is counted. `count` also holds processes that are idle: a `topopt run` that waits as a dashboard after its run is kind `run`, and the MCP servers of other sessions are `mcp_server`. An analysis that asks "did another optimizer run next to this one?" reads `by_kind`, not `count`. | no process list (a system that is not Linux or macOS), or the read fails |
| `version` | object `{topopt, git_sha, numpy, scipy, pypardiso}` | `topopt.__version__`; the commit that HEAD names in the `.git` folder of the code folder, READ FROM THE FILES (`.git` as a folder, or the file `gitdir: <path>` of a linked worktree; `HEAD`; the ref file in the git folder or in `commondir`; `packed-refs`): no `git` command runs, so there is no timeout and no `xcode-select` on a Mac; `importlib.metadata`, or `__version__` of a module that is loaded already | `git_sha`: the code folder is not a git checkout (an installed wheel): `null` and NO note, so `null` with no note means "not a checkout"; `null` WITH a note when the files cannot be read (no `HEAD`, a ref that is nowhere). A package that is not installed: `null`, no note (`pypardiso` is an optional extra) |
| `low_power_mode` | bool | macOS: the `lowpowermode` line of `pmset -g`. Linux: does not apply | Linux (no note); macOS when the command fails or has no such line, for example a desktop Mac (a note) |
| `notes` | list of text | one sentence for each fact that could not be read, as `<fact>: <ErrorType>: <text>` | empty list for none |

The thermal state of a Mac is not read: `pmset -g` does not print it (that is the second command `pmset -g therm`, which has not been run on a Mac).
The command timeout of every read-only command that remains (`ps`, `sysctl`, `pmset`, macOS only) is `hostinfo.COMMAND_TIMEOUT_S` (5 s, the value that
`runjob`, `solver_choice` and `environment` already used). The git commit needs no command.

The keys that the end of the job adds next to `wall_s` (all are `null` when the source fails; a sentence goes to `host.notes`):

| Key | Type | Source (Linux / macOS) |
|---|---|---|
| `peak_rss_reset` | bool (at the start) | `true` when the write of `5` to `/proc/self/clear_refs` worked (Linux, source `VmHWM`). `false` on macOS (no note), when the write is refused (a note), and when the command asked for no reset because it built the problem before the job (a resume, a continuation: a note). See "Peak memory" above. |
| `cpu_time_s` | number, seconds | `getrusage` (`RUSAGE_SELF` plus `RUSAGE_CHILDREN`, user plus system): the DIFFERENCE between the end of the job and its start. `RunJob.start` reads the first value (`hostinfo.usage()`, after the host facts and the reset), `finish` the second. It is the work of the job: the work of the process before the job (a test, a long server, the start-up of the command) and the work of another job of the same process (the MCP server runs `ratchet_approve` in its own process) are not in it. The children are those that the process has waited for during the job. `null` (and a note) when a read fails. |
| `cpu_time_children_s` | number, seconds | the part of `cpu_time_s` that belongs to the waited-for children (the same difference of `RUSAGE_CHILDREN`) |
| `ctx_switches_voluntary`, `ctx_switches_involuntary` | int | `ru_nvcsw` and `ru_nivcsw` of this process, as the same difference (a high involuntary count with a high load says that the host was busy) |
| `load_avg_end`, `procs_running_end` | as `load_avg` and `procs_running` | the same reads again at the end |
| `setup_s` | number, seconds | `topopt run` only: from the start of the command (`t_start` of the run, which is also the start of the job) to the first pass (state `running` of `status.json`): the voxel build, the labels, the solver set-up |
| `loop_s` | number, seconds | from the first pass to the end of the last pass (state `postprocess`, or `stopped`) |
| `post_s` | number, seconds | from the state `postprocess` to the state `done`: the post step (threshold, smoothing, STL, metrics; the buckling check, if asked). The refine step is not in it. |
| `peak_rss_loop_bytes` | int | the peak of this process (`peak_rss_info`) read when the loop ends. With `peak_rss_bytes` it separates the peak of the loop from the peak of the post step. |

The phases come from the times at which `RunWriter` changes the state (`RunWriter.phase_times()`). They are `null` for a job that has no run
writer (the ratchet, a probe), and a phase whose start or end was not reached is `null` (a run that failed in the set-up has no
`loop_s`). `setup_s + loop_s + post_s` is a little less than `wall_s` (the YAML read, the lock and the refine step are outside of the three).
The start of the phases is the start of THIS command, also for `--resume` and `--continue-from`: `RunWriter` moves its `t_start` back by the elapsed
time of the parent run there, so that `status.json` `elapsed_s` goes on from the parent, and the phases do not follow that clock (they keep
`RunWriter._phase_t0`, the start of the command). So the sum is not more than `wall_s` for every kind of run.

**Job lock.** One job per run folder. The lock holds the pid and the start time of the process. A process is alive when the pid
exists (a zombie is not alive where `/proc` says so) and it is the same process as the one that wrote the lock:
- Linux (`/proc` exists): the record has the raw start ticks (field 22 of `/proc/<pid>/stat`) and the `boot_id` of the machine
  (`/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id`). Another `boot_id` or other ticks mean another process (a reused pid). A step of the wall
  clock does not move the ticks, so it cannot make a live holder look reused. (The epoch time that is made from the boot time
  moves with the wall clock; it is in the record for text only.)
- macOS, and a record without ticks: the start time from `ps -o lstart=` (second resolution) equals the recorded epoch start time
  within 1 s.
- If the system gives no start time, a live pid counts as alive. `holder_state(rec)` gives `live`, `dead` or `reused`. Since P9-14 it is a wrapper of
  `identity_state(rec)`, which gives `live`, `dead`, `reused` or `unconfirmed`: `unconfirmed` is a live pid with no start time to compare (the system
  gives none, or the record has none). `holder_state` maps it to `live`, so a lock is never taken from a process that may still hold it. A reader
  that must not say "live" without proof (the registry of servers, section 43) uses `identity_state`.
- A file system with no `flock` (`flock` fails with `ENOLCK`, `ENOTSUP`, `EOPNOTSUPP`, `EINVAL` or `ENOSYS`, for example a network share
  without a lock daemon): the helper goes on without the guard and checks the record only. Two starts at the same moment can
  then both take the lock. A fact says so (`job lock: the file system of the run folder gives no flock ...`) in `notes` of
  `job.json` and in `run.log`. The override works as always. It is not an error.
- Held by a live process: `JobHeld` (a `UserError`, exit code 1 in the CLI). The text has the holder pid, the start time and the folder, and names the
  override. The folder is not changed. `run_topopt` returns the same text as `error`, with `job` (`pid`, `started_at`, `run_dir`).
  It checks the lock before it stops the old run process of the server, so a refusal does not close the old dashboard. The old
  process of the server itself is not a conflict: it is stopped as before.
- Held by a dead pid, or by a reused pid (the pid exists but its start time differs): the lock is replaced. A fact says which. It goes
  to `notes` of `job.json` and, in `topopt run`, to `run.log` as `warning: job lock: ...`.
- Override: CLI `topopt run ... --override-lock`; MCP `run_topopt(..., override_lock=true)`. The run takes the lock and says so as a fact. Nothing
  is stopped. The first process can still write to the folder, so the two runs can damage each other's files. When the first process ends, it sees
  that its token is not in the lock (or that the record in the folder is not its own), writes nothing, and prints one line to stderr.
- A person can remove `job.lock` to free a folder. The run that held it then still writes its record and marker at the end.
- One lock per run folder. There is no lock per work folder. The lock is for one host: a folder that two hosts share is not covered.

**run_status.** The result has `job`: `null` if the folder has no job files, else the fields of `job.json` (no token) and `state`, `holder`,
`marker`, `summary`. `state` is:
- `running`: a live process holds the lock;
- `done`: the job ended with a success code;
- `failed`: the job ended with another exit code (`exit_code` has it);
- `stopped`: the job ended with `STOPPED_EXIT` (5): a request to stop ended the run (marker `job.STOPPED`);
- `stale_lock`: the lock is there, and its process is dead or its pid is reused. `marker` is null, or it is the marker of an earlier job;
- `unfinished`: `job.json` says running and there is no lock.

`summary` gets one more sentence, for example `job: done (exit 0, 569.2 s, peak memory 2.05 GB)`, `job: FAILED with exit code 2 (...)`,
`job: stopped by a request (exit 5, ...); the checkpoint is kept and --resume continues`, or
`job: stale lock. The process of the lock (pid 123, started ...) is not running, and there is no done or FAILED marker`. The `state` of
`status.json` is not changed. For a run that this server started, a job record that is older than the start of that run gets
`earlier_run: true` and the prefix `job (an earlier run; the new run has not written yet):`. If that run process has ended
and the folder holds no run data newer than its start (a YAML error, for example), `run_status` does not show the old run as the
current one: `state` is `error`, `process_alive` is false, `summary` is `error: the run process ended with exit N before it
wrote any run data (see <run folder>.stdout)` (`was stopped by signal N` for a signal), and `job` is `{state: "no_record",
exit_code, log_file, summary, earlier_job}`. `run_status` also returns `history_facts` in every reply (a list of strings; empty
if no line was skipped).

### 24.2 Checkpoint, resume, stop rules and the verdict (B-042, added with D1b)

Code: `topopt/checkpoint.py` (file, comparison, resume plan, `Checkpointer`), `topopt/verdict.py` (stop rules, verdict), the loop in
`topopt/optimize.py` `run()`, and the flags in `topopt/cli.py`. They use numpy and the standard library only. No new dependency.
The Linux x86_64 paths are run and tested. The macOS arm64 paths have not been run on a Mac. The one platform call is the flush of the file (below).

**Checkpoint.** Every pass writes `checkpoint.npz` in the run folder (pass 0 and the last pass too). The file holds the whole state that
the next pass reads. A run that is killed and resumed gives the same result as a run that is not killed.
- One file is one `np.savez` (no compression): arrays by name, and the array `meta_json` (uint8) with a JSON text. One file means one
  atomic write: arrays and text are never from two passes.
- Write order of a pass: the snapshot, the history line, then the checkpoint. The checkpoint is written to `checkpoint.npz.tmp`,
  flushed to the drive, the old `checkpoint.npz` is moved to `checkpoint.prev.npz`, the temp file is moved to `checkpoint.npz`, then the folder is flushed.
  A kill at any point leaves at least one valid file. The flush of a file is `fcntl.F_FULLFSYNC` where `fcntl` has it (macOS: there `os.fsync` does not
  flush the drive cache), else `os.fsync`; a file system that refuses `F_FULLFSYNC` gets `os.fsync`. Fact: after a power cut the reader finds the
  last file that reached the drive, so the loss is at most the last pass or two; a process kill loses nothing. The history and the snapshots are not flushed (as before).
  The run log gets one `fact:` line at the end with the count, the size and the time of the writes (the flush can be turned off with
  `topopt.checkpoint.FSYNC = False`).
- Arrays: `x` (the design after the step; at the last pass, the design that was measured), `mma_low`, `mma_upp` (n,1), `mma_xold1`, `mma_xold2`,
  `mma_x` (only if `MmaState.x` differs from `x`), `design_mask` (the design voxels of the grid as packed bits, 1 bit for each grid voxel in C order: about 14 KB on the
  1.2 mm hook grid; a resume uses it to put the saved values on the right voxels), `carry_U` (the solve of the design that step acceptance accepted: see section 17),
  and the arrays of the objects that offer state, as `<owner>__<name>` (today `solver__x_prev`: the AMG warm start), and the arrays of the row states, as `rowvec_<n>`
  (float64, exact: the start vector `v0` of the buckling row, section 39; `meta.mma.rows` and `meta.rows_before` hold `{"npz_array": "rowvec_<n>"}` in its place, and an array that is equal in both is stored once).
  A run without a buckling row has no such array, and its file is as it was.
- `meta_json` keys: `kind` (`topopt-checkpoint`), `format` (1), `topopt_version`, `written_at`, `platform`, `iteration` (the last finished pass),
  `n_iterations`, `complete` (this is the last pass of the run: its last pass, or a stop rule), `stop` (the stop rule that fired, or null),
  `n_design`, `elapsed_s` (the run time until now, it goes on after a resume), `mma` (`it`, `f0_ref`, `rows`, `move`, `x`: `none`, `same` or `saved`),
  `step_acceptance` (`counters` [passes, rejected tries, passes with a rejected try, forced steps] and `carry_beta`), `prev` (the last history record),
  `inputs`, `resume_points`, `extras` (names of the `<owner>__<name>` arrays), and for the solver `gpu-mg` `gpu_mg` (`tol`, `backward_error`: the numbers of the loop, section 20; a checkpoint from
  before G2 has none, and the resume says so).
- `inputs` (the hashes live here only; `run.json` has none): `yaml_sha256`, `yaml_parsed` (the YAML as parsed data, `yaml.safe_load` through JSON), `regions` (SHA-256 of each region file. The hash is `topopt.runinfo.sha256_file`; the keys come from
  `topopt.runinfo.region_files` (section 24.1): `<field of config.regions>:<path relative to the YAML folder, with />`, for example `design:design.stl`,
  `fixed:regions/a/clamp.stl`, `load:tip.stl` (the path is the one the YAML names; a file outside the work folder has `<outside>/<12 hex>/<file name>`, no folder name). All fields are walked, so a later kind of region file has a key too. Two files with the same name in
  different folders have two keys. A checkpoint that has other keys, for example from an earlier build, gives a "no longer in the YAML" fact and a
  "new in the YAML" fact for each file, and needs the override), `effective` (settings, material and load cases as they are after the defaults, without the two voxel
  guards and `stop_rules`), `effective_sha256`, `solver` (the solver that ran), `grid` (`shape`, `n_design`, `origin` in mm, `h` in mm), `labels_sha256`.
- Reading: `checkpoint.npz` first, then `checkpoint.prev.npz`. A file is valid if every array reads (the CRC is checked), `kind` and `format` are right, and every core
  field is there with the right form: `mma.it`, `mma.f0_ref`, `mma.rows`, `mma.move`, `mma.x`, the arrays `x` (n), `mma_low` and `mma_upp` (n,1), `mma_xold1` and `mma_xold2` (n; from the first MMA step on),
  `mma_x` (if `mma.x` is `saved`), `design_mask` (its design voxels are `n_design` on the grid of `inputs.grid.shape`), the `step_acceptance.counters` (if given), `inputs`, and every array that `mma.rows` or `rows_before` refers to (`rowvec_<n>`). A file that fails the check goes to
  the older file, or to a refusal with the reason; this happens before any change of the run folder. A temp file is never used. A file with another `format` is not used and not deleted; the text names its `topopt_version`.
- State that a later item adds goes through the hook: an object (the model, the solver) with `checkpoint_state() -> {name: array}` and
  `restore_checkpoint_state({name: array}) -> [facts]`. A field that the file lacks gives a `resume:` fact in the run log, not an error.

**Resume.** `topopt run <file.yaml> --out <dir> --resume [--allow-changed-inputs]`. MCP: `run_topopt(..., resume=true, allow_changed_inputs=false)`.
The folder must exist (a resume of a folder that is not there is a user error). `--allow-changed-inputs` needs `--resume`.
1. The command reads the YAML and the region files again, builds the problem and the solver choice, reads the checkpoint and compares. All this
   happens before anything is written, and before the job files of section 24.1: a refusal writes nothing to the run folder, and a finished run keeps its `job.DONE`
   and `job.json`. The plan is made again under the job lock (the problem is not built twice).
2. If the resume goes on: it removes `checkpoint.npz.tmp` and a checkpoint that failed the check; it cuts `history.jsonl` to the checkpoint pass (the kept lines keep their
   bytes; a line that does not parse is dropped; a last line without a newline gets one, so the next line never joins it); it removes the snapshots after the checkpoint pass
   and `*.tmp` snapshots; it removes `result/` and `verdict.json`; it writes `run.json` and `labels.bin` again with the first `started_at`; the run time goes on from `elapsed_s`.
   With the solver `gpu-mg`, the solver cuts `gpu_mg.jsonl` to the same pass when it starts, and appends (section 20); a new run starts a new file.
   It does not call `clean()`. The plan (the facts) goes to `run.log` first, then the folder changes, so a resume that stops inside this step has left its facts. Each of these steps that
   changed something is one `resume:` line in `run.log`.
3. The run goes on at pass `iteration + 1`, then ends as always (post step, refine, `verdict.json`). A checkpoint with `complete: true` has no pass left: the resume only runs the post step again.
4. The job lock of section 24.1 applies. A stale lock is replaced with a fact. A `job.FAILED` marker does not block a resume (the helper removes old markers at the start). `job.DONE` is written at the end.
5. `run.json` `started_at` stays the start of the first run. Each resume adds an entry to `resume_points` (in the checkpoint, in `verdict.json` and in `metrics.json`
   `verdict`): `iteration`, `checkpoint` (the file used), `resumed_at`, `dropped_history_iterations`, `dropped_snapshots`, `changes`.

Equality: with one thread and a direct solver (PARDISO, Cholesky) the resumed run equals the run that was not killed byte for byte (history without the timing fields,
snapshots, `final.stl`, `preview.bin`, `labels.bin`). With more threads, or with AMG, the numbers are close, not equal. AMG is not reproducible from run to run
even with one thread (pyamg draws random numbers for its spectral radius estimate).

Inputs that changed (a fact for each, and the override; `settings.objective_scale: first -> <not set>` is such a fact for a checkpoint with `first` and a YAML with no key, section 13): the whole parsed YAML, key path by key path, also a key that the loader does not turn into a setting
(`name`, `assumptions`, a later key such as `mirror`), the content of each region file (keys of section 24.1 `region_files`), the voxel labels, the solver that runs, and the effective settings
after the defaults if the parsed YAML is the same (a default of topopt changed). The facts name each key path with the old and the new value: `settings.volume_fraction: 0.3 -> 0.35`,
`name: cantilever -> other`, `load_cases[0].forces[0].force: [0, 0, -2.0] -> [0, 0, -3.0]`, `mirror: <not set> -> ...`. A list that holds no mapping is one value; a list of mappings goes by index.
Regions that fill other voxels (the grid is the same): the fact gives the counts, "N of the M saved design voxels are design voxels in this run too, K are new, J are dropped". With the override the saved arrays
(`x`, the MMA state: `mma_low`, `mma_upp`, `mma_xold1`, `mma_xold2`, `mma_x`) go onto the new design voxels by position (flat grid id): a voxel in both keeps its saved values, a new voxel starts as in a new run
(`x` = `settings.volume_fraction`, `xold1` = `xold2` = `x`, the asymptotes `x -/+ 0.5 (xmax - xmin)`), a dropped voxel is left out. A region file that has the same content under another path of the same role is one fact
("region file design:a.stl is now design:b/a.stl: the content is the same"). The step acceptance solve `carry_U` is used only if no input changed; with a change the next pass solves the design again, and the log says so.
Not a change: `settings.stop_rules`, `settings.max_active_voxels` and `settings.max_grid_voxels` (they do not change the numbers of a pass): each is a note. A YAML text with other bytes and the same parsed content
(comments, the order of keys, the format) is a note (`resume: the YAML text changed (comments or format only) ...`), not a refusal. The refusal is a `UserError` (exit 1, one line): `Resume stopped: the inputs changed since the checkpoint
(iteration N): <key: old -> new; ...>. ... Options: ...`. With `--allow-changed-inputs` the run goes on with the new inputs, and says so in `run.log` and in `resume_points[].changes`. A checkpoint without `yaml_parsed` (an earlier build)
is compared by the effective settings. For a run with `settings.target_mass_g` (I7) the effective settings hold the asked mass and not the derived fraction (section 3), so the same YAML gives the same
effective settings before and after the problem is built.
A new setting, whose default changes the numbers of a pass, follows one rule. It is left out of the effective settings at its default, so an older checkpoint resumes.
A `resume:` fact says that the checkpoint is from before the setting, and what the run does now (`gpu_tol` and `gpu_backward_error`, section 20; `objective_scale`, section 13).
A value that is not the default stays in the effective settings, so a change of it is a change of the inputs.

Resume stops with no override that works (the text names the reason and the options):
- no checkpoint file (the folder is not a run, or the first pass did not end), or no file that reads;
- a checkpoint with another `format`;
- another grid: the grid shape or the voxel size differs, or the grid origin moved by half a voxel or more (the saved design does not fit). An origin that moved by less is the same grid (a fact; the saved design goes onto the cells with the same index);
- a checkpoint of a run that finished (`complete`) with another `settings.iterations`. `--resume` does not make a finished run longer (a resume repeats its post step only). The route for more passes is a new run folder: `--continue-from` (section 24.3). The refusal names it;
- a checkpoint at or past the last pass of a run that did not finish.
`settings.iterations` can be made shorter for a run that did not finish (with the override).
A run that is a continuation (section 24.3) takes its pass count from its own checkpoint (`continued_from.iterations`), not from the YAML, so a plain `--resume` of a killed continuation needs no other `settings.iterations`. `config_of_continuation` does this before the plan (`topopt run --resume`, and the resume check of `run_topopt`);
`plan_resume` only adds a fact.

**Stop rules.** YAML `settings.stop_rules`: `false` (default), `true`, or a mapping (a mapping turns the rules on unless it has `enabled: false`). Keys: `enabled`,
`objective_change` (default 1e-4, relative), `window` (5 passes), `grayness_max` (0.1), `time_budget_s` (none). CLI: `--stop-rules` or `--no-stop-rules` wins over the YAML. MCP: `run_topopt(stop_rules=true|false)`.
The rules are off by default, so a run without the key has the same passes as before D1b. The decision is made after the sensitivity step and before the update step of a pass. A pass at which a rule fires makes no step
(`change` 0), like the last pass, and its checkpoint has `complete: true` and `stop`. The rules, in this order:
- `converged`: the objective has settled and the run is feasible: the four tests of the verdict are met (below).
- `time_budget`: the run time (it includes the time before a resume) is at or above `time_budget_s`. The text gives the convergence tests at that pass, each with its value, threshold and met or not met.
  The run time is read at the end of a pass: it counts the loading, the setup and the passes, not the post step (section 11). A mapping with only `time_budget_s` also turns on `converged`.
`stop` in `verdict.json`: `rule`, `iteration`, `text`, `measures` (or `elapsed_s` and `time_budget_s`).

**Stop on request** (P4b-4, F4-11). A person or an agent can ask a running run to stop at the end of its current pass.
Code: `topopt/runjob.py` (`request_stop`, `read_stop`, `read_own_stop`, `clear_stop`, `stop_reply`, `is_run_folder`), the loop in `topopt/optimize.py` (`RunStopped`),
`topopt/cli.py` (`cmd_stop`), and the MCP tool `stop_run`.
Tests: `tests/test_run_stop.py`. The helper `tests/stop_at.py` writes the request from inside the run at a fixed pass (no sleep, no timing).
- The request is the file `<run_dir>/job.stop`. It is JSON with these keys:
  - `format`: 1.
  - `requested_at`: local time with the UTC offset, ISO (as in `job.json`).
  - `by`: `topopt stop` or `mcp stop_run`.
  - `target_pid`: the pid of the run if the caller knows it, else null.
- A file that is there but does not parse is also a request (a person made it with `touch`). `read_stop` then gives `by`, `requested_at` and `target_pid` as null.
- If a request is there already, `request_stop` writes nothing again.
  Two writers can find no request at the same time. Each writes its own temp file in the run folder (`job.stop.<pid>.<8 hex>.tmp`).
  Each moves its temp file to `job.stop` with `os.replace`, and the last move wins. Then each reads the file back and replies from what is on disk.
  A writer whose request did not win gets `already_requested`.
  The temp file is removed in all cases. A writer that crashed can leave one.
  No reader of run folders is confused by it (audit of `list_runs`, `feedback`, `cleanup`, `apply_marks`, the replay and the post step).
- No signal is sent and nothing waits. The run reads the request at two points:
  1. At the end of each pass, after `checkpoint.save`. This read is for a pass that is not the last pass, and at which no stop rule fired.
     It is one file read for each pass, with no polling.
  2. Once before the post step (`cli._run_folder`). This read is for a request that came during the last pass, or during a pass at which a stop rule fired.
- The run does not read the request during the setup, the post step and the refine step. All passes are done then, so the reply `postprocess` below writes nothing. The one exception is the first run of `--fine-pass` when a fine pass follows (see section 24.6): the request is written, and the driver of `--fine-pass` reads it before it starts the fine pass.
- A request that comes during the post step is removed at the end, and the run ends with exit code 0.
  The `run.log` fact is `a request to stop (...) came after the last pass. The post step does not read requests and the run is finished, so the request is removed.`
- A process acts on a request only when `target_pid` is null or is its own pid (`read_own_stop`). A request for another pid stays in the folder for that process.
  With `--override-lock`, two processes can work in one folder. `stop_run` names the one that holds the lock, which is the newer one.
- A stop has this sequence:
  1. `optimize.run` writes `verdict.json` (state `stopped_by_request`, below), frees the solver and raises `RunStopped`.
  2. `topopt run` writes `status.json` `{"state": "stopped", "iteration": k, "message": ...}` and removes `job.stop`.
  3. It writes the `run.log` line `stop: stopped by a request at pass k of N; --resume continues at pass k+1. The request (...) is removed.`
  4. It skips the post step and the refine step. There is no `result/`.
  5. It ends the job with exit code 5 (`job.STOPPED`, state `stopped`, section 24.1).
  6. The process continues to serve the dashboard, unless `--no-wait` is given.

  A stop before the post step (`RunStopped.complete`) leaves the verdict of the finished optimizer. Its message says that `--resume` runs the post step only.
- The history line, the snapshot and the checkpoint of pass k are those of a run that goes on. They are written before the request is read. The history gets no extra field.
  The stage facts of the stop pass (`stage_facts.stage_end`, no solve) go to `run.log` as `fact: stop at pass k: ...` and into the verdict `facts`. They do not go into the history.
  `robust.finish_run` and the end value of the perimeter row wait for the resume.
- `--resume` of a stopped run needs no `--allow-changed-inputs`, because the inputs did not change.
  `plan_resume` adds the fact `resume: the run was stopped by a request at pass k (requested by B at T).` This happens when `status.json` says `stopped` at the pass of the checkpoint.
  For a complete checkpoint, the fact says that the optimizer is done and that the post step runs now.
  With one thread and a direct solver, the resumed run equals the run that was not stopped, byte for byte (the rule of "Equality" above).
- The start rule (section 24.1): the job start removes a `job.stop` that does not name the pid of the new run, with a fact. This includes a request with `target_pid` null.
  So an old request cannot stop a new run.
- `stop_reply(run_dir, by, starting_pid=None)` is the one function that the CLI and the MCP tool call.
  `starting_pid` is a process that the caller started and that has not taken the job lock yet.
  The reply is a dict with these keys:
  - `state`, `run_dir`, `pid`, `iteration`, `phase`, `message`, `options` and `note`.
  - `job` (section 24.1, or null), `stop_request` and `checkpoint` (`checkpoint.describe`, or null).

  The values of `state`:

  | `state` | When | Written |
  |---|---|---|
  | `stop_requested` | a live process holds the job lock, or `starting_pid` has not taken it yet. The run is in the optimizer loop or before it | `job.stop` |
  | `already_requested` | the same, and a request is in the folder (or the request of another writer won) | nothing |
  | `postprocess` | a live run with status `postprocess` or `done`: no pass is left to read the request. Options: wait; or end the process yourself (`--resume` then repeats the post step only). The first run of `--fine-pass` with a fine pass to follow (`job.json` `fine_pass.first_run`, and `run.json` `part_voxel.recommend` or `fine_pass.forced`) gets the state `stop_requested` (or `already_requested`) instead, see section 24.6 | nothing (the exception: `job.stop`, read by the driver before the fine pass) |
  | `nothing_to_stop` | the job ended (`done`, `stopped`, `failed`), or it is closing (status `stopped` or `error`, lock still there). Options: the `--resume` route where a checkpoint is there | nothing |
  | `gone` | `stale_lock` or `unfinished`: no live process. Options: `--resume` (it replaces the stale lock, with a fact). MCP also: the run process of this server ended before it took the job lock, and the folder has no job files | nothing |
  | `none` | (a) no job files and no live process. (b) The folder does not exist (no folder is made). (c) A live process holds the job lock in a folder that is not a run folder (no `status.json`, no `run.json`) | nothing |
  | `several` (MCP only) | several live runs: `runs` lists them | nothing |

  - `status.json` is used only if it is not older than the start of the job (`_current_status`). So the status of an earlier run is not read as the phase of the new one.
  - For case (c) of `none`, the message names the marker that it sees: `ratchet.json` or `ratchet.jsonl`. A ratchet job does not read `job.stop`.
  - The texts of `none` and `nothing_to_stop` add (`runjob.NOT_SEEN`): a run that is starting and has not taken the job lock yet is not seen. Call again.
  - `note` (`runjob.STOP_NOTE`) is in every reply: a topopt build from before this change does not read `job.stop`. A run of such a build ignores the request.
    The file stays in the folder then. Only a job of this build removes it.
- `stop_run(run_dir=None)` (MCP) adds `run_dir_rel`, `found_by` and `process_alive`. Without `run_dir`, it picks the run like this:
  1. The run that this server started and that still works.
  2. Else the scan of the work folder and its `runs/` folder for a live `job.lock`. This finds a run that the CLI started.
     The scan counts run folders only: a folder with `status.json` or `run.json` (`is_run_folder`, the rule of `list_runs`).
     The folder of a ratchet job holds a job lock too, and it is not a run.
     A run that has only just taken the lock and has not written `status.json` yet is not found. Call again.
  3. Several live runs give `several`, and nothing is written.
  4. Else the last run of this server, or the default run folder.

  If `run_dir` names a folder with a live job lock that is not a run folder, the reply is `none` and nothing is written.
  For `nothing_to_stop` and `gone`, `message` names a pid of this server that is alive: it only serves the dashboard.
  If the run process of this server ended before it took the job lock, and the folder has no job files, the reply is `gone`. `message` has the exit and the log file.
- `run_status` and a stop:
  - State `stopped`: `status.json` says `stopped`, and `summary` starts with `stopped: <message>`.
  - Every reply has the field `stop_request`: the request in the folder, or null if there is none. This includes the replies `starting`, `none` and the early `error`.
    For a pending request on a running run, `summary` has a sentence about it.
  - The resume hint tests the job state. A checkpoint is there, no process is alive, and there is a job record or no pid of this server.
    Then `summary` says that `run_topopt` with `resume=true` continues the run. For a complete checkpoint, it runs the post step only.
  - `run_result` of a stopped run returns `{"done": false, "stopped": true, ...}`.
- Readers (P4b-4 audit):
  - `feedback.run_facts`, `run_history` and `compare_runs` show the verdict state as a string. They need no change.
  - `list_runs` shows the status `stopped` as `state`.
  - `cleanup`, `apply_marks` and `topopt buckling` add a sentence to their "no result" error. The sentence names the stop and `--resume` (`runjob.stopped_hint`).
  - The replay shows `stopped` at its end.
  - The dashboard has a STOPPED pill and a banner with the status message.

**Verdict.** `verdict.json` in the run folder (written at the end of `run()`, atomic) and `result/metrics.json` key `verdict` (the same object). A folder without `verdict.json` gets one that the post step
computes from `history.jsonl` with the default thresholds (`source: "history"`, and a note). Keys:
`format` (1), `state`, `text`, `final_iteration`, `iterations`, `converged`, `feasible`, `measures`, `stop_rules` (the settings), `stop`, `resume_points`, `notes`, `facts` (added with P3a: the `stage_end` of the last pass, with its `iteration`, or null; section 13), and `stop_request` (P4b-4: only in the state `stopped_by_request`; `requested_at`, `by`, `iteration`). Every other verdict keeps its bytes.
- `state`: `stopped_by_rule` (a rule fired), `stopped_by_request` (P4b-4: a request to stop ended the run at the last pass, which is not the last pass of the settings; the text is `stopped by a request at pass k of N. Tests: ...` with the same tests as the other states), `converged` (the last pass is `settings.iterations`, `converged` and `feasible` are both true), `iteration_limit` (the last pass is `settings.iterations`, and `converged` and `feasible` are not both true), `unfinished` (the history ends earlier and no rule fired).
- `feasible` and `converged` are two separate facts. `feasible`: every constraint row is met (`g <= 5e-3` = `formulation.NOT_MET`), and no row is without a result (below). `converged`: the objective has settled: the objective change, the grayness and the last beta stage are met (no constraint row is read).
  A run can be feasible and not converged, and it can be converged and not feasible. The text never calls a run infeasible because it is not converged, and never calls it not converged because a row is not met. The state `converged` and the stop rule `converged` need both facts.
- `text`: facts only. It gives each test with its value, its threshold and "met" or "not met", for example "iteration limit reached at pass 80. Tests: objective change 0.000144 (relative) in the last 5 passes (threshold 0.0001: not met); grayness 0.035 (threshold 0.1: met); largest g -9.83e-06 (row volume, threshold 0.005: met); the beta schedule has reached its last stage (beta 8 from pass 65)."
  For a run with a volume row the text ends with ` Facts: volume: 0.47 of the allowed volume used (projected design), 0.40 (thresholded part at 0.5).`
  It adds `; load path: ...` when a load region is not joined (section 13). A mass run with no volume row has `material: ...` in the same place (F1-3a), and `grey design: ...` after it when its
  last pass has a grayness above `grayness_max`: the grayness value, the volume at the cuts 0.4, 0.5 and 0.6 with the spread, and the body count at the three cuts (section 13). The facts are not tests.
  No state, `converged` or `feasible` reads them.
  A settled run with a row that is not met starts with "The objective has settled; row X is not met (g ..., threshold ...)." A settled run with a row that is not judged starts with "The objective has settled; row X is not judged (no result at the last pass (status ...; ...))." The default thresholds are not tuned for a part; the text does not judge the run.
- `measures` (the rule and the verdict call the same function): `objective_change` (the largest relative change of `objective.value`, the physical value of the objective and not the scaled one of MMA (section 13), between two passes in the last `window` passes at one beta; needs `window + 1` passes in a row at that beta, else `value` is null),
  `grayness` (of the last pass, at most `grayness_max`), `last_beta_stage` (the last pass is at or after the start of the last beta stage: `verdict.reaches_last_beta_stage`, the function that the fact before the run uses, section 13), `max_g` (the feasibility test: the largest linear `g` of the rows, and its `row`, at most 5e-3), and `last_step_change` (information, no threshold). Each of the four tests has `value`, `threshold` and `met`; `converged` is the first three, `feasible` is `max_g`.
  **A row with no result at the last pass** (`formulation.no_result`: the entry has `evaluated` false and a `status` other than `skipped`, or `evaluated` false and no `last_eval`; the buckling row after a failed evaluation, section 39) is not judged, in the way of `objective_change` with no value. `max_g` then names that row (the first one, in the order of the rows), with the extra key `judged` (false; a judged `max_g` has no such key, so the verdict of a run without a failed row keeps its bytes), `met` false, `value` the `g` of the value that the row holds, `status`, `held_from_pass` (the pass of that value, or null) and `text` ("not judged: no result at the last pass (status ...; the value held is from pass N)"). So `feasible` is false, and it stays a bool. The rule `converged` does not fire at such a pass. The value that a skipped pass holds is a result: the row is judged.
- `interface_tests` and `region_integrity` (added with H1 PR 3; only in `metrics.verdict`, not in `verdict.json`, which the run wrote before the post step): facts of the finished part, not tests of the convergence. `interface_tests` is there only if a YAML interface has `full_surface: true`: the list `interfaces.full_surface_tests` of section 23, one test for each such interface (`full_coverage` at least 0.98: met). `region_integrity` is there only if a frozen region keeps under 0.97 of its volume (section 23, check C): `region`, `role`, `kept`, `threshold`. The text then ends with one more sentence for each key present, for example ` Interface tests (full surface): socket_bore 0.75 of its full area (threshold 0.98: not met); socket_bore_b 0.371 of its full area (threshold 0.98: not met). Frozen regions that keep less than the limit: sleeve 0.447 of its volume (threshold 0.97: not met).` `state`, `converged` and `feasible` do not read them, and `verdict.json` does not have the two keys: they are only in `metrics.verdict`. A run with neither key keeps the bytes of its verdict.
- The name `verdict` also appears in section 17 (`stress` report: pass or fail of a voxel statistic, none today). They are not related: the key `metrics.verdict` is the convergence verdict, and `metrics.stress.cases.*.verdict` is the accuracy verdict.

**MCP.** `run_topopt(yaml_path, out_dir, override_lock, resume, allow_changed_inputs, stop_rules)` (and `continue_from`, `more_iterations`: section 24.3). A resume that is refused returns `{"error", "run_dir", "resume": {"facts", "options", "checkpoint"}}` and starts nothing (the old dashboard process is not stopped).
Without `resume`, in a folder that holds the checkpoint of a run that did not finish, the reply has `earlier_checkpoint` (the fields of `checkpoint` below and a `note`: the new run deletes that checkpoint, `resume=true` continues the old run), and the run starts.
`run_status` has `checkpoint` (null, or `file`, `iteration`, `iterations`, `complete`, `written_at`, `elapsed_s`, `topopt_version`, `format`, `stop_rule`, `resume_points`, `yaml_path`, and `continued_from` for a continuation) and `verdict` (null until the run ends) in every reply, also in the replies
for `starting`, `error` before any data, and `none`. If no process is running (no pid of this server, and the job state is not `running`) and the checkpoint is not complete, `summary` says that `run_topopt` with `resume=true` continues the run. `skills/start-here/SKILL.md` tells the agent to report the verdict and to use `allow_changed_inputs` only if the user wants it.

### 24.3 Continue a finished run in a new folder (P4b-5, finding F4-14)

Code: `topopt/checkpoint.py` (`plan_continue`, `apply_continue`, `Continuation`, `check_more_iterations`, `check_new_folder`, `config_of_continuation`,
`diff_inputs(soft=)`, `Checkpointer`), `topopt/optimize.py` (`rows_before`), `topopt/cli.py`, `topopt/snapshot.py` (`run.json`), `topopt/gpu_mg/model.py` (the timing file),
`topopt_mcp/server.py`. Tests: `tests/test_continue.py`, `tests/test_continue_mcp.py`, `tests/test_continue_gpu_mg.py`. No new dependency, and no new limit, wait, retry or timeout.

**Command.** CLI: `topopt run <file.yaml> --out NEW --continue-from PARENT --more-iterations N [--allow-changed-inputs] [--stop-rules | --no-stop-rules]`.
MCP: `run_topopt(yaml_path, out_dir=NEW, continue_from=PARENT, more_iterations=N, allow_changed_inputs=false, stop_rules=None)`. The two options go together, and they do not go with `--resume`.
N is a whole number of 1 or more. There is no upper limit. A wrong value or a wrong mix is a `UserError` (exit 1, MCP `error`) with options, and nothing is written.

A continuation is a NEW run in a NEW folder. It starts from the last checkpoint of PARENT (pass K) and has K + N passes, as a run of K + N passes has. The parent is only read:
no lock, no write, no new file, no change of a modification time. `settings.iterations` of the YAML is not used (a fact says so). The YAML and the region files are read again and compared with the checkpoint, as for a resume
(section 24.2), with one exception: `settings.iterations` is a soft key (`diff_inputs(soft=)`; the YAML and the effective settings), so a YAML that says 12 or 24 passes is not a change.
Another change of an input is a refusal with facts and options, or goes on with `--allow-changed-inputs` (MCP `allow_changed_inputs`). A grid that differs, a checkpoint that cannot be read, and
a checkpoint of another `format` stop as for a resume. A parent that is still running is not refused: a fork from its checkpoint is a valid step. The process reads the checkpoint once, and that one read gives
the pass K, the pass count K + N, the plan, `run.json`, the log, `checkpoint_sha256` (the hash of the bytes that were read, not of the file name read again) and the copy (the history lines
and the snapshots up to pass K only). The parent goes on and its later passes are not in the new run. A fact says so (`continue: the parent is running now ...`).

**Two kinds of parent.**
- The checkpoint is complete (`complete: true`): the parent finished, or a stop rule or a request ended it at its last pass. That pass only measured: it made no MMA step. The new run
  runs pass K again, now with its update step (`last=False`), and goes on to pass K + N. This is a replay (`continued_from.replay` true). The history lines, the snapshots and the lines of `gpu_mg.jsonl` of the passes 0 to K - 1 are copied. Pass K is written again.
- The checkpoint is not complete: the run was stopped (section 24.2), killed, or ended with an error. The new run is a fork. It starts at pass K + 1 and runs no pass again. The files of the passes 0 to K are copied. The pass count of the parent
  does not matter: the fork has K + N passes (it can be fewer than the parent planned).

**Order of the work.** (1) The arguments and the new folder are checked, then the checkpoint is read (once: the plans below use this one read), the problem is built and the inputs are compared. All this writes nothing, not even the new folder:
a refusal leaves no folder. (2) The new folder is made and the new run takes its own job lock (section 24.1). It plans again under the lock, with the same read of the checkpoint (the YAML and the region files are read again, so they can have changed
since step 1). A refusal there ends the job with exit code 1 and `job.FAILED`, and the folder holds the job files only. Then it calls `RunWriter.clean()` on NEW like any new run (it deletes the run files of an older run there, also the checkpoint of an unfinished one: the log says so). When NEW holds an older run, the checks of the model that follow the plan (the union piece with no fixed voxel, the piece with no support, the perimeter bound) come before that call, and a refusal keeps the older run (section 24.1, "A refused run keeps the earlier run"). The call moves the older run into `.earlier-run/`, and the first saved pass of NEW deletes it (F4-47). (3) `apply_continue` writes the facts
(`continue:` lines in `run.log`), then copies. History lines keep their bytes. Each snapshot goes through a temp file and `os.replace`. The run time goes on from the parent (`elapsed_s` of the checkpoint), so a time budget includes the time of the parent.
`resume_points` starts empty. `started_at` is the start of the new run.

**The new folder must not change the parent.** NEW is refused (exit 1, options, nothing written) when it is PARENT, when it is inside PARENT, or when PARENT is inside `NEW/snapshots`, `NEW/result` or `NEW/verify`
(a new run deletes those folders). The folders are compared by identity (`os.path.samefile`: device and inode) and not by the text of the path, so a link, a bind mount and a path in another letter case on macOS (APFS) are found.
For a NEW that does not exist yet, the deepest folder of its path that exists, and each folder above it, are compared with PARENT. A parent can be a continuation, so a chain works (the checkpoint of the parent holds its own `continued_from`; the new record names the parent, not the first run).

**Disk.** The copy has no cap. The fact before the copy gives the bytes: `the new run folder gets a copy of the history up to pass P, S snapshots (B bytes) ... The copy uses at most T bytes of disk space`,
and the fact after the copy gives the lines and the bytes copied. The snapshots are about K times the size of the grid in bytes.

**What the checkpoint adds.**
- `meta.rows_before`: `MmaState.rows` at the start of the pass (JSON, with the arrays of the row states as references into the `.npz`, section 24.2; the stress row keeps its KS scale, the buckling row keeps its state and its start vector `v0`). Only a complete checkpoint has it (the replay needs it, as the rows in the file are those after the pass). It is an optional key.
  A checkpoint without it (from before P4b-5) works: the replay uses the rows after pass K, and a fact names which rows can differ (see the table). No other pass uses the key.
- `meta.continued_from`: the record of section 5. Each checkpoint of a continuation has it. A killed continuation resumes with a plain `--resume`: `config_of_continuation` (called by `cmd_run` and by the resume check of `run_topopt`) takes the pass count (`continued_from.iterations`) from there,
  and `plan_resume` adds a fact (`resume: this run is a continuation of ... Its pass count is 24, from the checkpoint.`).
- A replay restores `first = K`, the rows from `rows_before`, `prev` = the history record of pass K - 1, and `stop = None`. The beta schedule and the reset of the objective scale (section 13) go by the absolute pass number, so the passes K to K + N follow the schedule of a run of K + N passes.
  Everything that only the last pass does (`last=True`: the spring reactions, the `stage_end` facts, `robust.finish_run`, the perimeter end value, the verdict) moves to pass K + N.

**A parent that a stop rule ended.** The stop rules come from the YAML or the flags of the new run. With the rules on, the rule is judged again at pass K with the same numbers, so it can end the new run at pass K again. The fact names the rule and the options:
`--no-stop-rules` (MCP `stop_rules=false`), or other thresholds in `settings.stop_rules`. With the rules off, the run goes on to pass K + N. This item does not change the stop rules. A request to stop (section 24.2) that ended the parent is not read by the new run: it reads the `job.stop` of its own folder only. The fact names the request; for a request after the last pass
(a complete checkpoint, so a replay) it says that the new run runs that pass again and that the request does not stop it.

**What the output states.** The facts of the plan, one `continue:` line each: the parent, the checkpoint and its pass; replay or fork; the pass count and where it comes from; the stop rule; the grid origin; the notes; and the step settings (`continued_from.step_settings`): the passes
(`first_pass`, `last_pass`), the beta of each stretch, the move limit (the setting, and the value in the checkpoint if step acceptance changed it), the objective scale (mode and the passes where it is set again), the stop rules, the solver, and whether `rows_before` is used
(`used`, `missing in the checkpoint; the rows after pass K are used`, `not used: no pass runs again (a fork)` or `not needed: no row keeps a value between passes`).
A continuation that ends before the last stage of `settings.beta_schedule` also has the `fact:` line of section 13 ("A run that ends before the last beta stage") in `run.log` before pass 0, with the pass count K + N and the option `more_iterations`; it is not a `continue:` line.

**MCP reply.** A refusal: `{"error", "run_dir", "continue": {"facts", "options", "checkpoint"}}` (`checkpoint` is `describe` of the parent). The old dashboard process is not stopped. A wrong argument: `{"error"}`. A run that starts has the key `continue`:
`parent`, `iteration` (K), `parent_iterations`, `iterations` (K + N), `more_iterations`, `pass_runs_again`, `step_settings`, `facts`. `step_settings.solver` is the setting as it is: the server does not resolve `auto`
(the run process can be another Python), so the reply says `auto`, the fact says that the run process picks the solver, and `run.json` of the run names it. The reply comes from a read of the checkpoint before the run process starts, and the run process reads
the checkpoint again; its read decides. If the parent runs (a live job lock), the pass of the run can be later than the pass in the reply, and `facts` says so; `run_status` and the `continued_from` record of `run.json` name the pass that the run read.

**Equality and measured differences.** With one thread and a direct solver (PARDISO, Cholesky) a continuation equals the run of K + N passes byte for byte (history without the timing fields, snapshots, `final.stl`, `preview.bin`, `labels.bin`, `metrics.json`;
`run.json` differs by `continued_from`, `started_at`, and the YAML path if the YAML is another file). Measured on Linux x86_64 (PARDISO, 1 thread; `tests/test_continue*.py`):

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| cantilever, K 12 (mid stage), 19 (the pass before a stage start), 20 (a stage start) | byte-equal to the run of 24 passes |
| cantilever, K 12 and N 6 (the YAML says 24) | byte-equal to the run of 18 passes |
| stress rows with step acceptance, K 9 and 17 (the pass before a stage start), with `rows_before` and without | byte-equal. The KS scale comes from the design and the beta of the stage, so the rows after pass K give the same numbers as the rows before it |
| stress rows with step acceptance, K 10 and 18 (a stage start), with `rows_before` | byte-equal |
| stress rows with step acceptance, K 10 and 18 (a stage start), without `rows_before` | the numbers, the snapshots and `final.stl` are equal. Only the label `c_changed` of each stress row at pass K differs (the run of 24 passes: true, the continuation: false), and a stage-start note of a small `c` can go with it |
| buckling row, K 4 and 12 (tests; K 3 and 9 were measured in a scratch script, not in a test), with `rows_before` | byte-equal |
| buckling row, checkpoint without `rows_before`, K 12 (test; K 9: scratch script) | the numbers are equal (compliance, volume, row value, last snapshot, `final.stl`). Only the label `reason` of the row entry can differ (pass 12: `stage_start` against `near`) |
| buckling row, checkpoint without `rows_before`, K 4 | the evaluation schedule moves: the run of 24 passes skipped the passes 2 to 5, and the continuation evaluates from pass 4. Compliance differs by 6.7e-7 and the volume by 8.0e-7, in relative terms (a scratch script at K 3: 3.0e-6 and 1.8e-6; not a test). The row value differs by up to 0.59 at a pass that one run evaluates and the other does not. The last snapshot and `final.stl` are equal. The test limit is 1e-5 |
| AMG, K 12 | close, not equal: compliance 1.3e-8, volume 1.7e-11 (relative, largest over the run) from a straight run. Two straight runs differ by 1.3e-8 and 4.4e-11. The test limit is 1e-6. The lines before pass K are those of the parent, not of the straight run |
| gpu-mg on pocl (CPU), 2 mm cantilever, K 10 + 4 (replay) and K 6 + 8 (fork from a killed run) | compliance 3.0e-9 and 2.5e-9, volume 9.3e-11 and 3.9e-11; no voxel of the last snapshot and no byte of `final.stl` differs. Two straight runs are equal. The test limits are 1e-7 and 1e-8 |
| more than one thread | close, not equal (as for a resume) |

**gpu-mg timing file.** `gpu_mg.jsonl` of the new folder holds the lines of the parent with `iteration` below K (a replay), or up to K (a fork), byte for byte. The solver cuts the file to the same pass when it starts and numbers its lines after them
(section 20). The replayed pass has its lines once.

**Pass numbers above 9999.** There is no upper limit for N, so a run can pass pass 9999. The name of a snapshot stays `it_{:04d}.bin`: from pass 10000 it has five digits. A text sort of the names is then wrong (`it_10000.bin` comes before `it_9999.bin`).
Every reader takes the number from the name and orders by the number. Tested with a made-up folder of 10,004 passes (`tests/test_continue.py`): `dashboard_server.RunSource.snapshot_iterations` (`\d{4,}`), `replay.Replay` (`\d+`), `post._last_snapshot`,
`checkpoint._snapshot_number` (used by `apply_plan` and `apply_continue`, which also check the `missing` snapshots with a `range` and the same name format), `snapshot.RunWriter.write_snapshot` (the writer), `feedback.run_facts` (a count) and
`tools/compare_runs.py`. Read, and not tested: `tools/fake_run.py` (a writer with the same name format) and `scripts/ci/short_run.py` (it removes the folder). The dashboard script reads no snapshot name (the server gives integers).
Two readers sorted the names as text and now order by the number: `tools/compare_runs.py` (its report; the verdict was never wrong, because both lists were sorted the same way) and `tools/calibrate_min_member.py` (it took the wrong last snapshot above pass 9999).

**Platforms.** The code uses the standard library and numpy only. The Linux x86_64 paths are run and tested. The macOS arm64 paths have not been run on a Mac; they use the same code.

### 24.4 A run that ended with no result: the facts and the options (P9-6, finding U9)

A run process can end with no result: a kill by a signal before it wrote run data, a kill in the middle of a run, an exit with an error.
`run_status` and `run_result` then say what is known and what the user can do. They state facts, and a possible cause only as a possible cause:
the exit code of a process that a signal ended does not name the sender (the system for lack of memory, this server, the user, a force quit).
The peak memory is written only when the process reaches `RunJob.finish()` (section 24.1), which a kill never reaches. No engine file changed.

**When.** `run_status` adds the keys below when the run process of the folder has ended and left no result (`server._ended_without_result`):
the status is `error`; or the job state is `failed`, `no_record`, `stale_lock` or `unfinished` and the status is not `done` or `stopped`; or the status is
`starting`, `running` or `postprocess` and no process is alive (for a run that this server started, or with a dead job record). A done run, a run
that a request stopped (`stopped`) and a run with a live process that works have none of the keys. A `none` reply (no `status.json`) has them if the job
record ended with no status file. The `summary` keeps its start, and gets one clause at its end: `possible cause: ...` (`possible cause (the exit code does
not say): ...` when this server did not stop the process), or `last log line: "..."`, and `first option: ...` (not repeated when the summary already says
that `run_topopt` with `resume=true` continues the run).
A busy status with no live process also gets `(warning: the process has stopped)` after the first numbers of the summary: for a run that this server started,
and for a run whose job record says that its process has ended (a CLI run too, #448). The `state` key stays the state of `status.json`. A process that ends
natively in the post step (libgomp ends it with exit 1 after a failed thread start, or a SIGSEGV in native code) cannot write its status, so `state` stays
`postprocess`; the end shows in `failure` (the exit code or the signal for a run of this server; `exit_note` for a CLI run), `job` (`stale_lock`), `log_tail`
and the summary, and `run_result` returns no result (#448, `tests/test_native_exit_post.py`).

**Which run the facts are about.** The run process of the folder is, in this order: the process that this session of the server started
for this folder; the pid in the job record (`job.json`) of the run; the pid file `<run folder>.pid` of this server. The pid file comes last: a run of
the CLI does not write it, so it can name the process of an older run in the same folder (P9-6 review F1). A file counts for the run only if it is
not older than the start of the run (this session's start, else `started_at` of the job record, with the tolerance of one second that `_is_busy` has).

| Key | Content |
|---|---|
| `log_tail` | the last 12 lines (`_tail`, the helper of `verify_status`) of the newest log of this run: `<run folder>.stdout` (the output file of this server; a CLI run does not write it) and `run.log` of the folder (deleted when a run starts; a resume does not delete it). Each counts only if it is not older than the start of the run. If both count, the file with the later write time comes first, and on a tie the output file. With no start time known, only the output file counts. Absent if no log counts. |
| `log_tail_file` | the file of `log_tail`. |
| `failure` | the facts, below. |
| `options` | a list of short texts, only those that apply. Order: `run_topopt` with `resume=true` (a checkpoint is there; a complete one runs the post step only); then, with a positive memory fact (below), a larger `voxel_size` and a solver with less memory, on Linux the kernel-log text (`journalctl -k` or `dmesg` has the line `Killed process <pid>` if the kernel stopped the process; a text, this server does not read that log), read `log_tail` (an exit with a message), `check_problem`; without a positive memory fact, `check_problem` comes before the memory options. The memory options come only when memory is a possible cause: a stop by SIGKILL or with no record of its end, and not a stop by this server; or the status message or the log tail names memory. |
| `possible_causes` | only for a stop by a signal (or no record of the end) when the run wrote no error message. If `stopped_by_this_server` is true: that one cause (a stop by this server, with its time). Else the list has: a stop by the user or another program; the system stopped it for lack of memory (only for SIGKILL or an unknown end; with the memory estimate, the RAM, and the words that an estimate is a model and can be lower than the real peak); a crash in native code (a signal other than SIGKILL, SIGTERM, SIGINT, SIGHUP). A stop by this server is in the list only when its mark is set. Order, from facts of the reply only (no threshold): with a positive memory fact the memory cause is first; else the stop by the user or another program is first. A positive memory fact is: the message or the log names memory (`MemoryError`, `Unable to allocate`, `out of memory`, `cannot allocate`, `bad_alloc`); or an estimate of the run (the line `memory estimate`, or the buckling-row line) is above the RAM that the run itself saw (`memory_estimate.ram_gib`). |
| `possible_causes_note` | with `possible_causes`, unless the stop by this server is known: the exit code does not say who stopped the process, and the order of the list is not a ranking. |
| `dashboard_note` | for each ended run with no live process: the dashboard ran inside the run process (`cli.start_dashboard`), which has ended, so the link of `run_topopt` does not answer. It names `topopt dashboard <run folder>` and the saved passes (`up to pass N`), or says that the run saved no pass. `dashboard_url` is not changed. |

`failure`:

| Key | Content |
|---|---|
| `pid` | the pid of the run process (see above), or null. |
| `exit_code` | the exit code (negative for a signal) of the process that this server started, else the `exit_code` of a `failed` job record, else null (then `exit_note` says why). |
| `signal` | the name of the signal (`SIGKILL`) when `exit_code` is negative, else null. |
| `run_data` | `none` (no `status.json` of this run), `setup only: no pass is done`, or `up to pass N` (the last row of `history.jsonl` that parses). After a refused run over an earlier run: `setup only: no pass is done (the passes in the folder, up to pass N, are of an earlier run: see earlier_run)` (section 24.1, P9-18). |
