| `stopped_by_this_server` | true when `_stop` (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL; `run_topopt` uses it for the process of an earlier run) signalled this pid in this session of the server, for this run folder, and not before the start of the run (`stopped_at` has the time); false for a process that this server started and did not stop; null when the process was not started by this session, because an earlier session can have stopped it. `stop_run` sends no signal: it writes `job.stop`. |
| `peak_memory`, `peak_memory_bytes` | the peak of a job record that ended with a failure (`failed`), as text in GB (1e9 bytes) and GiB with the source, and in bytes; else the text `not recorded: the process did not reach its end` (a process that ended by itself with no record: `not recorded: the process wrote no job record of its end`) and null. |
| `memory_estimate` | the last line `memory estimate: about X GiB of Y GiB RAM (...)` of the newest log that has one (`topopt run` writes it before the solve; a resumed `run.log` holds one for each run): `{gib, ram_gib, line, source}`, and `with_buckling_row` (`{gb, line}`; GB = 1e9 bytes, as the line says) if the log also has the line `buckling row: on in the YAML (...): memory estimate about X GB with the row`; else `{gib: null, reason}`. Nothing is computed for the reply. |
| `ram` | `{total_gib, available_now_gib, note}` from `topopt.environment._ram()` (the cgroup is counted). The room is the room now, after the process ended. |
| `exit_note`, `stopped_at` | `exit_note` only when `exit_code` is null (the process is still alive and ends after the error, or the exit is not known); `stopped_at` only when `stopped_by_this_server` is true. |

**run_result.** `run_result` reads the state from `run_status` (so a `status.json` or a result of an older run in the folder is not returned for a new run that
died or works). A run that ended with no result (the same test) returns `{"done": false, "state", "run_dir", "run_dir_rel", "summary", "message", "log_tail",
"log_tail_file", "failure", "options", "possible_causes", "possible_causes_note", "dashboard_note", "checkpoint"}` (the keys of section 24.4 that the run has; after a refused run
over an earlier run also `earlier_run`, section 24.1, P9-18). With
the status `error` of this run the `message` is `The run failed: <status message>`. A run that is at work (`The run is not done yet. Call run_status.`), a folder
with no run (`No result yet. Call run_status.`) and a run that a request stopped (`stopped: true`) keep their replies.

### 24.5 The live time estimate after pass 2 (E1-P2)

Code: `topopt/eta.py`. It uses the standard library only. No new dependency. `topopt check` gives the start estimate of the run time (section 11 and the
`check` output). **The start estimate of `check` is unchanged.** This section is about a run that is at work: once its process has made 2 passes, the run
itself predicts the time that is left better than the start estimate does (experiment E1).
The estimate is a fact for the reader. No code stops a run, refuses a run or changes a setting because of it.

**The function.** `eta.time_left(records, planned, n_free_dofs, start=0)` returns `(estimate, None)` or `(None, reason)`. It reads no file. The estimate is a dict
`{"left_s", "up_to_s", "after_pass", "basis"}`; the numbers have one decimal. Pass numbers are those of `history.jsonl`: pass 0 is the first pass. After the pass k:

    left_s  = mean(t_iter_s of the passes S+1 and S+2) * (N - k) + POST
    up_to_s = left_s * 1.33

- `S` is the first pass of THIS process: 0 for a new run. A resume or a continuation (section 24.2, 24.3) starts later, and `status.json` key `first_pass` says where
  (below). The probe is the passes `S+1` and `S+2`, so the run that was probed before the resume does not count. Pass `S` is not in the mean: E1 measured the passes 0
  and 1 and found them slower (abs log of the total 0.211 and bias -0.19, against 0.136 and 0.002 for the passes 1 and 2).
- `N` is `run.json` `iterations`: the last pass number, also for a continuation (K + `more_iterations`). `optimize.run` runs the passes `first` to `N`, so after the pass k
  there are `N - k` passes left. E1 model C counts the same way (`N - 2` passes left at the end of pass 2). A count of `N - 1 - k` would be one pass short.
- The mean stays the one of the passes `S+1` and `S+2` at the later passes. There is no other rule in the code: this item keeps the rule that E1 measured. E1 measured the windows 2-3 and 1-3
  (abs log of the total 0.130 and 0.129, against 0.136 for 1-2). A running mean over the passes `S+1` to `k` was measured in E1-P2 and is better at the later passes (table below). It is not shipped.
- `after_pass` is the last pass in the history. `basis` has `pass_s` (the mean), `probe_passes`, `passes_left`, `post_s`, `post_band`, `bound_factor`, `assumes` and `measured`.
  A run of less than 10,000 free dofs also has `not_measured`.
- The estimate is for the planned passes: "if no stop rule or request to stop ends it earlier". A stop rule (section 24.2) or a request to stop can end the run before pass `N`.
  `assumes` and the line of `run.log` say so.
- A run that has not made the pass `S+2` has no estimate: `run_status` has `time_left: null` and `time_left_note` with the reason (for example `no estimate before pass 2 is done (the last pass done is 1)`).
  So has a run that is not in its passes (state other than `running`), a record without a usable `t_iter_s`, and a `run.json` without `iterations` or `n_free_dofs`.
  A process that starts after the last pass (the resume of a finished run: `first_pass` is `N + 1`) has the reason `no pass is left to run`.
- **A run process that has ended has no estimate**, also when this server did not start it. A kill leaves `status.json` at `running` with no marker, so `status.json` alone cannot tell. The job record can
  (section 24.1): `job.state` `failed`, `no_record`, `stale_lock` or `unfinished` (`eta.ENDED_JOB_STATES`, `eta.job_ended`) gives `time_left: null` with the note `the run process has stopped`, in `run_status`
  and in `/api/status`. A job with no record (a hand-made folder, a replay) is not "ended".
- GPU runs and every solver: the same rule. `t_iter_s` is written for each solver. The error differs by solver (below).

**Constants** (in `topopt/eta.py`; the only new numbers of E1-P2). Source: experiment E1 (run-time study, 2026-10-23; the runs were made by the code revisions before main bb6e193; one shared Linux host),
the 586 runs with 10,000 free dofs or more that have `t_iter_s` for the passes 1 and 2 (111 problems). `POST` is the median of `post_s` (`metrics.json` `run_time_s` minus the last `elapsed_s` of `history.jsonl`)
by the size bands of `models.ModelC.band`:

| Name | Free dofs | Value | Runs (problems) in E1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `POST_S_BELOW_50K` | below 50,000 | 4.43 s | 435 (74) |
| `POST_S_50K_TO_200K` | 50,000 to 199,999 | 7.51 s | 145 (32) |
| `POST_S_200K_UP` | 200,000 and more | 21.67 s | 6 (5): a thin band, a rough number |
| `BOUND_FACTOR` | | 1.33 | the q0.9 multiplier of model C (E1 section 3.3) |

`POST` is all the work after the loop in the E1 rows. A run with an opt-in post check (for example buckling) has a longer post step than these medians.

**Error measured in E1** (leave-one-problem-out for the models; the probe has no fit, but the POST medians pooled over the same rows (no hold-out; E1 found the difference small); 10,000 free dofs and more; one shared Linux host; runs of the code revisions before main bb6e193):

| Quantity | n | Median | p90 |
|---|---|---|---|
| remaining time after pass 2, abs log of actual / estimate | 585 | 0.156 (a factor 1.17) | 0.496 (a factor 1.64) |
| total time (model C), abs log | 586 | 0.138 (a factor 1.15) | 0.447 (a factor 1.56) |

- The estimate has no bias (the median of log actual / estimate is 0.003). For comparison the start estimate of `check` had an abs log of 0.642 (a factor 1.9) on the 596 runs of 10,000 free dofs and more.
- The bound `up_to_s` (x1.33): 88.0 % of the 585 runs ended inside it for the remaining time at pass 2 (the q0.9 of actual / estimate is 1.37), and 90.3 % for the total time.
  By planned passes the coverage of the remaining time was 87 % (12 or fewer; n = 142), 91 % (13 to 40; n = 277) and 84 % (more than 40; n = 166). It is a fact about those runs, not a limit.
- The error of the total is higher at 12 or fewer planned passes (abs log 0.196, n = 143) and at more than 80 (0.216, n = 55), and for 200,000 dofs and more (0.291, n = 6).
- By solver (remaining time after pass 2, the shipped constants, abs log median / p90, share inside x1.33; recomputed in E1-P2 fix round 1 from `dataset.csv` with the selection of `e1/probe.py`; no number differs from the gate review):
  `pardiso` n 535 (103 problems): 0.150 / 0.497 / 89 %; `gpu-mg` n 28 (11 problems): 0.246 / 0.413 / 79 %; `amg` n 22 (12 problems): 0.237 / 0.472 / 77 %. The last two are thin samples.
- Not measured: a run below 10,000 free dofs (the same constants are used; `basis.not_measured` says so), a Mac, and a host with another load. The same hook run took 99 s to 1,469 s on the E1 host (62 runs, same setting, E1 section 8): the host state decides most of that spread, and the probe sees the state of the passes 1 and 2 only.

**The later passes** (E1-P2, not in the E1 report; a copy of the logic of `e1/probe.py` that also reads the per-pass `t_iter_s` of `history.jsonl` of the 586 E1 runs; scratch script `scratch/e1-p2/window_check.py`; abs log of
actual / estimate for the remaining time, and the share of runs inside x1.33). At pass 2 the script gives the E1 numbers (0.156, 0.496). The rule of the code is "fixed 1-2"; "running" is the mean of the passes 1 to k.

| After pass | n | fixed 1-2: median / p90 / inside x1.33 | running 1 to k: median / p90 / inside x1.33 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 585 | 0.156 / 0.496 / 88 % | the same (one window) |
| 5 | 562 | 0.161 / 0.499 / 88 % | 0.127 / 0.479 / 90 % |
| 10 | 491 | 0.156 / 0.516 / 88 % | 0.113 / 0.395 / 95 % |
| 20 | 399 | 0.136 / 0.459 / 86 % | 0.095 / 0.283 / 94 % |
| 40 | 166 | 0.173 / 0.524 / 81 % | 0.103 / 0.382 / 90 % |

So the shipped rule keeps its error at the later passes (a median factor of about 1.15 to 1.19), and its bound covers less (81 % at pass 40, n = 166). A later item can change the window; the numbers are the evidence.

**Where it shows.** One function, three outputs:

1. `run.log`: one line after the pass `S+2` of each process (a resumed process writes its own line), only if a pass is left to run:
   `fact: time: about 93 s left after pass 2 (up to 124 s; the passes 1 and 2 took 1.84 s on average, passes left: 48, the post step takes about 7.51 s; this holds if no stop rule or request to stop ends the run earlier)`.
   A run below 10,000 free dofs adds `. Experiment E1 (run-time study) did not measure runs of less than 10,000 free dofs`.
   `optimize.run` writes the line before it reads a request to stop at the end of pass `S+2`, so a request that came in that pass can end the run right after the line: the words "or request to stop" say it. It is a `fact:` line, not a `warning:` line. There is no line for the other passes.
2. `run_status` (section 10): `time_left` (the dict, or null) and `time_left_note` (the reason, or null). The `summary` gets `about 93 s left (up to 124 s)` after the volume. `run_status` reads `history.jsonl`
   and `run.json` for it.
3. The dashboard (section 7): `GET /api/status` is `status.json` and, for a run in the state `running` that has an estimate, the key `time_left` (the same dict). Without an estimate the answer is the bytes of the file, as before.
   The bar shows `about 93 s left` under the timer (`#b-left`); its title has the bound and `basis.assumes`. The line is in the bar from the start and is empty before a value exists
   (CSS: the span has `display: block` and a minimum height of one line, and a hidden `::after` text keeps the width of a value), so the label and the timer do not move when the text appears.
   In live mode the dashboard server reads the job record (two small files) at each poll of `/api/status` and does not cache that test; it caches the estimate on the size and time of `history.jsonl` and `run.json`
   (`stat`), so a poll without a change reads nothing of the history.
   In replay mode the key follows the replay clock. `Replay.status()` has no `first_pass`: the replay of a resumed run probes the passes 1 and 2 of the first process, and the replay of a stopped run can show a value
   for the short time between its last history row and the `stopped` state.

**`status.json` key `first_pass`.** `RunWriter` writes `first_pass` only when the process does not start at pass 0: a resume (section 24.2) and a continuation (section 24.3). It is `null` until `optimize.run` has read the checkpoint,
then the number of the first pass that this process runs (`Checkpointer.restore`: `first`). A new run has no such key, so its `status.json` is as it was. A reader that finds no key counts from pass 0; `null` means no estimate yet.

Tests: `tests/test_eta.py`.

### 24.6 Fine pass: a new run on a finer voxel from the design of a finished run (#318)

Code: `topopt/fine_pass.py` (the voxel of the part, the guards of the fine grid, the settings, the parent, the start design), `topopt/config.py` (`FINE_OBJECTIVE_CHANGE`, `FinePassSettings`: `settings.fine_pass`), `topopt/region_rules.py` (`MIN_REGION_VOXELS`, `MIN_REGION_THICK`, `REGION_ACROSS`: one place for the numbers of the region check),
`topopt/verdict.py` (`SETTLED`, `settled_met`, `stop_decision(settled=)`), `topopt/checkpoint.py` (`plan_fine`, `FINE_SOFT`, `config_of_fine`, `Checkpointer(fine_from=)`), `topopt/optimize.py` (`run(x0=)`),
`topopt/snapshot.py` (`run.json`: `fine_from`, `part_voxel`), `topopt/cli.py`, `topopt/part_card.py`, `topopt_mcp/server.py`. Tests: `tests/test_fine_pass.py`, `tests/test_fine_cli.py`, `tests/test_fine_mcp.py`, `tests/test_region_rules.py`, `tests/test_verdict.py`.
No new dependency. The tools give facts, estimates and options; the agent decides. A plain run is unchanged (the golden file of the hook, section 27, is the same).

**Command.** CLI: `topopt run <file.yaml> --out NEW --fine-from PARENT [--fine-voxel H] [--fine-passes N] [--fine-tol T] [--allow-changed-inputs]`.
MCP: `run_topopt(yaml_path, out_dir=NEW, fine_from=PARENT, fine_voxel=None, fine_passes=None, fine_tol=None, allow_changed_inputs=false)`.
One command for both runs: `topopt run <file.yaml> --out D --fine-pass` (MCP `fine_pass=true`). It makes the normal run in `D`, then the fine pass in the sibling folder `D-fine`
(`cli.fine_folder`; a sibling, because `check_new_folder` refuses a folder inside the parent). The reply of `run_topopt` has `fine_run_dir`, `fine_run_dir_rel` and `fine` (`first_run_dir`, `fine_run_dir`, `facts`).
`run_status` of the first folder has `fine_run` (`run_dir`, `state`). While the process lives, `state` is `not started` or the state of the fine run. After the process has ended it is the real end state: the state of the fine run (`done`, `stopped`), `failed` (the fine run wrote the status `error`; `message`, `log`), `refused` (the process ended and the fine run never started: a guard or the plan refused it; `message` has the exit, `log` the file) or `none` (no fine pass was needed or made, with a `note`). One background process does both runs, so the server counts as busy until the fine pass has ended.
`stop_run()` with no `run_dir` stops the run that works now: the fine pass when it runs (the reply names its folder in `run_dir` and `found_by`), and the first run while that works (the process then ends with exit code 5 and starts no fine pass). From the post step of the first run until the fine run has written its status (the post step and the refine step, the gap between the two runs, and the plan and build of the fine grid), it writes the request `job.stop` in the FINE folder with the pid of the process (the first run does not read a request in its post step), and the reply has `state` `stop_requested` (or `already_requested`) and the fine folder in `run_dir`; it is not `none`. The driver of `--fine-pass` (`cli._stop_before_fine`) reads a request for its pid in the first folder (the first run keeps a request that came after its last read, when a fine pass is to follow) and in the fine folder before it starts the fine pass, and once more after the plan of the fine grid. It removes the request and an empty fine folder, writes the fact `fine pass: a stop request came after the first run: the fine pass did not start.` to the console and to the log of the first run, and ends with exit code 5. The first run is finished and keeps its result. `run_status` of the first folder then has `fine_run.state` `stopped` with that note. The CLI has the same route for the post step and the refine step of the first run: `topopt stop <first folder>` there finds `fine_pass` in `job.json` (the first run of `--fine-pass`), sees in `run.json` that a fine pass follows (`part_voxel.recommend`, or a given `--fine-voxel`), writes `job.stop` in the FIRST folder with the pid of the process (`runjob.stop_reply`: `stop_requested`, exit 0), and the driver reads it before it starts the fine pass. In the short gap after the first job has ended and before the fine run has a folder with a status, `topopt stop <first folder>` finds a finished job (`nothing_to_stop`, exit 1) and writes nothing, and the fine folder may not exist yet: the MCP tool `stop_run` is the route in that gap. A part that needs no fine pass has no such window: a request in its post step is removed as in any run, and `topopt stop` there writes nothing.
`--fine-pass` tests the planned fine pass BEFORE the first run (`cli._fine_pass_precheck`), and a refusal is exit code 1 with options and writes nothing: (1) a `--fine-voxel` that is equal to or coarser than the voxel of the first run is refused ("--fine-pass: --fine-voxel H mm is the same as / coarser than the voxel of the first run"); the options name what the user typed: give `--fine-voxel` a value below the run voxel, remove `--fine-voxel` to use the voxel that the part needs, remove `--fine-pass` to make the first run only; (2) the planned fine grid fails a guard (below). Without `--fine-voxel`, if the voxel of the part is not below the voxel of the run by 0.05 mm or more (`part_voxel.recommend` is false), `--fine-pass` makes the first run, logs a fact and ends with exit code 0: the pre-check says this at the start of the first run too, in a line right after `topopt run:` in the log (`fine pass: --fine-pass is on, but the part needs a voxel of X mm ... There will be no fine pass`). A `--fine-voxel` that is finer than the run voxel wins (tools inform, the user or agent decides; `--fine-from PARENT --fine-voxel H` forces a voxel too, so the one-command form agrees): `--fine-pass --fine-voxel H` makes the fine pass at H also when the part needs no finer voxel (MCP `run_topopt(fine_pass=true, fine_voxel=H)` the same). The fact `fine pass: the part needs about X mm (...), which is not finer than the voxel of this run, R mm, by 0.05 mm or more. --fine-voxel H mm is finer, so the fine pass runs at H mm as asked.` (`cli.forced_fine_fact`) is the line right after `topopt run:` in the log of the first run and a line of the log of the fine run, there is no "no fine pass" note for this case, the first run logs `The fine pass starts next ... at H mm as --fine-voxel says`, the grid at H goes through the guards before the first run, and `cli._run_then_fine` does not end after the first run. The server keeps `fine_voxel` of the run (`_current`), so `fine_run.state` is not `none` and the server is busy until the fine pass has ended. If the first run ends with another code, there is no fine pass. The sibling folder is built from the resolved `--out` path (`--out .` works).
A fine pass starts only with `--fine-pass` or `--fine-from`: no other command starts one.
`--fine-voxel`, `--fine-passes` and `--fine-tol` go with `--fine-from` or `--fine-pass` only. `--fine-from` does not go with `--resume`, `--continue-from`, `--more-iterations` or `--fine-pass`; `--fine-pass` does not go with
`--resume`, `--continue-from`, `--more-iterations`, `--fine-from` or `--allow-changed-inputs`. A wrong value or a wrong mix is a `UserError` (exit 1, MCP `error`) with options, and nothing is written.

**What a fine pass is.** A NEW run in a NEW folder on a finer grid of the same problem. It starts from the design of PARENT, a run folder that finished (its checkpoint is complete). The parent is only read: no lock, no write, no change of a modification time.
A parent whose checkpoint is not complete (stopped, killed, error) is refused with options: its design is not at its end. A parent with no usable checkpoint is used through the density of its last snapshot (a fact says so) if its `status.json` says `done`; a parent with no checkpoint and no snapshot, a damaged `labels.bin` and a folder with no `run.json` are refused with options.
NEW is refused when it is PARENT or inside it (`checkpoint.check_new_folder`, section 24.3). The same YAML works: the fine pass overrides `settings.voxel_size` (also `auto` or a number), `settings.iterations`, `settings.beta_schedule`
and the stop rule `settled`. The YAML and the region files are read again and compared with the checkpoint of the parent (`checkpoint.plan_fine`, `diff_inputs(soft=FINE_SOFT)`): a changed key other than the soft keys is a refusal with the change and options,
or goes on with `--allow-changed-inputs`. The soft keys are `settings.voxel_size`, `settings.iterations`, `settings.beta_schedule`, and `settings.filter_radius` when it is the default of 1.5 voxels or the radius of the wall rule (`settings.robust: wall`, section 22b: `members.radius_for_grid` gives `max(w / L(eta_e), 1.5 voxels)` for the voxel of the fine pass, so the record and the facts of the fine run state the radius that it uses; a fact says so with its own text).
A filter radius that the YAML gives (`settings.filter_radius` or `settings.min_member_mm`; for the wall rule an explicit `settings.filter_radius`) stays the same in mm. The text "the voxel labels are not the same" is dropped (another voxel gives other labels), and a changed solver is a fact (the solver is chosen for the grid of the fine run).
The voxel guards (`max_grid_voxels`, `max_active_voxels`), the memory estimate and the platform checks apply to the fine grid as for any run. An error of the build of the fine grid names `--fine-voxel` (MCP `fine_voxel`) and not `settings.voxel_size` (`fine_pass.name_fine_option`).

**Voxel of the fine pass.** By default the voxel that the part needs, tested on the grid of the fine pass (`part_voxel` with `verify`, below): the measured voxel, or a few steps of 0.05 mm below it, and a fact says which. `--fine-voxel H` (MCP `fine_voxel`) sets it, a number of mm above 0. A voxel equal to the voxel of the parent is refused (the options name `--continue-from`
with `--more-iterations`, which add passes on the same grid). Without `--fine-voxel`, a voxel of the part that is not finer than the voxel of the parent is refused in the same way, with the options `--fine-voxel H` (forces a voxel) and `--continue-from`; `--fine-pass` then ends after the first run with the fact "no fine pass". A `--fine-voxel` coarser than the parent is allowed, with a fact. The record names where the voxel comes from (`voxel_from`: `part_voxel` or `fine_voxel`).

**Start design.** `FineStart` maps the design of the parent to the design voxels of the fine model by physical position: the mean of the parent values over the parent design voxels around the centre of each fine voxel (a trilinear weighted mean; the
weights are those of the design voxels only for the source `x`; the origin of each grid is the minimum corner of all regions, and a mirror plane can move it by up to one voxel). The source is `x`, the design variables of the checkpoint (`record.source`), or, if the parent has no
checkpoint file, `rho`, the density of the last snapshot, with a fact (the density has the filter and the projection in it, so the fine pass filters it twice; measured 2026-10-26 on a 5-inch drone arm at 0.7 mm, AMG solver: weighted compliance 854 against 726 at pass 0).
A fine voxel with no source voxel near it takes the nearest source voxel (`map.no_source`, `map.weak_source`). The volume is fitted to the target by one uniform shift of the variables (a bisection; `volume`: `target`, `target_from`, `mean_before`, `shift`, `mean_after`);
a target that the range cannot reach is printed as a miss. The target is `settings.volume_fraction` (`target_from`: `volume_fraction`). A run with `settings.objective: mass` has no volume row: `settings.volume_fraction` is only its start density, so the target is the final mean physical density of the parent (`target_from`: `parent`; from the history record of the checkpoint pass, else the last snapshot), which removes the drift of the mapping and a fact says so.
After the mapping the plan lets go of the arrays of the parent (`Parent.release`). Everything else starts new: the MMA asymptotes and history, the objective scale, the rows (the stress KS scale, the buckling start vector), the AMG warm start. `optimize.run(problem, out, x0=FineStart)` evaluates the start before it writes
`run.json`. Fixed and load voxels keep density 1 by themselves.

**Beta.** The schedule goes on from the passes of the earlier runs (`fine_pass.shift_schedule`): pass `j` of the fine pass has the beta of pass `offset + j` of the schedule, with `offset` = the pass of the checkpoint of the parent plus the `schedule_offset` of the parent
(a chain of fine passes adds up). No new number. Measured 2026-10-26 on a 5-inch drone arm at 0.7 mm, AMG solver, shared Linux host: holding beta 8 from the start gave the same result as the cold run at pass 30 (weighted 596.7 against 596.95 at pass 80); a restart at beta 4 was worse at the same pass and ended 0.7 % above.

**Passes and the stop rule `settled`.** `--fine-passes N` (MCP `fine_passes`) is the MAXIMUM pass count of the fine pass, a whole number of 1 or more, with no upper limit. Default: the pass count of the parent run (the pass of its last checkpoint, at least 1; `max_from`: `parent` or `fine_passes`).
`settings.iterations` of the YAML stays the pass count of the first run and is not used by the fine pass (a fact says so). A fine pass has a plateau stop on by default: the rule `settled` (`verdict.SETTLED`, state `stopped_by_rule`). It uses the measure `objective_change` of the verdict (section 24.2):
the largest relative change of `objective.value` between two passes in the last `window` passes at one beta (`settings.stop_rules.window`, default 5). The rule fires when that value is at or below the tolerance AND the constraints are met (`max_g`). It does not use the grayness test
and does not use the last-beta-stage test (on the 5-inch drone arm of the measurement the grayness is 0.22 in every run, so `converged` cannot fire there). The rule is judged before `converged`. The verdict text says which tests fired and their numbers.
The tolerance is, in this order: `--fine-tol T` (MCP `fine_tol`, a number above 0; `tolerance_from`: `option`), the YAML key `settings.fine_pass.objective_change` (a finite number above 0; `yaml`; it applies to every fine pass made from that YAML, `--fine-from` and `--fine-pass`), or `config.FINE_OBJECTIVE_CHANGE` = 1e-3 (`default`; the one default in code, next to the loader, with its evidence in the comment). The loader refuses a `settings.fine_pass` that is not a mapping, an unknown sub-key, and a value that is not a finite number above 0, with the key path and an example. The key is a soft input: a change of it is a note and not a change of the inputs for `--resume`, `--continue-from` and `--fine-from` (the fine run keeps the value of its record). The fine config carries it in `settings.stop_rules.objective_change` with `enabled` true,
so `StopRules` has no new field and the `verdict.json` of a plain run has the same bytes as before. `--no-stop-rules` (MCP `stop_rules=false`) is as in a plain run: NO early stop at all (`settled`, `converged` and the time budget are off) and the fine pass runs to its maximum; `fine_from.stop_rule` is then null and the log says so. Without it, the other stop rules and a time budget stay as the YAML has them. The log says which test fired
(`fine pass: the loss settled at pass N ...`), or that the maximum ended the fine pass before the loss settled (`fine pass: the maximum of N passes ended the fine pass before the loss settled ...`, with the objective change and the options).
Evidence for the default (offline replay of the history of two measured parts, window 5; measured 2026-10-26, AMG solver, shared Linux host): a 5-inch drone arm at 0.7 mm, beta 8 held: 1e-3 stops at pass 21 with weighted compliance 599.72 (+0.46 % against 596.95 of the 80-pass run from zero), 5e-4 at pass 30, 1e-4 does not stop in 30 passes;
examples/hook/hook_short.yaml at 1.2 mm, beta 8 held: 1e-3 stops at pass 15; a restart at beta 4 then 8 does not stop in 16 passes (the beta step restarts the window), and the maximum ends it. The default is for the first fine passes of a part and is not a limit.

**Voxel of the part (`part_voxel`).** The largest voxel that keeps enough voxels across the thinnest feature: 2.8 voxels across the thinnest fixed, load and solid region and the smallest keep-out region (`region_rules.REGION_ACROSS`, the number of the region check), and 3 voxels across
`settings.min_member_mm` (`members.MEMBER_ACROSS`), rounded DOWN to 0.05 mm (`STEP_MM`). It is ONE value: no band and no levels. The thickness of a region is twice the radius of the largest sphere inside its mesh: the same quantity as the region check (the largest distance to the outside). It is measured on the exact mesh, with the closest-point query
of `trimesh.proximity` (`fine_pass.inscribed_radius`), so the cost does not depend on the voxel, the grid or the size of the region. The search has two parts. First `THICK_SAMPLES` = 512 surface points (chosen by area, fixed seed): at each point a ball that touches the surface there starts at half the chord along the inward normal and shrinks to the nearest surface point inside it,
until it is empty (a relative `THICK_TOL` = 1e-4). Then `THICK_ROUNDS` = 20 rounds of `THICK_TRIES` = 32 new surface points around the best one, the distance of the points halving each round, until the gain is below 1e-6 of the first spacing (far below a step of 0.05 mm). A point that can not beat the best radius so far stops early. A region of several bodies is searched body by body, largest volume first; a body that can not hold a ball larger than the best so far is not searched.
The last ball is tested with the signed distance of its centre. Every ball that is returned lies inside the region, so the measure is never above the exact thickness. The numbers are precision constants of the measure, not limits for the user. A measured thickness within `THICK_SLACK` = 0.05 % below a step counts as on the step (a 2 x 2 x 3 mm box measures 1.9998 mm).
Measured 2026-10-26 on a shared Linux host (one thread, CPU time), diameter of the largest sphere against the exact value (a linear program for a convex body): slabs of 1, 2 and 3.5 mm, also tilted by 20 and 45 degrees, and a 200 x 200 x 2 mm plate: exact, 0.02 to 0.03 s; cuboids up to 0.016 % low; a rod of 64 sections 0.01 % low (0.1 s); the wall of a tube of 96 sections 0.03 % low (0.12 to 0.15 s);
a sphere of 5120 faces 0.12 % low (5.3 s), of 1280 faces 0.34 % low (1.2 s); a cone of 64 sections 0.55 % low (0.14 s); a plate and a ball in one mesh 0.29 % low (1.3 s). The worst case is a coarse sphere (800 faces: up to 3 % low in some orientations; the cost is 0.7 s on the gravy space of the ladle). Real regions (thickness in mm, CPU time):
hook_short: wall plate 3.5 (0.03 s), tip 4.2017 (0.04 s), screw holes 8.9801 (0.14 s); ladle: grip 16.0, bowl 8.9898 (0.13 s, 3360 faces), gravy space 51.5117 (0.70 s), opening 45.0; 5-inch drone arm: frame clamp 6.0, motor mount 4.0, plate stack 6.5, root bolt holes 3.198, motor bolt holes 6.0, motor shaft 6.9956 (6.9962 exact), motor bell 6.5 (0.03 to 0.13 s each).
A feature gives a voxel (the thickness over 2.8, or `min_member_mm` over 3). `voxel_mm` is the smallest one, rounded down. `limiting` is the feature that sets it: `role`, `name`, `thickness_mm`, `across_at_run` (voxels across at the voxel of the run) and `across_needed`. `recommend` is true when `voxel_mm` is below the voxel of the run by `STEP_MM` or more; a value that is equal to the voxel of the run after the rounding gives no recommendation.
**The test on the grid of the fine pass.** The thickness gives the voxel as a number; the grid decides how many voxel centres a region holds (a slab of 2.8 voxels holds 2 or 3 rows, by its place on the grid). When a fine pass is planned or starts (`--fine-from`, `--fine-pass` with its pre-check and its start, `topopt check --fine-from`, MCP `fine_from` and `fine_pass`; `part_voxel(verify=True)`), the voxel is tested:
each load and solid region and the limiting region is voxelized at that voxel on the grid of the fine pass (the lattice of the fine grid, over the box of the region only, as `voxelize` does) and the measure of the region check is applied: `thick`, the largest distance in voxels to the outside, must be at least `MIN_REGION_THICK` = 1.9. If a region fails, the voxel goes down by 0.05 mm, until none fails; `CHECK_STEPS` = 8 steps at most.
A run log or plan fact says it: the region that failed, the voxel before, the steps and the voxel used. A region whose box has more voxels than `settings.max_grid_voxels` is not tested (the guards refuse such a grid); a fact says so. Steps that run out leave the last voxel and a fact. A plain `topopt check`, `check_problem` and the end of a run print the measured value without this test, so a fine pass can take a voxel below the value they state, by steps of 0.05 mm; the fact line says so, and the log of the fine pass names the region and the steps. The reason is the grid: a thin end of 2 mm holds too few rows at the measured voxel (the cantilever below: `topopt check` says 0.7 mm, the fine pass takes 0.65 mm).
The cantilever of the tests at 2 mm: both numbers are 0.7 mm for a wide tip; for the tip of 2 mm width the grid at 0.7 mm holds 2 rows (voxel centres at 18.65 and 19.35 mm), so the fine pass takes 0.65 mm. `examples/hook/hook_short.yaml` at a run voxel of 2.0 mm: the wall plate is exactly 3.5 mm thick, 3.5 / 2.8 = 1.25 mm, which holds 3 rows on the grid: 1.25 mm, not 1.2 mm (the two-level measure of the first version gave the lower end, 1.2 mm, of a band).
The block `part_voxel_block` has `voxel_mm` (the measured value), `run_voxel_mm`, `recommend`, `max_passes`, `tolerance`, `limiting`, `estimate` (`voxel_mm`, `active_voxels`, `free_dofs`, `grid_voxels`, `max_passes`, `time_s_max`, `time_s_from_zero`, `time_s_run`, `memory_bytes`, `memory_model`, `memory_phase`;
estimates from the model of `check`, not measurements; `memory_bytes` is the memory model of the solver that the fine pass runs with: for `gpu-mg` the gpu-mg model of section 20 with the filter terms of the fine grid (`memory_model` `"gpu-mg"`, `memory_phase` the phase that sets the peak), else the Cholesky model (`"cholesky"`, phase null); computed at `voxel_mm`), `guards` (only with `estimate`: `ok`, `failed`, `voxel_pass_mm`, `text`; the test of the fine grid below), `fact` (the one line, only if `recommend`) and `error` (if the measure failed: then `recommend` is false, and a failure never stops a check or a run).
The fact line says what sets the voxel, what the run uses, that a fine pass tests the voxel on its grid and can go down in steps of 0.05 mm, the option, when the fine pass ends, that in two measured parts the result came within 0.5 % and 2.1 % of a run from zero at the fine voxel with fewer passes at the fine voxel, that the first run is extra time, and the estimate (time and memory are estimates). It makes no claim of a speed-up.

**Guards of the fine grid (before the first run).** `fine_pass.fine_grid_guards(config, check, voxel, passes)` tests the planned fine grid against `settings.max_active_voxels`, `settings.max_grid_voxels` and the memory block (the memory estimate above the RAM of the machine: the estimate of the solver of the fine pass, as `topopt check` warns with it; for `gpu-mg` the text says "the gpu-mg memory estimate is ... (peak in the mesh step)" and the phase can be `build`, `loop` or `mesh`). The counts scale with the cube of the voxel ratio (`fine_estimates`). It returns `ok`, `failed` (a list of `guard`, `value`, `limit`, `text`), `voxel_pass_mm` (the finest voxel, a multiple of 0.05 mm with the margin of 3 % of `voxelize.suggest_voxel_size`, that passes all three, or null when no voxel finer than the run voxel does) and `text`. The text is the fact with the options: `--fine-voxel H` (MCP `fine_voxel`) with that voxel, or a higher setting in the YAML, or a machine with more memory. `topopt check` and `check_problem` put it in the block `fine_pass` (`guards`) and in the fact line; there the voxel is the measured one (the fine pass can take a lower one after its test on the grid, which only makes the grid larger by a few steps). `--fine-pass` builds the check of the first run and tests the fine grid (at `--fine-voxel` when given, else at the voxel of the part tested on the grid of the fine pass, `part_voxel(verify=True)`: the voxel that the fine pass will take) before it writes anything: a failure is exit code 1 with the text, and no first run is made.

**Where the recommendation shows.** Plain `topopt check` prints the fact line (one line, only when `recommend` is true); `topopt check --json` and `check_problem` have the key `fine_pass` (the block; None for a check with `--fine-from`). The end of the run log has the same line.
`run.json` has `part_voxel` (the block, written after the last pass). The part card (`result/report.md`) has the line, and a block "Fine pass" for a fine run. `run_result` has `fine_pass` (the block) and, for a fine run, `fine_from`. No recommendation is shown when `recommend` is false.

**`topopt check --fine-from PARENT`** (also `--fine-voxel`, `--fine-passes`, `--fine-tol`, `--allow-changed-inputs`) writes nothing. It prints the plan of the fine pass (the first line of the log, the facts of the parent and of the comparison) and then the numbers of the fine voxel
(grid, active voxels, free dofs, estimates). `--json` adds the key `fine_from` (the record without the numbers of a mapping, and `facts`). A refusal that the run would give is the same error with options. `check_problem` has no `fine_from` argument; `run_topopt(fine_from=...)` returns the plan in `fine` before it starts
(`parent`, `iteration`, `parent_voxel_mm`, `voxel_mm`, `voxel_from`, `max_passes`, `max_from`, `tolerance`, `tolerance_from`, `window`, `schedule_offset`, `source`, `facts`, and with the voxel of the part `part_voxel_mm`, `limiting`, `limiting_role`, `limiting_thickness_mm` and `grid_check`) and a refusal with `fine.facts` and `fine.options`; both write nothing.

**Records.** `run.json` of a fine run has `fine_from`: `run_dir`, `iteration`, `parent_iterations`, `parent_voxel_mm`, `parent_shape`, `schedule_offset`, `voxel_mm`, `voxel_from`, `max_passes`, `max_from`, `stop_rule` (`settled`, or null when `--no-stop-rules` turned every stop rule off), `tolerance`, `tolerance_from`, `window`, `source`,
`checkpoint`, `checkpoint_sha256` (the hash of the bytes that were read), `topopt_version`, and, when the voxel came from the part, `part_voxel_mm` (the voxel after the test on the grid), `limiting` (the name of the feature), `limiting_role`, `limiting_thickness_mm` and `grid_check` (`voxel_mm`, `start_mm` (the measured voxel), `steps`, `region` (the region that failed last, or null), `ok`, `skipped`), and from the mapping `map` (`points`, `no_source`, `weak_source`), `volume` (`target`, `target_from`, `mean_before`, `shift`, `mean_after`) and `origin_shift_mm`. `tolerance_from` is `option`, `yaml` or `default`. The key is absent in any other run.
Each checkpoint of a fine run has the same record in `meta.fine_from`, and `describe()` (so `run_status`) shows it.

**Resume of a killed fine run.** A plain `--resume` continues it. It does not read the parent: `checkpoint.config_of_fine` takes the voxel, the maximum, the schedule offset and the tolerance from the record of the checkpoint (the config of the YAML is not trusted for them), `plan_resume` adds a fact
(`resume: this run is a fine pass from ...`), and `x` comes from the checkpoint of the fine run itself (the `x0` path is not used). **The stop rules of a resume.** The state of the stop rules (`settled` on, or all rules off) comes from the record of the run itself, in this order: an explicit `--stop-rules` / `--no-stop-rules` of the resume (it wins, as for a plain run), else the step settings of the continuation (`continued_from.step_settings.stop_rules.enabled`), else `fine_from.stop_rule` (`checkpoint.fine_early_stop`). The same order serves `--continue-from` a fine pass or a continuation of one: a continuation of a continuation with `--no-stop-rules` keeps the rules off without the flag. The resume fact says the state that is used (`as the checkpoint has it`, or `the checkpoint has the stop rules on; --no-stop-rules of this resume sets them off`), and a flag that changes the state is written into `fine_from.stop_rule` (and the step settings) of the resumed run and its checkpoints. (Before, a resume of a continuation turned `settled` on again from the record of the fine pass.) Measured: a killed and resumed fine run, with the parent moved away, equals the run that was not killed (bit-equal with one thread and a direct solver, as in section 24.2). A fine run is a normal run:
`--continue-from` works on it with the same YAML: the continuation takes the voxel, the beta schedule seen from the parent chain, the window, the tolerance and the stop rule from the record of the checkpoint (`checkpoint.config_for_continuation`; the grid comparison uses the fine grid), adds K + N passes, and the new checkpoint and `run.json` keep both records (`continued_from` and `fine_from`). A parent that `settled` ended is judged again at its last pass when the rules are on (the fact of section 24.3); `--no-stop-rules` goes on to K + N. A continuation of a continuation works the same way. It can be the parent of the next fine pass (for example 1.0, 0.7 and 0.5 mm; the offsets add up).

**Relation to the other commands.**

| | `--resume` | `--continue-from` | `--fine-from` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Folder | same | new | new |
| Grid | same | same (else refuse) | finer (equal refused) |
| Start | checkpoint state | checkpoint state (replay or fork) | mapped design, new MMA state |
| Pass count | from the checkpoint | K + N | at most `--fine-passes` (default: the passes of the parent), or when the loss has settled |
| Beta | schedule | schedule | schedule seen from the parent chain |
| Changed inputs | refuse | refuse (soft: iterations; of a fine parent also voxel, beta schedule, the default filter radius) | refuse (soft: voxel, iterations, beta schedule, the default or wall-rule filter radius) |

`settings.fine_pass`, `settings.stop_rules` and the two voxel guards are soft in all three: a change is a note.

**Guards.** All checks come before the first write (the order of F4-43, section 24.1): the arguments, the read of the parent, the plan and the problem of the fine grid, then the job lock, then the checks of the inputs, then the clean of NEW. A refusal leaves no folder, and an earlier run in NEW stays.
The parent is not changed by any of these steps.

**Lever cards** (section 41): `run_topopt:fine_from`, `run_topopt:fine_pass`, `run_topopt:fine_voxel`, `run_topopt:fine_passes` and `run_topopt:fine_tol`, layer 2, and the YAML keys `settings.fine_pass` and `settings.fine_pass.objective_change` (kind `method`, layer 1); the evidence rows are the measured runs of a 5-inch drone arm and of examples/hook/hook_short.yaml (2026-10-26, AMG solver, shared Linux host).

Tests: `tests/test_fine_pass.py`, `tests/test_fine_cli.py`, `tests/test_fine_mcp.py`.

## 25. Role playbooks, `team_guide`, and the Claude Desktop extension (added with V4)

This section specifies the role playbooks of the topopt team, the tool `team_guide`, the MCP prompts and resources that
serve the same text, and the `.mcpb` extension for Claude Desktop with its build script. The engine (`topopt/`) does not change. Texts that agents read give facts, estimates
and options. They have no habitual "must" or "never" (the rule for agent texts). A test checks this.

### 25.1 Role playbooks (one source)

- Files: `topopt_mcp/roles/<id>.md`, one for each role. The ids are `lead-design`, `cad`, `fea`, `print` and `finish`
  (`team.ROLE_IDS`, in the order of the list: the order of the work, `finish` last because it follows the print check after a run; added with FIN-1, #361). The wheel ships them as package data (`topopt_mcp = ["roles/*.md"]`).
  `topopt_mcp/team.py` reads them with `importlib.resources`. It needs only the standard library.
- File format: a header between two `---` lines with the keys `title` (a name for a menu) and `summary` (one line,
  at most 120 characters, no line break), then the body. The playbook is the body without the blank lines around it.
  A header key that is missing, an empty body or a missing file is a `RoleFilesError`.
- The body is the same text as the body of `agents/<id>-engineer.md` (25.4). It says who the role is, who decides, which
  tools the role can use today, what does not exist yet (the sentence "does not exist yet" is in every role), how the
  role works, and what it reports at the end. It is short (under 4,000 characters). It has no `${...}` text (the
  manifest field `prompts` treats that as a template variable). It holds no material of a talk or a demo day.
- A role works in two modes. As a sub-agent it cannot ask the user and returns open questions to the caller. When one
  agent does all the roles, it asks the user when an answer changes the part. The text says both.
  Items that need a shell or a skill exist in the Claude Code plugin. The text names them (the line near the top of
  each role, and "(needs a shell)" on the items where it fits) and says that another client can lack them.

### 25.2 The tool `team_guide(role: str | None = None) -> str`

- Returns the playbook of the role as plain text, equal to the playbook of the role file.
- `role` is a role id. Also accepted: any case, `_` for `-`, the plugin agent name (`cad-engineer`,
  `topopt:cad-engineer`), the resource URI (`topopt://roles/cad`), and a prefix that names one role (`lead`).
- No role, an empty role, or a name that matches no role: the answer is the list of the roles with one line each
  (`- <id>: <summary>`), the ways to read a playbook (the tool, the prompts, the resource URIs) and, for a wrong name, a
  first line that says so. The list is a fact. It is not an error, and the call does not raise.
- The result has text content only (`structured_output=False`).
- The tool sits in its own block at the end of `topopt_mcp/server.py` ("Team guide"). No other tool changes. The server
  `INSTRUCTIONS` name `team_guide` in their last line, the line of the tools whose descriptions say when to use them (since #380;
  before, the sentence `team_guide() lists the role playbooks.`). The length bound of the instructions stays one bound: since #380
  it is `OLD_CLIENT_CUT` of `tests/test_plugin_manifest.py`, 2,048 characters for the whole text (before: fewer than 2,400 characters
  in `tests/test_mcp.py`, then from P9-3 `MCP_TEXT_LIMIT`, 4,096 characters, with the key text in the first 2,048).

### 25.3 MCP prompts and resources

- One prompt for each role. The name is the role id. The title is `title`, the description is `summary`. A prompt has no
  arguments. It returns one user message that holds the playbook.
- One resource for each role. The URI is `topopt://roles/<id>`. The MIME type is `text/markdown`. The name is the role id,
  the title is `title` and the description is `summary`. The resource has the playbook as text.
- A client lists them with `prompts/list` and `resources/list`. Claude Code shows a prompt as `/mcp__<server>__<id>`. The
  `<server>` part depends on how the server starts: `topopt` in a checkout with the repo-root `.mcp.json`
  (`/mcp__topopt__cad`), and `plugin_topopt_topopt` for the server of the plugin (`/mcp__plugin_topopt_topopt__cad`; the tools of
  the plugin server have that prefix, `skills/start-here/SKILL.md:22`; not tested for prompts).
  Where Claude Desktop shows prompts and resources is not documented. So `team_guide` is the tool that every client has.
- If the role files cannot be read (a broken install), the server logs one line to stderr and serves no prompt and no
  resource. The tool `team_guide` then answers with the cause as text (`The role playbooks are not available: <cause>.
  The other tools work.`; it does not raise), and the other tools work.

### 25.4 The agent files

- The body of `agents/<id>-engineer.md` (after its own header: `name`, `description`, `color`) is equal to the playbook of
  `topopt_mcp/roles/<id>.md`. The role file is the source. The header of the agent file has one YAML comment line
  that says so and names the test: `# The body is a copy of topopt_mcp/roles/<id>.md. tests/test_team_guide.py checks it.`
- There is no generation step in V4. The test `tests/test_team_guide.py::test_agent_body_equals_the_role_file` fails when
  the two differ. Its message names both files and shows the lines that differ. (The numbers of the diff count lines of the
  body; the message says how many lines to add for a line of the file.) To change a playbook, make the change in both
  files.

### 25.5 The `.mcpb` extension

- Build: `uv run --no-project --python 3.13 packaging/mcpb/build.py [--out DIR]` writes `<DIR>/topopt-<version>.mcpb`. The
  default `DIR` is `dist/mcpb`. It is in `.gitignore`: some tools cannot publish a binary file, so nobody commits a
  `.mcpb`. The script needs Python 3.11 or newer and the standard library. A Mac without a newer Python has Python 3.9 as
  `python3`, so the command above lets `uv` fetch a Python for it. With a Python below 3.11 the script prints one line with
  that command and exits with code 1 (before `import tomllib`, so there is no traceback). It makes the zip itself (sorted
  names, fixed times, fixed modes: the same files give the same bytes on the same Python build; another zlib can give
  other compressed bytes). If the `mcpb` CLI (npm `@anthropic-ai/mcpb`, MIT) is on PATH, the script also runs
  `mcpb validate` on the manifest. Without it, the script says so on stderr.
- Template: `packaging/mcpb/manifest.json` (a complete, valid manifest). The script writes the manifest of the zip from it
  and sets three things: `version` (from `pyproject.toml`),
  `tools` (the name and the first docstring line of each function that `@mcp.tool` registers in `topopt_mcp/server.py`,
  read with `ast`) and `prompts` (one entry for each role: `name` = id, `description` = summary, `text` = playbook).
- Manifest facts:
  `manifest_version` is `0.4`. The server type is `binary`: the host runs the command of `mcp_config` and installs nothing.
  `entry_point` is `scripts/topopt-env.sh`, the launcher of the plugin (#206). `mcp_config` is `/bin/sh ${__dirname}/scripts/topopt-env.sh mcp`
  (`/bin/sh` runs the launcher, so the mode of the unpacked file does not matter), with the env var `TOPOPT_WORKSPACE`
  from the user option `workspace` and the env var `TOPOPT_DEFAULT_WORKSPACE` = `${HOME}/Documents/topopt`. The option is a directory
  with no default and `required: false`. Claude Desktop does not replace a variable inside the default of an option (version 3.6556.2,
  macOS 15.3: the server got the text `${DOCUMENTS}/topopt` and made the folder in the extension folder), but it replaces `${HOME}` in
  `mcp_config`. An empty option gives the server the text `${user_config.workspace}` or an empty text; the server takes this as "not set"
  and uses `TOPOPT_DEFAULT_WORKSPACE`. Claude Desktop starts the server in a folder that the user does not know, so the user can pick
  the work folder in the settings of the extension. A change needs a full quit of Claude (Cmd+Q): a new chat or a new Code tab session
  keeps the old server process. Section 10.1 has the rule of the server.
  The first start is the one of the plugin (section 34.1, the launcher; #370): it connects at once with all the tools (the snapshot of
  the lists), answers a tool call with the setup status, sets up the environment in the background and then hands over to the Python server,
  in the same chat. The environment is in `<extension folder>/.plugin-env` (the default env dir of the launcher; the host sets none of its
  variables). It holds the pins of the lock file and `topopt` (a test checks it), on a uv-managed Python 3.13 (PY-1, #422): the launcher makes it with
  `uv venv --python $LAUNCHER_PYTHON` (3.13), whatever `requires-python` allows. An environment of an older launcher (Python 3.12) is made again once, at the first start after the update:
  the first line of the stamp holds `python=<LAUNCHER_PYTHON>`, and `install_all` makes a venv whose Python is another major.minor again with `uv venv --clear` (one stderr line names both versions; the packages download again, so it needs the network;
  offline the setup stops and the next start online ends it). `status` and `doctor` name the Python as the reason. The manifest names no runtime in `compatibility`, because the host needs no Python.
  `compatibility.platforms` is `["darwin", "linux"]` (no `win32`: the server uses POSIX calls).
  The manifest schema has no field for the CPU architecture. The target, macOS arm64, and the Linux architecture
  (x86_64) are in `_meta["io.github.chartergroup.topopt"].architectures`, and in the long description.
  `tools_generated` is `true`. The license is `MIT`.
- Zip content: `manifest.json`; `pyproject.toml` (made from the one of the repo: the same name, version, `requires-python`,
  pins, scripts, `license` and `license-files` (when the repo has them) and build rules; the pins of the extra `mcp` are in
  `dependencies`, so an install of the folder without the extra also gets the server; the extras of the repo stay (nothing
  installs an extra unless someone asks for it, and the install offers of `environment` name them); the lines of
  `requirements.lock` are in `[tool.uv] constraint-dependencies`, for a `uv run` in the folder); the launcher
  `scripts/topopt-env.sh` and the lock files `requirements.lock` and `requirements-macos-x86_64.lock` (the build stops when one of
  the three is missing; no other file of `scripts/` goes in); `topopt/`, `topopt_mcp/`, `examples/`, `tools/check_part.py` (the only file of `tools/` that the role texts and
  the server name; the developer scripts stay out), `CONTRACTS.md` and the license files (`LICENSE*`,
  `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES*`, when they exist). In a git checkout only the files that git tracks go in; the script prints the
  names of the files that it left out (a local file, an ignored run folder). Without `.git` (a tarball) every file of
  those folders goes in. The zip has no cache file, no built library (`*.dylib`, `*.so`), no test, no recording and no
  agent or skill file. `*.sh` files have mode 0755 and every other file 0644. `environment` returns the unpacked folder
  as `code_folder`, so the role playbooks find `tools/check_part.py` and `CONTRACTS.md` there.
- pyopencl is a main dependency on macOS arm64 and Linux x86_64 (section 20, "Install"), so the extension has the GPU solver `gpu-mg` and the
  rule of `auto` (a GPU that passes the self-test) without an extra. The wheel has no OpenCL driver: on a machine with no OpenCL device `auto` runs a CPU
  solver. Nobody has run the extension with pyopencl on a Mac or in Claude Desktop yet.
- Needs on the machine: `/bin/sh`, and for the download of uv `curl` or `wget`, `tar`, and `sha256sum` or `shasum` (a Mac has them; section 34.1
  has the list). No Python and no uv: the launcher uses the uv of the user, or downloads
  its pinned uv release and checks its SHA256 (section 34.1). The first start downloads that uv (when needed), Python 3.13 and the
  packages. Measured on Linux x86_64, 2026-10-27, Python 3.12 (empty home folder, PATH `/usr/bin:/bin`, the unpacked zip started with the command of
  the manifest): the tools after 0.03 s, setup ready after 59 s, the answer of the server after 77 s in the same session, about 530 MB in
  `.plugin-env` and 130 MB of uv cache and Python in the home folder. Claude Desktop replaces the extension folder on an update, so the
  environment goes away then: the next start sets it up again from the uv cache (measured: ready after 3 s, the answer of the server
  after 16 s). The unpacked folder must be writable: the launcher makes `.plugin-env` and `topopt.egg-info` in it.
- The native Accelerate library is not built (`topopt/native/build.sh` needs the Xcode tools). On a Mac without it,
  `settings.solver: auto` runs `amg` and prints the build command (section 4). Claude in Desktop chat has no shell
  (`environment` installs and builds nothing), so it cannot run that command. The user can run it in Terminal:
  `environment` quotes it. Claude Desktop replaces the extension folder on an update, so the library goes away then and
  the user runs the command again.

### 25.6 Platforms and limits

- macOS arm64 is the target of the extension. Nobody has installed it on a Mac or in Claude Desktop yet. Open: the install,
  the start of the `binary` server with `/bin/sh` by the host, and the first start in the app (the steps for a person to try are not written here).
- Linux x86_64: the manifest lists `linux`: the bundle runs there through the launcher (the opt-in test
  `test_unpacked_bundle_starts_with_the_command_of_the_manifest`, `TOPOPT_TEST_MCPB_LAUNCH=1`, needs the network). Claude
  Desktop has no official Linux build, so nobody tests the extension in Desktop on Linux. The build script and the tests
  run on Linux. Linux users have the Claude Code plugin or the `topopt-mcp` command.
- Claude Desktop chat does not load agents, hooks or a local MCP server from a plugin (the Claude docs, not tested here).
  A plugin upload there gives the skills. The extension gives the server. The skills run in the cloud sandbox of the chat, so a skill that runs a shell
  command (the launcher check of `start-here`) does not reach this machine. `team_guide('lead-design')` has no such need.

### 25.7 The material reference (added with P4b-1)

The file `topopt_mcp/materials/reference.md` is a read-only document. It shows data sheet ranges of printed PETG and PLA: the tensile
strength in the layer plane and across the layers, the test standard, how the bars were made, and what the numbers leave out. Each number has
the address of a data sheet and the date on which the sheet was opened. The file is package data, so the wheel and the `.mcpb` bundle ship it.
The server offers it as the resource `topopt://materials/reference` (`text/markdown`, name `material-reference`; code in `topopt_mcp/materials.py`).
Decision D7 was revised on 2026-10-24 (with PM-2): a sourced filament catalog ships (section 18.8), so the engine reads the numbers of a
filament that the user names (`material.filament`) and `find_material` returns them with their sources. This file stays a read-only reference
document: the engine never reads it, and the catalog is a second, separate file (`topopt/data/materials.yaml`). The rest of D7 stays: there is
no default allowable and no safety factor, and a number from a data sheet is a fact about printed test bars, not a limit of the part.
Without an allowable, the result of `verify` has the key `no_allowable` (`resource`, `package_file`, `note`). The note says that the result has
no limit block and no pass or fail, that topopt has no default allowable, and where the ranges are. It names the option of the caller
(`--allowable-mpa` or `allowable_mpa`), and `topopt verify` prints it as one `limit:` line. With an allowable, the key is absent. A reader ignores
unknown keys, and `format` stays 1. If the file cannot be read (a broken install), the server logs one line to stderr and serves no material
resource. The other tools and the role resources work. Tests: `tests/test_material_reference.py` and `tests/test_verify_run.py`. The test
`test_no_tool_returns_a_material_number` checks the revised decision: the three catalog tools are the only tools with `material` in the name,
and the reference is still the one resource with materials in its address.

### 25.8 The role `finish` (added with FIN-1, #361 steps 2 and 3)

- Files: `topopt_mcp/roles/finish.md` (the source) and `agents/finish-engineer.md` (the copy, 25.4). The role is the last of `team.ROLE_IDS`.
- Job: after a successful run and its print check (section 32), remove visible voxel steps and other surface defects of `final.stl` with the
  tools that exist, run the print check again, and report. It adds no tool, no key and no number. The step fact of #361 (step 1) is NO-GO: no
  measure of voxel steps passed, so the role checks the steps on the renders (`render_part`, views `front` and `fl2:-1.333,-1,0.373`, `regions`
  `off`), before and after, and states no threshold.
- Route, cheapest first (the role text names the tool and the section of each): look (render, `print_check` of `run_result`, `fine_pass`); a
  post-only change of `settings.mesh_method` (section 19; the resume of a finished run is 24.2, the new YAML goes in the folder of the old one, 9.1;
  the role reads `metrics.mesh.method` and `metrics.mesh.fallback` first); marks (`cleanup_list` 29.3, `apply_marks` 29, `ratchet_run` 36); the fine pass (`run_topopt` with `fine_from`, 24.6; the role reads the existing `part_voxel` block and computes none of it); a print
  check fail that is a design effect is reported with the options of the lever cards and their price, as a choice for the user.
- Requirements: method settings change freely with a report. A user requirement is tightened with a report and its price, and loosened only with the
  consent of the user. The price comes from the tools. The optimizer values (`compliance_final`, the stiffness of `compare_runs`) do not change with
  the mesh step: its stiffness price is the tet value of `verify_run` on both run folders with one `mesh_size_mm` and the facts of the lever card
  `settings.mesh_method`; its mass is in the metrics of the new run. `verify_run` reads a run folder, so the stiffness of an `apply_marks` edit is
  known only through a `ratchet_run` rule (`stiffness`, `stress`; a rule with a limit is a user requirement, a rule without one only adds a check);
  else the report says "not known". The print check after an edit uses `print_check` with the YAML and the voxel of the run, so the limits and the
  resolution are the same as before. A fine pass is a method choice; its estimate goes to the caller (a sub-agent) or to the user before it starts.
- Call: the skill `start-here` and the role `lead-design` call the finishing pass after each successful run, before the final report to the user.
  One agent that does all the roles does the pass itself.
- Tests: `tests/test_team_guide.py` (the role lists, the copy of the body, the freedom rule), `tests/test_plugin_manifest.py`, `tests/test_mcpb.py`,
  `tests/test_client_configs.py`, `tests/test_finish_role.py` (the tools and sections that the text names exist; the calls).

## 26. Mirror symmetry, load and support types, perimeter (added with A4)

Section 26.1 is A4a: the `mirror` key (backlog B-045). Section 26.2 is A4b (load and support types, B-046). Section 26.3 is
A4c (the perimeter bound, B-064). Do not renumber.

### 26.1 Mirror symmetry by an exact voxel index map (added with A4a)

The code is `topopt/symmetry.py`, with one call in `voxelize`, in `build_problem` and in `Model.density`,
`Model.chain_rule` and `Model.gradient_wrt_x`. `run`, `minimize`, `formulation.py` and the `gpu_mg` files do not change.

**The key.** `mirror` is an optional top-level key: a list of at most 3 planes with distinct axes. A plane is a mapping:

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `normal` | Required. `x`, `y` or `z`, in any case. A vector of 3 numbers with one non-zero component is also read (`[0, -1, 0]` is `y`). A plane has no direction, so a sign has no meaning. |
| `at_mm` | Required. The coordinate of the plane on that axis, in mm. A finite number. |
| `align` | Optional. `auto` (default), `face` or `centre`. It sets where the plane lies in the grid (see "Grid plane"). |

An empty list or `null` is the same as no key. These inputs are refused, each with one line that ends with the supported
form and the option to re-orient the part (the STL files and the loads) so that the plane is axis-aligned: a normal that
is not along an axis (for example `[0, 1, 1]`, or a name that is not x, y or z), the zero vector, a repeated axis, more
than 3 planes, a value that is not a list, an entry that is not a mapping, an unknown or a missing key, an `at_mm` that is
not a finite number, and an `align` that is not one of the three words.

**Grid plane.** Only the origin on the plane axis moves. `lo` is the minimum corner of all region STLs on that axis, and `k` is
the smallest integer with `at_mm - k h / 2 <= lo + 1e-4 h`. The tolerance 1e-4 h (`symmetry.GRID_TOL`) covers the float32
rounding of STL vertices, which is about 8e-6 mm at 123 mm from the origin and would otherwise add one EMPTY layer. The new origin
is `at_mm - k h / 2`. No voxel centre of a region is cut. With this `k` the shift is below half a voxel. The plane is `k` half voxels above the
new origin, and `k` is the number that the facts give. For `k` even (parity `face`), the plane lies on a voxel face (the node
`k / 2`). For `k` odd (parity `centre`), it goes through the centres of the voxel layer `(k - 1) / 2`. With `align: face` or
`centre`, `k` is raised by 1 if it has the other parity. The shift is then below one voxel, and the grid has at most one
layer more. `align: auto` takes the parity by the rule of "Parity choice".
The voxel `i` along the plane axis has the partner `k - 1 - i`. The node `i` has the partner `k - i`. The other
indices do not change. Without a `mirror` key, `voxelize` runs as before (`origin` and `shape` are bit-equal).
`build_problem` checks that each plane is a grid plane of the origin that `voxelize` returned: `2 (at_mm - origin) / h` must be a
whole number within `2 GRID_TOL`. If not, it stops with an internal error (`RuntimeError`, exit code 2, section 8) whose message
gives the origin, the voxel size and the number of half voxels. A map about another plane is not built.

**Parity choice.** For `align: auto`, the engine builds the labels for the parity of the smallest shift, counts the label
mismatches (below), and builds them for the other parity. It keeps the parity with fewer mismatches. A tie keeps the
smaller shift. With `align: face` or `centre`, the parity is given and the run uses it: the engine does not change it. The engine
also builds the labels for the other parity, as a fact (F4-33): the plane gets `other_parity` (see "Facts"), and the `mirror:` lines
get one more line when the other parity has fewer label mismatches (see below). With several planes, the planes are decided in list order, and each plane
sees the parity that an earlier plane got; a given plane keeps its parity, so it does not change what a later plane sees. The cost is one more voxelization of the regions for each plane (`auto` or given), and one
at the end. In `label_mismatches`, the count of the other parity is `null` when it was not tried (a given `align`: its count is in `other_parity`; or the other grid cannot be built, for example because of the grid guard).
A voxelization of the hook at 1.2 mm takes about 0.03 s (measured at load 4.6).

**Label mismatches.** The number of voxels whose label differs from the label of their mirror image. A voxel whose image is
outside the grid is compared with EMPTY. A pair of voxels counts twice. The load region ids are not compared. The count is a fact.
It stops no run. A part that is symmetric about the plane gives 0 for the parity that fits it. Why the parity matters: the
voxelizer decides a voxel by a ray with a fixed small offset (`_JITTER`, in x and y). A region face that goes exactly through
voxel centres is decided with the sign of that offset, and its mirror image gets the other sign. On the hook (plane y = 0 mm,
voxel 1.2 mm) a load region has faces at y = -9.0 mm and y = 9.0 mm, which are 7.5 voxels from the plane. With the face parity
they go through voxel centres: 134 mismatches, all in the two layers at y = +-9.0 mm. With the centre parity they are voxel
faces: 0 mismatches.

**The index map.** For each plane, `perm` is an array over the design voxels, in the order of `x` (the order of the flat grid index).
`perm[p]` is the design voxel at the mirror image of the voxel `p`. It is an exact map, not a nearest-neighbour search. It is an
involution: `perm[perm[p]] = p`. A voxel on the plane (centre parity) is its own partner.

**Orphans.** A design voxel whose image is not a design voxel has no partner. Its `perm` is itself, so it stays a free variable.
No label changes and nothing is refused. The facts give, for each plane, the count, the share of the design voxels, and the count
for each cause of the image: `outside_grid`, `empty`, `keep_out`, `fixed`, `load` and `other` (a label code that has no name
here; 0 today). A voxel with the label LOAD counts as `load`. This includes the solid regions of section 22a, which have the label
LOAD. The causes add up to the count. On the hook, the centre parity gives 0 orphans. The face parity gives 24, all `load`.

The texts say what the orphans mean for the plane, as facts with options. Without orphans: no extra words. With some: the design is
symmetric on the paired voxels, and the text gives the share of the paired voxels. At or above half of the design voxels
(`symmetry.ORPHAN_MOST` 0.5): the mirror has little effect on this plane. For all design voxels (for example a plane that is far
from the part): the mirror has no effect on this plane, and the load is not mirrored. In these two cases the text gives the extent of the
grid along the plane axis (`grid_range_mm`) and the options: check `at_mm`, move the plane, make the regions symmetric about it, or
remove the key. The run goes on. No text says "the design is symmetric" for a plane without partners, and the end-value line of such a plane says that its values say nothing about symmetry (every voxel maps to itself).

**The average.** In `Model.density`, before the filter: `x` goes to `0.5 (x + x[perm])`, once for each plane in turn (list order).
Then the filter and the projections as before: `rho_tilde = F @ x_avg + b`. In `Model.gradient_wrt_x` (every `wrt` kind: `rho`,
`rho_tilde` and `x`, and `rho_stiff` of section 22b) and in `Model.chain_rule`, after the transposed chain, the gradient goes to `0.5 (g + g[perm])`
once for each plane, in reverse list order. The reverse order makes this step the exact transpose of the first. The maps of two
planes commute where the labels are symmetric about both planes. Orphans are where they are not, and there the order can matter.
An orphan keeps its value exactly (`0.5 (a + a) = a`). With no key, both steps return their input (the
same object) and the default path is bit-equal to the path before A4a.
The design that the model uses is `A x`, the average of `x`. `Model.design_point` gives it as `point.x`, so a response of kind `x`
reads the averaged design, and the transposed average in `gradient_wrt_x` is the exact gradient of that response. A response that
read the raw `x` would have the gradient of another function, and so would a response that averages `point.x` again (with two planes and
orphans `A` is not a projection, so `A A x` is not `A x`). The response reads `point.x` as it is.
`A x` is exactly symmetric about the last plane of the list (`a + b = b + a`). About the other planes it is symmetric where the maps
commute, that is, where the labels are symmetric about both planes. The raw optimizer variable `x` is a different thing. With one
plane (or planes whose maps commute) the gradient is symmetric to the bit, the update of `x` is elementwise, and `x` stays
symmetric (bit-equal needs one MMA row: with more rows the products in the dual solve can depend on the BLAS kernel). With two or
more planes and orphans, the reverse order ends with the first plane, so the gradient and `x` are symmetric about the first plane only.
The physical density is symmetric to rounding (about 1e-16) where the labels are symmetric: the sums of two mirror rows run in
another order. Near orphans it is not symmetric (a fact that the end values give). The pipeline method is the same (`pp_core_final.py` `sym` and `symT`). It does not need the filter to commute with
the map. The filter does commute for a symmetric label field: `F P = P F` and `b = b[perm]` (measured: 3.3e-16 on the hook grid; 2.2e-16 with the rule
`density_one` and 1.1e-16 with the rule `ignore` of section 22a, on 40 symmetric grids). `F` is not a symmetric matrix.

**Order with the robust form (section 22b).** The order of the steps is: the average of `x` (planes in turn), then the filter
(`rho_tilde`), then the nominal projection (`rho`: the volume, the snapshots, the final mesh) and the eroded projection
(`rho_stiff`: the stiffness). Both projections use the one symmetric `rho_tilde`, so the eroded density is after the average. The
reverse chain: a slope with respect to `rho` or `rho_stiff` goes through its projection slope, then `F^T`, then the average
in reverse plane order as the last step.

**The loads are not mirrored.** The finite element model has the full grid and the real loads. The optimizer minimizes the
function of the averaged design. For a load that is not symmetric, the result is the best symmetric design for that load. The
facts give, for each load case and each plane, `|f - R f| / |f|`. `f` is the nodal force vector of the case, `R` moves each nodal
force to the partner node and flips the force component along the plane axis, and a node with no image in the grid has no
partner. The value is `2 |f_anti| / |f|`, with `f_anti` the antisymmetric part of `f`: 0 for a symmetric load and 2 for an
antisymmetric load (a force with no image node gives 1). At or below 1e-9, the text says "symmetric". A symmetric force on a load
region whose voxels are not symmetric about the plane can read as not symmetric (on the hook at 2.0 mm, `hang` reads 0.447 with 12
design voxels of cause `load`). The text then names the count of the design voxels of cause `load`.
On the hook: `hang` 0 and `pull_off` 0.347 about y = 0 (Fy = 5.21 N of 30.0 N). A case that has a symmetric and an antisymmetric
part makes a gradient of the compliance that is not symmetric. The transposed average is what keeps the gradient exact.

**Facts.** `Problem.mirror` is `None` without the key, else a dict (all numbers are JSON values):

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `planes` | One entry per plane, in YAML order: `axis`, `at_mm`, `align` (as given), `parity` (used), `k`, `plane_index` (the node `k / 2` for `face`, the voxel `(k - 1) / 2` for `centre`), `label_mismatches` (`{"face": n or null, "centre": n or null}`; the count of the parity that is used is for the final grid), `orphans` (`count`, `share`, `outside_grid`, `empty`, `keep_out`, `fixed`, `load`, `other`), `grid_range_mm` (`[lo, hi]`: the extent of the grid along the plane axis), and, for a plane with `align` `face` or `centre` only, `other_parity` (`{"parity": "face" or "centre", "label_mismatches": n, "orphans": n}`: the other parity on its own grid, as `resolve` measured it for this plane; the key is missing for `auto` and when the other grid cannot be built). |
| `design_voxels` | The number of design voxels. |
| `load_asymmetry` | One entry per load case: `case` and `planes` (one ratio per plane, in the order of `planes`). |
| `end` | Written when the run ends: `x_deviation` and `rho_deviation`, one value per plane. They are `max abs(v - v[perm])` for the last call of `Model.density`, with `x` the **averaged design** `A x` (the input of the filter; not the raw optimizer variable) and `rho` the physical density. `x_deviation` of the last plane is 0 by construction. `rho_deviation` is the fact about the physical design: about 1e-16 where the labels are symmetric, and larger near orphans. |

`run.json` has the dict as `mirror` (and the end values, written when the run ends). `check_data`, `topopt check --json` and MCP
`check_problem` have it as `mirror` (`null` without the key). Text lines (`topopt check`:
`mirror:` lines; `topopt run`: `mirror:` lines in `run.log`; the builder check: `mirror:` lines) give, for each plane, the
parity with both counts, the orphans with their causes, and for each load case and plane the ratio with the words
"symmetric" or "not symmetric"; the run adds the end values. All of them are facts. None blocks a run. The
spec of `build_regions` has an optional `mirror` key, copied into the YAML as given. The loader checks it.

**A given `align` whose other parity fits better (F4-33).** When the plane has `align: face` or `centre` and the other parity has
fewer label mismatches (any lower count; there is no threshold), the lines of the plane get one more line, right after its orphan
line, with both counts and the options. The run still uses the given parity. For `centre` given, the card case (`examples/hook/hook_short.yaml`, voxel 2.0 mm,
the plane `y = 0`) reads:

    plane y = 0 mm: parity face has fewer label mismatches than parity centre, which align centre sets (face: 50 label mismatches and
    12 orphans; centre: 1140 label mismatches and 570 orphans). The run keeps centre. Options: set align: auto, or set align: face

(one line). The orphan counts are left out if `other_parity` has none. If the other parity has the same count or a higher one, there is no line, and
the `other_parity` fact is still there. `auto` has no `other_parity` and no such line: its facts and lines are as before F4-33.

**What does not change.** Without a `mirror` key the default run is bit-equal at 1 thread (hook `compliance_final`
1.3891411615538347, every snapshot, `final.stl` and `preview.bin`). The mirror gives no speed-up: the finite element
model, the solver and MMA keep the full size, and the extra work is two vector averages for each plane and each pass. The
`gpu-mg` model inherits the map through `Model` (`GpuModel` does not override `density`, `chain_rule` or `gradient_wrt_x`);
this path is not run-tested. The code is plain numpy and has no platform branch. `topopt.cli` still loads no numpy at import
(`symmetry.py` loads numpy only inside functions).

**Not in 26.1.** A half model, an automatic mirror load case, a mirrored output mesh, marks (the refine step) with a plane from the
YAML, and the load and support types of 26.2.

### 26.2 Load and support types (added with A4b)

Every key of this section is optional. A YAML without them gives the same run as before (bit-equal at 1 thread).
`Config.uses_extended_loads()` is True when the YAML has a moment, a remote force (`at`), a pressure or a per-axis
support (`Config.has_partial_supports()`). A reader that knows only plain forces and full clamps tests it.

**YAML keys.**

| Key | Form | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
