| `forces[].moment` | `[Mx, My, Mz]`, N mm | A moment about the node centroid of the region. `force` is then optional (default `[0, 0, 0]`). |
| `forces[].at` | `[x, y, z]`, mm | The point where `force` acts (a remote force). It needs `force`. It need not be inside the region. |
| `forces[].coupling` | `distributing` | The only coupling. `rigid` (RBE2) is refused (see below). |
| `pressures[]` | `{region, value_mpa}` | A pressure in N/mm2 (MPa) on a name of `regions.load`, in a load case. A case needs a force or a pressure. |
| `fixed[]` | a path, or `{file, axes}` | `axes` is a list of `x`, `y`, `z` (distinct). Only these axes are fixed. A path is a full clamp. |

A pressure on a `fixed` file or on the design STL, and a name that is not a key of `regions.load`, are refused with
a fact. `solid` regions are not a target. Messages are one line and end with `(file: <yaml>)`.

**Moment and remote force (distributing coupling, RBE3-like).** The force `F` and the moment `M` of an entry are
spread over the nodes of the region (every node of every voxel of the region, each once, as the plain force).
The reference point is the node centroid `c` of the region. A remote force adds the moment `(at - c) x F`, so the
applied moment is `M_c = M + (at - c) x F`. With `r_n = x_n - c`, `I = sum(|r_n|^2 E - r_n r_n^T)` and `w = I^-1 M_c`:
`f_n = F / N + w x r_n`. This is the least-squares spread of the force and moment (the nodal forces have the smallest
sum of squares). The sum of the nodal forces is `F` and their moment about `c` is `M_c`. No stiffness is added and no dof is
constrained. A moment about an axis where the nodes lie on a line (an eigenvalue of `I` below 1e-6 of the largest) cannot
be carried: the entry is refused with a fact (the axis, the eigenvalue ratio, the options). The audit of each entry
(force and moment, relative to the larger of the value and the sum of the terms) is at most 1e-9; else `UserError`.
`rigid` is refused: a rigid coupling (RBE2) needs constraint elimination, which this engine does not do. The message names
the distributing coupling (RBE3-like), the option to model a stiff link as a load region of solid voxels, and a later
option: a rigid segment in a bordered system (KB `capabilities/elastic-supports`).
The spread uses equal weights on all nodes of the region (also the inner ones), as the plain force does, so the result
depends on the thickness of the region and on the voxel size. Edge case of the 1e-6 limit: a one-voxel-thick rod region
that is longer than about 2450 voxels (the ratio is `6 h^2 / L^2`) cannot carry a torque about its own axis, and the
text says that the nodes lie on a line. A torque on a bar of 8 mm square section gives the rotation of beam theory
`T x_c / (G J)` with `J = 0.1406 a^4`: 0.939, 0.981 and 0.994 of it at h = 2, 1 and 0.5 mm (it converges from below). A
tip moment on a cantilever gives 0.941, 0.975 and 0.986 of `M x_c / (E I)` at the same h (measured, `tests/test_load_types.py`).

**Pressure.** The loaded faces are the faces of the voxels of the load region whose neighbour is EMPTY or KEEP_OUT,
or lies outside the grid. A face toward a design, fixed or other load voxel gets no pressure. A positive value pushes
into the body: the force on a face is `-p h^2 n_out`, split in four equal parts on the four nodes of the face. Nodes
that faces share add up. The resultant is `-p` times the vector area of the loaded faces. For a region that stands on the
design it equals `p` times the projected area. A closed region in free space has the resultant 0. A region with no
loaded face is refused. The audit compares the nodal sum with `-p` times the vector area (1e-9 relative).
The face distribution on a slanted surface is a staircase. The resultant is exact for the voxel faces (`-p` times the
vector area of the staircase). Against the STL surface it has the error of the voxelization. Measured on a plane patch
of 12 x 6 mm at 0, 15, 30 and 45 degrees and h = 1, 0.5 and 0.25 mm: the resultant differs by 0 to 1.7 percent
(the tangential part, by quantization), and the lever arm of the moment about the patch centroid by at most 0.28 h.

**Per-axis supports.** The fixed dofs of an entry are the chosen axes of every node of the voxels that the entry keeps
after the label priority (keep_out > fixed > load > design). A node that two entries share gets the axes of both.
`Problem.fixed_dofs` stays a sorted unique int64 array of dofs. A per-axis support region is a solid body: its voxels
are label FIXED, with full stiffness, and they are in the final mesh. Its nodes are fixed along the named axes only, so
the body carries load along the other axes and adds its stiffness to the part. For a full clamp all dofs are fixed, so
a clamp adds none. Measured with a symmetry plane (a half bar with a roller slab [y] at the plane, half the force, against
the full bar; the exact value of `2 c_half / c_full` is 1; pardiso, rho = 1): a slab of one voxel outside the part gives
0.79 at h = 1 mm and 0.88 at h = 0.5 mm (the half model is too stiff, and the error does not go to 0 with h: it is
material); a slab of 3 mm outside gives 0.60; a slab of one voxel inside the part gives 0.97 and 0.98; of 3 mm
inside, 0.91. For a symmetry plane, put a slab of one voxel inside the part, or use `mirror` (section 26.1) for a
symmetric design. Before the first solve (`build_problem`, so for every solver and for `check`),
the six rigid-body modes are tested on the fixed dofs. If one is free, a `UserError` gives the number and the names of the free
modes and the options. Facts: `fixed_dofs`, `free_modes`, `singular_value_ratio` (`Problem.extended["supports"]`,
`run.json` `supports`, `check` key `extended`). The test does not look for separate pieces of the part.
AMG runs in scalar mode when a node has fixed and free dofs together (no new code: `fe.triplets_aligned` is false). The
setup of the hierarchy takes 2 to 3 times as long as in the 3 x 3 block mode of a full clamp (measured on 80,000 to
90,000 free dofs: 3.0 to 4.3 s against 1.4 to 1.6 s), and the number of CG iterations is the same (8 to 14). The direct
solvers need no change.

**Lost force and moment.** `lost_force` counts the force on fixed dofs, not on fixed nodes: a per-axis support drops
only the force along its axes. A case that has a moment, a remote force or a pressure is measured on its nodal forces:
the basis of the percents is the sum of the sizes of the nodal forces (for a plain force it is `|F|`, so a case of
plain forces has the numbers and the keys of a YAML without the new types). A lost force or moment at or below 1e-9 of
that sum is round-off and counts as 0. A case with no resultant force (a pure moment) has `lost_percent` null, and the
text says so; `lost_percent_of_sum` gives the lost force against the sum of the nodal force sizes. Such a case has the
lost moment as a fact (section 5, `lost_force`): the case value is the sum about one point, the origin of the part
coordinates (`lost_moment_about_mm`), and the value of each region is about the node centroid of the region. A case of
plain forces has no lost-moment keys: its moment about the origin is the lever arm times the lost force, so it is
not a new fact, and a plain case reads the same next to a case with a moment.

**Output.** `run.json` `load_cases[].forces[]`: `force` (the resultant, `[0, 0, 0]` for a pure moment) and `kind` (section
5). `metrics.json` `stiffness_cases[].N_per_mm` is `null` with a `reason` for a case with a moment, a remote force or a
pressure. `topopt check` and `check_data` have the key `extended` (the entries with their audits, and the supports) and print
`load:`, `pressure:` and `supports:` lines. `topopt run` writes the same lines to `run.log`. The dashboard draws the
arrow of a remote force at its `at` point; a moment has no glyph.

**Other readers.** `topopt verify` does not know these types. `topopt verify` refuses in `preflight`
(after `read_run`, so the CLI and the MCP tool both stop before any mesh) with a fact and the options, when
`Config.uses_extended_loads()` is True and the YAML has a moment, a remote force, a pressure or a per-axis support: its P2 model clamps all 3 dofs of a fixed region and loads a plain traction.
`gpu-mg` takes the moments, remote forces and pressures (the solver takes any right-hand side), and a per-axis support since P2c
(section 20; before, `cli.GPU_MG_AXES` refused it).
A spring (section 35) or a joint (section 38) makes `uses_extended_loads()` True, but `topopt verify` does not refuse it since K1-A (section 16, "Joints and springs"). `gpu-mg` takes springs and joints
since P2b (section 20). `topopt_mcp`,
the dashboard (`null` stiffness, no arrow for a zero force), `tools/check_part.py` and the stress and refine steps
read the new fields.

**Limits.** No distributed moment on a surface of arbitrary shape, no rigid coupling, no body force,
no pressure on the design surface. Spring supports are in section 35. A pressure acts on every exposed face of its region: shape the region so that only the
wanted face looks into free space.

### 26.3 Perimeter bound (added with A4c)

One optional key adds one constraint row of the A1 API (section 13): `P <= settings.perimeter_max_mm2`. `P` is the surface area of the
physical density of the part, counted in voxel faces. The code is `topopt/perimeter.py`. A YAML without the key gives the same run as before (bit-equal at 1 thread: the hook example, every
snapshot and `compliance_final` 1.3891411615538347).

**The key.**

```yaml
settings:
  perimeter_max_mm2: 12000     # optional. A number > 0, in mm2. YAML 1.1 loads 1.2e4 and 1e4 as text; they are read as numbers.
```

`P` is voxel face area in mm2 (a staircase surface; in one measured problem about 1.24 times the area of `final.stl`). The loader
refuses 0, a negative number, a text that is not a number, a bool, `null` and a value that is not finite. The message names the key
and the value, ends with `(file: <yaml>)` and has one line (section 2). The part builder (`build_regions`) passes the key from the spec
`settings` to the YAML.

**What `P` is.** `P = h^2 * sum over faces of f(d)`, where `d` is the jump of the density across a face and
`f(d) = (sqrt(d^2 + eps^2) - eps) / (sqrt(1 + eps^2) - eps)`, with `eps = 1e-3` (`perimeter.EPS`, written to `run.json`). So
`f(0) = 0` and `f(1) = 1`: a binary jump is exactly one face. One design voxel in void has `P = 6 h^2`, two neighbouring voxels `10 h^2`.
The term has the slope 0 at `d = 0`. A gray design has `P` at most its exact total variation. `eps` shapes the gradient. It is not a limit.
The faces count as follows.

| Voxel | Density of the voxel |
|---|---|
| design voxel | its physical density `rho`: the nominal density, also in robust mode (section 22b), after the filter, the projection and the mirror average |
| FIXED or LOAD voxel (this includes `regions.solid`, interface unions and spring regions) | 1 |
| EMPTY or KEEP_OUT voxel | 0 |
| outside the grid | 0 |

Every face that touches a design voxel counts. A face between two voxels that are not design voxels is a constant: 1 if one is solid and
the other is void, else 0. The sum of the constants is the **fixed part** (`fixed_part_mm2`). It is in `P` and in the bound, because the printed part has
that surface. The pipeline does not count faces on the border of the mesh. Here a face to the outside of the grid counts as a face to void.

**The row.** Name `perimeter`. Linear form: `g = P / bound - 1`, met when `g <= 0`. Price 1000 (the default of a linear row, as the volume
row), and no price key. The gradient is with respect to `rho` (`wrt="rho"`): `Model.gradient_wrt_x` multiplies by the Heaviside slope and applies the
filter transpose and the transposed mirror average, so the row works with the filter rule, `min_member_mm`, `robust` and `mirror` with no code of
its own. `P` needs no solve, so the row adds no adjoint solve. The face list is built at the first use, from the labels, and it holds two index
arrays for the faces that touch a design voxel (measured: 2.3 MB held, 45 MB peak at the build and 15 MB peak for one evaluation at the 5M-voxel guard with 99k
design voxels; 2 to 7 ms for P and the gradient on the hook, with a load average of 17 on the host, against 2.6 to 2.9 s for a pass). Order of the rows: the volume row, the compliance limits, the stress rows, the displacement and
alignment rows (section 31), and the perimeter row last. It comes after the fallback of the volume row: a mass run with no other row keeps its
volume ceiling, because the perimeter row does not hold material (in the measured problems the empty design had the smallest `P`; it is not a general law: a pocket in the solid regions has a smaller `P` when it is filled). `problem_facts` says it in one line.
The row works with `objective: compliance`, `case_combine: max` and `objective: mass`.

**The smallest possible `P` and the refusal.** `p_min_mm2` is the smallest `P` of any design with the density 0 or 1 in every voxel (and, by the
co-area formula, the smallest exact total variation of any density in [0, 1]). It is a minimum cut of the design graph: one node for each design voxel, an
edge of capacity 1 for each design-design face, edges from the solid side and to the void side for the faces to solid and void voxels. `scipy`
finds it in 0.07 s on the hook and 0.14 s for 99k design voxels (host under load). `p_min_mm2` is the fixed part plus the faces of the cut. A bound below
`p_min_mm2` cannot be met by a design with density 0 or 1, so `topopt check` and the start of `topopt run` refuse it before the model is built. The text
has the bound, `p_min_mm2`, the fixed part, the unit and the options:

`settings.perimeter_max_mm2 is 1000 mm2, and no design with density 0 or 1 can have a perimeter below 6776.0 mm2 (the minimum cut of the design space, rounded up to 0.1 mm2). The solid regions alone (fixed, load, solid and spring voxels) have 4640.0 mm2 of surface to void, and any design adds at least 2136.0 mm2 more. P is voxel face area in mm2 (a staircase surface; ...). Options: raise settings.perimeter_max_mm2 to 6776.0 mm2 or more; reduce the solid regions; make the design space bigger (file: ...)`

A bound that equals `p_min_mm2` (to 1e-9 relative, round-off) is not refused. The statement is exact for designs with density 0 or 1. A gray design
can have a smooth `P` a little below it, only for gray near-void designs (the hook_short example: the smallest smooth `P` over all densities in [0, 1] is 6773.09 mm2,
0.043 % below `p_min_mm2` 6776.0, at a design with all densities at 0.0063 or less). The text shows `p_min_mm2` rounded up to 0.1 mm2 (6779.52 shows as 6779.6), so the number
in the advice is a bound that the check accepts; the `perimeter:` line and the run log show it in the same form. The filter can keep a design above it: with the default rule
(`filter_solid_neighbours: density_one`) the filtered density near a solid region is above 0 even for `x = 0` (the "solid pull"). So `p_min_mm2` is a floor and not a
promise that a bound above it is met. A script that calls `formulation_from_config` with a model, or `optimize.run`, gets the same `UserError` at the
build of the formulation. A script that gives no model gets it at the first pass.

**Facts, no threshold.** `topopt check` prints one line `perimeter: bound ...; fixed part ...; smallest possible ...; bound / smallest = <ratio>.` and the unit,
and `check_data` / `check_problem` have the key `perimeter` (`max_mm2`, `eps`, `fixed_part_mm2`, `p_min_mm2`, `p_base_mm2` (null: it needs the filter),
`bound_over_p_min`; `null` without the key, and `bound_over_p_min` is `null` when `p_min_mm2` is 0, which the check prints as "not defined"). The ratio is printed for every bound. The code has no limit on it: a bound near `p_min_mm2` is allowed. One measured problem
shows what it can cost (the hook_short example, 2.0 mm, 40 passes, linear row, price 1000; `p_min_mm2` 6776, fixed part 4640, the free run has `P` 15,855 and compliance 1.3964):

| Bound (mm2) | Bound / `p_min_mm2` | Compliance | Volume | `P` at the end | g of the row |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 14,270 | 2.11 | 1.472 (x1.054) | 0.1999 | 14,277 | +5e-4 (met) |
| 11,891 | 1.75 | 1.866 (x1.34) | 0.1766 | 11,901 | +8e-4 (met) |
| 9,513 | 1.40 | 11.54 (x8.3) | 0.107 | 9,602 | +0.009 (not met) |
| 7,928 | 1.17 | 169.6 (x121) | 0.054 | 8,089 | +0.020 (not met) |
| 7,135 | 1.05 | 2,011 (x1,440) | 0.028 | 7,383 | +0.035 (not met) |

This is one problem. It is context for the choice of a bound and not a rule.

**Reports.** `P` of the start design is `p_base_mm2`: `x = volume_fraction` in every design voxel at the first beta of the schedule. It
depends on the config alone, so a resume gives the same number. It equals the value of the row at pass 0.
- `run.json` `perimeter` (section 5): `max_mm2`, `eps`, `fixed_part_mm2`, `p_min_mm2`, `p_base_mm2` before the first pass, and `p_final_mm2` (the value
  of the row at the last pass) after the last pass. `constraints` has `{"name": "perimeter", "limit": <bound>}` (section 13).
- `history.jsonl` and `metrics.json` `constraints`: the row, with `value` = `P` in mm2 (section 13). `metrics.json` `rows` has the entry of section 31
  with `kind` `perimeter` and `unit` `mm2`; `value_start` is `p_base_mm2` and `value_end` is `p_final_mm2`.
- `run.log`: at the start `fact: perimeter: bound ...; ... P of the start design ...`; at the end, if `g > 0.005`, `constraint not met: perimeter ... the bound is <r> times the
  smallest possible P (<p_min> mm2)`, the cause and the options (`raise settings.perimeter_max_mm2, or relax the other rows (volume_fraction, compliance and stress limits)`),
  and, in every run, one line `fact: perimeter: P of the start design ..., P of the last design ..., bound ... (met|not met); smallest possible ...`.
- No snapshot field (the snapshot files have no metadata; `history.jsonl` has `P` for every pass) and no dashboard change.

**Checkpoint and resume.** `checkpoint.effective_settings` leaves the key out when it is `None`. A checkpoint written before A4c, and one of a run without the key,
have the same effective settings and the same hash, so they resume with no change. A resume that adds or changes the key is a change of the inputs
(`settings.perimeter_max_mm2: <not set> -> 12000`) and needs `--allow-changed-inputs`. The row has no state.

**Combinations (facts).**
- With the mass objective: the row does not hold material. A bound below the `P` that the other rows give can make the optimizer add material (cantilever example of
  the tests: volume 0.177 without the bound, 0.187 with a bound at 0.97 of that `P`; hook_short, 40 passes, with two compliance limits: 0.1497 without the bound and 0.2115 with a bound at 0.9 of its `P`, measured on this branch; the research prototype gave 0.2193). The price of the row is 1000 and the
  price of a compliance limit is 100, so a tight perimeter bound can leave a compliance limit not met. The log says it in two places. `problem_facts` (start of the run,
  `topopt check`): `The perimeter row has price 1000 and a compliance limit has price 100, so a tight bound can leave a compliance limit not met.` At the end of the run, when a compliance
  limit is not met and the perimeter row is met, the summary line names the row as a possible cause and gives the option:
  `the other rows are met, and this limit is not met at the end of the run; the perimeter row has price 1000 and a compliance limit has price 100, so a tight perimeter bound can be a cause; options: raise settings.perimeter_max_mm2, or relax the limit`.
  The cause is a possible one: the log does not say that the row is the cause. Under the mass objective this summary has no volume option and no mass-objective option, with or without the perimeter row
  (`the other rows are met, and this limit is not met at the end of the run; options: relax the limit`). The text of a run with the compliance objective is the text of section 13.
- With `case_combine: max`: the row is one more constraint row after the bound rows of the cases.
- With robust mode (section 22b): `P` is of the nominal density, the shape that the printer makes. The compliance rows use the eroded density.
- With mirror (section 26.1): `P` is of the averaged design. The gradient is symmetric. `p_min_mm2` is the minimum over all designs, so it is also a floor for the symmetric ones.
- With the stress rows (section 17): the row has no `measure`, and the step acceptance does not check it.
- Solvers: the row calls no solver. It is tested with `amg` (every platform), PARDISO (Linux x86_64) and the Accelerate Cholesky (Apple silicon, the CI legs). The `gpu-mg` model
  (section 20) inherits the density chain and `design_point`, and the shared `run` loop builds the row, so the row works there by code reading; a gpu-mg run with the row is not made.
- `topopt verify` (section 16) reads the YAML with the same loader and does not check this row. The refine and feedback steps read `run.json` generically.

**Platforms.** The module is numpy and scipy, with no platform branch. macOS (Apple silicon) and Linux x86_64 give the same row. The Mac run is not made on the build machine.

**Limits.** No objective weight (`w P / P_base`) and no price key. `P` is the voxel (staircase) area, not the area of the mesh. No dashboard view. No override for a refused bound.
The face list belongs to one label array: a second model gets a new list. The pipeline form `sqrt(d^2 + eps^2)` (not shifted) is not used: it adds `eps` for each internal face (+0.6 % to +1.7 % on recorded hook designs).

## 27. CI, golden values and tolerance tiers (added with V6)

CI runs the tests and one short hook run on Linux x86_64 and on macOS arm64.
The step logic is in `scripts/ci/*.py`. The workflow file only calls them. The facts that differ between the legs
are in `scripts/ci/legs.toml`. `tests/test_ci_scripts.py` checks that the workflow, `legs.toml`, the golden file and this
section agree. E4 adds a Linux leg with the pins of the Intel Mac lock, a manual workflow for a hosted Intel Mac runner and a
check of the lock files (27.10).

### 27.1 Files

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `.github/workflows/tests.yml` | The workflow: jobs `plan`, `test` (one job for each leg, each Python of the leg and each shard of the leg, 27.2, 27.3.2), `test-after`, `wheel` and `report` (27.3.2, 27.6). It starts by hand only: its only event is `workflow_dispatch`, and a push or a pull request never starts it. Its input `legs` is a choice, `linux` (the default) or `all`. `linux` runs `plan`, the leg `linux-x86_64` on Python 3.13, and `wheel`; `all` also runs `macos-arm64` (a macOS minute counts more than a Linux minute) and `linux-x86_64-intel-pins`, both on 3.13. `plan_legs.py --legs` writes the matrix. Start it from the Actions tab (workflow `tests`, Run workflow) or with `gh workflow run tests.yml --repo chartergroup/topopt -f legs=linux`. |
| `.github/workflows/intel-mac.yml` | The manual workflow for a hosted Intel Mac runner (E4, 27.10): jobs `plan` and `test`, event `workflow_dispatch` only (a push or a pull request never starts it). A run takes 15 to 25 minutes (estimate). |
| `.github/workflows/evals.yml` | The manual workflow for the plugin evals on the MCP mocks (`claude plugin eval`, `evals/README.md` "Run the evals in CI"): one job `evals` on `ubuntu-24.04`, event `workflow_dispatch` only (a push or a pull request never starts it). The inputs `model`, `judge_model` and `threshold` go to the runner as they are; `threshold` `0` turns the score gate off, and the job then fails only when the run fails. The other inputs are `tag` (`smoke` or `mock`), `case`, `runs` and `max_cost_usd`. The credential is the secret `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`. Each case is a real model call. |
| `.github/actions/plugin-eval/action.yml` | The composite action of `evals.yml`: Node.js 22, the pinned Claude Code, `scripts/ci/run_evals.py` (input check, the run, the job summary) and the upload of the output folder. `check_workflow.py` checks it (`runs.using` composite, a `shell` for each `run` step, a `description` for each input). |
| `scripts/ci/legs.toml` | The legs, the tolerance tiers and the allowed skips. |
| `scripts/ci/license_policy.toml` | The decided licence exceptions (27.7). |
| `tests/tiers/durations.json` | The seconds of each test file (`all`, and `not_slow` without the tests of `slow.txt`), made by `scripts/ci/make_tiers.py durations` from junit XML files. `scripts/ci/shards.py` splits the test files with it (27.3.2). |
| `scripts/ci/*.py` | One script for each step. Standard library only, apart from `check_workflow.py` and `short_run.py` (PyYAML). |
| `tests/test_locks.py` | The offline check of the platform markers against both lock files, and the tests of `check_locks.py` (27.10). |
| `examples/hook/hook_short.yaml` | The short hook run (27.4). It is the hook with a coarser grid, 40 iterations and a shorter beta schedule. No code is specific to it. |
| `ci/golden/hook_short.json` | The golden file (27.4). Text, not binary. |

### 27.2 Legs

| Leg | Runner | Extras | Expected solver | Runs with `legs=linux` | Pythons |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `linux-x86_64` | `ubuntu-24.04` | `dev`, `mcp`, `pardiso`, `step`, `tet`, `verify` | `pardiso` | yes | `3.13` |
| `macos-arm64` | `macos-15` | `dev`, `mcp`, `step`, `tet`, `verify` | `cholesky` (the Accelerate shim is built first) | no, only with `legs=all` (value `on_pull_request` in `legs.toml`; the key name is historic) | `3.13` |
| `linux-x86_64-intel-pins` | `ubuntu-24.04` | `dev`, `mcp`, `pardiso`, `step`, `tet`, `verify` | `pardiso` (lock `requirements-macos-x86_64.lock`) | no, only with `legs=all` (E4, 27.10) | `3.13` |
| `macos-x86_64` | `macos-15-intel` | `dev`, `mcp`, `step`, `tet`, `verify` | `amg` (lock `requirements-macos-x86_64.lock`) | no: `intel-mac.yml` starts by hand only (E4, 27.10) | `3.13` |

The table applies since the workflow became active (2026-10-24, 27.1). Since the same day no event but `workflow_dispatch` starts a run: the column
`Runs with legs=linux` says whether the choice `linux` of the input `legs` runs the leg (the choice `all` runs every leg of `tests.yml`).

The column `Pythons` is the key `pythons` of the leg in `legs.toml` (required). `plan_legs.py` makes one matrix entry (`label`, `os`, `python`, `shard`, `shards`, `suffix`, `part`) for each Python and shard of a
leg, so a leg with two Pythons is two jobs (more with shards), and the workflow makes its venv with `matrix.python`. The supported Pythons have one source:
`SUPPORTED_PYTHONS` in `scripts/ci/_common.py` (3.13 only, since #469). `requires-python` in `pyproject.toml` must allow exactly these versions, the keys `pythons`
pick from them, and `check_locks.py` and `wheel_check.py` check each of them (27.8, 27.10). `tests/test_ci_scripts.py` checks that these places agree. Every leg
lists 3.13 only (since 2026-10-27; before, Linux x86_64 and macOS arm64 listed both and the Intel legs 3.12). The launcher makes Python 3.13 (the Python of every leg); the lock check of CI
resolves the locks for each supported Python, and the wheel job installs the wheel on each. To support a new Python, add it to `SUPPORTED_PYTHONS`, to `requires-python` and to `pythons` of a leg.

An extra that `pyproject.toml` does not declare is dropped and the log names it (the extra `verify` comes with PR #21). No `gpu`
extras are installed. pyopencl is a main dependency on Linux x86_64 and on an Apple silicon Mac, so it is installed. The Linux leg has no OpenCL
platform (pocl is in the extra `gpu-test` only): a test that needs a device skips with `no usable OpenCL device: ...` through the fixture `dev` of its
file, and a test file that needs pyopencl skips with `could not import 'pyopencl'` where it is not installed (27.6). The install command is `uv pip install -c <lock> -e ".[extras]"`: the lock gives the pinned versions. The lock is
`lock` of the leg in `legs.toml` (default `requirements.lock`; the two Intel legs use `requirements-macos-x86_64.lock` with `install_mode = "lock-first"`, 27.10).
The Linux leg installs the apt packages `libglu1-mesa`, `libopengl0`, `libxft2`, `libxinerama1`, `libxcursor1`, `libxfixes3`,
`libxext6` and `libgl1` (the gmsh wheel loads them). The `macos-arm64` runner label is `macos-15`: GitHub retires `macos-14`
on 2026-11-02.

### 27.3 Steps of a leg, in this order

Each step runs when the install step passed, also after a failed step. Each step writes a table to the job summary.

| Step | Script | Fails when |
|---|---|---|
| Install | `install_env.py` | a command fails |
| Licence check (shard 1 only, 27.3.2) | `license_check.py` | see 27.7 |
| Expected solver | `check_solver.py` | `topopt check examples/hook/hook.yaml --json` does not report the CPU solver of the leg in `solver.cpu_solver`, or exits non-zero. The step prints what `auto` picks (`solver.resolved` and the line of `solver.choice`) as information and does not compare it: a runner that shows an OpenCL GPU can pick `gpu-mg`, and the CPU solver stays the same |
| Lock files (shard 1 only) | `check_locks.py` | the leg has `check_locks = true` and a lock file does not resolve for its platform with its own pins for a supported Python (the step passes no `--python`), or a control does not fail (27.10) |
| Short run (shard 1 only) | `short_run.py run` | a metric is outside the tier, the inputs differ from the golden file, or the run takes longer than `short_run_limit_s`. The run names the CPU solver of the leg (`--solver <expected solver>`, 27.4) |
| pytest | `run_pytest.py` | pytest exits non-zero. The tests of the chosen tier (of the shard, 27.3.2) run, with the gmsh tests, in parallel with pytest-xdist (27.3.1). |
| Skips | `check_skips.py` | a skipped test matches no `allowed_skip` entry of the leg (27.6) |
| Artifacts | `actions/upload-artifact` | never (it runs on failure too) |

#### 27.3.1 The parallel pytest step

`run_pytest.py` starts `python -m pytest -n <workers>` and sets the thread variables for the tests. Both values are data of the leg in
`legs.toml`: `pytest_workers` (`"auto"` or a whole number) and `pytest_threads` (the value of `OMP_NUM_THREADS`, `MKL_NUM_THREADS`,
`OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS` and `NUMBA_NUM_THREADS` in each worker; a variable that the caller has already set keeps its value). The options
`--workers` and `--threads` override the leg; `--workers 0` runs one process, as a plain `pytest` does. If pytest-xdist is not installed
the step runs one process and the log and the summary say so. Every test of a job runs in its one parallel run: no test file needs a separate serial
step, because the tests of `tests/test_environment.py` that read the thread variables clear them themselves (they failed when a caller set
`OMP_NUM_THREADS`). The summary table shows the workers and the thread variables. The values are measured: on 4 CPUs (`taskset -c 0-3`, 4 workers) the full suite took 619 s with 1 thread, 646 s with 2 threads and
757 s with no thread variable set, so both legs use `pytest_threads = 1`. The short run (27.4) is a step of its own: it is not a pytest step and it sets its own thread variables to 1.

**Tiers (`--tier fast|full`, input `tier` of the workflows).** `fast` is the default of the workflows. The key `pytest_fast` of a leg
is a marker expression for `-m` (`not slow` on Linux; `platform_sensitive and not slow` on macOS; `none` runs no pytest and writes a junit XML file with
zero tests). `full` runs every test, except what `pytest_full` of the leg leaves out (`not slow` on the Intel-pins leg). The markers come from
`tests/tiers/slow.txt` (the tests of 5 s or more) and `tests/tiers/platform_files.txt`; `tests/conftest.py` adds them, and `scripts/ci/make_tiers.py`
writes both lists from junit XML files. A test that is in no list is in the fast tier.

The artifact `ci-<leg label>-py<Python>` (with the suffix `-s<i>of<N>` when the leg has N shards, 27.3.2) holds: `junit.xml`, `pytest.log`,
`shard.json`, `topopt-check.txt`, `topopt-check.json`, `pip-freeze.txt`, and with N above 1 `collect.xml`. The artifact of shard 1 (the only one
when N is 1) also holds `licenses.json`, `short-run-deviation.json` and the folder `short-run/` (the run folder without `snapshots/`). Retention: 14 days.

#### 27.3.2 Shards and the job `report`

Shards (key `shards` of the leg in `legs.toml`, default 1; a whole number of 1 or more, else `CiError`): `linux-x86_64` has 2, `linux-x86_64-intel-pins` 2, `macos-arm64` 2 (a
macOS minute counts more than a Linux minute, and each shard pays its own setup), `macos-x86_64` 1. `plan_legs.py` makes one matrix entry for each Python and shard, and `--tier` gives one shard to a leg that
runs no pytest in the tier. `run_pytest.py --shard i/N` collects the tier, splits the test FILES by their times (`scripts/ci/shards.py`, `tests/tiers/durations.json`: longest file
first into the lightest shard; a file that is not listed gets the median; ties break by name) and passes the files of shard i to pytest, so no test is deselected or shown as
skipped. The licence check, the lock check and the short run run on shard 1 only; the install, the solver check and pytest run on every shard. Each shard writes `shard.json`
(leg, Python, shard, `tier_total`, the node ids it ran) to its artifact `ci-<leg>-py<Python>-s<i>of<N>` (no suffix when N is 1). The job `report` (runs also after a failure) downloads
the `ci-*` artifacts and fails when a shard is missing, a test ran in two shards, the shards of a leg and Python ran another number of tests than `tier_total`,
or a skip of the junit files or of `collect.xml` matches no `allowed_skip` entry (27.6) (`scripts/ci/report_shards.py`). It writes the 30 slowest tests to the job summary. `intel-mac.yml` has no job `report`, so `macos-x86_64` keeps
one shard (`tests/test_ci_shards.py` checks it).


### 27.4 The golden file

`ci/golden/hook_short.json`, written by `python scripts/ci/short_run.py make-golden`:

```json
{"format": 1, "case": "examples/hook/hook_short.yaml",
 "inputs_sha256": {"examples/hook/hook_short.yaml": "<hex>", "examples/hook/design.stl": "<hex>"},
 "metrics": {"compliance_final": 1.3963757322862906, "volume_fraction_final": 0.19999265534613847,
             "volume_final_mm3": 22663.3, "mass_final_g": 28.1},
 "info": {"iterations": 40, "triangles": 27626, "solver": "pardiso", "watertight": true},
 "made_by": {"platform": "linux-x86_64", "cpu": "...", "solver": "pardiso", "threads": 1, "python": "3.12.13",
             "packages": {"numpy": "2.5.3"}, "topopt_base": "7555b19", "date": "2026-10-20", "wall_s": 19.8, "load_average": "..."}}
```

- `compliance_final`, `volume_final_mm3` and `mass_final_g` are the keys of `result/metrics.json` (section 5). `volume_fraction_final` is
  `volume_fraction` of the last row of `history.jsonl`. `volume_final_mm3` has 1 decimal and `mass_final_g` has 2 decimals in
  `metrics.json` (`topopt/post.py`), so a tier gives each of them an `atol` of one rounding step.
- `inputs_sha256` holds the sha256 of the YAML and of each STL that it names. If an input changes, the step fails with the text that
  the golden file needs a new run. The deviation of a changed input is not shown as a deviation of the optimizer.
- `info` and `made_by` are facts for people. The step does not compare them.
- The run uses one thread: `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS`, `OMP_NUM_THREADS`, `MKL_NUM_THREADS`, `NUMBA_NUM_THREADS` and
  `VECLIB_MAXIMUM_THREADS` are 1. The command is `topopt run examples/hook/hook_short.yaml --out <dir> --solver <expected solver of the leg> --quiet`.
  The solver is named because the golden file is a CPU result and `settings.solver: auto` can pick `gpu-mg` on a machine with an OpenCL GPU.
  `make-golden` does the same: `--solver` (default `pardiso`) names the CPU solver, never `auto`.
- A new golden file or a new tier value is a change of the repo and goes through a review. A tier value needs a measured or cited basis in 27.5.

### 27.5 Tolerance tiers

A metric passes when `|measured - golden| <= atol + rtol * |golden|`. The values are in `legs.toml`:

| tier | metric | rtol | atol |
|---|---|---|---|
| bit | compliance_final | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| bit | volume_fraction_final | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| bit | volume_final_mm3 | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| bit | mass_final_g | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| cross | compliance_final | 1e-8 | 0.0 |
| cross | volume_fraction_final | 1e-8 | 0.0 |
| cross | volume_final_mm3 | 1e-6 | 0.1 |
| cross | mass_final_g | 1e-6 | 0.01 |

- `bit`: the same machine, the same pins, the same thread count. The numbers repeat exactly.
- `cross`: another CPU, another operating system, or another direct solver library (PARDISO against Accelerate). Both legs use `cross`.
  The golden file was made on Linux with PARDISO, so the macOS leg compares across the platform and the Linux leg across the CPU.

Measured basis (Linux host Intel Core Ultra 9 185H, 22 threads, load average 4 to 9; deviation of the second number from the first):

| Pair | compliance_final | volume_fraction_final | volume_final_mm3, mass_final_g | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mac recording (Accelerate Cholesky, a Mac, 2026-10-08) against Linux PARDISO at 1 thread, hook 1.2 mm, 80 iterations | 3.5e-13 | 1.9e-14 | equal (21362.8 and 26.49); triangles 85610 in both | a recorded run of an older build |
| Linux PARDISO, 1 thread against 1 thread, short run, 4 runs | 0 | 0 | equal | measured |
| Linux PARDISO, 1 thread against 4 threads, short run | 1.4e-13 | 1.6e-14 | equal | same |
| Linux PARDISO against AMG (default tolerance), short run | 4.5e-10 | 9.6e-10 | equal | same |

The value of `cross` for `compliance_final` and `volume_fraction_final` is 10 times the largest measured deviation (9.6e-10, the
AMG pair, a looser solver than the direct solver of macOS). The values for `volume_final_mm3` and `mass_final_g` are the rounding step
of the file plus 1e-6. `volume_final_mm3` is the volume of the smoothed mesh (`topopt/post.py:115-185`), not a voxel count. An estimate, not measured: a design
change of one voxel (8 mm3 in the short run) moves it by much more than 0.1 mm3. A change of the mesh method moved it by 2005 mm3 (27.9).
The first run of the macOS leg on GitHub gives the first measured deviation of that leg.

### 27.6 Expected skips

Skip check with shards (27.3.2): each shard runs `check_skips.py` on its own junit XML (an entry that matches nothing is not an error, so a shard needs no
change), and `report` runs it again on all junit XML files of a leg and Python together (`--junit` can repeat), with the `collect.xml` of one shard. A test
file that skips at import (a module-level skip) has no node id, so no shard runs it; the collect step writes its skip to `collect.xml`, so the check still
sees it.

Every skipped test in `junit.xml` must match one `allowed_skip` entry of the leg in `legs.toml`: the same test file, and a skip message
that contains the `reason` text. A skip that matches none is a test that the leg expects to run (for example a gmsh test whose
library does not load). Each entry has a `why`. An entry that matches nothing on a run is shown in the summary and in the log and is
not an error. The tet test files have no allowed skip on any leg.

The `file` of an entry is a glob pattern (`fnmatchcase`, so `*` also crosses a `/`): a plain path matches only that file. The legs use one
glob, `tests/test_*gpu_mg*.py`, for the two skips of the gpu-mg tests in CI (`could not import 'pyopencl'`, `no usable OpenCL device`), and
`macos-arm64` uses it for a third skip (`use a real GPU only when TOPOPT_TEST_REAL_GPU=1`, from `tests/conftest.py`). The entry `no usable
OpenCL device` is on every leg. The entry `could not import 'pyopencl'` is only on a leg where the install gives no pyopencl (the two Intel legs:
the marker of pyopencl leaves an Intel Mac out, and the Intel lock with `--no-deps` adds none); on the Linux x86_64 leg and the Apple silicon leg
it must not be there, so an import skip there is a fault. A test evaluates the marker for the runner of each leg. A glob must match at
least one test file and must not match a tet test file. Because the legs start by hand only, the local tests (`tests/test_ci_scripts.py`)
check the plan before a run. They read the test files with `ast` (not as text), so they see the imports and the uses, and not the comments:
- each test file that imports a shared skip marker (`needs_accelerate`, `needs_pardiso`, `needs_direct_solver` of `tests/helpers.py`, and
  `needs_direct` of `tests/test_checkpoint.py`, with or without an alias, or as `helpers.<marker>`) and uses it has an entry on each leg
  where the marker skips (the `expect_solver` of the leg decides);
- each test file that calls `importorskip("pyopencl")`, or imports a test module that does, has the entry `no usable OpenCL device` on every
  leg and the import entry on each leg where the install gives no pyopencl; each other file that a pyopencl glob matches is in the list `GPU_MG_WITHOUT_OPENCL` (gpu-mg tests with a faked device, which must
  run), so a new gpu-mg test file is put in one of the two groups;
- each test file with the marker `opencl_context` has the real-GPU entry on `macos-arm64`.
A skip that a platform check makes in a test body, or in a marker that a test file defines for itself (not a shared marker), is still found
only by a run on that leg; so is a copy of a skip fixture in another file.

An expected failure (xfail) is not a skip. Pytest writes it as `<skipped type="pytest.xfail">` in the junit XML. The step leaves these
elements out and gives their number in the summary.

Every `why` is a current fact. The entries for the pyopencl modules (PR #25), for `tests/test_mcpb.py` (PR #29) and for
`tests/test_runjob.py` on macOS (the run helper, PR #34) were first written while those PRs were open; all three are in main now, and the
skips stay (no gpu extra in CI, no mcpb command on a hosted runner, no /proc on macOS). A skip that a new PR adds and that no entry names
fails the step of the second PR. That PR adds its entry.

Since pyopencl is a main dependency (Linux x86_64 and Apple silicon), the pyopencl modules import it on a leg. A leg with no OpenCL platform
(the Linux leg: pocl is only in the extra `gpu-test`) then skips each test that needs a device with the message `no usable OpenCL device: ...`.
Only the fixture `dev` of the test file gives this skip (`pytest.skip(f"no usable OpenCL device: {e}")`), and a module-level
`pytest.importorskip("pyopencl")` gives `could not import 'pyopencl'` where the package is not installed. The files are `tests/test_*gpu_mg*.py`.
A test that needs no device fakes the device list (`fake_cpu_device` in `tests/test_gpu_mg_x_merge.py`) and does not skip. `tests/test_solver_choice.py`
fakes every device and never skips for a missing device.

### 27.7 Licence step

`license_check.py` reads the installed metadata of every distribution of the leg venv except the project (`importlib.metadata`). The
venv is clean, so this holds the core dependencies, the installed extras and everything that they pull in, also a package that a
requirement with an extra marker brings (`mcp` requires `pyjwt[crypto]`: `cryptography`, `cffi`, `pycparser`). It sorts each licence into `permissive`, `copyleft`, `proprietary` or `unknown`
(`License-Expression`, then the `License ::` classifiers, then the `License` text). It fails when:

1. a package is not permissive and `license_policy.toml` has no `allow` entry for it. Each entry holds the decision that accepts it.
   The entries today are gmsh and cholespy (extras), cadquery-ocp-novtk (the extra `step`), and the Intel packages of the `pardiso` extra.
   An `override` entry replaces the category of a package whose metadata does not match its files (cholespy).
2. a core dependency, a package of an installed extra, or a package with an `allow` entry is not named in `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`
   (a table row or a bold name). This rule runs when the file exists, or when `pyproject.toml` lists it in `license-files`.
   The file comes with PR #27. Before it merges, the step says that the rule did not run.

`tests/test_third_party_notices.py` (PR #27) checks the declared packages and their pins against the notices file. The CI step
checks the installed set and the licence text. The two do not replace each other.

### 27.8 Wheel job

`wheel_check.py` runs on `ubuntu-24.04`. It builds the wheel (`uv build --wheel`) and checks that the wheel holds the data files of
`tests/test_packaging.py` and the files of `license-files`. Then, for each supported Python (27.2), it installs the wheel with `[dev]` and `requirements.lock`
in a new venv of that Python outside the repo (`--python V` limits it to one), copies `tests/test_packaging.py` to an empty folder, checks that `import topopt` comes from the venv, and runs that test file
there (without `test_wheel_lists_data_files`, which builds a wheel from the source tree). It also runs `topopt --version` and
`topopt check examples/hook/hook.yaml` with the installed wheel. Last, it runs `pytest --collect-only -q tests` in that venv (extra `dev`
only, no `mcp`) and reports the modules that do not collect. This step does not fail the job: on `main` the modules that import `mcp` with no
`importorskip` fail to collect (B-017 is open).

### 27.9 Changes of other PRs that move the golden file

The golden file holds the final mesh of the short run. A PR that changes the default mesh method changes it. The change of the default to `mesh_method: sdf`
does. Measured on scratch merges with V6 (Linux x86_64, PARDISO, 1 thread):
`compliance_final` and `volume_fraction_final` do not change; `volume_final_mm3` goes from 22663.3 to 20658.5, `mass_final_g` from 28.1 to 25.62
and `triangles` from 27626 to 20416 (the C2 values are equal). Of the two changes that touch this file, the one that merges second runs
`python scripts/ci/short_run.py make-golden` on Linux with PARDISO and commits the new `ci/golden/hook_short.json`. The macOS values for the new mesh are not measured.

P3a (`settings.objective_scale`, section 13) moves the golden file too. The default `stage` takes the objective scale again at the first pass of each beta stage.
So the optimizer path of the short run (beta 1, 2, 4, 8 at passes 0, 16, 26, 34) changes. Measured on Linux x86_64, PARDISO, 1 thread, with the same inputs.
The code before P3a reproduced the old golden file to the last digit on the same host. The change: `compliance_final` 1.3963757322862906 to 1.3777520293840457,
`volume_fraction_final` 0.19999265534613847 to 0.2000291240085193, `volume_final_mm3` 20658.5 to 20738.6, `mass_final_g` 25.62 to 25.72, `triangles` 20416 to 20586.
The file `ci/golden/hook_short.json` was made again with `python scripts/ci/short_run.py make-golden`. The macOS values are not measured. The `cross` tier is the one that a Mac leg uses.

F4-51 (the cut to the envelope, section 19) moves the golden file too: the short hook result has material past its design space, so the cut takes
257 mm3 (1.25 %) and the calibration pays it back. Measured on Linux x86_64, PARDISO, 1 thread, same inputs: `volume_final_mm3` 20742.0 to 20736.0,
`mass_final_g` 25.72 to 25.71, `triangles` 20198 to 19762. The same new file also has `compliance_final` 1.3777520293840457 to 1.3777520284094718 and
`volume_fraction_final` 0.2000291240085193 to 0.20002912402522363: that move is not from F4-51. Main `6154411` (before F4-51) gives these two values on
the same host (inside tier `cross`, not inside tier `bit`), and F4-51 does not change the optimizer. The file was made again with `make-golden`.

F4-55 (the envelope fill, section 19) does not move the golden file: the default is `off`, so the mesh is the one of the code before F4-55. With `auto`, the fill skips itself on the short hook run (it would add 8.9 % of the volume target inside the design
space, above the 5 % cap), so the mesh is the same. With `on` the fill runs there; the four metrics stay inside tier `cross` (`volume_final_mm3` 20735.9 against 20736).

### 27.10 Lock checks and the Intel Mac legs (added with E4)

A Mac with an x86_64 Python (section 28) installs `requirements-macos-x86_64.lock`: the main lock with
four pins moved back (numpy, numba, llvmlite, cryptography). Three checks keep it in step with the main lock:

- **`scripts/ci/check_locks.py`** (network; `uv` on PATH). It runs `uv pip compile <lock> --python-platform <P> --python-version <V> --no-build`
  (wheels only) for each supported Python V (`SUPPORTED_PYTHONS`, 27.2; the CI step passes the Python of its entry with `--python`, so the entry of 3.13 checks 3.13) for: the Intel lock on `x86_64-apple-darwin`, the main lock on `aarch64-apple-darwin`, and the main lock on
  `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`. Each must resolve, and the resolved name-to-version map must equal the map of the lock (an added, a dropped or a changed pin
  is a wrong result with the pin in the detail). A lock line with an environment marker, and a lock with no pin, are wrong results. Three controls must fail: the main lock on `x86_64-apple-darwin`, the Intel lock with `numba==0.67.0`
  and `llvmlite==0.49.0` together, and the Intel lock with `cryptography==50.0.2`. A control is ok only when uv says "No solution found" and the text
  has `<name>==<version> has no usable wheels` for a pin of the control (the main-lock control: for any pin). So a network error, a package that is
  not in the cache and a version conflict are not a pass. That is the wording of uv 0.12.1, the version that both workflow files pin
  (`UV_TEXT_VERSION`, a test compares them); another wording gives a false fail, never a false pass. numba and llvmlite move together because numba 0.67.0
  with llvmlite 0.45.1 is a version conflict on every platform, so it would not prove a missing wheel (measured on `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, where
  all three controls resolve, and a test runs that). The step runs on the legs that have `check_locks = true` (the leg `linux-x86_64`). The compile logs
  go to the artifact folder `lock-checks/`. A pass proves a wheel for the one macOS version that `uv` assumes, not for every Intel Mac OS version.
  A package that is missing from the lock shows as an added pin when another pin needs it; the name test sees the other cases.
- **`tests/test_locks.py`** (offline). For an Intel Mac, an Apple silicon Mac, Linux x86_64 and Linux arm64 it evaluates the platform markers of every
  requirement of `pyproject.toml`. A requirement that applies must have the pin of the lock of that platform. A pin that differs between the two
  locks must have a requirement in `pyproject.toml`, except `llvmlite` (numba holds it). The `pardiso` extra gives no pin on a Mac. The same file
  runs the check of `check_locks.py` with the real `uv` (it skips when `uv` or the package index is not reachable).
- **`tests/test_plugin_launcher.py`** (V5): both locks have the same names and differ in four pins.

Keys of a leg in `legs.toml` (all optional, except `pythons`, 27.2): `lock` (the lock file of the install; default `requirements.lock`), `install_mode`, `workflow` (the workflow
that runs the leg: `tests` by default, `intel-mac` for the manual file; `plan_legs.py --workflow <name>` writes its matrix) and `check_locks`.
`install_mode = "project"` (default) is `uv pip install -c <lock> -e ".[extras]"`. `install_mode = "lock-first"` is **close to** the install of the launcher on an
x86_64 Mac, not equal: `uv pip install --only-binary numba --only-binary llvmlite --only-binary cryptography -r <lock>`, then
`uv pip install -c <lock> --no-deps --no-build-isolation -e .` (the link of the launcher, #397), then the requirements of the extras of the leg with `-c <lock>`. The workflow makes the venv with
`uv venv --python <the Python of the entry> --managed-python` (3.13 for the two Intel legs, as the launcher). What stays different from the launcher:

1. The flag spelling. The leg passes `--only-binary <name>` for numba, llvmlite and cryptography (no source build for the three packages; a pin without a wheel
   stops the install). The launcher on main before PR #50 passes `--no-build-package <name>` for the same three packages. `uv pip install` of uv 0.12.1 and 0.13.4 rejects
   that spelling (`unexpected argument`, exit code 2; the flag exists for `uv sync`). PR #50 changes the launcher to `--only-binary <name>`; then this difference is gone.
   A test compares the three names, and does not check the spelling of the launcher (the test of PR #50 does, against the real `uv`).
2. The third command. The leg installs the requirements of its extras (`dev`, `mcp`, `pardiso`, `step`, `tet`, `verify`) with `-c <lock>`; the launcher installs no extra.
3. The fallback of the launcher (the pins of `pyproject.toml` when the lock install fails) is not tested by the leg: a failed lock install fails the leg.
4. The detection and the venv remake of the launcher (`detect_x86_mac`, the Rosetta note, `uv venv --clear`) do not run; the leg names its lock in `legs.toml` and the workflow makes a new venv.
5. `linux-x86_64-intel-pins` installs Linux wheels. The macOS x86_64 wheels are only proven to exist by `check_locks.py`, not installed there.

A follow-up: after PR #50 (the launcher) merges, a leg step can run `sh scripts/topopt-env.sh sync` itself, which makes the leg the install of the launcher.
The two Intel legs need it: on Linux the markers of `pyproject.toml` ask for numba 0.67.0, and the Intel lock holds 0.62.1, so the mode `project` has no
solution there (the markers agree with the Intel lock on an Intel Mac only).

`linux-x86_64-intel-pins` is the leg `linux-x86_64` with the lock `requirements-macos-x86_64.lock`, `install_mode = "lock-first"` and
`on_pull_request = false` (a test checks that no other key differs). Both legs with the Intel pins compare the short run with the golden file at tier `cross`.
`macos-x86_64` runs only in `.github/workflows/intel-mac.yml`: runner `macos-15-intel`, expected solver `amg`, no Accelerate shim.
`check_workflow.py` checks each workflow file against its own rule for `on`: since 2026-10-24 `tests.yml` and `intel-mac.yml` both need `workflow_dispatch`
and no other event (the rule of `tests.yml` was `pull_request`, `push` and `workflow_dispatch` before). The `test` job of `intel-mac.yml` is the same as the one of `tests.yml`.
Nothing of this ran on a Mac or on GitHub.

## 28. x86_64 Python on a Mac: Intel Mac and Rosetta (added with V5)

Sections 16 to 27 belong to other items. This section changes nothing for macOS on Apple silicon and Linux x86_64.
This item is best effort for an x86_64 Python on a Mac (release tier MVP: "all that is practical on Intel Macs"). The Intel Mac is
not a target platform of the tests. Nothing was tested on a Mac.

- **Kind of Python.** `topopt.solver_choice.mac_python_kind()` returns `None` (not a Mac), `"arm64"` (a native
  Python on Apple silicon), `"rosetta"` (an x86_64 Python on Apple silicon), `"intel"` (an x86_64 Python that
  is not translated: an Intel Mac) or `"unknown"` (an x86_64 Python on a Mac, and the check did not run). The
  check is the read-only command `/usr/sbin/sysctl -n sysctl.proc_translated` (bare `sysctl` if the full path does not
  exist). The value is `1` for Rosetta and `0` for an Intel Mac with macOS 11 or newer; the key does not exist on an
  older macOS (the command fails). It runs only for an x86_64 Python on a Mac, never on macOS arm64 or Linux. The
  result is cached for each process.
- **Solver rule (changes section 4).** On an x86_64 Mac, `auto` gives `amg` (as before). `cholesky` is a user error
  (exit code 1, one line: "needs the Apple Accelerate shim, and topopt supports it on Apple silicon only", with the
  options `amg` and `auto`). Section 4 says that `cholesky` runs on macOS; it runs on macOS with Apple silicon.
  `pardiso` is a user error as before, and its line does not offer `cholesky` on an x86_64 Mac.
- **`hint`.** The key `hint` of `check --json` (section 8) and the line `hint:` of `check` are `null` on every
  platform except an x86_64 Python on a Mac. There it is one line. It names the kind (Rosetta, Intel Mac, or unknown),
  says that `auto` gives `amg`, and says that this is best effort: topopt was tested on Linux only, the lock for
  macOS x86_64 is older than the main lock, the time model is fitted to a native M1 run with Cholesky (not
  calibrated here), and the `amg` factor 4.1 of the time model was measured on one Linux machine. For Rosetta and
  unknown it gives the commands to a native arm64 Python: `file "$(command -v uv)"` (or `file <TOPOPT_UV>` when the launcher downloaded the uv) (it must say arm64), then
  `rm -rf <the folder of this Python>` (the environment), then a new setup from a Terminal that does not use Rosetta.
  `run` prints the same line as a `warning:` line in `run.log`.
- **`environment` (section 10).** `platform` has two more keys: `mac_python` (the value above) and `hint` (the text of
  `hint`, or `null`). `backends.cholesky.note` names Rosetta or an Intel Mac on an x86_64 Mac.
- **Lock files.** `requirements-macos-x86_64.lock` is `requirements.lock` with four pins moved back, because the
  versions of the main lock have no macOS x86_64 wheel (numba, llvmlite, cryptography) or need a newer numpy: numpy
  2.3.5, numba 0.62.1, llvmlite 0.45.1, cryptography 48.0.1. The header of the file says why. `pyproject.toml` has the
  same four pins as markers (`platform_system == 'Darwin' and platform_machine == 'x86_64'`); `uv pip compile` of
  `pyproject.toml` for aarch64-apple-darwin and x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu gives the same result as before. A change of
  a pin in `requirements.lock` has to be checked against the Intel lock.
- **Launcher.** `scripts/topopt-env.sh` decides by the Python of the environment (`platform.machine()`), and by
  `uname -m` only if that Python does not run. For an x86_64 Python on a Mac it installs from
  `requirements-macos-x86_64.lock`, adds `--only-binary numba --only-binary llvmlite --only-binary cryptography`
  (a missing wheel stops the install at once with the package name; `TOPOPT_ALLOW_SOURCE_BUILD=1` lifts this; the flag is
  `--only-binary` because `uv pip install` has no `--no-build-package`, which `uv sync`, `uv lock` and `uv run` have: uv stops with
  "unexpected argument"; a test checks every flag that the launcher passes to `uv pip install` against the real
  `uv pip install --help`), prints the
  facts above, and writes `pins=lock-macos-x86_64` in the stamp. If the shell runs natively (`uname -m` is `arm64`) and the
  venv has an x86_64 Python, it makes the venv again (`uv venv --clear`). On every other platform the calls of `uv`
  are byte-equal to those before V5, except the Python version of `uv venv` (#422) (L1a adds `--reinstall` to the install calls only after a marker of a cut setup, and the import check before the stamp, on every platform: section 34.1). The `lock=` checksum in the stamp is the one of the lock file that the platform uses (the Intel lock on an x86_64 Mac). The stamp line ends with `python=<LAUNCHER_PYTHON>` since #422 (section 25.5): it is the one change of the text since V5, and it makes an environment of an older launcher run the setup once.
- **Probe.** `tools/platform_probe.py [--json] [--no-import]` reports the machine, the Rosetta flag, the Python build,
  the import status of each package (each import runs in a child Python), and the solver rule. It uses only the
  Python standard library (Python 3.8 or newer). It makes no network call and writes no file outside a temporary folder.
  Its exit code is 0.
- **Not specified.** The speed of `amg` on an x86_64 Mac, and the time model there. Nothing was measured on a Mac.
- **Checks (E4).** The Intel lock and the markers are checked as in 27.10. The state of each open item, the facts about `cholesky` on an Intel Mac
  (it stays a user error; cholespy cannot serve the optimizer; an x86_64 Accelerate shim is an option that needs a Mac test). The official uv installer
  gives an arm64 uv on an Apple silicon Mac, also from a Terminal that opens with Rosetta.

## 29. Apply marks to the finished part (added with C3a)

`topopt/apply_marks.py` edits the finished part (`result/final.stl`) at the marks of the Refine page. It gives facts and
options. The agent decides. The MCP tool `apply_marks` (`topopt_mcp/server.py`) is a thin wrapper around it. The CLI has
no command for it: use `python -m topopt.apply_marks` (below). The module imports numpy and scipy at the top; scikit-image,
trimesh, manifold3d, the voxelizer and `topopt.tet.surface` (the surface definitions of `topopt verify`: numpy, scipy and numba;
it does not import gmsh) load when a function needs them. It adds no dependency.

**Boundary.** `apply_marks` writes one NEW folder (`edited.stl` and `apply_marks.json`) and nothing else. It does not edit
the run folder, `final.stl`, a YAML, a region STL or a marks file. It makes no FE run, so the stiffness and the stress of the
edited part are not known. It gives no KEEP or REJECT verdict. The optimizer, `topopt run`, `post.py` and the refine page do
not change. The re-run route of section 21 (`marks_to_hints`) stays the other option, and the report names both routes.

### 29.1 `apply_marks(run_dir, marks, *, out_dir=None, options=None, overwrite=False, allow_stale=False, yaml_path=None)`

The arguments after `marks` are keyword-only. The MCP tool (29.2) has `marks` first and `run_dir` second, the order of the
tools of the feedback family (`marks_to_hints`); the module function keeps the order of its siblings (`run_dir` first).

**Input.** The run folder needs `run.json` (`shape`, `h`, `origin`), `labels.bin` and `result/final.stl` (a closed solid; the
call stops with `{ok: false, error}` when one is missing). `result/stress.npz`, `result/metrics.json` and the YAML of the run
are used when they are there. `marks` is as in 21.3 (`read_marks`: the path, the JSON text or the dict).

**Values of a mark.** The page values are used. A value that the page does not record is the value of the pipeline stage
`s7_cleanup`, and the report names it (`defaults_used` for a mark, `pipeline_defaults` with the source line for each
operator).

| Mark | Used | Not used |
|---|---|---|
| `remove` | `points`, `radius_mm`, `mirror`; `amount_mm` only in `remove_mode: shave` (the depth) | `normals`, `note`, `strength` |
| `add` | `points`, `radius_mm`, `amount_mm` (the neck offset), `mirror` | `normals`, `note`, `strength` |
| `smooth` | `points`, `radius_mm` (`iso` and `fair`; `smooth_mode: tube` does not use it), `strength` (a multiplier of the pipeline sigma and window), `mirror` | `normals`, `note`, `amount_mm` |

`radius_mm` is multiplied by `options.radius_scale`. A mark with no `radius_mm` gets 4 mm (the page default).

**Optional mode keys of a mark (added with C3b).** A `smooth` mark can carry `smooth_mode` (`auto`, `tube`, `iso`, `fair`) and a
`remove` mark can carry `remove_mode` (`cut`, `shave`). The page does not write them; a producer of marks (the list command of 29.3)
does, so that the file states the operator for each mark. The order for one mark: `options.per_mark[id]`, then the key of the mark,
then `options.smooth_mode` / `options.remove_mode`, then the default (`auto`, `cut`). The options always hold a value, so a global
option cannot be told from the default: a mark that states its mode keeps it, and `per_mark` keeps the last word. A value that is
not in the list, or a key of the other type (`remove_mode` on a `smooth` mark), is a fact in `problems` and is not used. A mark
with no key behaves as before. The entry shows the mode that was used (`values.smooth_mode`, `values.remove_mode`). A mark can also carry
`cleanup`, the facts of a candidate (29.3). Nothing reads it: `values_not_used` of the report names it (the hints of section 21 name
`smooth_mode`, `remove_mode` and `cleanup`).

**Steps.** A mark is one step: the signed distance field of the current part in a crop box around the mark, the edit of the
field, the new surface put into the part, the checks. A mark with `mirror` has one path for each image in the group of the
reflections about the mirror planes (2 images for one plane, up to 8 for three). Images that are closer than twice their reach
(`radius_mm`, and for `remove` also `remove_dom_mm`) are one site, with one edit whose weight is the larger of the paths, so an
overlap is not edited twice (`pitfalls/mirror-commit-double`); the sites are the closure of this rule over all pairs. Each
other site is a step. A mark that lies on a plane is its own image (one path). The threshold of the neck rule of `add` (0.4 g in
the pipeline, counted over both sides) is shared by the images: a site that holds k of the n images gets k / n of it. The order is `remove`, then `smooth`, then `add`, and
file order inside a kind (the pipeline order of `apply_marks3.py:115`). Each step sees the part that the steps before made.

**Mirror plane.** `options.mirror_plane`, else `mirror_plane` of the mark, else `mirror_plane` of the marks file (one plane
each), else `run.json["mirror"]` (engine item A4a, section 26.1: `{planes: [{axis, at_mm, align, parity, k, plane_index}, ...],
design_voxels, load_asymmetry, end}`; up to 3 planes with distinct axes; a list of planes or one plane is read too, and `normal`
may be a letter or a 3-vector), else y = 0 (the plane of the page; the report says `default`). A plane of `run.json` that has the
axis of an earlier plane, or that cannot be read, is not used, and `marks[].mirror.plane_facts` says so. The planes and their
source are in `marks[].mirror.planes` (`mirror.plane` is the first).

**Crop box and field.** The nodes are `lo + pitch * (i, j, k)`. `pitch` is `options.pitch_mm`, else the voxel size of the run / 4,
kept between 0.2 and 0.5 mm. The box is the mark (or the path) plus a reach that depends on the operator, cut to the bounds
of `final.stl` plus a margin: 3 mm, and at least the reach of the operator (so a filter reads real field and not the box
face). The field is the signed distance of the current part (negative inside): the inside mask by ray parity
(`voxelize.inside_mask`), the distance to its boundary by the Euclidean transform, the exact distance on the layer of nodes each
side of the surface, clipped to +-8 mm. Deeper than that layer the field is within half a node of the distance. The box has no
wall: a solid that reaches its face goes on outside it. A ray of the inside test that crosses the surface an odd number of times
(it grazes an edge) is cast again with a small shift (`odd_rays_repaired` in the step); a column that stays odd is counted
(`odd_rays`), and above `options.max_odd_rays` (0) the step is rolled back (`odd_rays`).
A node counts as changed (it sets the splice zone) when the field moves by more than 0.0001 mm and it is within two nodes of
the zero level before or after, or it changes sign; the smoothing of the field far from the surface does not move the surface.
**Guards.** A box above `max_crop_voxels` (8 million nodes) or a call above `max_total_voxels` (60 million) is not made. The
step has status `guard`, with the node count, the memory estimate (200 bytes per node plus about 300 MB for the process, so
the fact says), `pitch_that_fits_mm` and the options (a coarser `pitch_mm`, fewer marks, a larger guard). It is a fact, not a
crash and not a silent fallback.

**Operators**:

- `remove`, `remove_mode: cut` (default): the feature is the solid within `radius_mm` of the path. The parent is the union of
  the medial balls that are not close to the feature, closed with a ball and grown by 0.5 mm. The cut is the removal domain
  (the feature plus 2 mm) minus the parent, beyond `frozen_keep_mm` of the frozen regions, plus a thin foot; the cut field is
  smoothed and the scar polished outside the parent. The step gives the parent check (`parent_check`: `within_tolerance` is true
  when the medial inscribed diameter near the feature does not drop, the skeleton of the solid (scikit-image `skeletonize`) keeps
  its inscribed diameter (`min_drop`, `mean_drop` and the largest local drop, as `lib2.parent_check`), and the cut does not
  enter the closed parent by more than `parent_tol_mm`, 0.2 mm; it is a fact about the cut, not a verdict on the part). `options.parent_check`: `report` (default: the edit is made and the check is a fact) or `enforce`
  (a failed check rolls the step back). A cut on a flat face with no feature is a pit that the check does not see; the facts
  show it (volume, thickness), and a note says so.
- `remove`, `remove_mode: shave`: the README meaning of the page: the surface moves in by `amount_mm` (1 mm when the mark has
  none) at the path, with a cosine falloff to `radius_mm` in the tangent plane (the weight is that of the point on the surface
  below the node). It does not protect the parent. The step gives `depth_at_mark_mm` (planned) and `depth_reached_mm` (the depth of
  the new surface below the mark, along the old normal; it can differ from `amount_mm` by about half a node).
- `add`: a closing with a ball of `close_mm` (3 mm) on the part, smoothed, blended in with the cosine weight of the distance to
  the path (`radius_mm`). When the closing adds less than `neck_min_mm3` (51.8 mm3, 0.4 g), the surface also moves out by the
  neck offset (`amount_mm` of the mark, else 0.5 mm) in the weight. Material is only added, and only inside the design domain.
- `smooth`: `auto` (default) is `iso` for one point and `fair` for a stroke; both use `radius_mm` and `strength`, so the edit stays
  in the zone that the page shows. `options.smooth_mode` (or `per_mark`) asks for another mode. `tube` is asked for only: it
  rebuilds the whole strut under the stroke, does not use `radius_mm`, and its mark line gives the planned volume and the edit
  reach (`edit_note`). A tube that cannot be made (the stroke is under 6 mm, no strut axis, or the section of the solid at a
  point of the stroke is not bounded: a block or a wide face) falls back to `iso`, and `mode_reason` says why. `tube`: the strut
  axis is the stroke snapped to the ridge of the inscribed radius and extended while the section stays alike; the radius is the
  area-equivalent radius smoothed over a window of 10 mm x `strength`; the old strut is removed and the tube joined with a
  smooth minimum. `iso`: the field is Gaussian smoothed (1 mm x `strength`) in the cosine zone. `fair`: a Gaussian of 4 mm x
  `strength` along the web direction (the path tangent) in the cosine zone.

**Frozen regions.** The fixed, load and keep-out voxels of `labels.bin` are frozen. The weight of an edit is 0 within
`frozen_keep_mm` (3 mm) of a frozen voxel and 1 beyond `frozen_full_mm` (6 mm), with a linear taper (`remove` does not cut
within `frozen_keep_mm`). No new material goes outside the design domain. The step reports the planned and the delivered edit
volume, `clipped_by_frozen_mm3` and its share, and the nearest frozen voxel to the edit. When the YAML of the run is on disk
(`yaml_path` for a moved run), each step checks the frozen regions with their STL files: the volume of the edit inside them
(the tolerance is 0.01 mm3, noise of the float32 files). An edit inside them is undone in the step (`frozen_restored_mm3`; the
mark line has `restored_in_frozen_mm3` and `frozen_note`, and `totals.restored_mm3` the sum). When the undo does not give a valid
closed part the step is rolled back (`frozen_restore_failed`), and the reason names the options (`frozen_keep_mm`, a smaller
`radius_mm`, `rerun_with_hints`). The end of the call checks the result as a whole (`totals.frozen_exact`); if that check still
finds a change that it cannot undo, every step of the call is rolled back. The check measures the part that it returns
(`added_after_undo_mm3`, `removed_after_undo_mm3`): `restored` is true only when the regions are exact within the tolerance; when
they are not, the note gives the volume that is left and the steps are rolled back. `regions.solid` (item #30) is added to the check when
the engine has it.

**Splice and checks.** The new surface is the zero level of the edited field (marching cubes). It goes into the part in a
zone, the nodes within 2.5 nodes of a changed node. Outside the zone the triangles of the part stay bit for bit
(`totals.triangles_replaced` counts the others).

*The seam* (C3a-fix). The old surface and the new surface are two triangulations of one surface. Along the wall of the zone they
differ by 0 to 65 um (the float32 rounding of the STL included) and they cross many times, so the boolean
`(part - zone) + (new surface ^ zone)` cannot tell which one is higher. It left a ribbon of sliver triangles of the wall:
fold edges (two faces that point back on each other), pinch vertices and non-manifold edges. printcheck and the report called
such a part closed, one body, and `topopt verify` refused it (exit 2). The step now makes the two pieces apart
(`part - zone` and `new surface ^ zone`, manifold3d), drops the triangles of the wall, and sews the two open boundary loops:
(1) edge to edge: the vertices of the new loop move onto the old loop (to a vertex of the old loop when it is within the shortest
edge that verify accepts, `MIN_EDGE_REJECT_MM`; an unclaimed vertex next to a claimed one, and the short edges of marching cubes,
stay, so edges under the limit can remain), the boundary triangles of both sides are split along the common chain, and the
inner vertices of the new surface within one node of the loop follow with a decaying share (never a vertex of the old part); a
check against the normals of the pieces refuses a move that turns a triangle over. In this tier the old part keeps its positions
and only its boundary triangles are split. (2) A loop pair that does not project (a loop that doubles back, a polygon
that is not simple, a triangle that would turn over) gets a strip between the two loops, and the edges of the seam that are
shorter than `MIN_EDGE_REJECT_MM`, and the fold pairs of the strip, are collapsed where the link condition and a flip check allow
(a strip between two loops that cross has a twist at each crossing, so a few fold edges can stay: the facts count them). In this
tier a vertex of the old loop can be removed: it moves onto a neighbour, by less than 0.05 mm for an edge under the limit, and by
the length of the edge for a fold pair (0.081 mm at most on the hook `remove_core`, 274 vertices; `old_vertices_removed` and
`old_removed_move_max_mm` give the numbers of each call). (3) The plain boolean, for one of eight reasons (`why_not_sewn`): the
module `topopt.tet.surface` cannot be imported; a piece (`part - zone`, `new surface ^ zone`) is empty or not a valid solid; a
boundary loop touches itself; the two cuts have another number of loops; a loop is more than 3 nodes (`SEAM_MATCH_NODES`) from its
partner; the sewn part is not a closed manifold or has no positive volume; manifold3d refuses the sewn part; and, for the undo of a
change inside a frozen region, the sewn undo changes the region by `FROZEN_TOL_MM3` or more. `steps[].seam` says which route ran
(see below), and `totals.surface_quality` gives the result. The constants of the sewing have these scales:
`SEAM_MATCH_NODES` (3) and `SEAM_REACH_NODES` (1) count nodes of the crop grid, so they scale with its pitch (0.2 to 0.5 mm);
`MIN_EDGE_REJECT_MM` (0.05 mm) is the absolute limit of `topopt verify` and does not scale; the area floor under which a triangle has no
normal is the float32 spacing at the largest coordinate times the pitch (`_area_floor`); `SEAM_WELD_PASSES` (20) is a guard of the
loop, and the facts say when it stopped the weld (`weld_stopped_by_guard`). The review found no scale problem. The step is
checked before it counts: the part is closed after a float32 reload from STL bytes (a pinch is repaired first by moving the pinched vertices apart
by 2e-4 x j mm against the vertex normal, into the own solid, up to 6 passes, as `f32_fix` of the pipeline; the same repair
runs on the part after the undo of a change inside a frozen region; then by
`Manifold.simplify(1e-5)`; `pitfalls/float32-stl-reload-pinch`); the part has no more bodies than before. A new body that holds
no fixed or load voxel (by volume) and is below `options.loose_body_mm3` (default max(10 x pitch^3, 0.001) mm3) is a sliver of
the boolean: it is dropped and reported (`dropped_bodies`: count, volume, the limit). Any other split rolls the step back
(`splits_part`), and the reason and `facts.bodies` give the volume of each body, whether it is a cavity inside the part, and
whether it holds a fixed or load voxel. A step that fails is rolled back and has status `rolled_back` with `rollback`
(`splice_failed`, `splits_part`, `parent_check`, `crop_edge`, `frozen_restore_failed`, `odd_rays`) and the reason. The
`crop_edge` reason names the face of the box, how near the edit comes, and the options. A step that changes nothing has status `no_effect`, with the reason and the options: a frozen region clips the edit to nothing
(`cause: frozen_clip`; the options are `frozen_keep_mm`, a mark farther from the region, `rerun_with_hints`), or the surface is
already as the operator makes it (`cause: surface_unchanged`; a flat face), or no solid lies within `radius_mm` of the mark.

**Stale marks.** When `source_sha256` of the marks differs from the hash of `final.stl`, the call stops before it writes
anything: `{ok: false, marks_match_final_stl: false, refused: {reason: "stale_marks", options}}`. With `allow_stale` the marks
are applied, and the report keeps `marks_match_final_stl: false` and a problem. A marks file with no hash gives null.

**Output folder.** Default `<run folder>-marks` beside the run folder (`-2`, `-3` when it exists). The call is refused (`{ok:
false, error, refused: {reason, path, options}}`) for: a run folder or a folder inside one (`run_folder`); the folder of the
YAML or of a region STL (`input_folder`); a symbolic link (`symbolic_link`); a folder that is a file (`not_a_folder`); a folder
with files when `overwrite` is false (`not_empty`); a folder with files that is not an earlier apply_marks folder
(`apply_marks.json` of format 1; `not_an_apply_folder`). The folder gets `edited.stl` (binary STL; not written when no step
changed the part) and `apply_marks.json` (the full report; paths relative to the folder).

**Report** (the return value; `apply_marks.json` has the same data with relative paths): `ok`, `format` (1), `run_dir`,
`run_name`, `marks_file`, `marks_sha256`, `marks_count`, `marks_match_final_stl`, `allow_stale`, `source.final_stl_sha256`,
`out_dir`, `grid` (`h`, `shape`, `origin`, `pitch_mm`, `pitch_is_default`, `pitch_rule`), `options` (the effective ones),
`option_catalog`, `marks`, `summary` (counts of `<type>:<status>`), `totals`, `files`, `routes`, `pipeline_defaults`,
`values_used`, `values_not_used`, `problems`, `notes`, `elapsed_s`, `peak_rss_mb` (the peak resident memory of the whole
process so far, in MB, not of this call alone), `load_avg` (the load average of the host at the end of the call).

Each entry of `marks`: `id`, `index`, `type`, `status` (`applied`, `partly_applied`, `no_effect`, `rolled_back`, `guard`,
`skipped_by_option`, `unreadable`), `reason`, `values` (`points`, `radius_mm`, `radius_used_mm`, `amount_mm`, `strength`,
`mirror`, `smooth_mode`, `remove_mode`), `defaults_used` (`name`, `value`, `anchor`), `values_not_used`, `surface_distance_mm`
(and `surface_note` above two voxels), `mirror` (`plane`, `planes`, `plane_facts`, `images`, `sites`, `images_per_site`,
`combined`, `gap_mm`, `mirror_surface_distance_mm`), `steps`, and from the applied steps: `edit` (`added_mm3`, `removed_mm3`,
`planned_mm3`, `clipped_by_frozen_mm3`, `clipped_share_pct`, `restored_in_frozen_mm3`, `part_volume_change_mm3`,
`part_mass_change_g`, `farthest_changed_node_from_mark_mm`, `edit_reach_mm` (the same number)), `edit_note` (a tube),
